chapters.html:
Phainon came to with the unmistakable, creeping sense that something was off.

The light spilling through the window was too warm—too settled to be early morning. The apartment was still. No alarm buzz. No hum from the morning news on low volume. No sharp, bitter trace of coffee lingering from the kitchen. Just the slow realization of stillness, and the weight of time already slipping past him.

His eyes opened.

8:39 a.m.

He stared at the numbers for exactly three seconds, his mind as blank as the ceiling above him. Then:

“…Damn it.”

He was up in an instant, pulling himself out of bed with the sort of fluidity that didn’t come from calm—just long-honed reflex. One hand dragged through his hair, the other already grabbing for clothes on instinct. No hesitation, no grogginess. That was the thing about being late often enough: the body adapted. It knew when the time for complaint had passed.

The shirt he’d ironed the night before was nowhere to be found—probably buried in a pile of laundry he’d sworn to deal with on Sunday. It didn’t matter. He grabbed a dark button-down from the closet—creased but wearable—and a pair of slacks already folded on the back of his desk chair. His socks were, unfortunately, mismatched. He didn’t stop to fix it.

He left them on the bed as he moved, feet bare against cold tile, into the bathroom. The water took a moment to heat; while it did, he stripped down and shoved a toothbrush into his mouth, multitasking with the determination of a man who knew exactly how long a three-minute routine could be compressed. Foam collected at the corners of his mouth as he stepped under the spray, bracing himself as cold hit skin first. He worked quickly—efficiently—mouth foaming, fingers scrubbing, water sluicing down his back. Two minutes. In and out.

He spat into the sink while toweling off, then turned toward the mirror and raked his fingers through his wet hair until it looked less like chaos and more like deliberate mess. Shaved just yesterday, thank god. He could skip the rest.

Back in his room, he dressed in quick motions, slipping into the shirt, slacks, and belt with the ease of routine. A tie was a luxury; today was damage control. He threw on a fitted jacket to give the illusion of intention and checked the time again: 8:47.

Technically, his lecture began at 9:00.

It was fine. It would be fine. Probably.

Shoes on—polished, at least, which felt like a small victory—he made his way through the apartment with purpose, grabbing his bag from the couch and slinging it over one shoulder. In the kitchen, he stopped only long enough to fill a water bottle and shove a slightly stale granola bar into his jacket pocket. The coffeemaker blinked at him, its timer long past. The carafe was bone-dry.

“Traitor,” he muttered.

Keys in hand, bag secured, he opened the door to leave—

And stopped.

There, just visible through the window, was his car. And on the windshield, vibrant against the dull grey of the dash, was a neon orange sticky note.

“NO GAS. Don’t push it. REFILL.”

He’d written it himself. Stuck it there last night in a brief moment of foresight—proof that at some point, he’d tried. A small part of him appreciated that. The rest wanted to tear it off and eat it.

He stood in the doorway for a moment, shoulders rising and falling with the slow exhale of a man not surprised, just deeply, deeply tired.

“…Right,” he said quietly.

And then he started running.

To call it a sprint would be accurate in the same way calling a lightning strike “a little spark” was accurate. Phainon didn’t run so much as descend upon the city streets—full force, half-dressed, and moving with the sheer unfiltered energy of a man who knew exactly how little time he had left to preserve his professional dignity.

The first block was a blur. He jumped a curb, nearly twisted his ankle on uneven pavement, and kept going without a second thought. His lungs burned. His bag slammed against his side with each step. He still tasted toothpaste. Somewhere in the flurry of movement, he remembered to breathe—but only just.

He vaulted over a knee-high fence meant to keep pedestrians out of a construction shortcut, immediately set off someone’s motion sensor, and offered a very genuine apology to the elderly woman whose dog leapt in surprise at his passing.

“Sorry!” he called over his shoulder, dodging a low-hanging branch. “Emergency academia!”

He wasn’t sure that meant anything, but she waved her cane after him all the same. Possibly in support. Possibly not.

He cleared a flight of stairs three at a time, ducked through a narrow alleyway, and took a bite of the half-stale granola bar he’d pulled from his pocket. It lodged somewhere in his throat. He coughed violently mid-stride, then kept running.

He didn’t usually have to run three and a half miles to get to work. But then again, he didn’t usually self-sabotage via poorly placed sticky notes and pretend “five more minutes” was a sustainable sleep strategy. Today was a day of exceptions, most of them stupid, all of them his.

A few pedestrians turned to watch as he passed. He couldn’t blame them. A grown man tearing across the city in business attire with wild hair and a messenger bag flapping behind him like a cape was probably not the most common sight on a Tuesday morning.

But fortunately for Phainon, he was fit.

Not in the “mirror selfie and macro counting” way, but in the kind of solid, quiet way that came from years of functional training. His body was used to movement—sharp, explosive movement. Sprints, climbs, hand-to-hand drills that weren’t technically legal, but didn’t leave marks if done right. There was a rhythm to it. His legs knew what to do. His lungs remembered the cadence. His mind locked into pace. It didn’t matter that he was wearing loafers and khakis—he made it work.

There was a moment, somewhere in the second mile, when time slowed. A bird crossed his path. A man with a coffee stepped directly in front of him. Phainon swerved, spun, caught himself with a hand on a lamppost, and kept going without breaking stride.

Someone shouted, “Hey—watch it!”

Phainon threw a hand up in apology and didn’t look back.

The campus gates came into view like a divine illusion—rising out of the morning haze, backed by the rising sun and the slight tremor of his vision from sheer exertion. He pushed harder, rounding the corner with all the grace of a missile.

When the university building finally loomed in front of him, he was soaked in sweat, half-blind with adrenaline, and actively seeing god. She had her arms crossed and looked unimpressed.

He hit the front doors with a force that made them shudder open on impact, and staggered through the threshold like a man just barely escaping death. His chest heaved. His vision stuttered. His heart pounded somewhere near his ears.

There were students in the hallway.

A few turned. One leaned back against the wall slowly, as if unsure if they were witnessing a crime or an art piece.

Phainon bent forward, one hand on his thigh, the other raised as a makeshift greeting. He was breathless, flushed, hair a damp mess across his forehead. He looked like he’d either just run a marathon or barely survived a kidnapping.

“Morning,” he croaked, still catching his breath. “Lovely day, isn’t it?”

There was silence.

Then, a girl dropped her coffee with a soft splatter against the tiles.

He stood straighter—forced himself upright, rolling his shoulders back like it didn’t hurt. Wiped the sweat from his brow with the inside of his sleeve. Straightened his jacket. Smiled.

It was the smile of a man who had almost certainly just violated several city ordinances, bodily limits, and laws of physics to make it here on time—and was absolutely not sorry.

One minute left.

Perfect timing.

The lecture hall was already half-full by the time Phainon swung open the door with all the subtlety of a man being chased by time itself.

Silence rolled over the room like a wave.

Dozens of students turned to stare, a few mid-sip with iced coffee, one midway through unwrapping a breakfast burrito. Phainon gave them all a winning, sweat-damp smile and tried to pretend his lungs weren’t actively suing for damages.

“Morning,” he wheezed. “Everyone’s so punctual today. Love the commitment.”

Dead silence.

Except for the unmistakable sound of one person slowly uncrossing their arms.

Anaxa stood at the front, stiff-backed, cold-eyed, the living embodiment of academic disappointment. His brow didn’t even twitch. His voice could’ve refrigerated milk.

“You’re late.”

Phainon didn’t flinch. Just took one dramatic step forward, arms slightly out like he was finishing a performance.

“Correction,” he said, catching his breath between syllables. “I am… not technically late.”

Anaxa blinked. Slowly. Like he was recalibrating his tolerance for idiocy in real time.

“You arrived at 8:59 and forty-eight seconds. Panting. Disheveled. And bleeding.”

“Surface wound,” Phainon said, examining the tiny cut on his palm. “Adds character.”

“You tripped over a bird feeder,” Anaxa said without missing a beat. “I watched the security feed.”

“And yet—” Phainon spread his arms wider, as if to showcase his very existence. “Here I stand. Against all odds. Truly, a tale of perseverance.”

There was a long, withering pause.

Anaxa reached into the front desk drawer, pulled out a flash drive, and slapped it into Phainon’s open palm like he was delivering a cease-and-desist.

“I fixed your lecture notes. Again. Three citation errors. Two incomplete slides. And you spelled ‘epistemological’ with an ‘f.’”

Phainon grinned. “And that’s why you’re the wind beneath my wings.”

“I’m the iron chain around your ankle.”

“Poetic.”

Anaxa just stared at him. Phainon could’ve sworn he saw the faintest twitch in the corner of his jaw—either a suppressed eye-roll or the beginning of an aneurysm.

“You’re lucky I respect punctuality more than I loathe you,” Anaxa muttered.

“Love you too, Ana—”

“Anaxagoras.” His voice cut clean. Sharp as glass. “Use my full name in front of the students.”

Phainon blinked. “Even when I say it with affection?”

“Especially then.”

And with that, Anaxagoras turned on his heel, coat flaring behind him like he’d practiced it in a mirror. The door shut behind him with a satisfying click.

Phainon turned back to the class, who were now watching him like they weren’t sure if this was part of the curriculum or a live-action breakdown.

He clapped his hands, the sound a little too enthusiastic for someone who’d just sprinted three miles and gotten publicly executed by his colleague.

“All right,” he said, grinning. “Who’s ready to learn how to professionally win arguments and ruin dinner parties forever?”

One student raised a hand. “Are you okay, sir?”

“I’m fantastic,” Phainon said, voice bright, as he casually wiped blood off his hand with a syllabus. “Let’s begin.”

By the time he reached the podium, Phainon was settled. Breathing steady. Hands relaxed at his sides.

The room had already quieted. A few students had been talking, but now they were shifting in their seats, pulling out their notes, straightening their posture as if anticipating the shift in atmosphere.

Phainon had a way of doing that. A presence that settled across the space— not oppressive, not dramatic, but measured. The kind that made people sit up and listen without realizing they were doing it.

He tapped the podium, and the screen behind him flickered to life, casting crisp lettering across the wall. No frills. Just the day’s subject, direct and to the point.

“Let’s begin,” he repeated, composing himself.

He let the words carry, unhurried and steady. He was never the kind of professor who filled silences out of discomfort. He let them breathe. Let them stretch just enough to draw people in.

“Your assignment,” he continued, “was to analyze existing cases and construct a counterargument for one you personally disagreed with.”

A flicker of movement—students shifting, hands tightening over their notes.

“Some of you,” he went on, “probably chose something easy. An argument so fundamentally flawed that it barely took effort to dismantle.” He exhaled lightly through his nose. “Which is fine, if you enjoy mediocrity.”

A murmur. A few wary glances.

“Others, I assume,” he said, glancing up, “chose something more… challenging.”

This time, there was more of a reaction—some straightened, some smiled. A few exchanged glances, the way students did when they were quietly measuring themselves against their peers.

Good.

He stepped out from behind the podium and leaned casually against the edge of the desk instead.

“The point of this wasn’t to regurgitate the easiest answer,” he said. “It was to engage with something that made you think. If you found yourself second-guessing your own stance while writing, congratulations. You did it right.”

Silence. Thoughtful. Expectant.

He tapped the desk lightly with his fingers.

“Who’s confident in their work?”

A few hands lifted. He scanned them, then gestured to the nearest one.

“Come up,” he said. “Convince me.”

There was a slight hesitation—just a fraction of a second, the universal moment of someone realizing they were about to be put to the test. Then movement. A student stood, stepping toward the front.

Phainon shifted slightly, making space.

“Keep it concise,” he instructed. “Direct. No rambling.” He tilted his head. “And if you try to sell me nonsense, at least make it sound good.”

The student nodded, took a breath, and began.

And just like that, the class was in motion.

For the next hour, Phainon listened, countered, redirected. He didn’t just lecture—he engaged. He challenged. He made them think on their feet, adjust, refine. And despite the occasional stumble, despite the inevitable nerves that came with speaking under scrutiny, the students adapted. They pushed themselves.

By the time the session neared its end, the energy in the room was sharper, more focused. No one had checked the clock in a while. No one had even noticed how quickly the time had passed.

Phainon finally leaned back against the desk, exhaling lightly.

“Better,” he said, nodding once. “Not perfect, but better.”

He glanced toward the clock. Just enough time to wrap up.

“Alright,” he said, “for next time—”

And just like that, the rhythm shifted again. The closing notes. The final instructions.

He watched as they packed up, murmuring amongst themselves—some clearly still turning over arguments in their minds, others already letting their thoughts drift toward their next class, their next obligation.

As they filed out, Phainon lingered at the desk, tapping a finger lightly against the wood.

There was a particular satisfaction in this part. The weight of a room that had been fully engaged. A job well done.

Outside, the day stretched on, demanding his next move.

He rolled his sleeves back down, buttoned them at the cuffs, and straightened his jacket.

He had just enough time to stop by the library.

And he knew exactly who he wanted to see.

The walk to the library was just long enough to justify. Long enough to pretend it was for the fresh air, the stretch, the change in scenery. Long enough to let him lie to himself with a straight face.

Phainon didn’t often take his full lunch break—there was always something else to be done. A paper to mark. A stubborn student to email. A system to mildly outwit. But today, he’d found himself drifting. Fingers tapping restlessly against his desk. Thoughts wandering in precise, unrepentant circles.

So he walked. Down the stone path flanked with overgrown hedges. Past the baker who always gave him judgmental looks for skipping breakfast.

Around the fountain some poor department kept insisting was “historical.”

The library stood at the edge of the square like it had been carved out of stillness itself. Cool stone, high windows, doors heavy enough to suggest silence wasn’t a suggestion but a commandment.

He pushed them open with one shoulder.

Inside, it smelled like old pages and whatever blend of tea Mydei had decided was acceptable this month.

Phainon’s footsteps were light. Quiet, but not sneaky. He wasn’t trying to hide—he just knew better than to provoke the wrath of the librarian with echoes.

And there he was.

Behind the counter, half-shadowed by a crooked lamp, Mydei was deep in a hardcover nearly as thick as his patience wasn’t. His posture was elegant in the way statues were—still, composed, absolute. He didn’t look up.

Which was fine. Phainon was familiar with the opening choreography of this little dance.

He leaned an elbow on the counter, smile already playing at the corners of his mouth.

“I’m beginning to think you’re avoiding me,” he said, voice low and easy. “That’s cruel, you know. I was almost forced to grade papers to fill the aching void.”

Nothing. Not even a blink.

Phainon let the silence stretch just long enough to be dramatic, then tilted his head slightly. “It’s alright. I forgive you. Mostly because you’re devastatingly attractive when you pretend I’m not here.”

Still no reaction.

He squinted. “You are going to speak to me, right? I haven’t been hallucinating this entire relationship?”

Finally—finally—Mydei turned a page.

“You’re early,” he said without looking up. “And loud.”

Phainon grinned. “You wound me, love.”

“I’ll do more than that if you don’t let me work.”

“Now, now,” Phainon murmured, clutching his chest like a man freshly stabbed. “Is that any way to speak to the person who brings light into your dreary little world?”

“You’re tracking gravel onto my floor.”

Phainon looked down. He was. He dragged one foot slowly back over the threshold like that might undo the damage.

“And your shirt,” Mydei added, finally glancing up, “looks like it lost a duel with a hedge.”

Phainon blinked. “It did.” Then, after a beat: “I won.”

Mydei’s expression didn’t change, but one eyebrow lifted.

Phainon took that as a victory.

“I suppose I’ll let you get back to it,” he sighed, pushing off from the counter. “Try not to miss me too much.”

“I won’t.”

He was halfway to the door when Mydei called, without looking: “You forgot your tie.”

Phainon paused, then turned slowly, eyes narrowing.

“…You noticed?”

“It was the only thing not wrinkled.”

Phainon’s smile spread, slow and utterly unrepentant.

“I knew you looked at me when I walked in.”

“Get out.”

He did. But he was still smiling.

The afternoon passed in the steady blur it always did—lectures, questions, the faint clatter of notes being taken by students who thought speed equaled substance. Phainon taught with sleeves rolled up, one hand gesturing broadly while the other kept time with the flow of discussion. His students were sharp today—almost too sharp. They volleyed arguments like seasoned debaters, snatching phrases out of the air and turning them like blades.

He didn’t mind it. He liked the back-and-forth, the momentum of minds stretching themselves. It was the kind of quiet power that didn’t need to shout.

The bell rang—figuratively. There were no actual bells at the university, just the subtle shift of bodies and the rustling of paper that meant class had ended and attention spans had been reclaimed by hunger or boredom.

Phainon was reorganizing a few papers on the podium when he caught the tail end of a conversation drifting in from the back row.

“…—the guy they caught last winter, yeah. I thought he was locked up for good.”

“They said he broke out. Again. Same as before. Three guards injured this time. And one—”

A low whistle. “Damn. How does he keep getting out?”

“No clue. You’d think the heroes would actually… I don’t know. Do something permanent.”

Phainon’s pen paused.

It was brief. A second, maybe two. But there it was—a stillness. A flicker behind the eyes, just beneath the surface of his usual calm.

Then, just as quickly, it passed.

He looked up, smile folding easily back into place.

“Gossiping during a lecture break?” he called out, voice lilting with mock disapproval. “What an impressive misuse of academic freedom.”

The students startled slightly, some laughing, others ducking their heads. One of them offered a sheepish shrug.

“We were just—”

“Plotting the collapse of public trust in the justice system?” Phainon offered. “Very on-brand for this department. But unless the accused is going to submit a thesis, I suggest we stick to the syllabus.”

There were a few more chuckles. The mood lightened.

But as the students gathered their things and filtered out, Phainon lingered.

He tapped the edge of the desk with one knuckle, eyes skimming across the now-empty room. Whatever warmth had been in them earlier was tempered now, like steel pulled from the flame and hammered cool.

He didn’t say anything. He didn’t need to.

He just adjusted his cuffs, straightened his posture, and moved on.

If his lips were curved up into a strange smile, no one mentioned it.

School ended and the the last meeting of the day bled into the early evening, dragging itself across the hour like it had nowhere better to be. Phainon had nodded through most of it, occasionally offering a well-placed comment that made the department chair purse his lips and scribble something into his notes. He’d pretended not to notice.

By the time the university building finally began to empty, the halls took on a quiet, echoing stillness. The kind that made even the lights seem tired.

Phainon leaned back in his office chair, one leg slung casually over the other, his fingers typing lazily across his phone screen. The glow lit his face in the dimness, his expression soft around the edges.

Phainon☀️:

Still working. Might be late tonight. Don’t wait up, darling <333

He watched the screen for a moment, then added:

Phainon☀️:

Or do. You’re very good at brooding into the evening.

A pause. Three dots flickered, then vanished.

Then:

Mydei🍷: I’m busy.

Phainon smiled. It was the same message he always got around this hour, when Mydei was finally closing up and done with social effort for the day. The man had the texting warmth of a glacier—but it was consistent. Familiar.

He typed again.

Phainon☀️:

Miss you anyway. I’ll see you tomorrow, alright? [ ♥ ]

He hesitated, thumb hovering.

Then added:

Phainon☀️:

Or this one if you prefer: (๑˘︶˘๑)

The read receipt popped up almost immediately. No reply.

He tucked the phone into his pocket, the smile still lingering.

“Playing hard to get after two years,” he murmured to himself, rising from the chair. “Bold strategy.”

The office was dim, but he didn’t turn on the overheads. He moved easily through the space, gathering a few things into his bag and slipping into his coat. His silhouette passed briefly by the window—just a figure against the deepening blue of the sky.

Campus after-hours had a different rhythm to it. Fewer voices. More shadow. The occasional echo of footsteps on stone.

He liked it. The quiet. The clarity.

Because soon, there’d be no more room for quiet.

Night wrapped itself around the city slowly, as if reluctant to settle in.

The sky had gone deep blue, starless, the kind of quiet evening that suggested storms on the edge of the horizon. Somewhere, faint sirens stitched themselves through the wind—too distant to mean anything. Not yet.

Phainon moved through the old stairwell with practiced ease, every step measured, silent. His usual stride had vanished; there was no flippancy now. No offhand grace or exaggerated flair. Just the low hum of breath and the sound of clothes adjusting as he shifted his shoulders beneath the cloak.

It wasn’t a disguise—not really. The world knew the Flame Reaver. Masked or not, there was no mistaking the man when the work began. But there were still rituals to be followed. The layering of fabric, the metallic glint of gauntlets cinched tight over his wrists, the whisper of a long coat as it unfurled behind him. Everything deliberate. Everything earned.

He paused near the rooftop exit, slipping a small device from his coat pocket—sleek, flat, nondescript. A single message blinked across the screen in clean white text.

Target spotted. Dockside. Level four clearance. Your call.

There was no sender listed. There didn’t need to be.

Phainon’s thumb hovered briefly, then tapped back one word.

Received.

No reply came, nor did he expect one. Anaxa was never one for sentiment.

He stepped out onto the rooftop, the wind cutting across his face with sharp, surgical precision. Below, the city pulsed with fractured light and fractured rules. Somewhere beneath it all, the subject of today’s whispered headlines was still walking free.

A repeat offender. A known threat. Caught, jailed, released. Again and again.

That was the problem with heroes, wasn’t it?

Phainon exhaled slowly, letting the air leave his lungs as he stared down into the night. Then, without hesitation, he moved—across the roof, over the ledge, into the alley below.

Gone.

Not a sound. Not a flash of flame. Just the ghost of motion and the quiet promise that someone had finally decided to finish the job.

Chapter Summary

A typical day in the life of Mydei: waking up too early, beating up criminals, riding motorcycles like traffic laws don’t apply to him—and somehow making it just in time to pick up his boyfriend.

Chapter Notes

Alright this was meant to be posted yesterday but I didn’t have time so I said fuck it, let’s write this at 2 in the morning to which I did cause sleep schedule? Never heard of her😍 I’ll revise any grammar errors I have later but if u see any plz point it out cause there are probably some in here💀

The alarm went off at six. A single chime, taut and immediate—silenced with practiced ease by the hand that reached for it.

Mydei opened his eyes.

He didn’t rise right away. The room was dim, washed in pale early light that touched the edges of the neatly arranged furniture. For a moment, he simply lay there, stretching—long and slow, joints loosening with the elegant indifference of a cat. His spine arched just slightly as he drew his arms over his head, all the way to the headboard, then relaxed back into the quiet.

When he moved, it was with the unthinking fluidity of someone who didn’t need to rush. The sheets folded themselves in his wake, the floor didn’t creak beneath him. Every motion belonged to a rhythm he’d long since mastered.

In the bathroom, the lights glowed on with a soft warmth. The tiles were cool beneath his feet, a contrast to the already-steaming shower he turned

on. He stepped in without hesitation, the water striking his skin in a clean, steady stream.

He stood beneath it for a while—shoulders relaxed, chin tilted slightly up. The warmth soaked into him, traced the lines of his back, and caught at the ends of his hair. He worked in silence, washing with slow precision, methodical and practiced. No wasted movements, no distractions. Just water and heat and breath.

When he stepped out, he wrapped the towel around his waist and wiped a hand across the fogged mirror. His own reflection gazed back: calm, composed, and still somewhat snappy from being awake so early. He didn’t linger on it.

He brushed his teeth next—still towel-bound, arms relaxed at his sides, the mint sharp against the lingering warmth of the shower. His gaze drifted toward the window. Beyond it, the day was starting.

The faintest twitch of an eyebrow. The smallest exhale of breath.

He rinsed. Spat. Swiped another towel once across his hair, then padded out into the apartment, leaving a faint trail of steam in his wake.

He dressed without much thought—layers folded neatly in drawers, socks stacked in perfect symmetry. Everything in its place.

Until the hoodie.

It was pink. Unapologetically so. The kind of soft, cozy pink that looked like it belonged to a sleep-deprived student with a fondness for bubble tea and pastel stationery. Not a six-foot-something wall of restrained muscle whose shoulders stretched most fabrics like it was on trial.

But the hoodie didn’t care. Neither did he.

It slid over his head, the hem brushing mid-thigh. Loose. Comfortable. The sleeves hung past his wrists and covered half his hands. It still smelled

faintly of clean cotton and some long-ago detergent he could no longer name.

No one had ever questioned it. Who would?

He reached for his usual pants—black, fitted—and tugged them on with the same calm efficiency as everything else. His movements weren’t rushed, just quiet and unbothered. Like a man whose priorities did not include justifying his fashion choices.

In the mirror, the hoodie looked absurd on him.

He didn’t blink.

It was warm. It was his. That was enough.

The kitchen was quiet when he entered, still touched by the gray-blue hush of morning. A filtered light spilled across the counters, catching on glass and brushed steel. He tied his hair back in a loose knot before he began.

He moved through the space with the kind of still confidence that suggested he’d done this a thousand times and never once fumbled. Ingredients were pulled from the fridge with a practiced hand—eggs, cream, sugar, a bar of dark chocolate already half-gone from some previous indulgence. A mixing bowl was spun out from the cupboard with the ease of muscle memory.

The smell of vanilla and cinnamon began to rise, slow and warm. French toast, thick-cut and golden, crisped in a pan while a second batch soaked nearby. He worked without noise, without clutter, the occasional hum under his breath the only sound besides the sizzle of the skillet.

The plating was clean—precise, even. Stacked slices dusted with powdered sugar, a drizzle of syrup in deliberate arcs, fruit arranged with a subtle sort of care that made it seem like it had just landed there on its own. He placed the plate on the table and poured himself a cup of coffee, black, before sitting down.

He ate in calm silence, enjoying the contrast between the crisped edge and the soft center, the way the sweetness lingered but didn’t overwhelm. The hoodie’s sleeves were pushed back just enough to keep them clean, the cuffs creased from habit.

It was, by all measures, a quiet morning. But it was his—and that made it perfect.

The screen lit up across the counter, humming once. Mydei glanced at it only because he always did—habit, not interest.

Phainon☀️:

Rise and shine, my sweetest librarian. Dream of me?

Mydei🍷: No.

A pause. Then another ping.

Phainon☀️:

Ruthless. Is this what love feels like?

Mydei🍷: …Yes.

A beat.

Phainon☀️:

:’(

Mydei scoffed quietly through his nose, but his thumb hesitated before setting the phone down. The corner of his mouth gave the smallest twitch— betrayal in its softest form.

Another message came in before the smile could fully form.

Phainon☀️:

Can you pick me up later? I’ll owe you one. Or two. Or all of me.

Mydei🍷: Fine.

Almost instantly:

Phainon☀️:

You’re an angel. (づ> v <)づ♡

Mydei stared at the emoticon. Then at the counter. Then back again.

He put the phone down with a sigh.

Ridiculous.

…But not unwelcome.

Mydei left the apartment with little fanfare.

The streets were still waking up—hushed and blue in the morning light, tinged gold at the edges where sunlight slipped through. He walked with the kind of ease that came from routine: hands tucked into the pocket of his pink hoodie, bag slung over one shoulder, footsteps quiet but steady.

There was a motorcycle parked a block away. Polished. Black. Unassuming, if you didn’t know what to look for. He didn’t take it this morning—didn’t need to. The library was only a short walk, and Mydei liked the stillness. It gave him time to think. Or not think. Whichever the day required.

When he arrived, he unlocked the heavy front doors and stepped into the silence.

The library was an older building, all high ceilings and sun-dappled windows, with the faint scent of parchment and dust lingering in the air. Not

affiliated with the university, but known well enough among those who preferred their solitude curated with care.

Mydei worked alone.

He moved quietly between the stacks, sorting returns into carts, shelving what needed shelving, straightening spines with unconscious precision. A few pages of inventory updates awaited him at the desk. He reviewed them without pause, fingers skimming the list as his mind filed the titles away automatically.

The morning passed like mist. A couple of regulars came in—one unsure, the other chatty. Mydei answered questions before they could fully form.

“You’re looking for something with a slower pace. Try the second shelf, to your right. Gold spine.”

“Something shorter? No romance? Top of the fiction display, third from the left. Yes, that one.”

He didn’t linger. Just nodded as thanks was offered, then returned to his sorting, sliding a volume back into place with the soft hush of cloth against wood.

The quiet suited him. Here, the world stayed still.

The minutes passed uneventfully. Mydei was halfway through reshelving a crate of archival editions when the panel on his desk blinked once—quietly, subtly. An ordinary drawer front shimmered with the faintest pulse of blue, then shifted, revealing a discreet interface beneath the wood.

He straightened. Brushed the dust from his hands. Stepped over.

The message was already waiting.

From: Hyacine

Priority: Elevated

Status: Request

—We need your assistance. Urgent, if you’re available, please.

He stared at the words for a breath, then let out a soft exhale through his nose.

So much for a quiet day.

He moved with purpose now—closed the panel with a gesture, rechecked the feed for the security cams, then began his practiced routine for shutting down. His hands were steady, but there was something tighter in his jaw, something quieter in the way he moved.

He flipped the “Quiet Study Hours” placard to “Closed for Maintenance” and calmly stepped into the main floor.

“Library’s closing early,” he said with a polite finality that left no room for negotiation. “Please wrap up your selections and exit.”

“One girl blinked at him, halfway through browsing the poetry shelf. “Is something wrong?”

“No.”

She stared at him a second longer, then wisely packed her things.

Mydei waited at the front doors, arms crossed, until the last few patrons filed out under his impassive gaze. Some left with questions in their eyes. None voiced them.

They knew better than to mess with the deranged librarian here.

He stepped forward and unlocked the door—just in time for it to swing open onto a man mid-knock, one arm raised awkwardly, mouth already

forming words.

“Hey, can I just drop—”

SLAM.

The door shut with a force that rattled the frame.

From outside: a stunned silence. Then a faint, bewildered, “…Alright.”

Inside, Mydei flipped the sign to Closed with the dead-eyed precision of a man who’d had enough.

He didn’t even sigh. Just turned on his heel, already walking away as he muttered,

“Tragic.”

Mydei exited through the back, the door shutting behind him with the soft hiss of an automatic lock. No one saw him leave.

In the narrow alley behind the library, leaning against the brick wall like a forgotten relic, sat a beat-up bike with one wheel slightly bent and a faded cartoon sticker peeling off the side. The sticker was smiling. Its origins were unknown. It had been there since before Mydei inherited the library, and in a display of both negligence and passive defiance, he’d never removed it.

So yes, the infamous Godslayer—the most feared operative in the Chrysos Heirs—was about to save the city in a pink hoodie and on a rickety two-wheeler with a grinning cartoon blob on it. Again.

He mounted it without comment and began pedaling.

The ride was smooth in the way only someone completely desensitized to potholes and poorly paved roads could find smooth. He coasted past sharp corners and winding lanes, letting the wind nip at his face. The city moved around him: alive, breathing, unaware. He didn’t rush. There was no need. The message had said urgent, not immediate.

It could’ve been a morning ride. A peaceful, if slightly uphill, commute from a man with a too-large clothing and somewhere to be. Mydei passed under iron bridges and between stone buildings, gliding in clean lines like he was drawing them.

He rolled to a stop in front of an unremarkable gray building tucked between a shuttered cafe and something else. Narrow windows. No signage. Just brick, concrete, and a locked steel door.

He parked the bike beside it, propped it with a foot, and opened the door.

The hallway beyond was pristine. Not a single mark on the marble floor. A wall panel blinked awake the moment he stepped in.

A soft chime. Then:

“Welcome. Identity confirmed: Mydeimos. Clearance: Class One.”

A portion of the far wall split and peeled away with a quiet hiss, revealing a hidden elevator of gleaming chrome and seamless walls.

He stepped inside.

“Please remain still for biometric authentication.”

There was a brief flicker of blue light.

“Retinal scan: verified. Vitals: stable. Aura signature: confirmed.”

“Descent initiated. Welcome to the Chrysos Heirs.”

The elevator dropped in a swift, perfectly controlled motion—silent, smooth, and fast.

He didn’t blink.

The doors opened to a cathedral of steel and glass.

Smooth marble floors stretched in clean lines under pale, ambient lights that hummed like something alive. Every footstep echoed faintly before being swallowed by the hush of controlled efficiency. Screens blinked with real-time feeds, teams moved with quiet intent, and distant murmurs of status reports carried like the low tide of an ocean. The Chrysos Heirs HQ ran like a heartbeat—steady, constant, indispensable.

Mydei walked in like it was a neighborhood bookstore.

He was still chewing.

A biscuit, half-wrapped in a linen napkin, rested between his fingers. Someone had offered it—he hadn’t looked up to see who—and he’d taken it without question, because regardless of whatever the hell was going on, it was still twelve in the godforsaken morning. Early by anyone’s standards. Even his. Even if he was an early bird (unwillingly).

He stepped onto the platform where she stood waiting.

Aglaea.

Goldweaver.

She was in full uniform, the folds of her tailored jacket resting like sculpture across her frame. Her presence was something like ancient nobility and something like cold fire—sharp, polished, and without flaw. Not a single strand of hair out of place. Not a single wasted word.

“Mydei,” she greeted, her voice clear, poised. “Thank you for coming on short notice.”

He nodded, tearing a clean bite from the biscuit. Crumbs landed somewhere on the left sleeve of his hoodie. He did not brush them off.

“We have a re-emergence,” she continued. “Designation: Obelis. A fracture-class anomaly, last seen six months ago in the Lower Sixth District.”

Her fingers moved across a console beside her, and a glowing outline flickered to life in the air—a vague, humanoid silhouette with spiked arms and pulsing veins of stone along its body.

“Abilities include: surface petrification, internal calcification, and blunt-force amplification. We believe he’s adapted since his last encounter with Castorice.”

Another flick of her wrist. Images changed: footage of a collapsed plaza, crumbling statues that had once been people. Charred outlines. A limp figure on a rooftop—Mydei didn’t react.

“Castorice was meant to intercept, but she’s currently deployed in the far north. She… hoped you wouldn’t be summoned so soon again.” Aglaea’s voice softened minutely. “She extends her gratitude. As do I.”

Mydei finally swallowed.

“Mm.”

Aglaea inclined her head in acknowledgment. Nothing more needed to be said.

“Oh,” she added with surgical precision, just as he turned slightly to leave, “and one more development.”

A final image, flickering into place. A security still of a burnt-out alley. At its center, a body. Unrecognizable.

“The Flame Reaver acted again last night. Another convict. Third this month.”

Silence.

Mydei licked the last of the crumbs from his thumb, pausing for a second before nodded once more, and throwing the napkin away in some trash bin nearby.

Then he turned to go, but not before he looked at the image one last time.

Obelis. Petrification. Amplification. Third this month. Castorice sends her regards. Etcetera, etcetera.

He exhaled softly through his nose, the sound the closest thing to a groan he could offer in polite company. Then: “I’ll handle it.”

Aglaea nodded, already turning to brief another agent, already trusting him to disappear and return with the problem no longer a problem.

He made his way down the corridor, past a few nodding operatives and a silent retinal scanner, until he reached the far wing—his designated quarter. Private. Stark. Familiar.

The door hissed shut behind him.

For a second, he just stood there, hand on the hem of his hoodie. Then, with all the energy of someone about to clock in at a very cursed shift, he pulled it off over his head in one long, reluctant motion.

Another sigh escaped him, quiet and resigned.

“So much for a quiet morning,” he muttered.

He folded the hoodie with unnecessary care, set it down on the chair like it was something sacred, and stared blankly ahead for a moment. Then he moved to the far end of the room, where the wall scanned him and began to shift.

Time to save the city.

Again.

Glass rained from the ceiling.

Mydei walked through it like it was mild weather. Shards bounced off his clothes. One sparkled dramatically past his ear. He didn’t blink.

The first man came at him with a crowbar, yelling something primal— probably meant to intimidate.

Mydei caught the crowbar mid-swing and stared at him, unimpressed.

Then he twisted. Crack.

The man screamed in a rather high-pitched tone and folded to the ground like bad laundry.

Someone behind him tried to be clever and swing a pipe at his back. Mydei stepped aside, reached back without looking, and grabbed the guy by the collar. A quick pivot, one neat slam into a support beam, and the second guy was down. Quiet.

“Two,” Mydei muttered.

Three more approached. Mydei sighed.

The first tripped over his own nerves. The second was yelling something about vengeance before Mydei stepped in and drove his elbow into the guy’s sternum with enough force to silence the rest of the speech. He crumpled with a wheeze.

The third paused. Considered her options. Ran at him anyway.

He caught her by the shirt, spun her in a wide arc, and let her crash into a pile of crates. A loud thunk, followed by a quiet groan.

He adjusted his sleeves. “Three.”

From the far side of the room, huddled civilians watched him with wide eyes, whispering behind hands. One of them mouthed what the hell, the other just nodded slowly like it was a religious experience.

It wasn’t. It was a Thursday.

At last, the villain emerged. Dressed in overdesigned black armor with pulsating neon lines and a gauntlet that looked like it had been soldered

together by a blind engineer with a grudge.

The guy grinned. “So you’re the Godslayer. I’ve been waiting for this moment.”

Mydei looked at him blankly. “Hm.”

“You think you can just walk in here, destroy my men, and—”

Mydei punched him in the face.

One hit. Lights out.

The man collapsed like a marionette whose strings had been cut, his fancy gauntlet flickering one last time before shorting out entirely.

Silence.

A long beat passed.

Then—tentative applause from one of the hiding civilians. Another gave a thumbs up. Someone else called out, “Yo, that was sick,” like they’d just watched a particularly clean trickshot.

Mydei touched the comm in his ear.

“Target neutralized.”

There was a pause on the other end, static crackling faintly.

“…Already?”

Mydei stared down at the unconscious body on the floor, then at his scuffed sneakers. “Yes.”

“Wow. Uh—okay. Stand by. Confirming clearance now.”

“Don’t sound so surprised,” he said flatly.

“Right. Sorry. You’re just… efficient.”

A civilian nearby coughed quietly. Mydei turned away, already heading toward the exit.

This was what passed for a warmup.

He barely had time to stretch his arms.

One moment, the air was thick with smoke and silence.

The next—reporters.

Where did they even come from? Were they hiding in the walls? Were they bred in the alleys like pigeons with microphones?

Mydei blinked as half a dozen cameras clicked in his face, lights flaring like miniature suns. Boom mics extended overhead with frightening speed, and a very chipper anchor in a magenta pantsuit shoved past the perimeter tape like it was suggestion-based.

“Godslayer!” she beamed. “How do you feel right now?”

“Tall,” he said.

That seemed to stun her for half a second. Not long enough. Another reporter chimed in: “What message would you like to send the people after this display of heroism?”

Ah, the PR part. Right.

Mydei stood a little straighter, his expression falling into the neutral, solemn default the press seemed to love. He prepared to deliver the usual message about hope, courage, resilience—all the buzzwords the Chrysos Heirs had approved.

And then he glanced down at the corner of his cracked comm screen.

4:25 PM.

There was a brief, almost holy silence in his mind. A quiet internal shattering.

Oh.

Oh no.

His eyes didn’t widen, his face didn’t shift, but his entire soul momentarily left his body. Not even during combat had he felt that cold pulse of dread. He had five minutes.

Five minutes.

Five minutes to get across the city, back in civilian clothes, and pretend he hadn’t just suplexed a villain through an industrial beam.

Phainon was probably already standing outside with his coat, checking his phone with one hand and looking devastatingly patient. He’d probably even made a joke earlier that Mydei would be late, and Mydei had said “I won’t be.”

He would be.

And he was going to look like the world’s worst boyfriend.

“Godslayer, your statement, please?” the reporter prompted.

Mydei stared blankly.

Then: “Stay safe,” he said quickly. “Avoid alleys. Eat protein. Hydrate.”

He turned and booked it.

Reporters called after him. Civilians tried to take photos. One confused fan tried to hand him a latte. Mydei ignored all of it, ducked into a side street, and made a break for his stored motorcycle like his entire reputation depended on it.

Which, tragically, it did.

They were too fast.

Mydei didn’t know if the reporters were genetically enhanced or just powered by the fumes of sensational headlines, but they were gaining. Cameras bounced behind him like caffeinated bloodhounds, chasing their next viral clip with the determination of people who had nothing to lose.

He took a sharp left. Then a sharper right. Someone yelled his name. Someone else yelled “marry me.” He did not look back.

With military precision and the calm of a man who had done this way too many times, he ducked into an alley, kicked off the nearest wall, climbed onto a dumpster, then a rusted fire escape, and vanished onto the roof like a very jaded, very tall alley cat in a pink hoodie.

When he finally reached his building, he didn’t even pause. Didn’t open the front door. That would take too long. That would look suspicious.

No. He vaulted onto his own windowsill—four stories up—and launched himself through the open window he always left unlocked for this exact kind of emergency.

He landed with the grace of a seasoned acrobat and the apathy of a man who’d done this too often to care about how absurd it looked.

His foot knocked over a chair. His hand hit a shelf. He didn’t stop.

Aglaea definitely had access to the cameras all the way here to Olympus’s surveillance grid. Half the Chrysos Heirs probably had bets on how long it’d take him to get back.

Whatever. They could keep their spreadsheets and silent judgment. He had exactly three minutes to stop being the God Slayer and start being a reasonably punctual boyfriend.

One problem though.

He didn’t have time.

The moment he landed, Mydei was already peeling off layers, hoodie hitting the floor like a fallen comrade. He kicked his shoes halfway across the room and beelined it to the bathroom, flicking on the sink with surgical urgency.

A splash. Then two. He scrubbed off the blood like it was just another stain on his reputation, wiping it clean with practiced indifference. The mirror fogged slightly, but he barely looked at it. There wasn’t time for vanity, only damage control.

Shirt off. Pants off. He yanked on a plain black tee that clung nicely to his frame—accidentally flattering, but whatever—and loosely tied a jacket around his waist. He looked normal. Civilian. Approachable. Definitely not someone who’d just reduced a minor crime ring to paste.

“Fine,” he muttered to himself, dragging fingers through his damp hair. “I look fine.”

And he did.

There was no time to celebrate that fact.

Motorcycle keys in hand, he was already halfway down the stairwell before the door even finished closing behind him. The second he hit the pavement, he swung onto the matte-black bike parked just where he always left it, engine purring like it missed him.

The machine was sleek. Fast. Clearly loved. Mydei treated it better than he did most of his own joints.

He revved the engine once, kicked off the stand, and was gone—cutting through traffic like sin through silk, disobeying at least five traffic laws with the casual ease of someone who had definitely done much worse and definitely gotten away with it.

Pedestrians stared. A few gawked.

Mydei didn’t even blink.

He had a boyfriend to pick up. And two minutes left on the clock.

The city blurred.

Back on the bike, Mydei slipped between lanes like smoke, weaving through traffic lights with a calm that suggested the law had no jurisdiction over him. Maybe it didn’t. No sirens dared chase him. No cameras dared flash. The wind tore through his hair and shirt as he leaned into a sharp turn, the machine beneath him responding like a loyal beast of war.

By the time he pulled up near the university gates, his expression was unreadable, visor still down. He parked neatly by the curb, engine purring once before dying to a gentle hum. Students were still loitering nearby, killing time, half-pretending not to stare as the tall, broad-shouldered rider stepped off with fluid grace.

Mydei exuded the same energy as someone stepping out of an explosion without checking behind him.

Heads turned. One girl muttered something like “Oh my god,” under her breath. Someone else dropped a water bottle.

Phainon was already waiting by the campus steps, messenger bag in hand. He looked up from his phone and paused.

“Oh,” he said, clearly taken aback. “I thought you’d be late.”

Before Mydei could respond, a voice from the side cut in—Stelle, one of Phainon’s more shameless students, waved a slow, impressed thumbs-up.

“Damn, professor. You bagged that?”

Phainon blinked. “Apparently.”

He walked toward the bike slowly, eyebrows slightly raised, gaze scanning Mydei like he was still trying to place this version of him. Mydei simply

stopped, one boot against the pavement, and lifted his visor with a slow flick.

Deadpan. “Well? Front or back? Which way are you riding.”

Phainon stared at him.

“…You.”

“…What?”

“Front, please.”

A long pause. Then, with no fanfare, Mydei wordlessly offered him the spare helmet.

Phainon took it with a blooming grin. He didn’t say anything, but the spark in his eyes said everything.

Mydei swung back onto the bike without a word.

Phainon followed.

“Anyway,” Phainon began, voice muffled slightly through the helmet. “I had this debate class today, and I swear to the gods, half the students didn’t even read the material. Do you ever get the urge to just—”

Mydei cut him off mercilessly, “Stop talking and hang on.”

Phainon’s voice lit up, a teasing tone creeping in. “Only if you promise not to crash.”

“Not unless you plan on doing something else on this bike.”

Phainon only chuckled, leaning back just slightly. “Fair enough.”

Mission accomplished.

Chapter End Notes

Chapter Notes
