The outskirts of the city were always too quiet.

No lights. Just neon glow bleeding in from miles away. No cars. Just the sound of electricity buzzing through frayed streetlamps that flickered like they were afraid to be seen. And no people—just whispers of them. A scarf left behind in a rush. A shoe discarded mid-sprint. The faint coppery scent of a skirmish long ended.

Phainon walked through it like a myth. Blade sheathed. Face masked. His breath steady and inaudible under the thick cloth and metal. Every step was measured. Silent. Like the ground didn’t dare echo back.

His comm crackled once, then cleared.

“Oh good, you’re not dead,” said Anaxa’s voice, clear with bored disdain. “Regrettable.”

Phainon didn’t respond. Just kept walking.

“I’m tracking movement four blocks east of your position,” Anaxa went on. “Possibly our slippery little parolee. And by ‘parolee,’ I mean government-sponsored moral collapse in a trench coat.”

A beat of silence.

Then Anaxa added, “And before you ask, yes. I’ve triple-verified the ID. Unlike you, I don’t conduct fieldwork based on ‘vibes.’”

Phainon gave the briefest hum, the kind that could be interpreted as either agreement or passive aggression.

Anaxa sighed, sharp and straight to the point. “You’re in one of Goldweaver’s zones, by the way. Try not to set anything on fire this time. Or do. Honestly, I’m torn between professional integrity and watching her file another seventy-page incident report.”

That earned the barest twitch of Phainon’s lip under his mask. Not quite a smile. More like a murder-adjacent smirk.

“Still nothing to say?” Anaxa asked, mock-sweet. “Charming. It’s like working with a particularly vengeful housecat.”

Phainon crouched low, eyes sweeping the ground. A drag mark. Blood, maybe. Fresh. Civilians had been here, and not long ago.

The comm crackled again.

“Anyway,” Anaxa said, more sharply now, “you’ve got ten minutes before that perimeter closes. Unless you’d like to get close with Olympus’ surveillance team, which, by the way, is still absolutely crawling with Goldweaver’s little pet projects. Including one intern who said your blade technique was ‘overly theatrical.’”

Phainon stopped.

“…He’s dead to me,” he said at last, voice low and dry as bone.

“Oh?” Anaxa said sweetly. “So you can speak. I was beginning to worry you’d taken a vow of silence for the aesthetic.”

Another pause. Then a calm, gliding voice from the shadows:

“I don’t speak unless I have to.”

“And yet you text with emojis,” Anaxa muttered. “Gods help me.”

Phainon rose again, gaze locked ahead as the faint outline of his target came into view—two floors up in a ruined building, hunched over a body that wasn’t moving.

No hesitation. No sound.

Phainon moved forward, blade unsheathed, and vanished into shadow.

The higher he climbed, the quieter the city became.

Not silent—no. Silence was clean. This was the low, muffled drag of something unfinished. Sirens echoed faintly, warped by distance. A dog barked once, then fell quiet. Somewhere below, glass crunched under a foot that wasn’t his.

Phainon stilled at the sound, hand on the hilt of his sword, before slipping through the fractured archway of an abandoned bank. The lobby was gutted —charred walls, vines curling through cracked stone, gold filigree blackened and peeling like old scabs.

Three bodies lay against the far columns, spaced with uncanny neatness. Two women, one man. All unconscious. All breathing.

“Unarmed,” Phainon murmured. “Breathing. Cold skin. Pulse slow.”

A pause.

Then, over comms, Anaxa’s voice filtered in—precise, detached, the kind of clinical you didn’t learn from med school but from years of field triage.

“Blue tint?”

“Yes.”

“Gas or contact agent. Circulatory suppressant. Five-minute exposure, maybe less.”

Phainon pressed two fingers to a woman’s wrist. “Non-lethal.”

“Not for long,” Anaxa replied. “Move.”

He did.

The stairwell creaked as he ascended. Fifth floor, Anaxa had said. Top of the tower. No working elevator, no time for dramatics. The shadows stretched longer here, twisted by broken windows and half-dead fluorescents flickering like dying stars.

It was when he paused to pass a wide, cracked window that he saw it.

A flurry of movement below—flames licking the edge of the street, smoke curling into the night. Somewhere, metal groaned. A public bus had crashed into the side of a half-demolished structure. Its front end was crushed into the scaffolding like a kneeling beast, windshield webbed with cracks. One of the tires was still spinning, aimless.

Civilians were crawling out of the windows.

One woman climbed down the side only to slip and tumble onto the asphalt. Another helped a limping man hobble away from the wreckage. A child was screaming somewhere, high-pitched and muffled by the smoke. Emergency response hadn’t reached them yet.

Phainon stilled.

The air around the bus shimmered faintly with that same synthetic gas— more subtle here, thinner—but unmistakable. He’d seen what it did when concentrated. This was already enough to ruin lungs.

And they were breathing it in.

One of the civilians, already staggering, collapsed against the curb. Another ran back into the wreckage. Phainon didn’t know why—maybe for a bag, or a pet, or something else no one would understand until it was too late.

His fingers curled slightly.

They wouldn’t all make it out.

For a moment, he stayed where he was, cloaked by shadow, eyes sharp and unblinking. He didn’t move. Didn’t flinch.

Then, Anaxa’s voice crackled in his ear.

“Still breathing, I assume?”

Phainon blinked, pulse sharpening again.

“Yeah,” he muttered, stepping back from the edge. “They’re still moving.”

He didn’t say for now.

He didn’t have to.

He bit his tongue and kept walking.

He didn’t have time for this.

He had to have trust in their capabilities, he had to.

Still, his next step up the stairwell was quieter than the last.

And faster.

The man at the top of the tower wasn’t going to kill himself.

Unfortunately.

He reached the upper floors without resistance.

No traps. No alarms. Just more signs of rot—offices gutted, desks overturned, ceilings sagging with moisture. A half-dead hallway light sputtered as he passed, casting sharp shadows across the limp bodies slumped against the walls.

Three. No—four.

None were dead. Not yet.

One man convulsed once, then stilled. Phainon didn’t stop walking.

He knew what death looked like. This wasn’t it. Just the threshold.

“Building schematics show no recent records past Floor Twelve,” Anaxa said, voice filtering in through his comm again. He sounded more like a war doctor now—detached, not disinterested. “No maintenance, no tenants, no surveillance footage. And then—suddenly—activity. Spikes in temperature. Magnetic readings. Toxic dispersals.”

Phainon stepped over another collapsed civilian. A brief glance—livid skin, dark veins. A quiet pulse.

“Unregistered tech?”

“Tech, or something playing at it,” Anaxa replied. “Too erratic for a sanctioned operation. And I ran the parole records again. Your guy’s clean on paper.”

Phainon scoffed. “They always are.”

“No. I mean clean. Like someone scrubbed it this morning. Name’s there. History isn’t.”

At the end of the hall, he saw the faintest glow.

Phainon didn’t run. He walked.

He stepped into the top floor like it belonged to him.

The man was already waiting.

Mid-forties. Bad posture. Jacket two sizes too big. He flinched at Phainon’s entrance, fingers twitching near a case of tools—vials, syringes, wires tangled like veins. The remnants of whatever horror he’d tried to unleash downstairs sat behind him in cold steel.

“You,” the man spat. “You’re—”

He never finished the sentence.

Phainon’s sword was a blur—one clean arc, not toward the neck or chest, but just above the hip. A vital-adjacent strike. Deep enough to send him sprawling, twitching, writhing. But not dying. Not even close.

The sword hummed softly in his hand.

The man hit the ground hard.

He tried to scramble away—stupid, futile—but Phainon didn’t even look winded. He walked up and, without so much as a warning, brought his heel down.

Hard.

The man screamed. Or tried to. It came out broken.

Phainon’s leg remained planted on his ribs, pinning him like he wasn’t even worth crouching for. A footnote. A smear.

“Name,” he said calmly.

The man didn’t answer. Just wheezed.

Phainon dug his heel in further, leaning slightly, just enough for bone to creak.

“No?” he asked, tone cool. “That’s fine.”

He stepped back, letting the man gasp. His blade stayed unsheathed, resting easily in one hand.

“Anaxa,” Phainon said.

“Yes?”

“Five minutes. Get what you can.”

There was a pause. The faint sound of keys tapping. Then:

“Already tracing the comms data. He used a portable relay to mask the gas dispersal signature. Stupidly. I’ve got half the call history.”

Phainon hummed once, low.

“Should I be worried?” Anaxa added mildly.

Phainon glanced down at the man, who had started to tremble.

“Not yet.”

He raised the sword slightly—just enough to catch the light.

“But soon.”

The man coughed, choked, then rasped out a wet, miserable plea.

“Please—please, I don’t—I was just paid to—”

He reached out with one shaking hand, fingers scrabbling against the floor like he thought he could crawl to mercy.

Phainon didn’t even look interested.

He shifted his weight again, slowly, deliberately, and pressed the heel of his boot into the man’s back—right between the shoulder blades. Not enough to kill. Just enough to crush the breath from his lungs.

The man let out a garbled, half-scream. No one heard it but the walls.

Phainon tilted his head, expression unreadable. His sword hung loose in his fingers, more a promise than a threat.

“Paid by who?” he asked quietly.

The man sobbed.

“Mm.” Phainon’s gaze didn’t change. “Let’s try that again.”

By the time he gave the name, his voice was raw from screaming.

He’d started bargaining somewhere around the cracked rib, but Phainon never even flinched. He’d worked methodically—almost professionally, distant, never once raising his voice. Just questions. Then silence. Then more pain.

“Alzourin,” the man finally wheezed. “It was—it was Alzourin, I swear— he said he had ties—he said—he said I’d be safe—”

Phainon’s head tilted at that. He crouched at last, the first time he’d so much as looked the man in the eye since it started.

“Alzourin,” he repeated, voice smooth, thoughtful. “Now that… that is helpful.”

The man blinked, dazed, but alive. Hope, pitiful and blinding, sparked in his battered face.

Phainon smiled.

It was almost kind.

“Thank you,” he said, and drove the blade clean through the man’s chest.

There was no pain in the expression that followed—just confusion. Like he’d expected mercy from the devil wearing a mask.

Phainon watched the light leave his eyes.

Then stood, wiped the blood from his sword, and said evenly into the comms, “Got a name. Make sure Goldweaver never gets to it first.”

Phainon wiped his blade clean on the man’s shirt with practiced apathy. No theatrics. No pause. The body was still twitching faintly when he turned away.

He didn’t make it far—just a single step toward the stairwell—before Anaxa’s voice filtered through his earpiece again.

“I’d hold your position.”

Phainon paused.

“Why?”

“There’s movement two rooftops east. Multiple heat signatures. The gas wasn’t coming from a single source—looks like auxiliary dispersal teams. Sloppy work. Likely untrained.”

Phainon exhaled slowly, adjusting the grip on his weapon. His gaze cut toward the skyline.

“How many?”

“Three, possibly more. Patterns are erratic. But one location stands out —heavier output. Sending coordinates now.”

A soft ping followed. He crouched low, tracking the line between buildings, already recalculating his path.

“Tell me it’s not a school.”

“Condemned residential high-rise. Structurally intact. You’ll need to cross two lots and take the west exterior. And—”

Anaxa’s voice hitched for a breath.

Phainon froze.

“There’s something else,” he said. “Near the node. Someone’s already up there.”

Phainon shifted upright. A new feed flickered across his visor—grainy drone footage, static in the wind, barely stable. But the figure it caught was clear.

His breath stilled.

No. Not here.

A man moved through the smoke. Sure-footed. Unarmored. Supporting someone with one arm while gesturing for another to follow. His shirt was streaked in soot, sleeves rolled up, hair tousled from the heat. Familiar in every way that mattered.

It was Mydei.

Phainon’s entire body went rigid.

He wasn’t supposed to be here. Not on this building. Not in this operation. No protective gear, no comms, not even a damn mask. What the hell was he doing?

Phainon’s foot slid toward the ledge before he registered the motion.

“He’s evacuating,” Anaxa said quietly. “Entered through the northeast stairwell. No surveillance coverage. Saw the gas. Moved on instinct.”

Phainon didn’t speak.

His eyes stayed on the screen.

Mydei was guiding another civilian forward, moving like he belonged in the firestorm. Calm. Efficient. Like this wasn’t the first time. But something was off. His posture was stiff, movements tight. Not rushed, but deliberate —like he was one step from collapse and wouldn’t let it show.

Phainon’s fingers flexed against the rail.

He could go now. Cut across the lot, clear the building, grab Mydei before anything got worse.

But—

“Don’t,” Anaxa said, quieter now. “You go down there, you compromise your route and him. He’s upright. He’s thinking. Let him do what he came to do.”

Phainon didn’t answer right away.

He hated how right Anaxa was. Hated seeing Mydei there, just close enough to reach—just far enough to lose.

His jaw clenched.

Of course he’d be there. Of course  he’s dragging people to safety with dust on his clothes and no plan at all.

“Tch.”

His voice was low when he finally spoke.

“He’s fine. He can handle himself.”

The words tasted like iron, but he meant them.

Phainon turned from the ledge, breath sharp, spine straight.

He had a job to finish.

Phainon was already halfway across the rooftop when Anaxa’s voice came through again—brisk, exacting.

“Change of plan. There’s a suppressant unit nearby.”

He slowed, barely.

“Neutralizer?”

“Something close. We detected trace readings—low-range dispersion tech. Primitive but effective enough to destabilize the gas on contact. You’ll want it before you hit the main site.”

“Coordinates?”

“Sending.”

The ping came a beat later. He veered off without hesitation.

The wind rose as he crossed the next lot, boots skidding briefly on gravel before finding grip again. His cloak snapped at his heels. Somewhere in the distance, a siren bled into static. He didn’t look back.

Anaxa’s voice cut through the crackle. “It’s a warehouse annex. North side. You’ll want to move quickly—the emissions are thickening.”

Phainon didn’t need the warning. He felt it in the air—sharp, acrid. Like something synthetic burning through metal.

The warehouse came into view two minutes later.

Which, of course, was when the ground blew up.

The explosion tore through the corner lot, flames bursting through concrete. Phainon twisted mid-air, thrown back by the shockwave—his cloak seared along the edge—but he hit the ground in a roll and came up with claws already drawn.

He didn’t miss a step.

“Traps,” he muttered, darting toward cover. “Of course.”

“Improvised,” Anaxa replied. “But targeted. Likely timed for your entry.”

“No shit.”

He sprinted low across the debris field, dodging the next detonation by inches. Smoke split wide as he lunged over a fallen pipe. Sparks flew. One side of the building cracked and groaned under stress.

Another blast tore through the side wall just as he hit the base of the structure.

“Top of the roof,” Anaxa said. “Confirming heat signature— neutralizer’s stored there.”

Phainon stared up.

“Of course it is,” he muttered.

Behind him, the second floor gave a warning lurch. Metal beams shrieked under pressure. The firestorm spread quick across the structure.

He didn’t wait.

With a single breath, he launched up—claws out. Steel tore into concrete with a sharp, scraping shriek. His body arced high, legs coiled tight as he hooked himself to the nearest ledge.

The wind buffeted him. Another explosion sent debris past his side.

He climbed.

Fast.

One claw after the other, driving into the wall like fangs into bone. Every movement deliberate. Balanced. Controlled.

Flames chased him halfway up, licking at the building’s side. A window blew out near his left arm. Shards grazed his coat but didn’t slow him.

Ten feet from the roof, he shifted his weight, swung to one side, and launched off the final ledge.

He landed on the rooftop in a crouch, dust rising around his boots.

The air up here was worse—thick, metallic. Acrid.

And in the center of it all, nestled beside a half-melted vent shaft: the neutralizer.

Small. Ugly. Functional.

Phainon rose, eyes narrowing.

“Got it,” he said. “What now?”

“Activate and deploy it near the node. You’ll have sixty seconds before it stabilizes the air. After that—”

“I know.”

His voice was low and focused.

He picked it up, turned toward the chaos below, and moved.

There wasn’t time for anything else, he had yet another flight of stairs to climb after this.

The rooftop was louder than expected.

Wind keened across the jagged edges of broken scaffolding, rusted beams rattled overhead, and the neutralizer at Phainon’s back gave off a low, steady hiss, thinning the last of the gas with every breath it expelled. The air still carried smoke, acrid and chemical, but visibility had improved.

He stepped into the open slowly, bootfalls silent across the scorched concrete.

And then—he saw him.

A lone figure, dressed in sharp black, moved at the edge of the dispersal core. He circled it like it belonged to him, like he was admiring the centerpiece of a gallery, not a makeshift weapon suspended over a gas-leaking conduit.

Phainon’s posture tensed.

“Someone’s here,” he muttered, gaze tracking the man’s steady movements.

Anaxa’s voice crackled through his comm. “Confirmed. No friendly markers. I’m running facial now.”

Phainon didn’t respond.

Something in the man’s demeanor itched at him. He wasn’t panicking. Wasn’t confused. He moved with certainty. Calm. And then he bent down, examined the device, and said something to someone just out of view.

A second figure was dragged forward.

Phainon went completely still for one reason.

The reason being?

It was Mydei.

On his knees, hands bound behind his back. Head up. Shoulders square. Blood ran down one arm, staining the fabric at the seam. His jaw was tight, eyes locked forward, glaring at the man with the cool precision of someone who’d already memorized a dozen ways to kill him.

The breath in Phainon’s lungs froze solid.

No gear. No support. Just Mydei in a torn shirt and that expression he wore when he was seconds from violence.

“What the hell,” Phainon whispered.

“I believe,” Anaxa said—tone neutral, almost bored—“that might be our guy.”

Phainon’s heart beat louder in his ears. “Alzourin?”

“Mmh. Lines up with movement reports from Sector 9. He’s been slipping through cracks for months—early parole, falsified IDs, access to tech far beyond his supposed means. Someone paid for this mess. We just found the check-writer.”

Phainon’s eyes hadn’t left Mydei.

How did this happen?

He’d been fine. Still standing. Still helping civilians not ten minutes ago. Phainon had watched him make it out of the haze—steady, methodical. Injured maybe, but not cornered.

So why is he here?

Why is he kneeling like that?

His pulse spiked.

Why did I let him stay?

Mydei was strong, of course he was strong, but this wasn’t strength. This wasn’t strategy. This was reckless. This was stupid.

Phainon’s hands flexed at his sides. The cold returned—sharp, numbing. Every instinct screamed to move. To strike. To grab Mydei and tear through the roof until nothing was left of Alzourin but blood and teeth.

But—

He froze.

Something shifted in the periphery.

Movement, fast and clumsy. A figure by the rooftop’s exit. Pale uniform. Nervous posture.

Phainon turned his head slightly, eyes narrowing behind the mask.

A vigilante.

Not one he recognized. Young. New. Maybe someone recruited recently, maybe not. Either way, he wasn’t acting like backup.

He was crouched low, hands shaking as he reached out toward a man in shadow. There was a brief exchange. Bills—thick, folded—passed quickly into the vigilante’s hand. He hesitated, then nodded, and stepped back.

A bribe.

Taken mid-crisis. In front of civilians. With Alzourin a dozen feet away.

Phainon’s expression flattened.

Not a word left his mouth.

He moved once.

There was no warning. No pause.

One clean slash.

Metal flashed in the low light, a single arc that cut the air like a guillotine— and the vigilante’s arms dropped to the ground with a dull, wet sound. Just above the elbows.

The man let out a choked scream, stumbled, collapsed.

Phainon didn’t look at him again.

He didn’t believe in vigilantes. But he believed in standards. And that man had none.

The rooftop felt quiet again. Not from silence, but from clarity.

Phainon turned his gaze back to Mydei.

His fingers tightened.

He wouldn’t let it happen again.

Not tonight.

He turned—

And saw Mydei, standing far too close to the edge.

Swaying.

One foot braced on cracked concrete, the other barely planted. Shoulders drawn taut. Head lowered like the weight of the night had finally caught up with him.

Phainon moved before he could think.

One breath, one heartbeat—and he was there.

An arm slid firmly around Mydei’s waist, pulling him back from the ledge with a grip that brooked no argument. Mydei tensed, instinctively twisting toward the touch—but Phainon was already steadying him, the line of his body acting like a barrier between Mydei and the drop.

“You’re fine,” he said, low, even. “I’ve got you.”

And for a moment, Mydei just… stared.

Wide-eyed. Breathing shallow. Shock tightening every line of his face.

Phainon knew why.

He wasn’t supposed to be here.

Not him. Not the Flame Reaver—the masked menace whispered about by heroes, feared by the corrupt. The vigilante who carved justice into every city block with surgical cruelty. Who showed no mercy. Who left no second chances.

And yet—here he was.

Holding him.

Mydei flinched slightly as screams rose again from behind them. The vigilante—young, foolish, now arm-less—still howled somewhere out of sight. The smell of blood was sharp in the air.

Phainon felt Mydei begin to turn. Just a fraction. Just enough to look.

His hand moved before Mydei could finish.

A gentle touch—two fingers beneath Mydei’s chin, tilting his face back toward him.

“Don’t,” Phainon said softly. “Not tonight.”

Mydei froze.

The contact wasn’t forceful. It didn’t need to be. There was something final in Phainon’s voice. Something immovable.

No more trauma for his idiotic, lovable boyfriend today. Not if he could help it. Not for him.

The city could burn. The rooftop could fall apart at the seams. But right now, Phainon only saw one thing worth holding onto.

And he was already in his arms.

Phainon didn’t speak as Alzourin monologued. He barely heard him, in truth. Words filtered through static—meaningless, slow, indulgent. The only

thing he registered was the strain in Mydei’s body.

It was subtle—barely a falter—but Phainon felt it. The slackness beginning to settle in his frame. The faint sway of his balance, like someone leaning too close to a ledge. He was still upright, still trying to mask the weakness, but Phainon could feel it beneath his palm, humming against his ribs like a wire pulled too tight.

Then came the words that cut through everything:

“He’s already marked.”

Phainon’s head snapped toward the sound, instinct sharp as glass.

“Poison,” Alzourin continued. “Or a curse. Whichever term feels more poetic.”

His fingers curled against Mydei’s side. That cold, creeping pressure in his chest sharpened into something jagged. Marked. Poisoned. He hadn’t seen a wound. No blood. That meant something internal. Inhaled? Ingested?

His mind moved fast. Faster than the fear. Faster than the dread clawing at the edges of his calm.

He scanned Mydei quickly—eyes flicking over his expression, the shape of his lips, the pallor blooming at his jawline. Still breathing. Still lucid. Whatever it was hadn’t hit the brain yet. That was good. That bought him seconds. Maybe.

Then—an idea. Fast, precise, ugly.

Chemical dispersal. Spell tracers. Inhaled airborne agents often rooted in the sinus cavity first—especially arcane ones. Slower if the respiratory tract was disrupted.

He’d seen this kind of thing before. A binding curse with a time delay, meant to cripple the target just long enough to make them helpless. Not enough to kill them outright—not yet. Enough to make them collapse in front of an audience. A performance.

The counter?

It had to be forced out. Diluted. Interrupted.

A neutralizer.

Or something that could neutralize.

His jaw clenched. There was no time to call for Anaxa. No time to find the source and burn it out. But he’d taken the antidote earlier—on Anaxa’s instruction, half-idly, not expecting to need it.

He had it in him. Right now.

His body was the filter. His bloodstream was the carrier.

And Mydei’s breath was already starting to hitch.

He looked at him again—really looked. The fall of his lashes. The way his lips parted ever so slightly, unaware. He was pale now. Too pale. Still blinking, still standing, but it wouldn’t last. A minute, maybe less. Then he’d crumple.

Phainon’s heart pounded once, hard enough to hurt.

He could do it. This would work. This was necessary.

And gods help him—that wasn’t all it was.

He took a breath and leveled his voice, crisp and direct.

“Close your eyes.”

Mydei blinked at him, sluggish and confused. “Wait—”

There wasn’t time.

Phainon moved.

His mask shifted just enough to bare his mouth. His hand caught Mydei’s jaw—not tender, not cruel, but commanding. A pressure honed in combat, the kind meant to say don’t argue. The other hand gripped tighter at his waist, an anchor against gravity and hesitation both.

Then—he kissed him.

No preamble.

It wasn’t gentle. Their mouths collided in a way that bordered on brutal— lips sealing with precision, breath forced into breath, blood forced down as we. There was no room for anything else. Not for hesitation. Not for sentiment.

But the urgency made it worse.

Because Phainon could feel everything: the tension in Mydei’s spine, the heat of his skin, the wavering fight in his breath. He could feel the way Mydei startled, tried to shift, maybe even open his eyes—

His grip crushed down for a heartbeat. A silent warning. Don’t. He was steadying him, yes, but it was also a threat—one Mydei knew how to read. A single twitch, and Phainon would let go. He wouldn’t, not ever, but Mydei didn’t know that.

He stayed still.

His breath hitched—shallow and sharp—and Phainon swallowed it like a man drowning. The taste of the curse was acrid, bitter, metallic. It clung to the back of his throat. But beneath it—there he was.

That trace of Mydei, familiar and infuriating, laced with defiance even now.

It hurt.

Because gods, Phainon wanted to touch him properly. To thread a hand through his hair, to cradle his face, to kiss him slow and deep until Mydei forgot what poison was. Until he forgot.

But he didn’t.

Because this wasn’t about want.

He held the kiss just long enough. Just until he felt the shift—the slightest ease in Mydei’s breathing, the release of something inside his chest.

Then he pulled back sharply.

The mask snapped down. His expression vanished behind it.

But his hands didn’t move.

One stayed at Mydei’s waist. The other hovered, still near his jaw, just in case.

He didn’t speak.

He didn’t need to.

Because Mydei was still breathing.

And that was the only thing that mattered.

The moment Mydei exhaled, Phainon stilled.

Alzourin had already begun to run—boots scraping against the rooftop edge, retreat sharp and graceless. Whatever contingency he’d counted on— poison, panic, spectacle—had unraveled the instant Mydei stayed upright. The instant Phainon intervened.

It was over, and the bastard knew it.

Phainon adjusted his mask back on as his muscles coiled, ready to pursue. The air crackled with the promise of movement—smoke rising in spirals behind him, steel still fresh on his tongue. He tilted forward—

Then froze.

A breath. Fragile. Hitching.

It came from behind him, quiet as a sigh—and yet it hit louder than the detonation that had rocked the street minutes before. He turned slightly. Didn’t need to look. He already knew.

Mydei.

The sound wasn’t one of fear. Not pain either. But there was something raw in it. Strained. As if just staying conscious required more effort than he wanted to show.

Phainon’s stance eased. Slowly. The sharp edge of momentum dulled.

He breathed out through his nose, jaw tight.

“Anaxa,” he said quietly.

“Already tracking him,” came the response, unsurprised. “He’s not gonna get far.”

Phainon nodded once and turned.

Mydei stood where he’d left him, upright by force of will alone. His hands were braced at his sides, but the tension in his shoulders betrayed him. His eyes were clearer than before—barely—but his mouth was slack with exhaustion, chest rising in shallow pulls.

Phainon approached without a word. When he reached him, he ducked low, arms moving with calm precision. One under the knees, the other bracing his back.

He lifted him clean off the ground.

Mydei startled slightly. Not enough to recoil, just a flicker of awareness in his brow, breath catching against Phainon’s neck.

“…what—”

His voice was hoarse, a whisper dragged through smoke.

“Don’t.” Phainon murmured.

He adjusted his grip, shifting Mydei’s weight closer, steadying his breathing by sheer proximity. The air still tasted like ash, but he could feel Mydei’s pulse now—fluttering too fast under his skin, but there.

“I can walk,” Mydei mumbled after a moment.

“You can pretend to,” Phainon replied evenly.

Mydei huffed, low and amused, or maybe just tired. His head tilted slightly against Phainon’s shoulder—wary, uncertain. But he didn’t protest again.

“You’re not supposed to be…” Mydei started, the sentence falling apart halfway through. He blinked slowly, eyes unfocused.

Phainon didn’t respond.

There were too many possible endings to that sentence, and he wasn’t sure he liked any of them.

Instead, he descended the rooftop, boot treads scraping against broken concrete. Mydei’s breath warmed his neck. The rhythm of it was still uneven, but steadying. Recovering.

That would do for now.

The descent felt longer than it should have.

Each step echoed against the warped stairwell, carved through smoke and ruin. The fire above was dying, but the heat still lingered—clinging to the walls, curling under their clothes. Phainon moved carefully, arms steady around Mydei’s frame, boots grinding ash into concrete with every step.

Mydei didn’t speak.

He hadn’t since the rooftop. Not a breath, not a sound.

And that silence—it wasn’t normal. Not from him. He wasn’t the type to chatter, sure, but he always said something. A half-dry remark. A curt protest. A pulse of stubbornness just to prove he still could.

But now? Nothing.

Phainon could feel the tension in his body, the rigid discipline holding him upright even as his strength clearly faltered. His jaw was set. Eyes half-lidded. Breathing shallow. Not from pain. Not fear, either. Just… exhaustion. Deep and buried. The kind you didn’t admit to until someone else pulled you out of it.

He held him a little closer.

The mask scratched cold against his own skin, its edges sharp against the warmth he wanted to give. He could hear Mydei’s heart now—steady but slow, like it was working harder than it should. It made something twist inside him. A feeling with too many names.

He wanted to speak. He wanted to.

To explain. To soften. To tell him he was alright, even if he wasn’t afraid.

To tell him he would always come for him.

That he’d never let him fall. Never let him be alone.

He wanted to press his forehead to his, to breathe against his skin until his pulse steadied. He wanted to kiss him again—really kiss him. Without poison in the air or blood on their hands or fear in the margins.

But he couldn’t.

Not like this.

Not with the mask still up. Not with the city watching, even if no one was looking.

So he said nothing.

Just kept walking, each step measured, each breath held just long enough to keep from shaking.

And Mydei stayed silent too.

But Phainon heard every word he didn’t say.

They reached ground level just as the sirens rolled in—low, layered, and unmistakable.

Not local authorities. Special Operations.

Phainon recognized the sound immediately. It was always them in cases like this—when containment broke, when dangerous tech or arcane weapons were involved, when the air itself turned hostile. They were the kind of unit that arrived not to chase suspects, but to clean up scenes: isolate toxins, collect samples, quarantine the aftermath. Efficient. Quiet. Not heroic, not glamorous—but necessary.

He hated them on principle.

Not individually, but as an institution. For how they’d look at a dying man crying out for help and think of a statistic. For their loyalty to protocol over people. For the way they’d send people to their deaths while they lounged comfortably behind government enforced steel, always showing up thirty seconds too late.

He glanced down at Mydei, still cradled against his chest. His breathing was thin, but steady. Pale. Cold. The effects of the curse hadn’t worn off yet, and Phainon couldn’t fix that alone. Not without tipping his hand. Not without compromising everything.

Tonight wasn’t about principle.

So, he stepped out of the shadows just enough to be seen.

The response was immediate. A pair of medics peeled from the arriving team, dressed in reinforced suits, visors up, already moving with purpose. They didn’t ask questions. Didn’t even look at him properly—just zeroed in on Mydei, recognized the symptoms, and moved to act. One had a scanner. The other was already prepping a spell-seal, muttering stabilization lines under his breath.

Phainon laid Mydei down, careful with every motion. He adjusted the cloak around his shoulders before the medics reached him, tucking it close. Like armor. Or a promise.

Then he turned to leave.

But fingers caught his wrist—barely a touch, too weak to hold him, but enough to stop him.

Mydei’s voice came quiet. Rough.

“…Thank you.”

Sincerity. Quiet, reluctant, and legit sincerity.

Phainon paused.

He looked at him—really looked, just for a breath—and gave a single nod.

Then he stepped back and was gone. Slipping between the noise and movement, into the empty spaces between units, unseen and unrecognized.

They’d fix him. They had to.

He wouldn’t be far.

The wind met him first—cool, sharp, and cutting as he scaled the last ledge and vanished into the dark. The city stretched beneath him in blur and noise, but he didn’t stop.

Not until the silence returned.

Not until he was alone again.

“Are you trying to incriminate yourself?” Anaxa’s voice sliced through the calm, laced with irritation. “You gave him your cloak?”

Phainon groaned, dragging a hand through his hair as he paced a few feet down the gravel-strewn rooftop. “I knowww, I know. I panicked. It was a gesture. A moment. I blacked out emotionally.”

“You blacked out emotionally.”

“It was romantic!”

A beat of silence. Judging.

“Drama queen.”

Phainon sighed, flopping into a crouch near the edge of the rooftop, one hand covering his face as he temporarily took off his mask. “I peaked. If I die now, bury me somewhere poetic.”

“You’re not dying.”

“I might. Emotionally. From the shame.”

Another pause.

Phainon stayed there for a moment, arms draped loosely over his knees, wind tugging at the edges of his suit. But slowly, the curve of his shoulders shifted. The weight of the last hour crept in again, heavier now that Mydei was safe, heavier because he wasn’t.

His voice when it came again was quieter. Sharper.

“…Do you still have the location?”

The humor had gone.

Anaxa didn’t miss a beat. “Always.”

Phainon stood slowly.

No theatrics this time.

He reached for the hilt of his sword and drew it in one smooth motion. The metal caught the faintest gleam of citylight—silver like a promise, like justice made manifest. He turned it in his grip once, steady. Controlled.

One slash was all he needed.

But that wasn’t all he planned to do.

Mydei🍷: I’m sorry.

Phainon blinked down at his screen.

Phainon☀️:

What happened? Did you kill someone. Did you touch my leftovers.

A pause.

Mydei🍷: I kissed someone else.

Phainon stared.

Then smiled.

He flopped back on the old couch that luckily was there, one arm tossed over his head, thumbs moving lazily over the screen.

Phainon☀️:

Was he hotter than me?

Mydei🍷: I’m being serious. I feel like I betrayed your trust. Even if it was to save my own life. It still counts. I should’ve fought it. Or told you right away.

Phainon kicked his feet in the air.

Actually kicked them. Like a teenager.

Phainon☀️:

So what you’re saying is You were thinking about me. While kissing someone else. Dear that’s the hottest thing you’ve ever said.

Mydei🍷: Phainon. I’m trying to be honest.

Phainon☀️:

And I love that for us. I forgive you. In fact I feel incredibly honored. You’ve basically declared undying loyalty via mouth contact. Very romantic.

Mydei🍷: You’re impossible. But thank you.

Phainon grinned down at the phone.

Then kicked a severed arm out of his path as he stepped over the pool of blood soaking the floor.

The silence in the warehouse was thick with finality. Broken only by the faint drip of something viscous down the wall and the hum of city static outside.

Alzourin’s body was sprawled across the broken concrete, head tilted back at an unnatural angle, his eyes frozen wide in disbelief—like he’d never thought it could end like this. That he’d never imagined someone could reach him.

Phainon tucked his sword away with clean, practiced grace, stepped around a chunk of ribcage, and leaned against a wall still streaked with soot.

He looked down at his phone.

Phainon☀️:

You’re cute when you’re guilty. I love you.

And with blood still drying on his boots and the last breath of a monster still lingering in the air, Phainon smiled.

And hit send.

Chapter Summary

A peaceful day off turns into light property damage, a tragic digital death, and deeply questionable vigilante mentorship. Somehow, it still ends with a date.

Chapter Notes

YIPPYYY FINISHED THE CHAPTER!! Fair warning the next one is probs gonna come in like 2-3 days depending on how fast I finish my sacrificial lamb ff so be warned😍

The strawberry parfait was almost offensively good.

Delicate layers of custard, sponge, and cream dissolved on his tongue like a sigh—soft, sweet, and unreasonably pleasant. Mydei sat at the corner window of Bitter & Sweet, one elbow propped against the table, the late morning sun slanting over his shoulder like an afterthought. The café had only opened last week, all pastels and woodgrain and mismatched mugs with personality, and yet here he was, already a regular.

He lifted another spoonful with methodical precision. Strawberry slice. Crushed biscuit. Whipped cream. It didn’t even occur to him to smile, but there was something distinctly peaceful about the line of his shoulders.

Across from him, the other half of the café’s couples-themed set menu sat untouched. A glossy, obsidian-black square of bitter espresso jelly with lemon zest and crisped sage, currently ignored in favor of sweetness.

He took another bite.

Somewhere between the caramel drizzle and the chocolate flake, a memory surfaced—brief, but sharp. The scent of smoke, his own blood—no, not his.

Someone else’s, darker than it should’ve been. The weight of a cloak pressed into his hands. The image of a man he didn’t know, or maybe knew too well.

The Flame Reaver.

He blinked. The spoon tapped gently against the glass cup. Right. That night.

The cloak had been turned in already. Standard procedure, even if the gesture had felt stranger than usual this time. The Chrysos Heirs had reacted fast—almost immediately. One of their elite containment-response units had been deployed within the hour, cordoning off the area, sweeping it for residuals, taking over the aftermath like it was a military operation. Which, technically, it was.

Mydei didn’t argue. He was one of them, after all. A vigilante, yes. But also Godslayer—one of the Chrysos Heirs’ top operatives, even if he didn’t flaunt the title.

Perks of membership: full access, full authority, and—on rare occasions like this—full emergency support.

He exhaled slowly and leaned back, spoon resting between his fingers.

The parfait really was good.

The door chimed.

Phainon strolled in like he owned the place, which, thankfully, he did not. In the span of ten steps, he managed to compliment three strangers and offend five, all with the same radiant smile and a tone that could only be described as well-meaning menace. Someone muttered something about “actors,” another about “flirts,” but Phainon just winked, found Mydei, and made his way over with the casual confidence of a man who’d once given a TED talk on charisma and didn’t remember doing it.

They’d both happened to have the day off—a rarity, considering Mydei’s secret career as an immortal black-ops vigilante and Phainon’s full-time profession as a charming academic nuisance to society—so they’d agreed to spend it together. Mydei had picked the spot. Bitter & Sweet.

The café’s couples pairing deal had been heavily advertised, promising a taste experience themed around contrast: one dish cloyingly sweet, the other soul-crushingly bitter. They were only served as a pair. Something about love and balance. It was ridiculous. Naturally, Phainon had agreed immediately.

When the dishes arrived, Mydei had leaned over his second parfait again with the focus of a man prioritizing joy. Across from him, Phainon stared down at his portion that looked exactly like the one from the dessert case: Still a pitch-black cube of espresso jelly, laced with activated charcoal and set atop a bed of bitter melon crisps. It was garnished with black salt, a scorched lemon wedge, and a sprig of something green and vaguely medicinal. The entire thing sat on a literal slab of slate, like it was being presented as evidence in a culinary crime.

Mydei blinked. “…You paid money for that.”

“I paid money so you could have that,” Phainon replied, nodding toward the parfait. “You deserve the sweet one.”

There was a moment.

Mydei didn’t move. Didn’t even blink.

Then he almost choked—not on his parfait, but on the sheer boldness of the line.

He recovered with practiced ease, face smoothing out like it hadn’t twitched at all. “…Shut up and eat your regret.”

And like a man, he did.

Phainon scooped up a bite of the jet-black abomination in front of him, posture dignified, eyes calm, like a man about to be knighted—not violently betrayed by his own tastebuds.

He chewed.

The silence that followed was deafening. His expression didn’t shift so much as crack. One eye twitched. A shiver ran down his spine. Somewhere deep within him, a part of his soul packed its things and quietly moved out.

“Mmm,” he said finally, voice dead and eyes hollower than the inside of a corrupt hero’s apology video. “Delicious. So… complex.”

Mydei didn’t look at him. Just lifted another generous spoonful of parfait to his mouth, entirely unfazed. He didn’t say anything. Didn’t need to. The way he lingered behind the silver spoon, clearly hiding a smile, said it all.

He didn’t offer to trade either.

Phainon, lips still stained with the taste of activated charcoal, lemon bitterness, and ego death, reached for his water like a man who’d just crawled out of the ruins of a desert temple. He downed it like it owed him child support.

“I’m fine,” he rasped after a second, blinking. “It’s…an acquired taste.”

“A tragedy,” Mydei murmured, still not looking up. “Is what it is.”

Phainon fanned his tongue with the menu. “You know, I thought it’d be like those dark chocolate types that taste rich and expensive and maybe a little melancholy.”

“And instead?”

“It tastes like if betrayal were a sweet.”

Phainon was still recovering—chewing ice now—when Mydei sighed, setting down his parfait with practiced patience. “You’re impossible,” he muttered, then scooped a spoonful and held it out toward him.

Phainon blinked, brightening instantly. “Are you feeding me?”

“It’s either that or I let you keep eating whatever that was.”

“That’s romantic,” Phainon said, already leaning in.

“Hurry up before I change my mind.”

Phainon accepted the bite with a soft, exaggerated “Ahh,” like he was auditioning for a toothpaste commercial, then lit up with delight. “Oh my gods. That’s so good.”

“You chose the bitter one on purpose,” Mydei reminded him, flicking his spoon in accusation.

“For you,” Phainon said, wiping a nonexistent tear. Scratch that, after the jelly there might have actually been one. “A sacrifice in the name of love.”

“You’re not dying, you’re eating jelly.”

“Same thing.”

But then—there it was.

A smear of cream at the corner of Phainon’s mouth. Small. Harmless. Ridiculous.

Phainon didn’t notice. Kept talking. Kept smiling.

Mydei’s gaze lingered for just a second too long.

It was such a cliché. The kind you rolled your eyes at in books. Wipe it off. Lick it away. Some stupid excuse to be closer.

He wasn’t going to do any of that.

Obviously.

He just noticed it.

That was all.

Still, he couldn’t help imagining it.

Not the casual wipe—it was too tame.

He imagined leaning forward. Not to be sweet. To be thorough. Tongue sliding over the corner of Phainon’s mouth, then shifting—barely—to his lips.

He imagined kissing him slow. Tasting sugar and laughter and something warm.

Then deeper. Messier. Until Phainon forgot to be smug. Until he forgot his own name.

He imagined biting his lower lip, tugging it between his teeth until it was red and flushed and a little swollen.

He imagined dragging his nails down Phainon’s back, just to see if he’d shiver. If he’d swear. If he’d beg.

Mydei blinked.

Across from him, Phainon was licking the spoon clean, humming like a man who’d never had a dark thought in his life.

Mydei took a slow bite of parfait, watching him over the rim of his spoon.

He was fine.

Totally normal.

Not thinking anything weird at all.

Not at all.

Mydei sighed, already waving the server over with a resigned flick of his fingers. “One order of honey cakes,” he said. “For the idiot.”

Phainon gasped like he’d been struck, pressing a hand to his chest. “You love me~” he sang, shameless and smug and absolutely not helping his case.

Mydei didn’t look at him. Didn’t blink. Didn’t move.

“You’re ignoring me. That means it’s true,” Phainon added, cheerfully unbothered by the silence.

The honey cakes arrived quickly—still warm, soft, and drizzled in a light syrup that glistened under the café lighting. Phainon, undeterred by pride or presentation, popped a piece into his mouth and visibly melted.

“Oh,” he breathed reverently, eyes fluttering shut. “Homely. Humble. Healing.”

Mydei side-eyed him. “You’re insufferable.”

“Not according to these honey cakes,” Phainon said, already forking up another bite. He looked so happy, so genuinely pleased with something so simple, it caught Mydei off guard.

And for a moment, Mydei just… watched him. The way his shoulders relaxed. The way his lips curved, unconsciously, around the next bite. The way the light caught in the soft strands of his hair and glinted off his lashes. He didn’t say anything, didn’t do anything. Just leaned on one arm, eyes fixed on the boy across the table as an inexplicable warmth bloomed behind his ribs.

He didn’t smile much. But one tried to form anyway—small, tentative, honest.

And then he heard it. The sharp, unmistakable sound of a camera shutter.

His gaze snapped up.

Phainon was holding his phone, angled just so, the smuggest look known to man plastered on his face.

Click. Another one.

“You took a picture,” Mydei said, deadpan.

“I took several,” Phainon said proudly. “And in some of them, you look like you’re in love with me.”

“Delete that.”

“Can’t. It’s art.”

Mydei reached for his drink instead of lunging across the table. Barely.

Then he caught a glimpse of Phainon’s phone screen as the other checked the time.

“My face is your lock screen.”

Phainon didn’t even flinch. “You look radiant in natural lighting.”

Mydei stood up.

Phainon immediately slapped his card down on the table and waved over the server. “One sakura blossom shortcake, please!”

The server blinked. “To pair with—?”

“Strawberry parfait,” Phainon said, gesturing at Mydei. “It’s for my emotionally overachieving partner.”

Moments later, a delicate slice of cake arrived—layers of fluffy vanilla sponge alternating with whipped cream and flecks of preserved sakura, topped with light pink glaze and a single candied blossom resting delicately on top. The scent was floral and airy, the kind of thing that paired perfectly with the tartness of strawberry.

Mydei sat down. He took one bite.

Appeased.

Phainon exhaled like he’d just negotiated peace.

“See,” he said, smug again. “Sweets fix everything. Including your wounded pride.”

Mydei didn’t answer. He just reached for the cake again and muttered, “I’m wiping your lock screen in your sleep.”

“Romantic and threatening,” Phainon said with a grin. “I knew you were the one.”

They finished their desserts at a leisurely pace, chatting between bites like there wasn’t a single looming catastrophe waiting in the wings. Phainon, now spiritually healed by sugar and the fact that he wasn’t getting stabbed for the lock screen incident, leaned back in his chair like a man who had conquered the world with charm and cake.

“So,” he said, licking a smudge of cream from his thumb, “how’s your day been?”

Mydei stirred what was left of his parfait. “Catalogued rare manuscripts. Helped a student who somehow confused ancient romance poetry with a cursed summoning scroll.”

Phainon blinked. “Okay, but you say that like it’s normal. What kind of library is this?”

“A public one,” Mydei deadpanned. “With extremely aggressive funding cuts.”

“Right. Of course. That explains the summoning scrolls. I’m assuming next week you’ll be fighting off eldritch horrors in the basement.”

“I already rescheduled that for Monday.”

Phainon laughed, tipping his head as he grinned at him. “Gods, I like you.”

“That’s sad,” Mydei said, scooping the last bite of his parfait into his mouth. “You’re already in too deep.”

Phainon retorted with, “I’d sink gladly.”

The bill came and was paid without much fanfare—Phainon insisted on treating Mydei—before they stepped outside together, sunlight softening into gold around them. The late afternoon breeze ruffled Phainon’s hair, and Mydei reached up to fix it without thinking.

Phainon blinked, caught off guard, but didn’t move. He only smiled.

They walked hand in hand, no destination in mind, letting the city buzz around them. Their fingers brushed and curled together naturally, like they’d done it a thousand times. Phainon launched into a story about a student who had tried to win a argument by quoting a novel that didn’t exist, and Mydei listened, amused, as if this weren’t the most peaceful he’d felt all week.

“Did you ever get that issue sorted with your class assistant?” Mydei asked after a lull.

“No, but I’m choosing to pretend I did. I’ve decided if I don’t look at the problem, it no longer exists. It’s called professor’s optimism.”

“Sounds like willful ignorance.”

“See? That’s why we work. You’re the voice of reason. I’m the voice of—” Phainon paused as they passed a pigeon wearing a leaf on its head. “—of avant-garde street fashion analysis. Look at that icon.”

Mydei shook his head, the barest trace of a smile curling his lips. He didn’t let go of Phainon’s hand.

Just the two of them, walking nowhere fast, one day off in a life of secrets and chaos.

And for now, that was all he focused on.

Phainon, in a move as inevitable as the sun rising dramatically behind him, decided they were going clothes shopping.

Mydei had barely blinked before he was being towed down the boutique-lined street, hand firmly in Phainon’s as if he’d lost the ability to steer himself. “You know,” Mydei said as they stepped into a store lined with honey-colored wood and soft ambient lighting, “I thought we were walking off dessert.”

“We are,” Phainon said cheerfully, already scanning racks like a hawk spotting prey. “You just happen to look edible in sweaters.”

The employee at the entrance looked up from her phone and paused. The new arrivals were, by all accounts, well-dressed already, but the taller one— the one with the wind-tousled hair and suspiciously good posture—was already holding three jackets and a button-up before she could even say welcome.

“You’re trying all of these,” Phainon said, piling items into Mydei’s arms with alarming efficiency. “No arguments.”

“I didn’t even say anything.”

“Your silence sounded judgmental.”

“I was breathing.”

“Exactly.”

Mydei sighed, shifting the growing stack in his arms. The first fitting room they passed was already being unlocked for him, the attendant giving a vaguely impressed nod as if she, too, understood that love sometimes looked like a personal stylist with no sense of financial restraint.

Every time Mydei stepped out, Phainon straightened in his seat, legs crossed, chin in his hand like he was watching the climax of a very high-stakes romance drama.

“This is stupid,” Mydei said after the fourth outfit, turning in the mirror. “It’s just a plain knit sweater.”

“Exactly,” Phainon said dreamily. “It’s criminal how good you look in beige. Beige!”

The fifth outfit earned a low whistle. The sixth prompted a hushed, “Are you trying to end me?”

By the seventh, the employee was no longer pretending to organize anything. She stood nearby, arms folded, quietly delighted.

The eighth outfit—tailored slacks and a dark, high-necked top that hugged just the right places—brought a rare silence from Phainon.

“…That one,” he finally said. “We’re buying that one twice.”

Mydei blinked. “Twice?”

“In case you spill something on it. Like your own blood. Or honey.”

“You think I’m going to bleed on expensive clothing?”

“I think I’d fight someone if they made you.”

The clothes piled up at the counter like offerings to a very well-dressed deity. The total racked up with quiet brutality. The employee looked mildly stunned. Mydei looked not even mildly surprised.

“You’re not putting any of it back?” he asked as they stepped away from the register, bags in hand.

Phainon didn’t hesitate. “You were hot in all of it. I have no regrets.”

“…You bought a scarf just to ‘frame my neck.’”

“And I was right.”

Mydei paused. Adjusted the very scarf in question. “Next time I’m picking the place.”

He didn’t protest. Didn’t insist they return a few things. Because if Phainon wanted to act like a man freshly whacked in the face by Cupid’s bat, Mydei wasn’t going to stop him.

He just hoped the bat had installment payments.

The moment they stepped outside, a quiet thought floated through Mydei’s otherwise fond haze:

How the hell does a professor afford this?

He glanced down at the bag in his hand. The receipt poked out, curled and long, like an ominous prophecy. He tugged it free.

Then stared.

Then stared harder.

The number on it made his soul flatline for a second. There were entire black-market relics that cost less than this total. He knew Phainon’s university paid decently—very decently—but this wasn’t decent. This was criminal financial decisions wrapped in tissue paper.

“…Are you going into debt over me?” he muttered with a hint of worry, eyes still fixed in disbelief.

Before the question could blossom into an actual confrontation, Phainon plucked the bag from his hand with a flourish and a grin that could derail logic. “Don’t worry about it,” he said breezily. “I’m not spending. I’m investing.”

“In what?”

Phainon turned and walked backwards a few paces, holding the bag like it was a bouquet. “My happiness,” he said sweetly.

Mydei squinted.

The employee waved them off from the storefront window, chin resting in her hand, giving Mydei a deeply understanding look. The kind of look that said, Could be your sugar daddy. Could be your simp. Either way? You’re eating, king.

Mydei sighed and looked away, scarf still warm around his neck, bags still heavy in his hand, and heart doing something annoying and fluttery in his chest.

He’d stop him next time.

Probably.

Maybe.

No, he wouldn’t.

Evening settled in slow and golden, blanketing the city in the kind of light that made even cracked sidewalks and crumbling rooftops look poetic. The day had mellowed into that soft in-between where time felt like it could stretch out forever, and the two of them walked without any real destination —just the lazy rhythm of their steps and the soft shuffle of shopping bags swaying at their sides.

Phainon had insisted on carrying most of them, but Mydei had managed to reclaim at least one bag under the guise of fairness, which Phainon protested against and then immediately forgot about.

They passed a bakery giving out samples, a couple tangled in matching jackets taking pictures by a mosaic wall, someone’s familiar fluttering overhead with a leash trailing behind it. Phainon kept glancing at them. Not the couple, not the samples—just the familiars, the pets, the companions. A dog in a bowtie trotted past with a bell on its collar and Phainon actually turned his head to watch it go.

Mydei noticed. Of course he noticed.

He let it sit for a while. Waited until they turned a corner onto a quieter street with soft lamps and window displays before saying, “Alright. Out with it.”

Phainon blinked. “What?”

“You’ve been watching every pet that’s walked by for the past ten minutes. I’m not judging. Just wondering if there’s a reason or if you’ve developed a sudden interest in domesticated creatures.”

Phainon laughed, rubbing at the back of his neck with the hand not holding six bags and a receipt that could have bought a small island. “It’s stupid.”

“Everything you say is stupid. Tell me anyway.”

He sighed, slow and a little embarrassed. “I lost my Tamagotchi.”

Mydei blinked. That was… not what he expected.

Phainon looked weirdly solemn. “I think I left it at your place last time I stayed over. I forgot about it until yesterday, and by then, I figured it was probably dead. And I know it’s just a dumb virtual pet, but I don’t know. I got attached to it.”

There was a beat. The air smelled like baked sugar and concrete.

Mydei stopped walking. He shifted the bag in his hand and reached into the inner pocket of his coat—then pulled something out and held it up between two fingers.

A Tamagotchi. Alive and well.

The screen lit up with a cheerful jingle, the pixelated creature bouncing in joy, little sparkles glittering around it. Clean. Fed. Very much not dead.

Phainon stared. “You’re joking.”

“Found it after you left,” Mydei said. “Been keeping it alive since.”

Phainon took it like it was a holy relic. Like he’d just been handed a second chance at life. He cradled it with both hands, bags rustling at his sides, and stared at the screen with a reverence that made Mydei feel like he was the weird one for not bowing.

Then, with all the seriousness in the world:

“I’m going to marry you.”

Mydei sighed. “Slow down.”

He didn’t look at Phainon. Just kept walking.

Didn’t stop the faint flush on his ears, though.

Internally? Yeah. Same thought.

They rounded a narrow alley—not because it was a shortcut or even remotely scenic, but because Phainon had seen a street cat with a heart-shaped marking on its back and absolutely had to follow it for photographic evidence. Mydei, who’d been dragged along mid-sentence and was now holding three shopping bags in one hand and a fourth looped around his wrist, said nothing.

He simply watched the cat disappear under a dumpster and then turned a slow look toward his companion.

Phainon, crouched like a hopeful cryptid with his phone out, was already sighing in disappointment. “It was perfect. Like a fuzzy little love confession.”

“I’ll be confessing something in a minute if you don’t keep walking.”

“Is it that you adore me?”

“No,” Mydei said, adjusting the scarf Phainon bought him out of spite and affection. “It’s that if I throw one of these bags at your head, it’s going to

hurt.”

Phainon laughed, stood, and bumped their shoulders together lightly. “You’re fun when you’re violent.”

They continued down the alley, shopping bags rustling softly between them. The sky had shifted from amber to rose, that soft twilight stretch where everything looked a little romantic, a little too quiet, the sort of lull that begged for gentle conversation and—

From the side, someone cleared their throat.

They hadn’t even made it halfway through the alley when four figures slipped out from the shadows with all the subtlety of a group cosplay gone rogue. One had a baseball bat. Another had what looked like a repurposed bike chain. All wore matching expressions of low-level menace and budget intimidation.

Mydei blinked. Oh good. The Discount Delinquents have arrived.

The one in front stepped forward, cocky. “Wallets. Bags. Phones. Now.”

Phainon took one glance, tilted his head, and murmured, “Really? You’re mugging us? In this economy?”

The guy with the bat scowled. “Try us.”

Mydei casually lowered one bag to the ground. It clinked. Phainon caught the sound and, without looking back, lifted his arm across Mydei’s chest— barely there, just a casual sweep of motion. A line drawn with his body: Stay behind me.

His smile didn’t drop, but it changed—less sparkle, more steel.

“Listen,” he said, tone still gentle. “You really don’t want to do this. There are heroes on patrol. City’s on edge after the last attack. You get caught with a weapon and attempted robbery? That’s not just gonna be a fine.”

“Then hand it over and we won’t get caught.”

Phainon shifted slightly. The bags on his arm swayed.

“I just spent a lot of money on tailored sweaters and an offensively expensive candle shaped like a duck,” he said, voice smooth but cool now, like honey drizzled over a knife’s edge. “And I’m going to be honest—I’m not in the mood to be inconvenienced.”

He smiled wider. It didn’t reach his eyes.

The air changed.

Mydei, who hadn’t moved, simply lifted his gaze and stared at the closest mugger like he was already cataloging how hard he’d hit the wall when thrown. He said nothing. Didn’t need to.

For the first time, the thugs hesitated.

Phainon took one small step forward, arm extended in the least-threatening gesture known to man—palms up, voice even, the faint beep of the Tamagotchi still chirping faintly in his hand.

“Look, we don’t want trouble. You can take the bags,” he said, all airy calm and professor-level diplomacy. “Just let us leave with our bones and dignity intact. And this.” He lifted the tiny toy slightly. “He has a job interview tomorrow.”

Mydei exhaled, barely stifling a huff. Even now?

One of the muggers—a guy who looked like he got kicked out of villain school for being too cliché—snorted. “What, this your emotional support keychain?”

He stepped forward.

Then, without hesitation or ceremony, smacked Phainon’s hand aside.

The Tamagotchi flew from his grip.

It hit the pavement with a crack so loud it felt personal. A glitchy buzz stuttered from the cracked screen before it sputtered out entirely, dark and dead.

Everything kept moving for a second—shouts, movement, threats. The muggers didn’t even register what they’d done. Just kept circling like budget hyenas.

But Mydei did.

And Phainon—Phainon just stopped.

His hand hovered midair, fingers still slightly curled as if the toy were still there. He stared at the shattered remains on the ground with a look of quiet devastation. His mouth opened a fraction, but no sound came out. His brows knit, just slightly, like the grief was settling before it even had a name.

The streetlight above flickered once.

Mydei turned toward him fully, watching with new focus.

“…Are you good?” he asked low, cautious.

Phainon gave a faint, brittle smile. “Totally.” His voice cracked slightly. “I mean, I only raised him for a week. Taught him how to eat. How to bathe. Taught him love.”

Mydei blinked. The thugs yelled louder. One of them laughed.

Phainon didn’t.

He crouched down slowly, collecting the broken Tamagotchi with deliberate care—as if he were picking up a fallen comrade on the battlefield. He turned it over once in his palm. The screen was fried. There was a tiny crack running through the casing.

He took a slow, deep breath. When he stood, he was composed. Polished, even. But something underneath had iced over. His eyes weren’t soft

anymore.

He slipped the broken toy gently into his pocket.

“Mydei,” he said calmly. “If I die tonight, avenge me.”

Mydei raised an eyebrow. “You’re not dying.”

“True,” Phainon murmured, lifting his gaze toward the circling muggers. “They are.”

And this time, the streetlight didn’t flicker.

It just went out.

Mydei didn’t rush.

He reached out, tugged Phainon gently back by the front of his shirt—and, with the calmest casualness in the world, pressed a kiss to his cheek.

It was a subtle thing. Quick. Dismissive, almost.

But Phainon went still like someone had cast a spell. Bags still looped around one wrist. Broken Tamagotchi cupped delicately in both hands like a drowned mouse. His mouth parted. His lashes fluttered. He looked like he’d just witnessed a marriage proposal, a live execution, and a one-man opera all in one breath.

Mydei stepped forward.

Behind him, Phainon remained frozen. Perfectly still. Gorgeously lit by the dying streetlamp. The light caught in his curls, he noted. One of the thugs actually glanced at him mid-fight like who is that—before promptly getting kicked in the ribs so hard he folded like paper.

The beatdown wasn’t fair.

Mydei didn’t let it be.

He moved like he’d decided gravity was optional. Every motion compact, controlled, efficient. One attacker rushed—Mydei ducked under his swing and drove a heel into the back of his knee. The man dropped with a strangled yell and didn’t get back up. Another came from the side; Mydei turned, caught his shoulder, and flipped him clean over like he was weightless. The sound of bones hitting concrete echoed sharp and final.

Nobody landed a hit on him.

Someone tried to grab his scarf. He didn’t even glance over—just seized the offending wrist, twisted until something snapped, and used the momentum to throw the guy into a dumpster.

Even the dumpster looked surprised.

Phainon remained off to the side, hands still clasped around the Tamagotchi remains like a grieving widow. His expression flickered between awe and how dare this be hot. A piece of glass crunched under his boot as he adjusted his stance—only to immediately stop, glancing down in vague horror as if worried about scuffing his shoe.

By the time the last thug scrambled away, breath hitching, Mydei didn’t even break stride. He rolled one shoulder back, adjusted his scarf again, and let out a quiet exhale like he’d just finished a workout, not a war.

He turned back toward Phainon.

Still there. Still cradling that ruined Tamagotchi like it needed last rites. Still pretty.

Mydei gave him a look. Phainon blinked.

“…You kissed me,” he said softly, like the thought had just now made it to the front of the line in his brain.

“I also flattened a small gang.”

“Yeah,” Phainon breathed. “You really did. I think I ascended for a moment.”

Mydei stepped forward, took the shattered plastic from his hands, and tucked it into his coat pocket alongside his keys.

“You looked like you needed saving.”

Phainon blinked again. “From what, emotional stability?”

Mydei handed him one of the shopping bags.

Mydei responded while repressing another sigh, “From yourself.”

They didn’t speak at first.

The alley was quieter now—save for the occasional groan, the steady drip from a broken pipe, and the sound of Phainon gently shifting one of the shopping bags back up his wrist, like he hadn’t just witnessed the love of his life send five men to the ER without breaking a sweat.

He still looked a little stunned.

Still clutching the strap of his coat. Still standing like he was halfway between proposing and fainting.

Finally, after a long moment, he said, softly:

“I want to say thank you. But I also want to dump you a little.”

Mydei, adjusting his sleeves, didn’t look over. “Why?”

“You let my Tamagotchi die.”

“You lost your Tamagotchi.”

“It was an accident.”

“I kept it alive for a week.”

“A week and a half,” Phainon corrected, which only made his case worse. “We were bonding. I named him after you.”

That got Mydei to look at him. Slowly.

Phainon pressed on like a man who had never once felt shame. “He had your discipline. Your emotional distance. Your raw, feral edge when hungry.”

Mydei blinked.

“You’re making this worse for yourself,” he said.

“I’m mourning,” Phainon insisted, straightening. “Don’t silence my grief.”

There was a brief beat of silence as Mydei glanced over the alley one more time. Unconscious bodies. Broken glass. A smear of blood halfway up a wall like it got lost trying to escape.

Phainon, in the center of it all, dressed like a vintage romantic drama and still somehow managing to look tragic instead of ridiculous.

Mydei sighed.

“I’ll buy you another one,” he said flatly.

Phainon blinked. “…Really?”

“No. I’m lying to keep you from crying.”

“Too late,” Phainon whispered. Then looked down at the bags in his arms. “But thank you for your service. And for letting me be uselessly decorative.”

“You do it very well.”

“Thank you,” he said again, quieter this time. “For real.”

Mydei didn’t answer, but his expression softened.

Just slightly.

But then a sharp metallic clang cut through the alley like punctuation.

One of the dazed muggers—brave, or perhaps just stupid—had managed to crawl upright. He didn’t get far.

A glowing baseball bat came down on him with a satisfying WHAM, and the man hit the ground like a sack of wet cement.

Standing over him was a figure in a star-dusted varsity jacket, glowing softly at the seams. The end of his bat pulsed faintly with pale light, as though it had been dipped in the cosmos. A matching cap shadowed his face, tilted at just the right heroic angle.

“Fear not,” he declared dramatically, flipping the brim of his cap up with one finger. “Justice has arrived.”

Mydei stared.

Phainon blinked once. Then, with the poise of a long-suffering mentor, clasped his hands behind his back and intoned, “Galactic Baseballer. A pleasure.”

The hero’s grin widened under the shadows of his cap.

“You’ve got a lot of nerve picking this alley,” he said to no one in particular, giving one of the bodies a mild nudge with the toe of his sneaker. “This is my territory.”

“I thought your territory was the arts building,” Mydei muttered.

“Quiet,” Caelus whispered, stage-whisper serious.

“My office is there,” Mydei continued blandly. “This is just off campus. You’re not even patrolling your own map.”

Phainon turned slightly, face bright with indulgence. “Let the hero work, Mydei. It’s important to support youth initiatives.”

“Do youth initiatives usually come with glowing weapons and probable head trauma?”

“Only the good ones.”

The Galactic Baseballer, completely unfazed, adjusted his grip and nudged another groaning thug with the bat.

THWACK.

No more groaning.

“You ever heard of choosing better targets?” Caelus called, though it was unclear if he was addressing the unconscious or the air. “No? Guess I’ll just make the lesson stick.”

He punctuated this by hauling one of the larger thugs over his shoulder like a laundry sack. His bat slung onto his back with a casual magnetic click.

Mydei narrowed his eyes. “You still haven’t returned your books.”

Caelus whipped around. “Why is everyone bringing that up tonight?”

“They’re mythological encyclopedias,” Mydei said. “In Latin. You do not read Latin.”

“It’s for aesthetic immersion!”

Phainon coughed gently. “He cited three Instagram infographics, two Tumblr posts, and a tweet thread last essay.”

“They were annotated,” Caelus huffed, grabbing the second goon and starting to drag him by the collar. “And accurate. I fact-checked.”

“With what?”

“…More tweets.”

Mydei didn’t even blink. “Return the books.”

“You’re ruining my mystique.”

“I don’t believe you have mystique.”

The hero groaned, defeated, but didn’t stop dragging bodies out of the alley like it was just another Wednesday. The soft glow of his bat, swinging gently from its strap, left streaks of pale blue across the ground.

As he reached the mouth of the alley, he turned back with a grin. “Well,” he called, “guess this night’s wrapped up! Tell Professor Phainon I said hi!”

Phainon raised a hand in correction. “Caelus, I am Professor Phainon. You missed our last debate tournament,” he said mildly. “Very irresponsible behavior for a hero.”

“I was fighting crime.”

“And losing participation points.”

Caelus blinked. “Okay, you know what? Whatever, I have a life. Later.” Just as he was about to leave, Caelus turned around and yelled, “Tell Stelle I’m cooler than she is!”

Phainon waved with two fingers. “Will do.”

And just like that, the Galactic Baseballer vanished into the dark—bat on his back, unconscious criminals in tow, whistling something suspiciously heroic. The glow from his jacket flickered like a misplaced constellation before he disappeared around the corner.

There was a long beat of silence.

Then Phainon turned, voice perfectly neutral. “He once cried when I played the opposing side during a mock debate.”

“Now he’s possibly concussing strangers.”

Phainon hummed, his voice somewhat fond. “Growth.”

Mydei rubbed his temple. “Your influence is catastrophic.”

“Thank you.”

And with that, they returned to their stroll—Phainon quietly radiant, Mydei quietly resigned, and justice, very dubiously, served behind them.

Distant city sounds filtered back in—the low hum of traffic, a siren somewhere far off—but here, beneath the pale reach of the streetlamps, it felt oddly hushed. Private.

Phainon adjusted the shopping bags in his hands. Mydei’s coat, folded neatly over one arm, had somehow survived the whole incident unscathed. Of course it had. Phainon would have committed murder over a bloodstain.

They walked a few steps more. Then Phainon stopped.

Mydei turned—just as Phainon stepped in, close and without warning, and kissed him on the cheek.

It was a soft thing. Simple. Just the faintest brush of lips beneath the eye, a hand lightly grazing Mydei’s sleeve for balance. Chaste, in theory.

But the angle. The closeness.

Deadly.

“My hero,” Phainon murmured, with all the flair of someone bestowing knighthood. “I’m positively swooning.”

Mydei exhaled, exasperated. “You’re so dramatic.”

Phainon leaned in further, just enough to brush his mouth near Mydei’s ear, breath warm against the skin.

“Does my hero,” he murmured, “want to claim his reward?”

Mydei didn’t move. Not right away.

Phainon tilted his head, just enough to clarify—soft, smug, and deeply unfair:

“A bath. A massage. Me.”

Mydei’s ears turned red. Entirely red. The tips looked like they might combust on contact.

“I just committed six misdemeanors,” he muttered.

“And I’m offering reparations,” Phainon said brightly. “Very hands-on ones.”

Mydei groaned. “You’re unbelievable.”

“And yet,” Phainon said, stepping closer, “you haven’t walked away.”

Mydei opened his mouth, but whatever retort he had dissolved as Phainon’s smile curved into something warmer. Not just teasing. Not just smug.

Affectionate.

And just a little bit daring.

“…The bath sounds fine,” Mydei muttered, eventually.

“Oh?” Phainon stepped beside him. “Not the massage?”

A beat.

Then, quieter: “Maybe the massage.”

Phainon grinned. “And me?”

Mydei let out the slowest sigh in recorded history. Took the shopping bags from his hand like it was a peace offering. Then turned, muttering, “Come on.”

“Where are we going?” Phainon asked, delighted, matching his pace.

“My place.”

Phainon blinked. “Is that where the bath is?”

No answer.

“Massage?”

Silence.

“…Me?”

Still no answer.

But Mydei’s face was pink. And he didn’t look back. Just kept walking.

Phainon followed, smug and satisfied.

The city around them buzzed quietly, neon and soft shadows folding back into place. Somewhere behind them, the alley faded into memory. The Tamagotchi had long since passed into digital oblivion. The jacket still looked perfect. The criminals were concussed. Galactic Baseballer had vanished into the night, whistling off-key.

And Phainon—still smiling, still unfair—had absolutely no intention of letting his hero sleep alone tonight.
