chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Phainon suffers. From sickness, from his boyfriend’s betrayal (he can cook?!), and from the sheer humiliation of forgetting their fancy date night. But somehow, between dodging Mydei’s concern, getting aggressively nursed back to health, and nearly exposing his secret life, he still ends up exactly where he wants to be—wrapped up in Mydei’s arms. Not a bad way to end the night.

Chapter Notes

I’m so consistent with updates🥲🥲

Phainon followed at a leisurely pace, each step echoing through the empty corridors like a promise. A quiet, patient promise.

Mydei was running.

Not in that graceful, confident way he always carried himself, but something messier. Desperate. His breaths were sharp and uneven, his shoulders tight with barely restrained panic. Every few steps, he glanced back, as if checking that Phainon was still behind him—as if he had any doubts.

Oh, he was watching. He hadn’t looked away for a second.

It was intoxicating, really, the way Mydei’s pulse must be hammering against his skin, the way his muscles tensed like a trapped animal’s. Did he realize how much he gave away? How every stagger, every quickened breath, only made him more irresistible?

Phainon could hear it—the fear. Feel it, even from here, curling in the air like a fine perfume. He let it linger, drinking it in, savoring the sight of Mydei’s back as he fled.

And still, he did not run.

There was no need.

Mydei was fast, but fear made fools of even the strongest men. His steps were rushed, reckless, and he made a fatal mistake—turning too sharply at the end of the corridor, misjudging the space. His back collided with the cold wall, and for a split second, his entire body stilled.

It was all Phainon needed.

He closed the distance between them in an instant, pressing forward, crowding into Mydei’s space as his hands found purchase against the wall beside his head. Mydei sucked in a breath, but there was nowhere to go now, no more space to flee. His throat bobbed as he swallowed, lips parting just slightly, eyes blown wide with something raw—something teetering between fear and anticipation.

Phainon leaned in slowly, deliberately, letting his breath fan against Mydei’s cheek before dipping his head lower, lips ghosting just above his racing pulse. So fragile, he thought. If he wanted, he could press just a little closer, let his teeth graze that sensitive skin—feel the warmth, the quickening beat of his heart beneath his lips.

“Mydei,” he murmured, voice a low rasp, silk spun over steel. “Why do you run?”

His answer was a sharp inhale, the tightening of his fingers against the wall as if searching for something to hold onto. He didn’t speak, didn’t move, only watched him with those deep, piercing eyes, as if torn between defiance and surrender.

It was beautiful.

Phainon smiled against his throat, lips barely brushing his skin. His fingers twitched against the cold stone beside Mydei’s head, aching with something wicked and possessive.

Then, ever so slowly, he tilted his head—his lips parting, teeth just barely grazing the soft skin of Mydei’s neck.

And Mydei shuddered.

Phainon let his teeth skim Mydei’s throat, savoring the way he trembled beneath him. His lips parted—this was it. He could feel Mydei’s pulse thudding wildly, his entire body taut with anticipation, with fear—

“AND—CUT!”

Phainon immediately abandoned all pretense of menace, his lips pulling into a delighted grin as he all but smashed his face against Mydei’s neck. He nuzzled into his skin with all the enthusiasm of an overgrown golden retriever, practically vibrating with affection.

“Mydeiii,” he whined climatically, refusing to budge an inch despite the exasperated groan from the man currently pinned beneath him. “I like it here. So warm. So comfy.”

“Get. Off,” Mydei gritted out, shoving at his shoulders with all the strength of someone who deeply, deeply regretting every life choice that led to this moment.

“Noooo,” Phainon hummed, rubbing his cheek against Mydei’s with such force it was a miracle neither of them got friction burns. “You smell nice. Like expensive soap and sweets.”

“That was perfect!” March 7th all but sang, practically skipping towards them with her camera in hand, beaming like she just won an Oscar. “I’m definitely getting an A for this.”

“Glad one of us is happy,” Mydei muttered, still trying and failing to pry Phainon off of him.

Phainon, meanwhile, was far too busy reminiscing about how exactly he got himself into this situation.

It all started when March 7th—student, menace, and self-proclaimed creative genius—had been given a film project for her university course. Something about narrative storytelling in visual media. Phainon didn’t really know the details. He had stopped listening after she said the words film project because the sheer look of desperation on her face told him exactly where this was going.

She had decided on a cliché vampire romance (of course she did), but there was one tiny problem—all of her friends were mysteriously unavailable.

Dan Heng, her ever-so-patient friend, had like ten different majors to juggle. Stelle, who could probably pull off being a vampire if she tried, had apparently chosen cleaning her toilet over acting. Which, honestly, Phainon kind of respected.

So, naturally, March 7th had gotten desperate.

And in that desperation, she had done something truly unhinged—

She had gone to an entirely different department and asked him, Phainon, a debate professor, to star in her little vampire movie.

He should have said no.

He tried to say no.

But then she hit him with the puppy-dog eyes, and his poor, bleeding heart caved faster than Mydei when confronted with a serious conversation about feelings.

Speaking of Mydei.

Getting him on board had been… a process.

Phainon had spent hours convincing him. Hours of bargaining, cajoling, and even resorting to the dirtiest trick in the book—pouting. And, in the

end, Mydei had relented. Probably out of sheer exhaustion.

And now here they were.

“Mydei, my love, my eternal muse,” Phainon drawled lovingly, finally pulling back just enough to look at him. “You were incredible. So convincing. I almost believed you were actually terrified of me.”

“I was terrified of you,” Mydei deadpanned.

Phainon beamed. “Acting! Amazing! My talented boy.”

“I will throw you into the sun.”

Phainon only snuggled closer.

March 7th, completely ignoring their nonsense, cheerfully checked the footage on her camera. “Yup! This is gold. Profess—uh, Phainon, you’re gonna be the best hot vampire ever.”

Phainon preened. “You flatter me.”

Mydei looked into the camera like he was in The Office.

Phainon was still grinning like a fool when he leaned in, his breath warm against Mydei’s ear. Mydei barely had time to react before—

Sharp teeth nipped at the tip of his ear.

Mydei shoved him. Hard.

Phainon went flying back with a delighted laugh, dodging a half-hearted attempt from Mydei to punch him square in the jaw. “Aww, you’re blushing~”

“I am not blushing.”

“Then why are your ears red?”

“They’re always red!”

“Uh-huh. Sure, honey.”

March 7th giggled as she checked the footage. “You two have way too much chemistry for this.”

Phainon wiggled his brows. “It’s called dedication to the craft.”

“It’s called being insufferable,” Mydei muttered, adjusting his now thoroughly wrinkled clothes.

Phainon ignored him, stretching his arms dramatically before flashing them both a dazzling smile. “Welp, that was fun! I’ll take my break now—be right back~”

And just like that, Phainon strutted off with all the confidence of someone who had never once in his life been bested. The laughter still lingered in his throat as he waved over his shoulder, utterly unbothered by Mydei’s very real threat of violence.

But the second he turned the corner, out of sight—

His soul left his body.

Gone was the smug grin. His posture collapsed. His swagger became a stiff shuffle. His face blanked out, eyes dead, like a puppet that had just had its strings severed.

He barely made it to the break room. The second he pushed the door open, he practically dragged himself inside, every step echoing the quiet agony of his existence.

A few students, clearly deep in conversation, turned to look at him.

Their expressions immediately shifted from casual disinterest to mild horror.

Phainon ignored them. His legs barely worked. His body screamed with each movement, the dull ache in his right side pulsing with every step. The bruise stretched over his waist like some grotesque inkblot, a brutal reminder that—

Oh yeah. He fell off a skyscraper last night.

Well, technically, he’d been caught mid-fall by something before he could go full street pancake, but that something had barely slowed him down before dropping him straight onto the pavement anyway.

The landing? Awful.

Right side first, bones rattling, nerves screaming, dignity obliterated. He had just laid there for a minute afterward, staring at the night sky, wondering if he should just start paying rent to the asphalt since he seemed to end up there so often.

And now? The bruising looked like he had angered a god and been smited accordingly. It wasn’t as bad as it looked, but holy shit did it hurt.

To top it off, because the universe apparently hated him on a personal level, he also woke up this morning with a fever.

Phainon grabbed a coffee cup with the hands of a man holding on for dear life.

The students at the nearby table watched in quiet horror as he filled it to the brim with boiling hot, pitch-black coffee—and then, without even waiting for it to cool, downed the entire thing in one go.

No reaction.

Not even a blink.

A freshman gasped audibly. Someone else scooted their chair away.

Phainon exhaled sharply, staring at the empty cup in his hand like it had personally failed him.

He debated getting another one but decided against it—not because it was a bad idea, but because it wasn’t bad enough.

Instead, he shuffled toward a chair and all but collapsed into it, groaning as if he was on his deathbed. His head hit the table with a dull thud.

A long, suffering sigh escaped him.

One of the students hesitantly leaned toward their friend. “Is… is he okay?”

“I don’t think so,” their friend whispered.

Phainon tuned them out. He just wanted to sit here and marinate in his own suffering.

With the last remaining ounce of his strength, he lifted his head just enough to glare at his empty coffee cup. His voice came out a hoarse, miserable mutter:

“Perfect day.”

And then, once again, he lay slumped over the table like a corpse abandoned in the middle of a battlefield.

For a brief, fleeting moment, he actually considered just giving up. Just lying here forever, letting the universe claim his body and soul.

This is fine, he thought, staring into the table like it could open a portal to another dimension. This is where I die. At least the pain will end.

But no. His suffering was far from over.

With the most painful moan known to man, he forced himself to move, stretching his arms up—

—and immediately regretted it.

Agony. Terror. A betrayal deeper than any greek tragedy.

It felt like someone had taken a flaming sledgehammer and slammed it directly into his right side. His ribs screamed. His muscles sang the song of their people—and their people were all dead.

For a brief moment, his brain was forcibly ejected from his body. He saw the other side. It was cold. Unforgiving.

One of the students at the next table over stopped mid-sip of their coffee, eyes wide as they watched Phainon freeze, tremble, and then very, very carefully lower himself back down with all the grace of a dying animal.

He clutched his side. Inhaled. Exhaled.

“This is actual bullshit,” he muttered.

There was a beat of silence.

Then—

Divine Enlightenment.

Like the second coming of the Buddha himself, Phainon rose.

Slowly, dramatically, his body straightened. The tension melted from his shoulders. His breathing evened out, his expression softened—no, serenely transformed—into an easy, relaxed smile.

His posture, once hunched in despair, became that of a man with infinite wisdom and composure.

His aura radiated nothing short of inner peace.

And that peace?

Was a lie.

The students gawked.

The girl who had watched him suffer so miserably just seconds before slammed her cup onto the table, looking personally offended at the mockery of human existence unfolding before her.

Another, barely whispering: “That’s not a real person.”

“And here I thought I was fake.”

“Look at Ken 2.0 over there…”

Someone crossed themselves.

Meanwhile, Phainon, now fully reborn as a divine being, dusted off his sleeves, casually adjusted his collar, and sauntered past the judgmental crowd like an untouchable deity.

He threw up a charismatic wave, flashing a smile that could charm the devil himself.

“Later,” he said smoothly, voice silk and honey.

And then, as though a god descending from the heavens, he left.

Because he had a film to finish.

Phainon strode back onto the set with the confidence of someone who absolutely did not just transcend mortal suffering through sheer force of will.

His energy was pristine. Controlled, even.

And then he stopped. Blinked.

“…Where’s my very attractive and endlessly amusing boyfriend?”

March 7th turned from reviewing the footage on her camera, hands still adjusting the settings. “Oh, Mydei? Yeah, he left.”

Phainon tilted his head, processing. “…What?”

“Said he had an emergency.”

Phainon squinted.

March 7th barely looked up as she casually scrolled through her clips. “Something about saving the city.”

A beat of silence.

Then Phainon snorted, crossing his arms. “Oh, come on. That’s cheating. He could’ve at least come up with a real excuse.”

March hummed, not questioning it.

At the same time, Phainon was now mentally filing through all the absolutely ridiculous things Mydei had done under the guise of “saving the city” before—

Like that time he single-handedly stopped a ten-car pileup just by existing at the right place at the right time. Or the time he “heroically” helped an old lady with groceries and acted like it was an epic quest of destiny. Or that one time he wrestled a loose sheep in the middle of a university campus, saying “someone had to do it.”

Phainon shook his head, grinning. “I swear, he says stuff like that so dramatically—”

(Meanwhile, somewhere across town, Mydei was absolutely demolishing a group of armed criminals, hurling one through a window and suplexing another into the pavement.)

Phainon chuckled fondly. He’s so silly.

March 7th snapped her fingers. “Oh, yeah, he said he’ll see you later.”

“Mm. Alright.”

Phainon didn’t think much of it. He was still mentally distracted by how dramatic Mydei was being.

Instead, he rolled up his sleeves and looked at March 7th, his usual easygoing charm settling into place. “Well, in the meantime, what else needs doing?”

March 7th lit up immediately, practically sparkling with joy as she spun on her heel to face him fully.

“Ohhh, you wanna help? That’s great! I was this close—” she held up her fingers an actual inch apart, “—to losing my mind because Stelle and Dan Heng are useless and you’re literally my last hope.”

Phainon chuckled, ruffling her hair without hesitation. “You say that like I wasn’t already the best choice.”

She huffed, swatting at his hand. “Okay, debatable,” Was that a pun? It definitely was, “but I’m too happy to argue.”

She handed him a clipboard. “Alright, you’re officially my assistant-slash-pack mule.”

“I am so honored.” He mock-bowed, flipping the clipboard. “What’s first, my mighty director?”

March clasped her hands behind her back, rocking on her heels. “Help me set up the lighting for this next shot, oh mighty  professor.”

“Say no more.”

And just like that, he got to work.

Phainon made himself useful.

Which, honestly, wasn’t hard—he liked being helpful, and March 7th was very easy to help. Mostly because she had the energy of a baby bird that had just been given coffee and needed someone to keep her from spiraling.

So, for the next hour, he adjusted lighting, held up props, carried equipment, and even made sure she remembered to eat while she ran around orchestrating her masterpiece.

At one point, he physically had to turn her away from the camera and push a granola bar into her hands. “Eat.”

March took an exaggerated, reluctant bite. “Ugh. This is what hell tastes like…”

Phainon arched a brow. “March. It’s chocolate chip.”

“Exactly.”

He sighed. This child.

Still, her enthusiasm was contagious, and despite the chaos, Phainon found himself genuinely enjoying himself.

“Alright, so this next shot?” March spun dramatically, eyes gleaming. “It’s supposed to be cinematic. Think: high contrast, deep shadows, the very essence of mystery and intrigue.”

Phainon, adjusting a light stand, nodded along. “So, basically every shot you’ve taken of Mydei so far.”

March gasped, clutching her chest like he’d just spoken truth beyond her comprehension. “Oh my God. You get it.”

Phainon smirked, tightening a bolt. “Of course I do. He’s the most photogenic man alive. Did you see the way his jacket flared earlier? That’s pure power.”

March sighed dreamily. “Right? Honestly, if I wasn’t terrified of him, I’d have asked him to model for me ages ago.”

Phainon hummed. “Oh, same.”

They shared a look, then cackled like gossiping old ladies.

By the time the sun dipped below the horizon, casting the campus in a soft amber glow, the shoot was finally winding down.

Phainon had helped with everything from holding reflectors to physically stopping March 7th from using a fog machine indoors (“March, I am begging you to think about the fire alarms.”). Now, as she reviewed the last few takes with a gleeful sparkle in her eye, he finally saw his chance to escape.

With a lazy stretch, he grinned and ruffled March’s hair one last time— because it was fun watching her squawk in protest.

“Alright, kid. I’m off.”

March swatted at him, but she was smiling. “Finally. Go be free.”

Phainon chuckled, stuffing his hands in his pockets. “Don’t miss me too much.”

March beamed. “Bye Professor!”

He winked and turned toward the exit, stepping outside into the cool evening air.

And immediately sighed in relief.

Finally. Peace. Quiet. No more fake vampire nonsense, no more dramatic lighting setups, no more—

A sudden gust of wind blasted through the quad.

Phainon barely had a second to register it before his bag exploded.

Papers. Everywhere.

Like a scene straight out of a sad indie film, loose sheets took flight— gracefully, mockingly—scattering across the pavement in slow-motion betrayal.

Phainon stood there, stunned, as his entire night’s worth of work transformed into a chaotic confetti storm.

“…Oh, you’ve got to be kidding me.”

The wind howled. The papers danced.

And so, the chase began.

Phainon bolted after them, narrowly avoiding trampling over a very confused teenager. “Move, move, move—”

One paper soared majestically onto a tree branch. Another cartwheeled into a fountain. One somehow made it inside a passing cyclist’s backpack (he’s never seeing that one again).

He hated this. He hated this so much.

After several minutes of desperate, parkour-level retrieval (and only mild public humiliation), Phainon finally managed to scoop up the last of his rogue documents.

Chest heaving, hair slightly disheveled, he stood there, victorious.

Then another gust of wind hit.

A single page slipped from his grasp.

Phainon locked eyes with it as it floated, tauntingly, toward the ground.

He inhaled sharply—

And stomped on it with finality.

Silence.

A passing person clapped.

Phainon slowly turned, giving them a dead-eyed stare.

They scurried away.

Shoving the papers back into his bag with great personal offense, Phainon straightened his clothes, exhaled slowly—

And marched off, like none of that had ever happened.

Because obviously it hadn’t.

(If anyone asked? No, it didn’t.)

In his head, a full-blown orchestral swell played—heroic, triumphant, worthy of a standing ovation.

He hrew back his shoulders, stretching and prepared to head home.

Then he heard it.

That sharp, thinly veiled fear in a woman’s voice. The tense, high-pitched note of a child.

His steps slowed.

A few meters away, at the edge of a quiet street, a man had a woman cornered against a storefront. His grip was tight around her wrist, his mouth twisted into a condescending sneer as he spoke too close, too casually.

The kid—a boy, maybe nine or ten—was pressed against his mother’s side, eyes darting in every direction like he was desperately hoping someone would intervene.

Lucky for him, I have time today.

Phainon’s fingers flexed as he changed course, each step measured, smooth.

He wasn’t reckless. He didn’t storm over with fists flying.

No.

He liked taking his time with people like this.

He liked the build-up.

He liked the moment they realized.

“Hey,” Phainon called, voice light, pleasant—just a touch intrusive. “Is there a problem here?”

The man turned sharply, annoyed at being interrupted. The woman looked startled—then almost relieved.

The man scoffed. “Nah, this is my wife.”

Phainon blinked.

Then blinked again.

Then slowly dragged his gaze to the woman and child, who were looking at the man like he had just threatened to skin them alive.

Ok, Phainon thought, so we’re lying today.

The man squared his shoulders. “Move along.”

Phainon didn’t move.

Instead, he tilted his head slightly, scanning the scene like he was considering something deeply.

“You know,” he said, voice still light, too light, “I find that hard to believe.”

The man’s face twisted. “I don’t care what you believe.”

Phainon hummed thoughtfully. “See, that’s the thing. Your ‘wife’ and ‘son’ look at you like you just crawled out of a sewer.”

The woman stiffened.

The man’s nostrils flared. “Mind your damn business.”

“Oh, but you see,” Phainon smiled, leaning slightly closer, “I love minding my business. And my business, right now, is making sure this woman and her actual son aren’t being pestered by some miserable little man.”

The guy bristled, stepping toward Phainon.

A mistake.

Because the second he got too close and reached out to him, Phainon’s hand shot out, catching his wrist in an iron grip.

The effect was instant.

The guy tensed as his wrist cracked. Not a break—just a warning. A cruel little preview of what could happen.

His breath hitched.

Phainon, finally, let his smile drop.

“You’re still talking,” he mused, pressing down just enough to make the guy’s fingers twitch involuntarily. “That’s annoying.”

Sweat formed at the man’s temple. “L-let go.”

Phainon’s grip didn’t budge.

Instead, he studied the guy—like he was a particularly uninteresting bug, something beneath his notice but still in his way.

He could break his fingers one by one.

He could twist his arm back until something gave.

He could drag him to the pavement and make him beg.

A pity, really, that the guy was stupid enough to try to punch him.

Phainon let it happen.

The impact was nothing. The weakest hit he’d taken all week.

The guy grinned, thinking he’d actually—

SLAM.

In an instant, Phainon had him pinned to the wall, one hand gripping his collar, the other forcing his arm into a brutal angle.

The woman gasped. The boy stared, wide-eyed.

Phainon leaned in, his voice dropping into something cold.

“Give me one good reason,” he murmured, “not to break your arms right now.”

The guy made a strangled noise, face pale, eyes darting—searching for some kind of out.

Phainon applied a little more pressure, just to hear him wheeze.

Then—

Sirens.

Phainon flicked his gaze down. The kid had his phone out. Likely called the cops a while ago.

Smart kid.

Two officers appeared at the scene, guns lowered but watching.

“Hands where we can see them!”

Phainon, without hesitation, let go and stepped back, hands raised in the most harmless civilian way possible.

His entire expression shifted.

Gone was the cold,menacing presence.

In its place—

A mild-mannered professor, polite, helpful, innocent.

One officer squinted. “What’s going on here?”

Phainon, effortlessly: “Oh, just a little misunderstanding.”

The man on the ground wheezed in sheer betrayal.

Internally, Phainon sighed.

Should’ve just broken his arm earlier.

The officers approached with caution, one of them already reaching for a notepad.

Phainon, ever the picture of innocence, took a half-step back and adopted the most agreeable expression in his arsenal.

“Good evening, officers.” He gestured lightly toward the wheezing man still crumpled on the pavement. “I was just passing by when I saw this gentleman harassing the woman and her son.”

The woman, finally free from the man’s grip, gave a frantic nod. “He wouldn’t leave us alone. He grabbed me—my son was scared.”

The officer turned to the boy. “Did you call us, kid?”

The boy swallowed and gave a firm nod. “Yeah.”

The other officer glanced between them all, then down at the miserable excuse for a man on the ground. “You want to press charges?”

The woman hesitated.

The guy—sweating buckets—started shaking his head wildly. “It was a misunderstanding—”

Phainon, watching the whole thing unfold, rested his hands in his pockets.

A small part of him wished the woman would say yes.

Because then he’d get to see this worm dragged away like he deserved.

But instead, she swallowed and shook her head. “No. I just—I just want to go home.”

Phainon sighed internally. That’s always how it goes, huh?

The officer still hauled the guy up by the arm, but his tone was lighter. “Alright, buddy. We’re taking you in for now. You can explain everything at the station.”

Phainon hummed, watching them go.

For all the things he hated about people like that, there was one thing that really got to him.

They never thought they were in the wrong.

They never understood what they did.

Even when thrown in cuffs, even when caught in the act, they always had some excuse. Always had some delusion that painted them as the victim.

It made Phainon sick.

But at least, for today, this one wouldn’t get to walk away so easily.

As the officers finished up, Phainon turned back to the mother and son, all his sharp edges tucked away once more. “Do you need me to walk you two back?”

The woman hesitated, then offered a small, grateful smile. “No, we’ll be okay. But—thank you.”

The boy, still clinging to her side, mumbled, “Yeah. Thanks, mister.”

Phainon softened slightly. “No problem. Good thinking, calling the cops.”

The boy beamed just a little.

And just like that, it was over.

Phainon turned on his heel, and finally left.

He didn’t look back.

His mind was already elsewhere, thoughts dragging behind him like shadows.

How many times had he seen this exact scene play out?

How many times had he watched the same thing—fear, hesitation, retreat— repeat itself over and over again?

How many more times would he have to?

Phainon’s jaw clenched.

Too many.

Too many people in the world thought they could get away with things like this.

Too many people did.

He could break them, one by one, and it still wouldn’t be enough.

It would never be enough.

A gust of wind swept past him, ruffling his hair.

He exhaled.

No use getting worked up now.

This wasn’t his fight to dwell on anymore.

Instead, he let out a long sigh and forcibly lightened his mood.

“Alright,” he muttered to himself, rolling his shoulders. “Time to go home and actually rest before I die.”

With that, he picked up his pace, winding through the city streets with practiced ease, until finally—

His apartment door came into view.

Phainon entered his apartment.

The door shut behind him with a quiet click, and immediately, his body sagged. He was done. Mentally, physically, spiritually. His bones felt like they were held together by sheer spite. His soul was peeling away.

Without even turning on the lights, he zombie-shuffled toward the bathroom, stripping off his shirt on the way and tossing it vaguely in the direction of the laundry basket. (It missed. He did not care.)

Shower. Blessed, holy shower. He stood under the hot water until it stopped feeling good and started feeling like a boiling pot. Only then did he move again, sluggishly scrubbing himself down before dragging himself out.

And this—this was where he gave up on life entirely.

Phainon didn’t even pretend to put together a reasonable outfit. No. That required effort. That required dignity. And he had none left.

So instead, he pulled on the most heinous outfit known to mankind.

A pair of sweatpants so loose they practically functioned as a dress. A t-shirt featuring an aggressively cursed, low-quality meme. A hoodie that was

once black but had been washed so many times it had become a depressing shade of charcoal. The sleeves were too long. The pockets were stuffed with mystery items.

And the slippers. Oh, god, the slippers. One was shaped like a bear, the other was from an entirely different set and had a hole in it. His socks didn’t match, either. They probably weren’t even his.

Looking in the mirror, he gave himself a slow nod of approval.

Perfect.

Then, with the grace of a dying man, he faceplanted onto his bed.

For a moment, there was silence. Peace. His body still ached, his brain was foggy, but he was home, and that was all that mattered.

And then his phone vibrated.

Mydei🍷: open up

Phainon cracked one eye open. Blinked.

Phainon☀️:

?

And then his stomach dropped.

Oh, fuck.

Date night.

Date night.

He shot up so fast his mind lagged behind.

A rapid-fire sequence of thoughts hit him at once:

1.He loved date night. 2.He forgot date night. 3.He was currently dressed like an escaped sewer creature. 4.He had exactly zero motivation to fix this.

…But then again.

Maybe it was a lazy date?

Fast food. Movies. He and Mydei both sprawled on the couch in oversized hoodies. It made sense, right? Mydei wouldn’t judge him. They’d just chill and eat junk food like the two barely-functioning adults they were.

Satisfied with this logic, Phainon lazily dragged himself off the bed, yawning as he shuffled toward the door. He even had a stupid little grin on his face, ready to say Surprise! like an absolute dumbass.

Then he opened the door.

Romantic music might as well have been playing in the background.

There stood Mydei.

In a suit.

A tailored suit. Black-on-black, crisp lapels, top two buttons undone, looking like he was about to ruin someone’s life. His hair was immaculate, his cologne was subtle yet devastating, and in his hands was a bouquet of flowers, like he had just walked straight out of a goddamn K-drama.

Phainon took exactly one second to process this.

Then, in complete silence, with an utterly blank expression, he shut the door.

Click.

The music cut off.

He stood there, staring at nothing.

Ah, he thought distantly. I have made a mistake.

He slowly turned back toward his apartment, eyes hollow.

Then, still in total silence, he faceplanted back onto his bed.

The void welcomed him.

Oh my god. Oh my god. Oh my god.

His body tensed, then convulsed into full-body cringe. His legs kicked helplessly against the sheets. His arms flailed once, then fell limp. His soul attempted to eject itself into the astral plane.

He saw. HE SAW.

His beautiful, perfect, devastatingly attractive boyfriend—his suave, elegant, K-drama-esque, romantic as hell, better-than-everyone Mydei—had just witnessed Phainon at his absolute lowest.

In The Outfit.

The slippers. The meme shirt. The mismatched socks. The pure, unholy combination of all things cursed in one single ensemble.

This is it. This is how I leave the mortal plane.

Phainon groaned, rolling onto his back, gripping his own hair like that would somehow erase the last two minutes from existence. His brain was burning, running at a million miles per hour, trying and failing to process the depth of his humiliation.

Okay. Okay. Deep breaths. This is fine.

Sure, his stupidly gorgeous, always-stylish boyfriend had just witnessed him in the worst state known to mankind, but that was okay. It was okay. Mydei loved him. He loved him no matter what. That’s what love was.

Right?

…Right?

His entire body twitched like a dying cockroach. I can never recover from this.

But no. No. He could fix this. There was still time. He just needed to change. Quickly, before Mydei got suspicious and—

Phainon practically dove into his closet. Ransacked it. Clothes flew everywhere. Shirts, jackets, a pair of pants that may or may not have belonged to Mydei, a single sock that definitely wasn’t his—

Nothing.

There was nothing.

Cold realization dawned upon him.

Oh fuck.

He forgot to do laundry last night.

His hands clenched around the last remaining hoodie in the depths of his closet. He pulled it out, eyes dark, filled with horror. It was a relic of his past—a neon green monstrosity from his university days, featuring a ridiculous slogan in Comic Sans that read DEBATE CLUB: WHERE ARGUMENTS GO TO DIE.

He held it. Stared at it. Considered simply walking into the ocean.

No. This wasn’t happening. He could not let Mydei see him like this again. There was only one solution.

Phainon gave up.

Quickly, he grabbed his phone.

Phainon☀️:

hey Mydei can’t do date night tonight actually I am dying. cancer. rip me. love u.

He pressed send.

Three seconds later:

Mydei🍷: open the damn door.

Phainon let out a long, suffering groan.

He squeezed his eyes shut. Took a deep, shuddering breath. He could fight this. He could stand his ground. He could—

No. No, he couldn’t.

With the weary resignation of a man condemned, he dragged himself toward the door.

And caved.

Phainon took a deep breath, backtracked into his apartment, and ransacked his closet for the only thing remotely presentable. It was a simple black button-up and dark slacks—decent, but standing next to Mydei, he might as well have been wearing a garbage bag.

Reluctantly, he returned to the door, dragging it open at an almost painfully slow pace, as if stalling would somehow make Mydei disappear. No such luck. The moment the door was fully open, Phainon was once again blessed (cursed) with the sight of his perfectly put-together boyfriend, who looked like he had just stepped out of a luxury magazine spread.

Mydei had the audacity to be standing there like some divine entity, all sharp angles and smooth confidence, the suit hugging him in a way that had to be illegal. His pale fingers adjusted his cufflinks like this was some casual outing and not an event that was actively ruining Phainon’s entire existence.

Phainon squinted, processing. Then, emotionally resigning himself to his fate, he sighed and muttered, “Don’t say anything. I know it’s bad.”

Mydei, expression unreadable, gave a slow, deliberate nod. “Mhm.”

Phainon groaned.

Before he could spiral again, Mydei held up a small, elegant envelope, sliding it into Phainon’s hand. “I got us a reservation at Kremnos,” he said, completely nonchalant, like he hadn’t just casually named one of the most expensive and exclusive restaurants in the city.

Phainon’s brain stalled. “I—hold on. Kremnos? You mean the place with a year-long waitlist? The place where they reject celebrities? The place that probably charges a small fortune just for breathing their air?”

Mydei, completely unfazed, adjusted his tie. “That’s the one.”

Phainon narrowed his eyes in deep suspicion. “…How?” Mydei was a librarian. That was self-explanatory.

Mydei simply smirked, mirroring the exact casual shrug Phainon had given him last month when he had spent an absolutely absurd amount of money on getting Mydei a custom-tailored outfit.

“Don’t worry about it.”

Oh, the hypocrisy.

Phainon opened his mouth, then closed it. His first instinct was to protest, to dig for the real explanation, but the look Mydei was giving him—the slightest softening of his gaze, the way his lips curled in amusement, the

way his entire demeanor practically radiated I wanted to do something nice for you, just take it—made Phainon hesitate.

He felt his initial guilt rise again, glancing down at his ridiculously mediocre outfit compared to Mydei’s, but… this was happening, whether he liked it or not.

Phainon sighed, but a small smile tugged at his lips. “Fine. Let’s go be disgustingly rich for the night.”

As they stepped out of the building, Mydei—ever the gentleman—reached for the car door and held it open.

Phainon, being the overgrown theatre kid he was, placed a hand over his chest, fluttering his lashes as he stepped in. “How charming.”

Mydei rolled his eyes but subtly smiled, following after him. The car interior was organized, dimly lit, and very comfortable. The second Mydei settled in, Phainon instinctively leaned into him, hands intertwining together.

For a brief moment, it was perfect. Peaceful. Romantic, even.

Then Phainon sneezed.

Loudly.

The force of it practically shook the car.

Mydei froze.

Slowly, ever so slowly, he turned his head, eyes narrowing as he observed Phainon like a scientist discovering an abomination under a microscope.

Phainon sniffled, rubbing at his nose. “What?”

Mydei didn’t answer. Instead, his gaze trailed downward—and that’s when he noticed it.

The faint discoloration on Phainon’s cheek. The subtle bruise, barely noticeable under the dim car lights but unmistakable once you knew what to look for.

In an instant, Mydei’s entire demeanor shifted. Concern Mode: Activated.

His fingers reached out, gentle but firm, brushing against Phainon’s forehead to check his temperature.

Phainon immediately recoiled like he’d been touched by holy water. “Oh, wow, look at that, we’re moving—”

The car had not moved an inch.

Phainon made a break for it anyway, attempting to dramatically slide further into the seat, twisting his body away as if sheer willpower alone could escape Mydei’s grasp. He looked like a scandal-ridden Victorian lady avoiding the touch of an eligible bachelor in a ballroom.

“Don’t be ridiculous,” Mydei muttered, leaning in further.

Phainon, full-on twisting himself into the most uncomfortable position imaginable, hissed, “I am never ridiculous—”

That was when Mydei moved and in a millisecond, straddled him.

Phainon choked on his own soul. “MYDEI.”

With the precision of a man who had clearly done this before, Mydei effortlessly swung a leg over Phainon’s lap, caging him in place with zero room for escape. The weight of him, the sheer presence, was completely unfair.

Phainon flailed weakly, pressing himself against the car door as if it was a hostage situation. “This is entrapment!”

Mydei, completely ignoring him, pressed the back of his hand to Phainon’s forehead.

A pause.

Then, his expression darkened.

“…You’re burning up.”

Phainon, sweating for multiple reasons, laughed weakly. “Well, you are on top of me—”

Mydei’s stare sharpened.

Phainon winced. “No, please, not the disappointment—”

Too late.

Mydei exhaled sharply, closing his eyes for a moment like he was deeply reconsidering his life choices the second time today. Then, he fixed Phainon with the most profoundly unimpressed look known to mankind.

Phainon wilted under it. His soul left his body. His ancestors turned away in shame.

“I can explain,” he tried.

“You’re sick,” Mydei stated flatly.

“Technically, I’m—”

“Sick and bruised,” Mydei continued, his voice taking on the cold efficiency of a doctor about to prescribe a lifetime of regret.

“I can see how that sounds bad, but—”

Mydei just stared.

Phainon shut his mouth.

This was going to be a long car ride.

The silence was uncanny.

Phainon, King of Shotgun, Lord of the Front Seat, had been unceremoniously demoted to the back like a misbehaving child. Mydei, ever the executioner, had not uttered a single word since slamming the driver’s side door shut.

The restaurant? Nowhere in sight.

Instead, the city lights blurred past as Mydei drove directly toward his apartment.

Not Phainon’s. His.

Which meant one of two things:

1.Phainon was being kidnapped. (Understandable, he was quite stealable.) 2. Phainon was in trouble.

Given the tense grip Mydei had on the wheel, the latter seemed more likely.

Phainon sunk deeper into the seat, feeling worse than the time he had accidentally—and he maintains it was accidental—started a city-wide pigeon war after feeding an unfortunate amount of bread to a particularly aggressive flock. (Chaos. Ruins. Avian carnage.)

The guilt creeping up his spine now was eerily similar.

Desperate to break the silence, he cleared his throat. “Sooo… nice weather we’re having?”

Nothing.

“Mydei?”

Still nothing.

Okay. He could work with this.

Phainon glanced out the window. “Sooo, uh. We passed the turn to Kremnos a while back.”

Silence.

“…That’s the restaurant, in case you forgot.”

Still, no response.

Phainon’s stomach churned. “…Are we not going?”

That did it.

“You think I care about that right now?”

His voice had changed.

Phainon winced. “I mean, I care—?”

Mydei exhaled, as if actively restraining himself from saying something much, much worse.

Phainon internally shriveled.

He’s mad but he won’t say anything.

Which, somehow, was so much worse.

Mydei obviously wanted to ask about the bruise. He obviously wanted to know why Phainon was burning up like he’d been thrown into a microwave. And yet, he was holding back.

For Phainon’s sake.

That was… kind of cute.

But also terrible.

Phainon sulked in the backseat, the weight of Mydei’s disappointment pressing down on him. He had faced down many people as the Flame Reaver. Corrupt politicians, crime syndicates, and multiple existential crises, but nothing—nothing—was as soul-crushing as his boyfriend being silently mad at him.

The second the car rolled to a stop, Phainon barely had time to register his surroundings before Mydei’s door swung open. His own followed a second later—ripped open with intent. Mydei had zero intention of letting him escape.

Before Phainon could even think about resistance, a firm hand grabbed his wrist.

“Mydei, wait—”

Nope.

He was dragged.

Not guided. Not led. Dragged.

Through the building, up the elevator, and straight into Mydei’s apartment.

Mydei ignored him entirely, closing the door behind them with a resounding click.

The bouquet.

Mydei still had it.

Then, with an almost comically gentle touch, he set them down on the side table.

Like they were sacred.

Like they mattered.

He braced himself.

Unfortunately, there was no bracing for Mydei aggressively taking care of him.

Because it wasn’t violent—no, it was far worse.

The exasperated-yet-careful way he pulled the blankets over him.

The mercilessly efficient way he undid the collar of Phainon’s (painfully inadequate) outfit, making quick work of ridding him of any uncomfortable layers.

Phainon swore he could feel his heartbeat increasing.

Mydei, fluffing his pillow with unnecessary aggression: “Oh, really?”

“…Yes?”

Mydei snorted.

Phainon pouted from under the covers. “You know I would’ve been fine.”

“You know that’s bullshit.”

Phainon opened his mouth. Closed it.

Fair.

For a moment, neither of them spoke.

Mydei’s hands stilled as he tucked the blanket around him.

No.

Mydei narrowed his eyes.

Phainon smiled weakly.

This was fine.

This was totally fine.

Wait.

You know what he was too old to care for this.

“I was being polite, Mydei.”

Silence.

Then, tentatively, “Phainon.”

No response.

“…Phainon.”

The blanket did not move.

Mydei sighed, rubbing his temple. He glanced at the soup, then at the blanket lump of his boyfriend, and exhaled through his nose.

“…Sunshine.”

A muffled groan. A victory.

Mydei pressed his advantage. “Come on. You need to eat.”

“No.” The response was sluggish, grumpy, full of sadness. “You lied to me.”

“I didn’t lie,” Mydei countered, shifting closer. “I just—” He hesitated. “— let you believe what you wanted.”

“That’s lying by omission,” Phainon grumbled, sinking further into the mattress.

Mydei stared at the ridiculous lump of blanket before simply deciding he was done with this. He reached forward, grabbed the edge of the covers, and ripped them away in one smooth motion.

“Backstabber,” Phainon whispered, eyes squinting at the sudden exposure to light.

Mydei ignored him, lifting the spoon with an expectant look. “Eat.”

Phainon, half-buried in the pillow, remained stubborn for a solid three seconds before the aroma of the soup hit him again. His stomach betrayed him with a low grumble.

Mydei’s lips twitched. “Oh?”

“…Fine.” Phainon grudgingly lifted his head just enough for Mydei to feed him, taking the first spoonful with a huff.

He chewed. Swallowed.

Damn it. It was good.

Phainon glared weakly at Mydei, eyes full of spite even as he reluctantly opened his mouth for another bite.

Phainon, ever the stubborn martyr, finished the last spoonful with exaggerated looks. He chewed climactically, swallowed like it physically pained him, and then turned his head away as if he was done with this entire existence and didn’t scarf down every bite, savoring it.

Mydei, undeterred, set the bowl aside and watched him in silence.

Then, without a word, he leaned down and pressed a soft, lingering kiss to Phainon’s turned cheek.

It was light, barely more than a brush of lips, but warm—warm in the way that settled deep in Phainon’s chest, in the way that said I see you, I appreciate you, even when you’re impossible.

Phainon froze.

Mydei pulled back just as casually as he had leaned in, standing up with no fanfare. “I’ll be back,” he said, voice as even as ever, before leaving the room like nothing had happened.

Phainon stayed perfectly still, brain completely short-circuiting.

Then, slowly, almost dazedly, he lifted a hand to press against his cheek where the kiss had been, eyes wide.

His face burned.

Mydei returned, this time with medicine and cooling pads in hand, his movements efficient, his expression unreadable. He didn’t say anything as he handed Phainon a glass of water and the pills, just watched with quiet expectation.

Phainon sighed through his nose, took the medicine without complaint, and swallowed. Mydei nodded in approval, then placed the cooling pad against his forehead with practiced ease, the coolness a sudden contrast to the feverish heat prickling against his skin.

Then, just as quickly, Mydei turned as if to leave.

Phainon’s fingers caught his wrist.

Mydei paused, glancing back. “I thought you were mad.”

Phainon hummed, voice turning smooth—too smooth, practically dripping with charm as he tugged just enough to get Mydei closer. “I was. Still am, maybe.” His grip firmed, slowly guiding Mydei down until he was hovering above him, knees sinking into the mattress on either side of Phainon’s hips. “But I’m also very weak to you.”

Mydei’s breath hitched, almost imperceptibly, but Phainon felt it. Saw the way Mydei’s throat bobbed as he swallowed. The way his fingers twitched like he wasn’t sure where to place them. Cute.

Phainon’s hands slid, slow and deliberate, up Mydei’s sides before settling at his hips, thumbs brushing over the fabric of his shirt. He felt the tension there, the hesitation. It made something dark curl in his chest, satisfaction winding into something sharper, something he didn’t bother naming.

Mydei’s lashes fluttered. “…You’re feverish.”

Phainon smiled, all teeth. “I was feverish before you got on top of me.”

Another barely-there shudder from Mydei, another point to Phainon. He tilted his head back against the pillow, gazing up at him, voice turning almost lazy as his hands kneaded at Mydei’s hips like he was making himself comfortable. “You always take care of me.” His voice dropped just slightly, enough to make sure Mydei felt it. “Makes me wonder what I’d do without you.”

He saw the effect of his words immediately. Mydei’s fingers curled into the sheets near Phainon’s shoulders, his gaze flickering as if debating something, but his body language—tense, unsure, a little too still—spoke loud enough.

Phainon’s grin softened into something slower, something more indulgent. His fingers flexed, pressing against Mydei’s hips just enough to remind him who was holding him there.

“Not leaving yet, are you?” he murmured.

For a moment, Mydei hesitated. Then, just as Phainon was about to tease him for it, Mydei moved.

It was slow, measured—like he was testing the waters, but undeniably deliberate. His hands slid up, tracing the shape of Phainon’s collar before his fingers curled slightly, gripping at the fabric just enough to make Phainon exhale through his nose, amused and intrigued.

Oh?

Phainon’s hands tightened where they rested on Mydei’s hips, grin widening. “Look at you,” he murmured, teasing but approving. “So bold—”

Then Mydei shifted, adjusting his weight—accidentally pressing down on Phainon’s side.

Pain flared up his ribs.

His breath hitched. It wasn’t much—barely a wince, a brief twitch of his lips—but Mydei caught it immediately.

Phainon knew he was screwed the second Mydei went still.

“…What was that?” Mydei’s tone was deceptively light, but Phainon could already feel the shift.

“Nothing,” he tried, too quickly.

Mydei’s expression remained unreadable. His hand, however, did not— because he suddenly gripped Phainon’s shirt and yanked it up before Phainon could stop him.

A sharp breath. Mydei’s fingers, ghosting over the deep, ugly bruise stretched across Phainon’s right side, stark against his skin. The dark splotches had bloomed outwards like ink, the worst of it concentrated near his ribs.

Phainon clicked his tongue. “See, now this is awkward.”

Mydei did not laugh.

Phainon, ever the optimist, tried anyway. “Listen, I know it looks bad, but —”

A hand pressed carefully, firmly, to the injury. Not enough to hurt, but enough that Phainon felt the weight of Mydei’s touch.

His head snapped up, mouth open to protest—only to falter when he met Mydei’s gaze.

The concern was there, yes. But beneath it, layered in the tense line of his shoulders and the way his fingers curled slightly as they rested against Phainon’s bruised skin, was something colder. Something sharp-edged and simmering, barely held back.

Mydei’s voice, when he finally spoke, was quiet.

“…Who did this to you?”

His grip tightened.

Phainon opened his mouth.

Closed it.

Opened it again—then shut it once more, because what the hell was he even supposed to say?

Oh, Mydei, my love, my moon, my eternity and more—I may or may not be the Flame Reaver, that notorious terrorist-slash-criminal you probably hate, thank you for asking. Oh, and by the way, I fell off a skyscraper last night, hope that’s cool with you.

Yeah, no. Not happening.

But Mydei was still staring at him. Waiting.

Damn it.

Phainon forced a grin, trying to wave it off. “Okay, so, funny story—”

Mydei just arched a brow.

“—Not actually that funny, but listen, I—”

The longer he spoke, the flatter Mydei’s expression became.

That patient silence. That expectant look. The quiet understanding that was somehow worse than any accusation.

Because damn it, Mydei and Phainon had trust and honesty. They didn’t lie to each other. And even when they did at first, they always came back and talked about it properly.

Phainon sighed, rubbing the back of his neck. “You’re not gonna drop this, huh?”

Mydei did not respond. Which was an answer in itself.

Phainon groaned. “Fine, fine,” he muttered, shifting slightly. He glanced away, voice softening. “Got caught up in something. It was… messy. I handled it, but—”

His fingers brushed against the bruise absentmindedly. “Didn’t walk away unscathed.”

Mydei’s gaze flickered over his expression, reading between the lines.

Not obscure enough to sound suspicious. But not detailed enough to raise more questions.

Still, his frown didn’t disappear completely.

“…You’re okay?” Mydei finally asked, quieter now.

Phainon smiled—smaller this time. “I’m fine.”

Mydei studied him for a long moment.

Then, after what felt like forever, he exhaled and finally—finally—relaxed a fraction, the tension in his shoulders lessening.

“…Alright,” he said, eventually.

Phainon felt something warm settle in his chest.

Healthy communication, baby. His younger self would be so proud.

Phainon could tell—Mydei was still tense.

He didn’t show it outright. To anyone else, he probably looked perfectly composed, just sitting there at Phainon’s bedside after moving away, fingers barely twitching against the sheets. But Phainon knew him too well.

Knew the way his hands curled slightly when he was thinking too hard, the way his breathing slowed like he was trying to contain something he didn’t want spilling over.

Yeah. Mydei wasn’t letting this go.

And Phainon, well—he was too exhausted to deal with it.

So he did the only thing that made sense.

He grabbed Mydei by the wrist for the second time today and dragged him onto the bed once again, this time next to him rather than on top.

Caught off guard, Mydei barely resisted as Phainon shifted them both, guiding him down. Then, without hesitation, Phainon wrapped his arms around him, pulling him close with the kind of ease that came with years of knowing exactly how Mydei fit against him.

It was instinctive. Natural.

Mydei, on the other hand, was completely still.

Slightly stiff, but not resisting.

He exhaled slowly, then muttered, “…You’re sick.”

Phainon blinked.

Oh. Right.

He hesitated, arms slackening a little as he prepared to let go. “Damn. Forgot about that.”

Mydei didn’t move.

Didn’t pull away. Didn’t push him back down.

He just… stared at him for a long moment. His expression was unreadable, eyes flickering across Phainon’s face like he was weighing something in his mind.

Then, without another word, he leaned in again—closing the distance, wrapping his arms back around Phainon, and burying his face against his chest.

Phainon stilled.

“…Uh,” he started, feeling Mydei’s warmth pressed against him.

“I have a strong immune system,” Mydei muttered, voice muffled against his shirt.

Phainon stared at him.

Then, after a long beat, he huffed out a laugh—something quiet and warm and helplessly fond.

“Alright,” he murmured, shaking his head, but not letting go.

The air settled, the tension ebbing away into something softer. Phainon let his hand drift up, absentmindedly stroking Mydei’s back, feeling the steady rise and fall of his breath.

Mydei fell asleep first.

His grip on Phainon remained firm, but his body gradually relaxed, breaths evening out. It was earlier than usual for him, but Phainon could feel the exhaustion in the way he held him—like he’d been holding himself together for too long and finally, finally let go.

Phainon stayed awake a little longer.

Just watching him.

He brushed a strand of hair from Mydei’s face, traced a thumb over his cheekbone, and leaned in to press a kiss against his temple.

God, he was so—

He exhaled softly, finally closing his own eyes.

And later that night, when Phainon had drifted off completely, he didn’t see the way Mydei’s eyes slowly opened again.

Didn’t see the way he lay there, quietly, just looking at him.

Didn’t feel the way Mydei’s fingers brushed against his wrist—light, careful, lingering for just a second longer than necessary before he finally, finally let himself relax again.
