chapters.title: Chapter 6: Godslayer’s Babysitting Duty
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei survives a catastrophic Black Tide breach, gets an earful from an angry Goldweaver, dodges politics, helps rebuild a city, entertains some kids, and somehow ends up walking a very tired (and very oblivious) Phainon home.

Chapter Notes

Sorry y’all I know I say this every time but this was pretty late😭 Won’t go into details but family drama gets exhausted REAL fast

The city groaned under the weight of its own destruction.

Smoke curled into the air in thick, suffocating waves, twisting between shattered buildings and flickering signs barely clinging to life. Sirens howled in the distance, a discordant symphony of emergency alerts and panicked broadcasts, all drowned beneath the far more immediate sound of people screaming.

And beneath it all, there was the Black Tide.

A pulsating, unnatural mass of shifting black and red, consuming everything in its wake. Like a virus given form, it spread over the streets in jagged, geometric patterns, warping metal and concrete alike, reducing them into something unstable, something wrong.

And at the center of it all, Mydei fought.

He dodged to the side just as a clawed hand swiped at where his throat had been moments ago, the air hissing from the sheer force of the blow. His gauntlets whirred as they absorbed the energy of his movements, golden

circuitry flickering as he twisted on his heel and slammed his fist into the creature’s face.

The impact sent it flying, crashing through what was left of an abandoned vehicle. The body convulsed once before going still, its corrupted flesh sizzling where his weapons had torn through it.

Another one lunged at him from behind. He moved before it could make contact, raising an arm to block the strike. The force rattled through his bones, but pain was an afterthought—irrelevant, temporary. Instead, he caught the thing by its neck and slammed it into the pavement, the crunch of bone sharp beneath the chaos.

Two down.

Mydei stepped over the body, scanning the street. Seven more. No—six. One of them had tripped over its own feet trying to lunge at him, landing in a heap against a wrecked motorcycle.

“Pathetic,” he muttered, raising his foot and stomping down without looking.

Five.

Somewhere in the distance, something hissed. He turned just in time to see a mass of tendrils lash out from the shadows, slicing through the air like whips. He barely dodged in time, the heat of the attack grazing his cheek as he reeled back, fists already raised.

Alright. Now they were getting serious.

His gauntlets hummed, energy coursing through the gold-plated metal as he rolled his shoulders. He exhaled sharply.

“Alright,” he said, shifting his stance. “Come on, then.”

The corrupted obliged, snarling as they charged.

He met them halfway.

The city was alive in the worst possible way.

Alarms blared from every direction, mixing with the sharp crackle of energy weapons and the distant, guttural howls of the corrupted. The skyline, once a proud testament to the city’s technological prowess, was now a fractured mess of collapsing towers, flickering neon signs, and spiraling drones struggling to navigate the chaos. But the worst part—the part that had everyone on edge—was that this shouldn’t have even been happening.

The Black Tide wasn’t just some natural disaster you prepared for like bad weather. It was an absolute, basically cosmic-level catastrophe. A dozen different failsafes were in place to stop it before it even had a chance to manifest—automated purifiers, reinforced containment fields, early-detection sensors, actual laws of reality—yet somehow, against all odds, it had breached the city.

Which meant someone, somewhere, had really screwed up.

Mydei didn’t have time to worry about that right now. He ducked under a massive, corrupted limb, bringing his gauntlet up just in time to obliterate the creature’s face in a crackling burst of energy. It staggered, barely registering pain before he finished it off with a brutal follow-up punch that sent it skidding across the pavement.

His earpiece buzzed to life, cutting through the din of destruction.

“Sector D secured. Moving civilians to the south tunnel.”

“Containment holding steady at the west perimeter, minimal casualties.”

“Black Tide exposure rates are dropping—Trinnon’s almost cleared the main access routes.”

Good. That was something.

The Chrysos Heirs had full authority over this operation—not that they wanted it, but the government wasn’t exactly in a position to argue. No one else could handle something of this scale, and by the time officials even started drafting a response, the Heirs were already in motion. The triplets took point on the evacuation, splitting up the work between them.

Trianne, the loudest and most chaotic of the three, had turned crowd control into something that shouldn’t have worked but somehow did.

“Keep it moving! No pushing! No trampling! If you shove one more person, I will personally throw you into the ocean—do NOT test me!”

People actually listened. Out of fear, efficiency, or sheer confusion, Mydei wasn’t sure, but the shelter lines were moving.

Meanwhile, Trinnon worked on purifying the Black Tide, her usually soft-spoken nature shifting into quiet, grim focus. The Tide wasn’t like normal contamination—it was aggressive, like a living infection that hated being removed. Every time she cleansed a section, it fought back, writhing and pulsing like something alive before it finally dissipated. The air shimmered where she passed, traces of corrupted energy breaking apart in her wake.

Tribbie, from somewhere high above, had locked onto the worst-hit areas, directing operators and scanning for survivors while also suppressing any contaminated points until Trinnon had time to get to them. She was the main reason Mydei knew where to focus his efforts, sending him alerts on where the biggest concentrations of corrupted were forming and where the Black Tide was spreading the fastest.

Despite everything, they were handling it.

Which was good, because Mydei had his hands full with the creatures that kept coming. Another one lunged, all jagged limbs and distorted features, and he met it with a well-placed strike to the gut. It crumpled instantly, and he barely had time to process before another took its place.

He breathed in, shaking out his hands as the gauntlets pulsed in response.

“Alright,” he muttered, cracking his neck as more shadows moved in. “Next.”

His earpiece crackled again, this time with a much more chipper voice.

“De! You’re still alive! Great news—there’s a lot less corruption now, and Trianne hasn’t started throwing people into the portals, so I think we’re winning!”

Mydei snorted, sidestepping a lunging corrupted and smashing its skull in with a brutal backhanded strike. “Yeah? Tell that to the ones still crawling out of the ground.”

“Oh, don’t worry, they’re thinning out. Mostly! You’re still needed in Sector G, though. Couple of stubborn holdouts who refuse to evacuate, and—oh, wait—uh, maybe don’t go there yet.”

He barely had time to process before the battlefield shifted.

A massive wave of force rippled through the air, sending cracks spiderwebbing through the pavement. Mydei pivoted sharply, muscles tensing as the already-ruined sky above twisted in on itself, energy flaring at the center of the battlefield. A shadow streaked through the air—fast, controlled, and deadly—before slamming into the ground with enough force to send debris flying.

And then, through the settling dust, he heard the roar.

Not the mindless howls of the corrupted. Not the eerie shrieks of the Black Tide creatures.

But the low, guttural rumble of something massive.

A pair of glowing eyes ignited in the haze, followed by the slow, deliberate stretch of wings that blocked out the colorful skyline. Its scales gleamed like obsidian, coiling energy crackling along its ridges as it exhaled a stream of searing-hot mist.

And at its feet stood Castorice.

Undertaker.

Her scythe gleamed in the dim light, the curved blade catching the crimson glow of the Black Tide like it was drinking it in. The contrast was almost jarring—her quiet, almost unassuming demeanor against the absolute carnage she commanded. Without hesitation, she twirled her weapon, fluid and practiced, before darting forward in a blur of motion.

The creatures never stood a chance.

Corrupted fell one after another, cut down in wide, precise arcs, their bodies barely hitting the ground before her dragon followed up with a well-placed blast of energy that vaporized whatever remained. She was methodical, efficient—focused entirely on the fight.

Which meant Mydei could switch priorities.

“De?” Tribbie’s voice hummed in his ear again. “Guessing you noticed the very big and very cool dragon? That means you’re good to move onto rescue!”

“On it.”

With Castorice taking point in combat, Mydei turned his attention elsewhere. His gauntlet pulsed as he activated a scanner, sweeping the crumbling landscape for any trapped civilians. Red markers lit up his visor —a few people stuck under debris, some huddled in barely-standing structures, others too injured to move.

He didn’t waste time.

For the ones he couldn’t reach, he sent direct coordinates to Trianne, trusting her to open gates for extraction. The rest—he got to work. Sprinting through collapsing streets, pulling people out from under rubble, hoisting them over his shoulder when they were too weak to run. Every second counted, and he moved like he knew it.

And above it all, through the chaos, Castorice and her dragon tore through the battlefield, ensuring nothing got close enough to stop him.

A soft chime echoed in Mydei’s earpiece, followed by the smooth, refined voice of Goldweaver.

“Mydei. I trust the battle is going well on your end.”

He took a moment to adjust his stance, letting his gauntlet recharge as he observed the battlefield. Undertaker was still holding the perimeter, and evacuation efforts were proceeding without issue.

“As well as it can be,” he replied. “Is this just a social call, or do you have bad news for me?”

A faint chuckle. “Straight to the point. Good. Due to the severity of this incident, a temporary alliance is being enforced between independent operatives and state-sanctioned responders. The Council has already approved it.”

That was expected. “Not surprising.”

“Then this next part won’t be, either. Some of the more… opportunistic individuals have attempted to use this disaster to their advantage.”

Mydei’s jaw tightened. “Escaped convicts?”

“Luckily, most were contained before they could flee. However, a handful slipped past the security measures. Your next priority is neutralizing them before they cause further harm.”

He could already tell where this was going. “Let me guess. They’re deep in the city.”

“Yes. The Black Tide concentration is significantly higher in that region, and most teams cannot risk prolonged exposure. You, however, are a different case.”

Of course. He was the obvious choice. His immortality gave him an undeniable advantage, even if he didn’t particularly like the reason why.

“Alright,” he muttered, rolling his shoulders. “Give me the locations.”

There was a brief pause, then two markers pinged onto his visor’s display.

“Sector M-13. Intelligence suggests possible hostages.”

“Sector R-4. Reports of a high-priority fugitive last seen in the area.”

Hostages took priority. He was already moving before Goldweaver could say anything else, sprinting toward the nearest operators.

“I need a mapped route through the contamination zones,” he said quickly enough. “Potential hostages in M-13. Figure out the best way in now.”

They scrambled to comply, pulling up

projections of the district and marking possible safe pathways. Mydei committed the fastest route to memory.

Then, just before taking off, his gaze locked with Castorice’s.

A brief look. Silent understanding.

He didn’t need to say anything. She was already shifting her stance, angling herself toward the direction he was heading.

By the time he dashed past her, she was already covering him.

The city was a warzone, but still manageable.

The Black Tide clung to the streets in thick, pulsating masses, twisting the very air with its unnatural presence. Anything it touched was corroded— metal rusting, stone crumbling, the very fabric of reality warping at the edges.

Didn’t matter. He pushed forward, dodging a collapsed tram with practiced ease. Something shrieked to his right—one of the larger mutations, its body barely holding shape as it dragged itself toward him.

Too slow.

His gauntlet flared. One hit, and it crumpled.

The deeper he went, the worse it got. The Tide was heavier here, thick enough to blot out the emergency lights and shroud the streets in an eerie, suffocating dimness. Every step felt like walking through a battlefield long since abandoned—except this one was still very much alive, shifting, waiting.

A lesser fighter would’ve hesitated. He didn’t.

He vaulted over a barricade, boots landing silently against the ruined pavement. Another group of corrupted creatures had formed ahead, grotesque and unstable, their bodies still struggling to adapt to their own mutations.

Pathetic.

He didn’t even slow down. The first one lunged, and he met it with an elbow to the skull, feeling the brittle crunch of bone beneath his strike. Before the others could react, he slammed a gauntleted fist into the ground, sending a shockwave rippling through the street. The force splintered the cracked asphalt, sending the weaker ones sprawling. The ones that weren’t dead yet wouldn’t be standing for long.

This wasn’t a fight, more a cleanup.

Sector M-13 loomed ahead. Buildings reduced to skeletal remains, streets littered with debris and the unmistakable marks of struggle. But even in the chaos, he could see movement—people trapped, survivors huddled in whatever cover they could find.

And between them and safety?

Escaped convicts. Armed. Opportunistic. And very, very unlucky.

He pressed a finger to his earpiece. “Goldweaver, I’m here. It’s bad.”

“Expected. What’s the situation?”

“Survivors spread across multiple buildings, too many hostiles for a direct engagement without risks. But we got lucky—some heroes are already in the area.”

A flicker of movement caught his eye—government-backed responders setting up defensive positions. Good. He could work with this.

“I’ll coordinate with them,” he said. “Fastest way to minimize casualties.”

“Understood. Keep me updated.”

He cut the line and moved, dropping down next to one of the nearest hero units. They flinched at first, but then recognition flickered in their eyes.

“It’s Godslayer,” someone muttered.

Damn right it was.

“Status?” he asked, wasting no time.

“We’ve secured two buildings, but the hostiles have barricaded the third. They’ve got hostages, and we can’t risk a frontal assault.”

Mydei nodded. “Alright. We do this clean. No unnecessary losses.”

A plan was already forming. He mapped out the quickest routes, calculated the points of least resistance, and—most importantly—determined exactly how hard he’d have to hit to get the job done.

He cracked his knuckles.

“Here’s how we’re doing this.”

The plan went off like clockwork.

The heroes took position at the north and south entrances while Mydei handled the rest. He moved fast—too fast for the convicts to react properly. The first was disarmed before he even realized someone was there, his weapon skidding across the floor as Mydei drove a knee into his gut. Another lunged with a blade, and Mydei let him land the hit—just to prove a point.

The knife slid in, piercing fabric and skin alike.

The convict grinned for half a second. Then that grin faltered as Mydei, completely unfazed, grabbed him by the wrist and yanked the knife out himself. He twisted, flipping the guy over his shoulder and slamming him into the floor hard enough to knock him unconscious.

“Didn’t even need that kidney anyway,” Mydei muttered, flicking the blood off the blade before tossing it aside.

The others weren’t as stupid. They tried to run. Mydei was faster.

One by one, they dropped—disarmed, disabled, unconscious. He didn’t need to kill them. He was methodical, and every move was aimed at maximizing speed while minimizing damage. Within minutes, the threat was neutralized, and the hostages were free.

Normally, he’d guide them out himself, but the moment he stepped outside, he knew something was wrong.

The Tide was getting worse.

The air felt heavier, thick with the sickly distortion that came with its spread. The streets trembled as patches of it pulsed and expanded, latching onto the ruined buildings like an infection. This wasn’t just lingering residue—this was active corruption.

He clicked his tongue. No time.

Digging into his pocket, he pulled out a standardized Chrysos Heir-issued communication device—smaller, simpler, nowhere near as advanced as what he usually used, but enough to get the job done. He shoved it into one of the hero’s hands.

“Use this to navigate out. I already linked it to the emergency channels— someone will guide you through.”

The hero looked at him, confused. “What about you?”

“Got my own.”

Every Chrysos Heir did. Their standard communicators were advanced, but their personal devices? Far more specialized, each tailored to their individual needs. Mydei’s was his terminal earring—direct access to Goldweaver, encrypted signals, and more secure channels. He didn’t need anything else.

“Get them out of here,” he ordered, already turning away. “I’ll handle the rest.”

He tapped his earring.

“Goldweaver, heading to the second location now. Give me the fastest route.”

“On it. Stay sharp, Godslayer.”

He inhaled, rolling his shoulders. He didn’t need to remember the pain from before—it was already gone. The wounds, the exhaustion, the damage— none of it mattered.

He started running.

The advantage of a disaster like this—if you could even call it that—was the instability it left behind. The Black Tide didn’t just corrupt the physical world; in some places, it tore through reality itself, leaving behind unstable rifts that could lead… well, anywhere. Dangerous, unpredictable, and usually lethal. But if you knew what you were doing?

It could be a shortcut.

Mydei’s terminal crackled to life, Tribbie’s voice cutting through the static.

“De! You’re heading the wrong way—wait, no, the right way—but also, uh, be careful?”

He arched a brow, sidestepping a pulsing vein of corruption as he sprinted down the ruined street. “You’re not making a strong case here.”

“Look, you’re near a rift—Sector R-4’s straight through it, so you could use it to get there faster. But also, it’s a rift. So, y’know. Do that thing where you don’t die. ”

He exhaled, shifting his trajectory. “Got coordinates?”

“Already linked to your display! It’s stable enough for a one-way trip, so—wait, before you go! How’s the purge looking?”

A new voice cut in before he could respond. Goldweaver.

“The threads are in place.” Her tone was smooth, measured, carrying that ever-present air of control. “I’m reinforcing Trinnon’s efforts—once everything is set, we’ll be able to cleanse a significant portion of the Tide in one go.”

That was good. That was necessary. The longer the corruption lingered, the worse the city’s chances were. Mydei gave a sharp nod, even though she couldn’t see it. “I’ll leave that to you, then.”

And with that, he stepped forward and plunged into the rift.

The world twisted.

For a brief moment, he felt weightless, the sensation of movement shifting in every direction at once. Color blurred, space bent—and then, just as quickly, everything snapped back into place.

He landed in a crouch, boots striking cracked pavement. A gust of displaced air rippled outward, sending dust scattering across the ruined street.

Sector R-4.

His gaze flicked upward, locking onto the building ahead.

That was way too close to the source of the Black Tide.

Even with the corruption spreading throughout the city, there were places that were worse than others—pockets where the contamination was so dense that even trained responders wouldn’t risk venturing inside. Civilians? They wouldn’t have stood a chance. If there had been survivors here, they were long gone.

Which meant the fugitive inside was a much bigger problem.

His visor flickered as real-time intel flooded in. The suspect’s profile was updating rapidly, a stream of encrypted data pulling from multiple sources. Mydei scanned through it, exhaling sharply.

“Of course.”

He had every reason to turn back. This area was unsalvageable, the probability of survivors was almost nonexistent, and the criminal inside? Probably already dead.

But still.

He wasn’t the type to leave things to chance.

Cracking his knuckles, Mydei rolled his shoulders and made his decision.

One way or another, he was checking it out.

He couldn’t die, anyway.

As Mydei approached the building, his visor continued streaming data on the target. The profile flickered with corrupted patches—interference from

the Black Tide—but enough came through for him to piece together the picture.

Alias: Red Ghoul Real Name: Unconfirmed Species: Mutant (Class Unknown) Known Affiliation(s): None (Suspected Mercenary) Threat Level: High Crimes: Multiple counts of homicide, illegal bio-modifications, suspected Black Tide experimentation

A mutant. Not just any mutant, either—Red Ghoul had a reputation. Reports painted them as a walking nightmare, something between an assassin and a scavenger, with cybernetic enhancements so invasive they blurred the line between organic and machine. Some claimed they harvested corpses for parts. Others said they could sense the dying, drawn to death like a vulture.

And now, they were here. In the dead center of one of the most contaminated zones in the city.

Mydei exhaled through his nose, stepping cautiously through the crumbling entrance. Even for him, this was dangerous.

The first thing that hit him was the stench.

Rot. Everything unnatural. It clung to the air, thick enough to taste. He ignored it, keeping his breathing steady as his gaze swept the ruined interior.

The place was beyond salvageable. Corruption twisted through the structure like veins, pulsing with a dull, malignant glow. The walls were warped, the floor cracked and uneven. Worse, it felt wrong. Even standing still, there was a sensation of movement, as if the space itself was subtly shifting, bending under the weight of the Tide’s influence.

Not good. Not good at all.

He should leave soon.

Even his internal systems were starting to register mild interference. He ran a quick check—still functional, but definitely not at full capacity. The longer he stayed, the more compromised his equipment would become.

His visor pinged, pulling his attention to the aerial surveillance feed from the council. The drones circling outside were barely holding together, their signals flickering in and out. The Black Tide wasn’t just distorting their visuals—it was breaking them down. Machinery didn’t last long in places like this. If they failed completely, he’d lose his external feed.

And he’d rather not be blind in a place like this.

Jaw tightening, he made his decision.

A quick sweep. Get eyes on the situation. Confirm the target—alive or dead —and get out.

At some point the aerial feed crackled with statistic again, its images distorted by the Black Tide’s corruptive reach. The drones were failing, barely holding together, but one managed to push through the interference —just enough to capture movement.

A figure, jagged and shifting through the flickering data.

Red Ghoul.

He moved like something not entirely human, a silhouette stretched and wrong, half-eaten by the feed’s decay. Mydei watched in calculated silence, waiting for the right moment to act, until—

“Leave.”

Goldweaver’s voice cut through the channel.

“This isn’t the time, Godslayer. He’ll come out. He has to. The Tide won’t let him last long, and when he does, we’ll take him down on our terms. Don’t risk yourself over this.”

She wasn’t wrong. Mydei hummed in agreement, already shifting his weight to leave—

—until the drone caught something else.

Another heat signature.

No. Two.

Huddled close in the same room as Red Ghoul, barely distinguishable through the noise of the malfunctioning surveillance. One smaller, child-sized. The other adult. Hiding.

They shouldn’t be here.

They couldn’t be here.

Everything about the situation was wrong—too close to the source, too deep in the contamination. No one should have even  lived. Yet the scan held, confirming the trembling figures against the ruin.

Something about the way they moved—the way they didn’t move—made the space feel heavier. A pressure, not against Mydei, but in the atmosphere itself. A presence that had no place in a dying cityscape, in a place where no one should have survived.

Mydei braced himself, already about to advance forth. He wasn’t leaving. Not now.

“Mydei.”

Aglaea’s voice slipped through the comms with a chilling precision. There was no plea in her tone, no room for hesitation.

“You will leave that building.”

Silence.

“They are dead.”

The way she said it left no space for argument. It was not a guess, it was a verdict.

“You are the strongest of the Chrysos Heirs. We do not waste you for sentimentality.”

His fists clenched at his sides, but he knew better than to argue. It was not the first time he had to walk away from the already damned. It would not be the last.

He turned back toward the exit, but his gaze flickered one last time to the screen. The drone’s battered feed stuttered, breaking apart into static, then snapping back into clarity for just a second—just enough for him to commit their shapes to memory.

He would find their families. He would apologize, personally.

And then the blur sharpened.

For a single, impossible moment, the image cleared.

White hair.

A familiar silhouette, too distinct to be a trick of the flickering lens.

And then, the final confirmation—

A pair of blue eyes staring directly into the drone’s dying lens.

Everything in Mydei’s mind went blank.

The screen shattered into darkness. The last drone collapsed.

“Mydei, move.” Aglaea’s voice was sharp, urgent. “You’ve lost visual. The Tide will—”

But he did not respond.

For the first time, in the heart of ruin and death, Mydei stood frozen.

A minute passed.

Too long. Far too long.

Aglaea, attuned to every breath of hesitation, hesitated herself.

“Mydeimos?”

Not Godslayer. Just his name.

His hands trembled at his sides.

Because the reason he froze was painfully simple.

It was Phainon.

Aglaea kept speaking, her voice threaded with urgency, her words deliberate and cutting.

“Mydeimos, respond. Now.”

Nothing.

“Mydei.”

Still nothing.

A pause. He could hear the flicker of her patience burning low, the weight of command pressing into her next words.

“If you—”

“…Sorry.”

It was barely a whisper, barely a word, but it was there. Numb.

Aglaea faltered, something rare flickering in her composure. “What?”

But before she could demand clarification—

The connection cut.

Silence.

True, suffocating silence.

Mydei had severed the link, shutting himself off completely. The last tether to Goldweaver, to Aglaea, to any semblance of control—gone.

The next second, he moved.

The wind howled around him as he took off in a dead sprint, his body reacting before his mind fully caught up. He was fast—too fast for the ruined structures around him to even register as more than a blur. Debris collapsed in his wake, the ground splintering beneath each powerful stride, but he was already past it, navigating the destruction with inhuman precision.

His mind was a storm.

Why?

Why was Phainon here?

He should have been evacuated. He should have been safe.

A flash of blue eyes in a dying screen.

He should not have been there.

His body weaved through the labyrinth of devastation, every movement with intent, yet his thoughts were chaos. A thousand possibilities crashed into him at once, each one more infuriating than the last.

Did he get lost? Did something happen?

Did he—

The thought solidified.

Did he leave?

Mydei’s breath hitched, realization slicing through his haze of panic.

Did he leave the shelters to give others space? To go save people himself?

Clarity hit him like a blade to the gut.

Of course he did.

That idiot. That complete and utter idiot.

Mydei cursed ten generations of Phainon’s ancestors under his breath, spitting out every insult he could think of as he neared the location. His worry twisted into pure, unfiltered frustration.

That absolute fool. That self-sacrificing, reckless, idiot.

He swore that if Phainon wasn’t already half-dead, he’d kill him himself.

But first—he needed a plan.

His pace slowed as he approached the ruined room, his movements shifting into something more slower. Reckless speed would get him caught; he needed to be quiet. Invisible.

Stealthy it is.

The interior was worse than expected.

The smell of rot was even worse here. Thick, suffocating, the walls slick with something that pulsed like a dying heartbeat.

And in the center of it all—

Red Ghoul.

The cameras hadn’t done him justice.

In person, he looked wrong.

His body had deteriorated, flesh hanging in strips, his limbs elongated beyond what should be possible. His face was barely recognizable, his jaw unhinged, a grotesque mimicry of something once human. The Black Tide had done more than just consume him—it had remade him into something eldritch, something that no longer belonged in this world.

But Mydei wasn’t focused on him.

His gaze swept the room, searching, calculating. He ignored the hushed, ragged breaths of Red Ghoul and instead traced the jagged lines of destruction, scanning—searching.

And then—

There.

His eyes locked onto a crumbled section of rubble, barely noticeable amidst the ruin. But beneath it, tucked in the shadows, were two shapes.

One small.

One familiar.

His breath caught.

Phainon.

Huddled there with the child, unmoving, hiding.

Mydei’s fingers twitched. His mind sharpened.

He had a target.

Now, he just needed to get them out.

Fighting Red Ghoul was out of the question—too unstable, too much risk. Instead, he slipped past the wreckage, using the jagged remains of the

building as cover, weaving through the ruined space toward Phainon and the kid.

He got close enough to see them properly.

Phainon looked wrecked.

Even in the dim, sickly light, exhaustion was written all over him—too pale, too still, eyes half-lidded with barely any strength left. He was barely upright, only held together by sheer stubbornness.

But when he spotted Mydei—really saw him—something flickered to life in his eyes. Recognition.

And then he moved.

Mydei watched, confusion sparking as Phainon shifted, pushing himself up just enough to do something. It wasn’t until Phainon struggled to lift the kid, an obvious take them in his expression, that Mydei realized.

You absolute moron.

Phainon—half-conscious, barely functioning—was still trying to help.

If it came down to it, he was planning to shove the kid into Mydei’s arms and run, even if it meant staying behind.

Mydei wanted to slap him.

Just stay put for once in your life, he wanted to say. Just rest. I’ve got this.

Instead, he exhaled sharply, stepping in. No time for arguing. He’d handle it.

With the child held securely in one arm, he gripped Phainon’s wrist with the other and pulled him along. He wanted to throw him over his shoulder, force him to rest, but Phainon was still standing, still moving—barely, but enough. So Mydei settled for dragging him at a pace just shy of urgent, putting as much distance between them and that place as possible.

They didn’t stop until the air felt cleaner, until the corruption wasn’t suffocating the very space around them, and until they were a safe distance away from Red Ghoul. Only then did Mydei slow, turn, and finally look at him.

“You absolute fool.”

It wasn’t shouted, wasn’t even particularly loud, but the sheer weight of those words could have crushed stone.

“What the hell were you thinking?” His voice was steady, too controlled. “Do you have any idea what would’ve happened if I hadn’t been there? If I’d been just a few minutes late?” He almost snapped, eyes flicking over Phainon’s exhausted frame, the barely concealed weariness in his stance. “You think you could’ve just handled it on your own? That you could’ve somehow saved both yourself and the child without consequence?”

His grip on Phainon’s wrist tightened for just a second before he let go.

“I don’t know what kind of martyr complex you’re running on, but I promise you—throwing yourself into a death trap isn’t heroism, it’s recklessness.” His tone wasn’t unkind, but it still cut deep. “And what’s worse? You didn’t even consider what your death would cause. Did you think about the people waiting for you? The ones who would have to carry the weight of your loss?”

His jaw clenched. He couldn’t say I would have had to carry that loss. He couldn’t say Do you have any idea how much worse this could have gone?

Instead, he calmed, voice dropping just enough to be softer—but no less firm.

“Don’t ever do something this stupid again.”

A pause. Then, curtly, “Are you hurt?”

Because no matter how angry he was, Phainon’s well-being still came first.

Phainon blinked, caught off guard, but he didn’t waver. “I’m fine,” he said, but there was no real point in pretending, so he pressed on. “But the important thing is—” He drew in a quick breath. “While I was hiding, I overheard something.”

Mydei said nothing, but his stance alone made it clear he was listening.

“The man,” Phainon continued, slower, like he was still working through what he heard. “I don’t know what he is, but he kept laughing. Kept saying it was finally happening. That he was finally going to be himself again.” He shifted slightly, glancing toward where he had been before Mydei arrived. “And he had machines. I didn’t see them, but he sounded desperate. Like they were his last chance.”

Something in Mydei’s expression hardened.

Figures.

Red Ghoul’s whole twisted goal had been to reverse what had been done to him. He had already tried using the Black Tide before. This had to be his next step—devices built to withstand the corruption long enough to force some kind of transformation.

Even if they purged the area, the effects wouldn’t end there. If those machines actually worked, the damage they left behind would be lasting.

Damn it.

“Let me help.”

Mydei nearly laughed. Instead, his hand caught Phainon’s shoulder, stopping him before he could say anything else. “No.”

Phainon stiffened but didn’t step back.

“You can’t help.” Mydei’s voice was firm, biting, and entirely unamused. “You don’t know what you’re dealing with. You don’t even know what he’s trying to do.” His grip tightened for a second before he forced himself to let go. “And you can barely stand.”

Phainon inhaled sharply. “I can still—”

“Don’t.” Mydei cut him off before he could even finish the thought.

This wasn’t just stubbornness—this was insistence. He actually thought he could contribute right now. That he should.

“You saved the kid,” Mydei said flatly. “That’s what matters. Now stop looking for a way to make things harder.”

Phainon looked away, jaw tight. Not out of regret, though. Not even out of embarrassment or shame. Like he was still trying to find an argument that would work.

Mydei closed his eyes, shoving down the very real urge to grab him and shake some sense into him. Instead, he reached out, catching Phainon’s chin just enough to make him look up again. “Listen.” His tone dropped lower, barely masking his irritation. “Do you think you’re helping? Throwing yourself around until you can’t even function anymore?” His fingers twitched, but he let go. “You already did your part. Now get out of here before you turn into another problem I have to deal with.”

He didn’t wait for an answer. He was already turning. “No arguments.”

Mydei scanned the area as his mind worked through the fastest way to get them out. No equipment, no backup, no way to call for help. That left only one real option—get Phainon and the kid out of the building, point them toward the rift, and let them handle the rest.

He didn’t like it. Leaving them behind in any capacity felt wrong. But Phainon could manage. He was capable enough for this, even if Mydei would rather be the one ensuring their safety the entire way through.

The child in his arms hadn’t stirred once. That wasn’t good.

His grip adjusted slightly, shifting the kid just enough to press two fingers against their pulse. Still there. Weak, but there. The Black Tide’s influence must have been creeping in. If that spread too far—

No. Mydei pushed everything else down, steadying himself. He couldn’t afford the distraction.

Then, without another word, he motioned for Phainon to follow.

Phainon hesitated. Mydei could feel it, even without looking. A pause just long enough to mean something, to make it clear that Phainon still wanted to argue.

But he didn’t. He only clenched his jaw and moved.

Good.

Mydei picked the best route in seconds, then they were running. He took the lead, clearing debris with quick movements, making sure the path stayed open. Phainon stayed close behind, steady despite how long he’d been in the contamination zone. He wasn’t faltering. Alright. That meant this was possible.

They just needed to make it out before anything else got in their way.

The child in his arms was still out cold—not ideal, but he could deal with that once they were safe.

He didn’t glance back when he asked, “You holding up?”

Phainon’s footsteps didn’t falter. “Yeah.” His voice was even, but something about it felt slightly off.

Mydei didn’t dwell on it. There were bigger concerns right now.

A sickening noise, wet and wrong, echoed through the hollowed-out building. Mydei immediately tensed, already bracing to deal with it—

But Phainon moved first.

By the time Mydei turned, Phainon had already grabbed a piece of broken piping from the rubble, wielding it with a grip that was too natural. He

didn’t fumble—he just moved. The pipe slashed through the creature before it could fully lunge, cutting straight through its barely-formed body.

A shriek, then silence.

The thing collapsed, its corrupted flesh warping and twitching from the Tide’s influence before finally going still.

Phainon barely reacted. His stance was solid, breathing measured, like this was nothing out of the ordinary. His mind seemed somewhere else entirely.

And then, suddenly, it wasn’t.

His expression flickered—like something had just occurred to him—before he abruptly let go of the pipe, letting it clang loudly against the ground.

Mydei’s eyes narrowed slightly. “You have training with a sword.”

Phainon blinked at him, then, after the briefest pause, smiled. It wasn’t forced, but it wasn’t quite real either. “Yeah. I had training.”

There was no tension, but there was something off.

Mydei’s gaze stayed firm. “From where?”

Phainon didn’t hesitate long. “An old instructor. Used to teach at a dueling hall before it shut down.”

That was a lie.

Mydei didn’t know if that meant Phainon had just never mentioned it before or if he was actively hiding something. But why lie?

His technique was too practiced for some amateur dueling lessons. He hadn’t just learned how to wield a blade—his body had memorized it. That kind of precision didn’t come from casual training. It came from repetition. From experience.

He was still Phainon. But the way he had moved, the way he had let that easy smile cover up whatever had crossed his mind before—there was a distance to it. A separation.

Now wasn’t the time.

Mydei sighed, nodding toward the pipe. “Pick it back up.”

Phainon hesitated.

“For protection.”

A beat. Then, finally, Phainon grabbed the pipe again.

Mydei turned away, focusing back on their path ahead. “We’re nearly there.”

And just as Phainon was about to come, because the world hated him, the air between them fractured.

A ripple tore through the space like a living infection, spreading outward in jagged lines. The corruption cut through reality itself, warping the air into something solid for half a second before unraveling again. Mydei didn’t wait to see what came next—he swerved.

So did Phainon.

They barely cleared the other side before the world broke. The structure beneath them twisted violently, as if the very ground had turned against itself. Stone and metal lurched, reforming into jagged, unnatural angles.

When Mydei landed, he steadied himself fast. Phainon wasn’t as lucky.

The shift had left him standing too high, balancing on unstable terrain that hadn’t been there a second ago. His footing slipped on the uneven incline, sending debris skidding down beneath him. He barely caught himself. One wrong move, and—

His stomach twisted.

Gritting his teeth, he called out without hesitation. “Phainon!”

He didn’t care if it was strange. If it gave away that he knew his name when he technically shouldn’t. It didn’t matter. Not when Phainon was in danger.

But Phainon froze.

It was barely a second, but Mydei saw it—the way his breath hitched, shoulders stiffened, fingers slightly curled as if bracing for something unseen. To anyone else, he would’ve looked merely winded, exhausted from the sprint and the sudden chaos. But Mydei knew better.

A shallow inhale. Too quick. His chest rising too fast, too unevenly.

Damn it.

Mydei forced himself to relax, pushing forward. “I need you to trust me.” His voice cut through the distorted air, steady despite the urgency of it.

Phainon looked at him now, eyes locked onto his.

Mydei adjusted his grip on the child, arms bracing. His voice softened, but the conviction behind it never wavered.

“Jump.”

Phainon hesitated. Just for a second. But it was enough.

Then, a sharp inhale. His body went rigid, like he was forcing himself past whatever was freezing him in place. And then he jumped.

Mydei caught him. Arms steady, the impact barely jarring, the weight settling against him as naturally as breathing.

I got you.

Phainon was stiff in his hold, his heartbeat too quick, too shallow, his fingers twitching against Mydei’s sleeve before he forcibly stilled them. But

Mydei didn’t let go immediately, holding him just a second longer, as if willing that lingering tremor away.

Then they were moving.

Fast. The ground beneath them was shifting unpredictably, the Tide still warping the air in sick, unnatural distortions, but Mydei didn’t falter. Phainon was silent in his arms, unnervingly so. If Mydei didn’t know him, he’d think he was fine.

But he did. And he wasn’t.

Then, finally, Phainon stirred, breath steadier, voice quieter than usual. “I know the way from here.”

Mydei shot him a look.

Phainon coughed, turning his head. “I… also took that rift.”

The words barely registered before something inside Mydei snapped.

He didn’t stop running, but his grip tightened, his jaw clenched so hard it ached, every instinct screaming at him.

You what.

He forced himself to inhale through his nose, but it didn’t help. His mind was already spiraling, conjuring every possible scenario, every horrible outcome. That rift wasn’t stable. That rift wasn’t safe. He had Tribbie’s guidance. He had a way back.

Phainon had nothing.

And yet he still took it.

His fingers twitched against Phainon’s side before he forcibly loosened them. Not the time. Not here.

When they finally reached stable ground, Mydei set Phainon down—not rough, but firm, his movements sharper than before. Then, he pressed the unconscious child into his arms, grip lingering just a second too long.

His voice came low, controlled, but edged with something raw. “Hurry up and get out. Stay safe.”

Phainon hesitated. Mydei didn’t. He was already turning away.

The tension in Mydei’s shoulders eased—just slightly—as Phainon finally disappeared from sight. Gone. Safe. He slowed down, steadying himself.

Now, there was nothing left to worry about.

His focus shifted, mind clearing as he assessed the situation. The structural integrity of the area was deteriorating, the air still thick with remnants of the Tide’s corruption, but none of that mattered anymore. The only thing that did was finishing this.

Then—an explosion.

It tore through the silence, rattling the foundations of the already broken city. But it wasn’t the erratic, unnatural rupture of the Tide. No, this was deliberate. Manmade.

Mydei’s lips curled slightly.

So, Red Ghoul was already moving. Good. That made things easier.

He rolled his shoulders, stretching out the tension left behind from carrying Phainon and the kid. His body was already adjusting, the strain fading. He was built for this—combat, pursuit, ending threats before they spread too far.

And right now, the threat was waiting for him.

He moved, each step carrying a purpose, slipping into the darkened remains of the city with an ease that was almost instinctual. No wasted movement. No hesitation.

If Red Ghoul wanted to burn the place down, fine.

Mydei would put him out himself.

The Rift Zone was a dead place. Not just in the way it looked—silent, empty, stripped of anything remotely natural—but in the way it felt. Reality itself seemed uncertain here, flickering at the edges like a dying signal.

Mydei moved through the collapsed research facility with practiced ease, scanning his surroundings as he stepped over fallen support beams and shattered glass. The place had been wrecked long before today—likely during the first Black Tide breach—but recent disturbances stood out. New scarring in the walls, footprints in the dust, and the faint, mechanical hum of something still running.

Then, he saw them.

Dark, metallic husks embedded into the ground and surrounding walls, pulsing with slow, unnatural light. Aberration Seeds.

Mydei’s lips curled, not in surprise, but in recognition.

Back at headquarters, he had seen something similar—an earlier prototype recovered after one of Red Ghoul’s failed attempts. Aglaea had called them parasitic stabilizers, a grotesque fusion of technology and Tide residue designed to force mutations into something… usable. Red Ghoul’s ultimate goal had always been the same: reversing his own condition. He had already gambled with direct exposure to the Black Tide and lost. Now, he was trying to reforge himself with something more controlled.

Or at least, something he thought he could control.

Mydei followed along, humming in morbid interest. So this is your last bet?

Destroying them one by one would be inefficient. It’d give Red Ghoul time to react, and who knew what kind of failsafes these things had? Instead, Mydei traced the connecting points between them, noting the thinnest links.

There.

The Seeds weren’t working independently—they were networked. If he severed the relay nodes, the entire chain would collapse.

Now for Red Ghoul himself.

With the Seeds out of commission, Red Ghoul would panic, his one hope slipping away. Mydei could use that, force him into a vulnerable position. If he could bait him into attacking prematurely, it’d leave an opening—one well-placed hit could disable him before he had a chance to adapt.

Plan set, Mydei rolled his shoulders, stretching briefly before adjusting his stance.

The source had to be somewhere central, somewhere that could have plausibly been the first point of the Black Tide’s breach.

Mydei’s mind ran through the layout of the facility as he moved, footsteps light against the fractured ground. Research centers like these were built with reinforced containment zones—labs, testing chambers, and most importantly, power cores. If there had been an experiment involving Tide exposure, the central containment sector was the most likely ground zero.

That was where he needed to go.

Navigating the ruins, he kept his profile low, slipping through broken corridors and past rusted terminals. The deeper he went, the worse the damage became. Walls warped as if melted and reformed, the floor littered with remnants of failed experiments—twisted metal, shattered glass, and decayed instruments.

Then, at last, he found it.

A massive containment chamber, once secured behind reinforced doors that now lay in ruins. The air here was thick, humming with an unnatural energy, and at the center of it all was the source.

Red Ghoul.

Or whatever he had become.

He was wired into the system.

Cables, grotesquely fused with flesh, ran from his spine and limbs into the Aberration Seeds, linking them directly to his body. It was as if he had made himself the central node, forcing their power through himself in a desperate attempt to override his condition.

Was he insane?

Trick question.

Yes.

The last time Mydei had seen him, Red Ghoul had already been inhuman— deteriorated, grotesquely elongated, his body barely holding together under the weight of Tide corruption. But now?

He was worse.

His form had twisted further, his flesh a shifting patchwork of unnatural textures—some parts decayed, others pulsating like something growing. His limbs were jagged, new segments forced into existence where there shouldn’t be any. And his eyes—if they could still be called that—were nothing but deep hollows, voids brimming with something that writhed and flickered.

Killing him would be easy.

Killing him without triggering a catastrophic reaction from the network? Less so.

Mydei needed a new plan.

Destroying the Seeds was still the key, but now that they were directly connected to Red Ghoul, severing them could cause unpredictable side effects. If he took them out too suddenly, the backlash could send whatever was left of Red Ghoul into a full-blown transformation.

No, he needed to overload the system first.

If he could force a surge—make the Aberration Seeds collapse under their own instability—then Red Ghoul wouldn’t just lose his connection. It would reject him. The backlash might be enough to kill him outright, or at the very least, weaken him enough for a finishing blow.

That meant targeting the conduits. The way the cables pulsed, he could see the flow of power. If he struck there—

Mydei’s grip shifted on his weapon.

Red Ghoul was motionless, save for the occasional twitch—like his body was caught in the aftershocks of something far worse than a nightmare. His breaths rattled through whatever remained of his lungs, shallow and uneven. If he was aware of his surroundings, he showed no sign of it. His entire being was tethered to the Aberration Seeds, to the corrupted network pulsing with unstable energy—his last, desperate grasp at something beyond his reach.

Good. That means I have time.

Mydei’s eyes traced the flow of energy through the cables, following their rhythm. Every circuit had a pattern, a sequence it relied on to function. Disrupting it wasn’t just about brute force—it was about precision. The conduits stabilized one another in a delicate balance. If he struck fast enough, severing them before they could recalibrate, the entire system would spiral into collapse.

His fingers flexed. Seven points. That was all it would take.

He moved.

A breath.

Then—

The first strike was clean. His blade cut through the conduit like it was paper, the severed link sparking once before dying. A ripple of energy

pulsed through the remaining connections, but Mydei was already gone, pivoting through the shadows.

The second fell just as easily. Sparks scattered across the floor, the circuit already starting to unravel.

Red Ghoul twitched. A sharp inhale—reactive, not conscious.

Mydei didn’t slow.

Third. Fourth. Fifth. Every strike landed in perfect rhythm, precise and merciless. The pulse of corrupted power stuttered, the Aberration Seeds flickering erratically.

The entire system was already failing by the time he reached the last two. Cables spasmed. Energy misfired.

Red Ghoul convulsed.

Not out of awareness—out of rejection.

The corruption that had once sustained him was turning against him, fracturing at its source. His body seized, the network unraveling, cables snapping one by one. His breath hitched, a garbled, wet sound tearing from his throat—

Mydei didn’t wait.

The final strike carved through the last conduit.

A shockwave burst through the chamber as the Aberration Seeds collapsed in on themselves. The cables shrieked, tearing free from Red Ghoul’s body like tendons ripping apart. The light in the chamber flickered, the unstable energy rupturing in its death throes.

And then, for the first time since Mydei had entered the room—

Red Ghoul screamed.

A sound that barely belonged to this world. A distortion of agony. Of something being unmade.

Mydei straightened himself as the dust finally settled. His plan had worked.

Now, it was just the two of them.

Time to finish this.

Red Ghoul lunged with a sudden, rabid force.

Mydei met it head-on.

They crashed, tangled in a violent grapple. Mydei ducked under a swipe meant to tear his face apart, bracing his stance before slamming his shoulder into the creature’s ribs. It staggered—but not out of pain. There was no pain left in that body, only instinct and rot.

Mydei caught its next strike mid-air and twisted, using the momentum to flip Red Ghoul down onto his back. The sound of bone grinding against stone echoed through the room. He didn’t let go. In one smooth movement, he pinned the thing’s chest with his knee, grabbing its arm and forcing it behind its back with practiced strength.

It screamed beneath him, wild and broken.

But Mydei didn’t move. He only looked down at what was left of the man.

“All this,” he said quietly. “For this.”

Red Ghoul bucked under him, a distorted snarl curling through its throat. Mydei leaned in, his tone sharp—not cruel, but cutting in the way truth always was.

“Look at yourself. Tell me this is what you wanted. Tell me this was worth the lives you’ve ruined, the cities you’ve infected, the people—”

His jaw clenched.

“—you dragged in with you.”

Red Ghoul writhed, muscles twitching under corrupted flesh. Mydei’s grip didn’t falter.

“You wanted to ‘be yourself again’? To prove you were more than what you did to yourself? And this is how you do it? Hooked into machines like some desperate parasite, too far gone to even remember what you were?”

His voice dropped, cold and controlled.

“Pathetic.”

The creature coughed something wet and foul. Then, barely audible, it rasped:

“Help me…”

A silence followed.

Mydei didn’t answer at first.

That voice—it wasn’t Red Ghoul anymore. It was the man underneath. Whoever he used to be. Whatever was left of him.

And Mydei almost moved. Almost reached for the blade that would make it quick.

Because death was mercy. Anything was better than the Tide consuming what little humanity remained.

But then he saw something else.

He saw Phainon again, high up on broken ground, breath shallow, hands trembling.

He thought of how close he’d come to losing him.

Of how this thing had caused it.

The offer of mercy shriveled in his chest.

Red Ghoul’s hand reached up, weakly clawing at his leg. Mydei looked down, gaze unreadable.

“Why should I?”

His voice cut clean, no softness left. Final.

The hand fell limp.

But something else began to stir—low and unnatural. The air thickened with pressure, a tension Mydei recognized too well. The Tide was shifting again, warping the space around it like a wound tearing further open.

Not now. Not here.

And Trinnon would be closing in soon. If the cleansing unit caught the edge of this new surge, it’d trigger a far more volatile reaction. He wasn’t about to be caught in that crossfire.

Mydei stepped back, casting one last glance at the barely-living husk, the failed dream rotting in real time.

Then he turned and left without hesitation, boots striking through the settling ash.

No satisfaction. No guilt.

Just a clean exit—and the knowledge that whatever came next, this wouldn’t follow him.

The blast nearly caught him.

Mydei tore through the collapsing hall, heat coiling at his back like a breath on his neck. The air had turned white—radiant, not with fire, but with something searing in its purity. Trinnon’s purge protocol had begun. The kind of cleanse that didn’t leave ashes behind.

It erased.

He vaulted over a fallen beam, boots skidding across rubble as he forced himself forward. Behind him, walls rippled before detonating into dust, swallowed whole by the advancing wave of light. Cables sparked and disintegrated midair. Stone boiled. The old research facility was coming apart at the seams, undone not by violence, but precision.

Each beat of light moved like a pulse of judgment.

Mydei didn’t stop until he burst through the exterior breach and into the unsteady rift somehow still standing, the pressure dropping in an instant as the light behind him slammed against the walls and swallowed everything within. The shockwave flared, kicked debris into the air, and rolled past him like a second wind.

He staggered forward a step, then dropped to one knee.

The world had gone silent. Not from peace—but from the absence left behind.

A long minute passed. Then another.

His chest rose and fell slowly, breath just now catching up to what his body had done. He leaned back, one hand braced against the broken earth, watching as white light flickered and dimmed inside the ruins. What was left was husk and cinder. No more Red Ghoul. No more Seeds. No more anything.

Just the residue of what nearly had been.

Static crackled softly in his ear.

Faint at first. Then clearer.

The comms were returning.

He reached up, pressing two fingers to his ears, ignoring the weight settling in his limbs.

“Primary threat neutralized,” he said, voice gravel-edged and low. “Facility purged. Mission status: complete.”

A pause.

He let the words hang for a breath longer, then added, quieter:

“Returning.”

No one responded. He hadn’t expected them to. But they were listening.

And that was enough.

He stood, dust trailing from his clothes as he turned from the wreckage and walked into the city.

The streets were hollowed echoes of what they had once been—cracked stone and twisted steel, pillars blackened with residue, and the occasional flicker of Tide-burned light, dimming by the second. The air felt thinner now, like whatever poisoned it had finally begun to withdraw. Mydei walked steadily, not hesitating. Not once.

His comm crackled to life again, clearer this time. Familiar frequency.

“Finally.” The voice slid through the channel like velvet over a blade.

Goldweaver.

He didn’t stop. He didn’t answer.

“Status acknowledged,” she continued, too composed to pass as calm. “But what happened down there? You went dark. No report. No signal. I was ready to list your name.”

Still, he walked. His fingers twitched once at his side.

”You were supposed to wait for reinforcement. You know protocol, Mydei. What if you’d fallen inside the Tide’s resonance zone? Do you know how close Trinnon was to declaring a full burn?”

He finally responded, voice even, detached.

“I contained it.”

“That’s not the point.”

Her voice was sharper now, pressed tight into that polished tone she wore like armor. “You’re not expendable. Don’t pretend this was part of the plan. You acted alone. You endangered yourself. Again.”

He didn’t answer, not really. Just a soft, brief noise that might’ve been acknowledgment, if only in theory.

“And the criminal?” Her voice slowed—just a fraction. Less fury now. More calculation. “We had systems in place for humane removal. Sedation injections. Tide-stabilizers. Even remote units we could have expended in worse case scenarios.”

He stopped.

The wind shifted around him, the scent of burnt circuitry and char still clinging to the air. He looked toward the heart of the city, the structures still standing like shadows behind stained glass.

“Unfortunately,” he said, voice cool as dusk, “he didn’t make it.”

Silence from the other side.

Not disapproval. Not shock.

Just silence.

Goldweaver had known him long enough to recognize when the conversation was closing, whether she liked it or not. She also knew what it meant when his voice slipped into that edge—where control overtook anything human, where he moved like something designed for aftermaths.

And yet—she still asked, quieter this time, “His name?”

The pause that followed stretched.

Too long.

When he answered, he didn’t look back.

“Doesn’t matter.”

He cut the channel.

Behind him, the remnants of the rift flared again—faint warping across the edge of the skyline, the Tide trying, stubbornly, to linger. It wouldn’t win. Not this time.

He pressed forward, pace quickening as the structure behind him groaned in warning. Another breach wave. He could feel it in the air, tension prickling like static on skin. Trinnon was almost there, which meant the final phase would begin soon—total cleansing.

He made it to the outskirts just as the sky above the facility blanched white.

The light wasn’t blinding—but absolute. A dome of purity, unfurling with precision, swallowing the corruption whole. The ground shuddered under the weight of it, the force of the purge cleansing every twisted remnant with brutal efficiency. Whatever was left in that building wouldn’t survive. Not even memory.

Mydei barely cleared the edge, stumbling forward onto a ridge of half-buried stone. Dust scraped at his lungs. He fell to one knee, bracing himself, breath caught in his throat.

He stayed there for a long moment, unmoving. His body wasn’t broken, but it had been too close. Far too close.

The comms crackled faintly again—no voice, just the quiet return of connection.

He didn’t answer immediately.

When he did, it was even.

“Chrysos Heir Mydeimos.  Returning to central node.” A pause. Then, steadier: “No casualties remaining.”

He stood, brushing ash from his sleeve.

There would be questions. Briefings. Reports.

But right now, all that mattered was that he walked away.

Then. The sky split with the rush of wings.

A shadow passed overhead—large, swift, scouting. Mydei barely needed to look up to know what it was. The rhythmic beat of its flight was too distinct, the presence too controlled to be anything else.

The dragon circled once, then descended, landing with a force that sent loose debris skittering. Dust kicked up, but before it could settle, a figure shifted from its back, peering down.

Castorice.

Blood streaked her clothing—none of it hers. Her scythe rested against her back, but she carried herself as if she could summon it to her hand in an instant. Her gaze met his, steady, unreadable. Then, with the barest tilt of her head, as if to say, You need a ride?

Mydei didn’t hesitate.

With practiced ease, he hauled himself onto the dragon’s back, settling just behind her. The moment he was secure, the beast moved, powerful muscles tensing before launching them into the air. Wind rushed past, the ruined cityscape shrinking beneath them.

From the corner of his eye, he caught the faintest curve of Castorice’s lips.

The Black Tide breach had been no accident.

It had taken only hours for the truth to surface—official negligence, a failure in oversight that had allowed the corruption to seep through the facility’s weakened defenses. The fallout was immediate. Arrests were made. Officials stripped of power.

But the consequences didn’t end there.

The department responsible for Tide containment, once an independent branch with near-total jurisdiction over incidents like this, was swiftly demoted. In its place, a new leadership structure formed—one that placed greater emphasis on cooperation with external forces.

Specifically, with vigilantes.

It wasn’t a complete shift. Vigilantes had always been legally recognized, but they operated outside the direct oversight of government-backed heroes. Now, their involvement was not only permitted but quietly encouraged. The public, still reeling from the devastation, placed their trust in those who had acted first, without hesitation—regardless of their official status.

Not everyone approved.

Tensions simmered between traditional heroes and those who worked outside the system. Some viewed the change as necessary, a long-overdue acknowledgment of the role vigilantes played. Others saw it as a threat—a blurring of the line between sanctioned enforcement and unregulated power.

For Mydei, it wasn’t his fight.

He stayed where he was needed, boots on the ground, helping with the cleanup effort. He hadn’t intended to linger—his original destination was elsewhere—but watching the city pull itself back together shifted something in him.

The streets were a mess. Ruined structures loomed like hollowed-out ribs, and the scars of the Tide’s presence remained in the blackened cracks and distorted surfaces. But amid the wreckage, there was movement.

People—volunteers, survivors, heroes, vigilantes—all working together. Clearing debris, offering supplies, ensuring no one was left behind. There was no division here, no argument over status or jurisdiction. Only action.

It was rare, seeing something like this.

A moment where the weight of everything didn’t crush people apart—but pulled them closer.

Mydei took it in. Then, without ceremony, he stepped forward and joined them.

For hours, Mydei worked alongside the volunteers, clearing rubble, stabilizing structures, doing what needed to be done. Some people approached him with quiet gratitude—shopkeepers, workers, people who had recognized his silhouette during the worst of the disaster.

Each time, he responded simply. “No need. This is my responsibility.”

It wasn’t humility. Just a fact.

Then the elderly came.

An old woman took his hand, squeezing it with surprising strength, her eyes shimmering with unshed tears as she whispered blessings. Another grasped his wrist, her voice trembling as she thanked him for saving her grandson.

And Mydei—who had faced horrors and monsters without flinching—stood still, uncertain.

He let them hold on as long as they needed. He bowed his head when they murmured their thanks.

And when a child tugged at his sleeve, he knelt.

A group of them had gathered near the cleared rubble, wide-eyed and whispering. One of them, a boy with dust-streaked cheeks, pointed at him.

“You’re really strong.”

A girl with a missing front tooth nodded. “Are you a hero?”

“No,” Mydei said, shaking dirt from his gloves.

The boy frowned. “A vigilante?”

“Something like that.”

“Do you fight bad guys?”

“Yes.”

The children exchanged glances, and then, as if on cue, they broke into action—punching the air, kicking invisible enemies, making exaggerated sound effects. One, for some reason, started rolling on the ground.

Mydei watched in silence, then huffed. Not quite a laugh, but close.

Then movement caught his attention.

A convoy of white vehicles pulled in, emblazoned with the insignia of the Special Medical Response Team. Their personnel stood out—clean, efficient, specialized for high-risk contamination zones.

And among them was a familiar figure.

Hyacine.

She moved quickly through the field, tending to patients with practiced ease. Unlike the other Chrysos Heirs, she wasn’t a fighter. She didn’t need to be. Her strength lay elsewhere—healer, assistant, support. Someone who saved lives in ways that didn’t require masks or codenames.

Then she saw him.

Her entire expression brightened.

“Mydei!” She practically skipped over, radiating warmth despite the destruction around them. “Oh, thank goodness—I was hoping I’d run into

you!”

She stopped in front of him, tilting her head as she scanned him over. “You’re all in one piece… right?”

“I’m fine.”

She let out a relieved sigh. “You look exhausted. Have you even sat down?”

“I’ve had worse.”

She frowned, hands on her hips. “That’s not the same as an answer.”

He didn’t respond. She sighed.

“Well, at least you’re alive,” she said, then added, more brightly, “Oh! Do you need medical attention? It’s not too late to sit down for a check-up, you know!”

He gave her a look.

She giggled. “Okay, okay, I won’t pester you… for now.”

There was a pause before Mydei spoke again, quieter this time. “You’ve been treating patients all day.”

“Yep! Non-stop since we got the all-clear to move in.”

His fingers twitched at his side. “Did you treat anyone with white hair? Blue eyes?”

Hyacine blinked, then tapped a finger against her chin, thinking. “White hair and blue eyes… oh! Yes, I did! He just left, actually.”

Mydei’s gaze sharpened. “Left?”

She nodded. “I know, right? I was surprised, too! He was in the worst part of the city for hours, but when he came in for evaluation—” she gestured vaguely, “—he was fine. Like, barely affected at all.”

Mydei frowned.

Hyacine continued, “Everyone was so shocked that they actually asked him to consider joining this new civilian defense program! He’s kind of a miracle case.”

He narrowed his eyes slightly. “And?”

She puffed her cheeks. “He refused. Completely.”

That wasn’t surprising. But still.

Hyacine sighed. “I tried to talk him into at least considering it, but nope! He just smiled and said, ‘I appreciate the offer, but I have my own path to walk.’”

Mydei exhaled slowly. That sounded about right. He loved Phainon, truly, but only he’d say something like that.

Hyacine rocked on her heels. “He was polite about it, but he definitely wasn’t changing his mind. Then he left! Not in a rush, just… like he already knew where he was going next, so he should be fine.”

Mydei didn’t say anything at first. Then, finally, he inclined his head.

“Thanks, Hyacine.”

“Of course! Let me know if you need anything, okay?” She beamed, then hesitated. “…And please try to rest at some point.”

He said nothing.

She sighed, shaking her head fondly before hurrying back to her work.

Mydei remained where he was for a moment.

Then, finally, he turned and walked away.

He had been searching for nearly an hour when he finally found him.

Phainon stood at the edge of a quiet street, leaning slightly against a railing, watching the remnants of the night’s disaster fade into the distance. The uneven glow of the streetlights cast long shadows over his figure, highlighting the exhaustion in his posture, the careful stillness of someone who had spent far too long holding himself together.

At Mydei’s approach, Phainon turned, his gaze honing as he took in the red-clad figure before him.

For a brief moment, there was hesitation—then recognition.

“…Godslayer.”

Mydei exhaled slowly. Even now, hearing that name directed at him felt strange. But he pushed that aside.

“You’re still standing,” he said. It wasn’t quite a question, but there was something pointed in the way he said it.

Phainon’s mouth quirked, something almost like amusement flickering in his expression. “I was given the all-clear by the medical team. They seemed more surprised about it than I was.”

Understandable.

“…And the child?” Mydei asked after a beat.

“Safe,” Phainon answered. “Reunited with her family.”

Something in Mydei’s chest eased, though he only gave a short nod. “Good.”

A pause. Then—

“I’ll walk you home.”

Phainon blinked, visibly caught off guard. “That isn’t necessary.”

“Didn’t ask if it was.”

Phainon gave him a long look, as if trying to read his intentions. “…I appreciate the offer, but I can assure you, I am not in any danger.”

“I know.” Mydei’s tone was unhurried but didn’t lack conviction, “I’ll still walk you home.”

Another hesitation.

Then, finally, with a quiet breath, Phainon gave a small nod. “…Very well.”

They started walking.

The city around them was still in disarray, but there was a quiet effort in the way people moved—volunteers clearing debris, healers tending to the wounded, small clusters of survivors reuniting under the pale glow of the streetlights. The aftermath of a storm, but one that hadn’t completely drowned the city.

Mydei let himself focus on that. The steady rhythm of footsteps, the distant murmur of conversation, the rare moment of quiet that settled between them.

Then—

“I take it there was some unfinished business.”

Goldweaver’s voice, smooth and unhurried, filled his earpiece.

Mydei’s stride didn’t falter, but his jaw clenched.

“And here I thought you weren’t the sentimental type.”

He didn’t hesitate. He reached up and disconnected the channel without a word.

Phainon glanced at him, faintly curious. “Something urgent?”

“…Nothing that needs addressing.”

Phainon didn’t pry. He simply nodded and kept walking.

And Mydei, without even realizing it, fell into step beside him.

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Mydei Jr. Deserved Better
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Phainon signs up for a civilian defense course without reading the fine print, promptly regrets it, names a training dummy “Mydei Jr.,” and nearly gets replaced by a clone with better posture. Mydei saves the day (and their fake child), Phainon flirts through an identity crisis, and somehow they leave more emotionally bonded than when they started. 10/10 romance, 0/10 government oversight.

Chapter Notes

Half of this was written pre 3.2 the other post, and then at the end (abt roughly at the clone scene) it was kind of rushed for certain reasons so sorry abt that💔

Hope the quality wasn’t too bad by the end, I needed a breather after that😭 Enjoy <33

Phainon sat on the park bench, gingerly pressing the side of his face. The sting had dulled, but the memory hadn’t. A few curious birds hopped near his boots, one of them tilting its head up at him like it, too, had just witnessed a man get obliterated by the palm of someone 2 centimeters shorter and way too handsome to be that violent.

“Damn,” Phainon muttered under his breath, flexing his jaw. “That man has arms.”

A squirrel chittered nearby, and for a second, he considered taking that personally.

The breeze was nice, at least. The kind of spring air that made the city feel deceptively normal again, despite the fact half of it had been swallowed by otherworldly corruption just last week. People passed by with coffee cups

and grocery bags, too busy returning to their lives to notice one of the Black Tide survivors sulking on public property. He had a hoodie pulled halfway up—not because he was cold, but because he was still emotionally nursing the absolute hellfire of a slap he’d received from his boyfriend.

Which, to be clear, was after the reunion. Not during. Not in place of it. After.

And oh, what a reunion it had been.

Phainon had turned a corner in the wreckage and found him—Mydei, alive, whole, shaken but standing. He hadn’t been expecting it. One second he’d been scanning the crumbled streets, the next there was Mydei, backlit by smoke and unnatural golden haze, eyes wide like he wasn’t sure Phainon was real. For a moment, neither of them said a word. Just looked.

Then Mydei broke. His knees gave out, and Phainon caught him before he could fall. The whole world around them had smelled like blood and ozone, but Mydei had buried his face in Phainon’s shoulder, breathing him in like he was air and safety and proof the sky hadn’t fallen completely.

Phainon remembered holding him, arms firm around that trembling back, and thinking something terrifying and stupid like I’d do it all again.

Then five minutes later, Mydei had stepped back, asked a single question —“Where were you?”—and upon hearing that Phainon had snuck out of the shelters, into the danger zone, and spent the next several hours helping pull survivors from buildings like he thought he was immortal—

Well.

Slap.

There was no ceremony to it. No windup. No dramatic monologue. Just pure, full-body fury compressed into a perfectly executed strike that damn near rearranged Phainon’s internal compass.

His teeth still felt slightly misaligned.

Phainon tilted his head back now, watching the clouds drift by. “To be fair,” he said to no one, “I did deserve it.”

He heard again, in memory, the sharp crack of that palm meeting his cheek. He could still see Mydei’s face—eyes rimmed with leftover grief and something that looked too much like betrayal. His lips had been pressed tight, fists shaking at his sides like he wasn’t sure if he wanted to hug Phainon again or throw him through a wall.

Probably both.

“He’d clearly been waiting to do that for a while,” Phainon murmured, touching his cheek again with something dangerously close to fondness. “Guess it was overdue.”

He sulked a little deeper into the bench, hoodie slipping further over his face. The ache was dull now, fading. What lingered was not pain, not really —just the warmth of knowing someone cared enough to be that furious. A slap laced with love. Or at least with deeply affectionate homicide.

God, he was in too deep.

He didn’t even know if he was more flattered or aroused.

Probably both.

The city had no right to look this normal.

Phainon’s fingers drummed against the bench slat, slow and irregular. A mother pushed a stroller past him. Somewhere, a construction drone hummed through a half-finished building frame, patching steel with movements too fluid to be human. Storefronts that were craters a week ago now shined with fresh paint. No one was smiling, exactly, but no one was screaming either. The city didn’t heal—it was forcibly stitched back together. Brick and glass and quiet desperation, dragged into place by people who didn’t sleep.

Or didn’t have to.

Phainon watched the clean horizon with the distant look of someone trying not to look too closely. He knew what was behind it. Who was behind it.

The Chrysos Heirs.

He didn’t hate them. It’d be too easy if he did. Easier to shove them in a box labeled problematic idols with a hero complex and toss it into the fire. But the truth was messier, more apathetic. He didn’t worship them, didn’t really care to understand them. They were just there. Vigilantes who operated above any law but their own, who pretended the world could be purified if you just pressed hard enough on the dirt.

He was different.

He didn’t bother purifying things.

Phainon shifted, arms draped along the back of the bench languidly. He’d killed people during the chaos. Only the worst ones. The ones looting through bodies, the ones dragging women into collapsed buildings. Not a court on earth would’ve touched them. They never did. But he did. Quietly, cleanly.

And he didn’t lose sleep over it.

But Godslayer…

His brow twitched.

Godslayer was also different.

Phainon hadn’t seen him coming—no heroic pose, no dramatic intro. Just a ripple of energy cutting through the Tide, breaking it apart long enough for the path to clear. And Phainon had followed. That had been the plan. He was almost out. Almost.

Then the Tide split the ground beneath him, and he’d frozen.

He hadn’t planned on that.

It came from nowhere—his muscles locked, lungs stalled, heart climbing his ribs with a quiet, rising panic. The Tide rose between them, a black wave with teeth, and he just stood there, feet cemented to the broken earth like a child watching the sea swallow something they couldn’t name.

Phainon’s hand curled loosely against his thigh. Skin taut across knuckles. Tension sinking in slow.

He thought he was over that kind of thing.

Apparently not.

He stared straight ahead, posture slack but coiled underneath. Then, with a sharp breath through his nose, he let it go. Hand loosened. Shoulder rolled.

“Anyway,” he murmured.

Godslayer had dragged him back across the barrier, voice sharp, movements tighter than necessary. He’d scolded Phainon like they knew each other. It was too close. Too personal.

He’d said his name.

I need you to trust me.

And he hadn’t asked. He hadn’t guessed.

He’d known.
