That was the part that didn’t sit right. Not the tone. Not the authority. Just the familiarity. The way Godslayer’s hand had lingered a second too long on his shoulder. The way his expression had cracked when Phainon winced. It wasn’t performative concern. It was worry barely restrained behind control. And not the general vigilante kind, either.

His.

And then there were the tics. Small things. The twitch in his left hand before speaking. The strange way he shifted his weight when standing still.

Even the phrasing—blunt and clumsy and weirdly endearing, like he didn’t want to intimidate him but still had to get his point across.

It reminded Phainon of someone.

He couldn’t put his finger on it, but it was like a word on the tip of his tongue, a voice echoing at just the wrong pitch, a face blurred at the edges of recognition. It crawled under his skin and settled in his ribs, right next to something he wasn’t ready to dig out yet.

He leaned back again, spine touching the cool metal of the bench rail. Breathing steady. Unblinking.

The sky was dull above him—washed gray like cheap fabric left out in the rain. The kind of day where everything felt paused, waiting for a cue that wouldn’t come.

He hated waiting.

He hated the way silence filled itself up with questions. The way his mind moved too fast when nothing else did.

He hated how long he’d been thinking about this.

Phainon ran a hand down his face, fingers brushing the edge of his jaw— still faintly sore from the slap.

“Gods,” he muttered, half-laughing under his breath. “I need a hobby.”

But he didn’t move.

He just sat there, letting the weight of everything he hadn’t said settle across his shoulders again.

And then, something bounced off the back of Phainon’s skull.

Not hard enough to hurt. Just enough to be intentional.

He blinked, turned his head, and stared down at the plush animal now rolling to a stop beside his foot. Chimera. Two-headed, stitched awkwardly together, little felt wings flopped sideways like they’d given up halfway through flying. Some kid’s toy.

Or, more accurately, his boyfriend’s.

Phainon picked it up and held it aloft by the scruff of its mismatched mane. “Really?” he called out, tone flat.

Mydei sat down on the bench next to him without a word.

Which was already suspicious. The silence. The weird, smooth calm. The way he didn’t even look at Phainon after pelting him with cuddly wildlife. That was the kind of composure only possible when someone was either plotting something or had finally lost their grip on reality. And with Mydei, it could honestly go either way.

Phainon eyed him sidelong. “So… you hitting me with adorable mythical creatures now? Is this a warning? A threat? A seduction?”

Mydei said nothing.

Even worse.

Phainon opened his mouth to speak again—but barely got the breath in before Mydei suddenly grabbed his collar.

“—wha—hello?”

His voice cracked upward in shock as Mydei tugged the fabric sharply, popping the first two buttons open with no hesitation. Phainon’s chest was suddenly on full display, pale and mostly unmarked except for the familiar smattering of old scars and the brand of someone who picked too many fights in his younger years and won most of them.

He blinked down at him.

“Bold of you to undress me in public. I mean—flattered, obviously, but I was hoping for dinner first.”

Nothing. Mydei didn’t even flinch.

Phainon smirked faintly, leaning back a little with all the faux-sultry bravado of a man very used to being ignored mid-flirt. “If you wanted me shirtless, you could’ve just asked. I have a whole routine for that. Music and everything. Real scandalous. Gets rave reviews.”

Still no reaction.

And that’s when he noticed Mydei’s hand. The way it hesitated, hovering near his sternum. The way his fingers lightly traced the edge of one rib, then slid to his side. He was through, too precise to be casual.

Phainon’s smile faded, eyebrows dipping just a little.

Ah.

He was checking.

The laughter stuck somewhere in his throat. Not because it was awkward— but because he didn’t expect it to hurt. Not like this.

“…Hey,” he said quietly. “I’m fine. I already got cleared, remember?”

Mydei didn’t answer. His gaze scanned across Phainon’s torso, sharp and quick and far too anxious for someone trying to act calm. His fingers twitched once, then steadied, brushing along skin like the residue of the Black Tide might still be lurking beneath it. Something clung to him, desperate and coiled.

Phainon didn’t move. Didn’t joke again.

He just watched him, eyes softening with a kind of ache he didn’t let out very often.

Because it wasn’t about the potential contamination.

It was about being sure.

Mydei finished a moment later, hand still at Phainon’s collar. He didn’t say anything when he let go.

Phainon reached up, slowly fixing the buttons himself—not that it helped. His chest still felt exposed. But not from the cold.

“…Thanks for the plushie, by the way,” he added, lightly, but his voice didn’t quite match the grin that tried to form. “Very aggressive delivery. I give it a seven out of ten.”

No answer.

Not yet.

But that was fine.

Phainon could sit with silence.

Especially if it was this kind.

Phainon barely had time to do anything before Mydei stood up like he was about to leave, brushing off his hands and turning halfway like he’d changed his mind mid-motion. Phainon opened his mouth to stop him—no clue what he’d say, probably something to stop him—but Mydei beat him to it.

“Phainon.”

He blinked, caught off guard by the way his name landed in the air—less like a question, more like a warning.

“Have you ever trained with weapons?”

There was a pause. Then a longer one. Then Phainon leaned forward slightly, squinting at him like he was trying to read through the question.

“…What an odd question,” he said at last, slow, measured, smile stretched too far. “Why? You planning to kill me?”

Mydei didn’t answer. His expression didn’t even twitch.

That made Phainon straighten a little. “Seriously though—any reason you’re asking?”

Silence.

He ran a hand through his hair, gears in his head beginning to click with more urgency than they should’ve. Something about the way Mydei asked felt targeted. Specific.

He thought back. Black Tide. The disaster. The chaos. The fact that he, against all logic, picked up a metal pipe and wielded it like a sword to draw a path for trapped civilians—an improvised solution. Godslayer had seen him do it. He was suspicious—Godslayer had questioned him even in the middle of an apocalypse—and Phainon, like the menace he was, said it was old training from an ancient dueling hall that got shut down. Total lie. Godslayer didn’t question it at the time.

But only Godslayer had been there. No one else.

So how the hell did Mydei—

The train of thought picked up speed. Phainon sat back a little, chewing the inside of his cheek. There were… ticks. The way Godslayer had spoken. Too familiar. Too worried. A hand twitch. Proximity issues. The way he’d yelled his name before pulling him across the broken barrier of the Tide.

His brows dipped.

No. That was impossible. Mydei couldn’t be—

His brain hit the brakes, practically skidding. No. No way. He dismissed the idea with a breath, waving it off internally like a bad punchline. He was spiraling. Overthinking. Godslayer had probably heard someone yell his

name. Or… maybe he’d mentioned the dueling hall lie to Mydei too, and just didn’t remember. Had he? When?

He started scanning through their past conversations like a mental archive, suddenly suspicious of every word he’d ever said to Mydei. Did he ever act out something dumb in front of him? Accidentally show off? Leave a trail?

He didn’t get to answer that. Because Mydei blurted:

“I wanna learn how to use a sword.”

Phainon blinked. Again.

Mydei immediately looked away, shoulders stiff. That… wasn’t what he’d meant to say. That much was clear.

“Wait, what?” Phainon said, but Mydei was already talking again, fast. If he didn’t know better he’d think Mydei was trying to bury a body and pretend he was gardening.

“There’s a new civilian defense program,” he said, eyes fixed on something very, very interesting on the floor. “It’s a government and vigilante collaboration. The Chrysos Heirs are involved. I thought—I don’t know. If something like that happened again… it’d be good to be prepared. And. I didn’t want to join it alone.” He shifted awkwardly. “But I figured you wouldn’t want to, anyway. So I was just asking. If you had experience. Or could teach me instead. If not. It’s fine.”

That was, objectively, the worst excuse Phainon had ever heard.

And still—adorable.

This man had baked up a whole half-lie, brought in vague governmental forces, vigilante programs, and an entire potential hypothetical natural disaster again—just to not say “please come with me.”

Phainon felt the laughter flickering in his chest and swallowed it down, smiling wide.

“Okay,” he said.

Mydei looked up, puzzled. “What?”

Phainon stood, dusted himself off with more flair than necessary, and said, “Let’s join the program.”

The silence Mydei gave him was too stunned to be anything but genuine.

Phainon grinned like the sun and reached forward, ruffling Mydei’s hair before he could duck away. “C’mon, you’re awful at asking for things. Lucky for you, I’m great at agreeing.”

He walked a few steps before throwing a look over his shoulder.

“What kind of idiot would do something like this for a guy?” he said, almost amused, hands in his blue hoodie pockets like he hadn’t just rearranged his schedule, risked a full month of violent, screaming admin hell from Anaxa, and tanked every ounce of free time he had for the next four weeks. “Anyway, I’m normal.”

And then, as if he hadn’t just dropped that emotional piano on the park bench and walked off, he was already pulling up his phone, tapping away as he murmured, “We should color-code our outfits. Coordinated vigilante aesthetics. I want a patch. A patch that says ‘Mydei’s Favorite.’ Or maybe ‘Assistant Sword Holder.’ Something with range.”

He didn’t see the way Mydei just stood there, staring at him like he’d made some grave, irreversible mistake.

The registration desk was chaos. Organized, orderly chaos, but still chaos.

They stood behind a woman loudly arguing about whether bringing her dog counted as “emotional support armament,” while a teenage recruit waved a digital clipboard in their faces asking if either of them had any experience with crossbows, civilian trauma response, or “chokepoint maneuvering” (whatever the hell that was).

Phainon blinked at him. “I once watched someone choke on a breadstick. Does that count?”

The clipboard kid moved on without comment.

When they finally reached the front, the clerk behind the desk—a tired-looking guy with a badge that read I Am Just a Volunteer—handed them each a stack of forms and an ocular scan pad.

Phainon didn’t even sit. He leaned on the counter, skimmed absolutely nothing, and began signing with the confidence of a man who hadn’t read a legal document in his life.

Mydei watched him, arms crossed. “You’re not even looking at the waivers.”

“That’s because looking implies I have something to lose,” Phainon replied, dotting the last signature with a flourish. “Also, I already memorized your emergency contact. I’ll just scream your name in case I die.”

Mydei pinched the bridge of his nose.

As Phainon handed back the tablet with a little bow, he turned and asked, far too casually, “Wait. Is it still legally binding if I didn’t understand anything I signed?”

The volunteer gave a thumbs up without looking up. Mydei, meanwhile, stared at his boyfriend like he was re-evaluating every life choice that had led him to this moment.

Phainon leaned toward him, stage-whispering: “If we end up conscripted into some government-blessed vigilante army, I want matching jackets. I was serious about that. Yours says ‘Sword Dad,’ mine says ‘Hot Liability.’”

Mydei didn’t respond. Just took his own clipboard, calmly filled it out, and submitted everything with silent, seething grace.

This was his life now.

And unfortunately, he loved the idiot.

“You know,” Phainon said as they rounded a corner, “if we die in this program, I want it noted that I won’t perish thirsty.”

Mydei didn’t slow his pace. “We start in five minutes.”

“That’s five whole minutes of hydration opportunity,” Phainon countered, already veering off the sidewalk toward the first vending kiosk he saw. “And I happen to think I’d fight better if slightly sugared and carbonated.”

Mydei gave him a weird look, but followed anyway. Phainon scanned the menu like he was evaluating fine wines, then jabbed a button with zero hesitation.

The machine rumbled before reluctantly coughing out a tall, unreasonably bright drink labeled Scorchberry Heat. It fizzed at the top like it might be flammable.

Mydei read the label. “That has chili extract in it.”

“Yeah,” Phainon said, already sipping. “Spicy.”

Mydei looked away like he couldn’t believe he was in love with this man.

They walked the rest of the path with only the occasional slurp from Phainon’s drink filling the silence. The streets were quieter here—closer to the training complex, more regulated, lined with caution signs and too-clean sidewalks. Even rebuilt, the city still carried the scent of sterilized aftermath.

Phainon was in the middle of recounting a story about a dog who had once stolen his sandal mid-street duel when Mydei suddenly stopped.

Someone had bumped into him.

The contact wasn’t aggressive—just a misstep, accidental. But the shift in the air afterward wasn’t.

Phainon paused mid-sip.

The man was older, taller than Mydei, with a sharp, weathered face and a soldier’s spine. His eyes—steely, worn—narrowed as they landed on Mydei. His tone, when he spoke, was deceptively soft.

“Mydeimos.”

Phainon blinked. Mydei had gone still. Tension rolled off him like waves of heat from a forge. His jaw set. His eyes narrowed. There was something ancient in that expression, some silent wildfire tamped behind his pupils.

Phainon, entirely out of sync with the moment, took another sip. Loudly.

“Mm,” he said. “Spicy.”

Neither of them reacted.

They just kept staring.

Mydei’s hand twitched slightly by his side—barely noticeable, unless you knew to look.

The older man’s gaze didn’t waver. His presence wasn’t aggressive, not exactly—but he held himself like someone used to being listened to. The kind of man who could command a room with a glance. A mentor. A general. A ghost from another life.

Phainon blinked once more, then leaned around Mydei slightly and said, with polite cheer, “Sorry, do you two know each other? Or is this just the world’s most intense sidewalk encounter?”

Still locked in the stare-down, Mydei exhaled slowly through his nose and said, “Phainon… meet Krateros.”

Phainon’s brain took exactly one second to compute. Then:

“Oh,” he said. And then again, brighter: “Ohhhh. Your teacher.”

Instant transformation. His voice took on that buttery, flirtatious lilt that usually preceded him getting slapped or kissed. “Sir. It’s an honor. I’ve heard so much about you. Your posture? Impeccable. Honestly, you carry yourself like someone who’s won wars and a pie-baking contest.”

Krateros looked at him. Once.

And then completely ignored him, eyes returning to Mydei without a word.

Phainon was not offended. He leaned in closer to Mydei and whispered, “He is kinda scary. I see the appeal.”

Mydei didn’t dignify that with a response. His focus was still on Krateros— jaw tight, gaze hard. Whatever history lingered between them, it wasn’t a soft one.

Phainon sipped again, the straw making a soft hollow sound at the bottom of the cup.

Silence.

Then Krateros finally spoke. “You’re participating in the Civilian Defense Course?”

Mydei’s mouth moved like he was about to answer—but before he could, Krateros glanced, just for a second, at Phainon.

That one look told him everything.

Mydei’s subtle shift. His unreadable glance. The small nod. Krateros didn’t ask again.

Instead, he said, “Good.”

And that was that.

The building rose from the ground like something carved from purpose itself—clean lines, gleaming panels, and the kind of reinforced structure

that screamed government money and lots of it. A wide banner above the entrance read: CIVILIAN DEFENSE INITIATIVE – IN COLLABORATION WITH THE CHRYSOS HEIRS.

Below that, in less glamorous text: Orientation Begins Promptly at 8:00 a.m.

Phainon and Mydei made it through the double glass doors at 8:00 and forty-seven seconds.

The instructor standing at the front—tall, tired, already regretting his job— clocked them immediately. His arms were crossed. His expression didn’t shift. Didn’t need to.

Phainon coughed.

Mydei looked away.

They shuffled into line like the picture of innocent punctuality. If innocent punctuality had shadows under its eyes and a Scorchberry Heat cup hastily shoved into the nearest trash bin.

Inside, the facility opened into an atrium that looked more like a military-grade training complex than a public civilian program. Floor-to-ceiling screens pulsed with digital maps. The walls were lined with reinforced padding and modular weapon racks. Observation balconies stretched high above them, most likely for supervisors or overfunded Chrysos interns with clipboards and superiority complexes.

Phainon tilted his head back and gave a low whistle. “Either this place makes superheroes… or war criminals.”

“Both,” Mydei muttered.

They were quickly ushered into an orientation hall, papers shoved at them, a woman in a blazer rapid-firing the rules in a monotone blur that sounded like she’d memorized it against her will. Phainon once again , signed everything upside down and backwards. Mydei didn’t comment until after.

“You know that might’ve signed you up for organ donation, right?”

“If I die in combat, my pancreas should at least get a shot at heroism.”

They were split into squads next, sent through sleek hallways into a second, expansive chamber: the training facility proper. Here, it was all polished impact floors, mirrored walls, and sectioned sparring rings. Equipment gleamed in tidy lines. Instructors stood at attention like someone had told them this was the Olympics. Probably had been.

Phainon’s voice dropped low. “Krateros definitely hates me.”

“He doesn’t hate you,” Mydei said. Then, after a beat, “He just doesn’t like you.”

Phainon slouched in melodramatic despair.

“Bad first impressions happen,” Mydei said, patting him once on the back with all the sympathy he could muster. “There’s always next time.”

“Next time he’ll poison my lunch.”

They were herded to their designated section—Station C—and paired up for warm-up drills. A nearby instructor barked the orders: “Combat stances! Basic counters! If your partner breaks a limb, do it cleaner next time!”

Phainon’s expression brightened. “They get me here.”

Most of the participants were clearly new—wobbly knees, late reactions, the occasional flinch when someone raised a fist. Phainon looked comfortably average by comparison. He moved well enough, like someone who maybe had seen combat but was humble enough not to brag about it.

Too well.

Mydei squinted at him as Phainon executed a near-perfect sidestep that flowed straight into a restrained counter-grab.

“You’re pulling your punches,” Mydei muttered.

Phainon blinked at him. “What? Me? Never. I’m average. Dangerously average. A solid C+ in fisticuffs.”

“You did a counter only trained scouts use.”

“I saw it in a documentary.”

“You adjusted your stance for southpaw three moves ago.”

“I’m adaptive. It’s my charm.”

Mydei stared at him like he was trying to x-ray his soul.

“You’re hiding how good you are.”

Phainon shrugged with zero guilt. “Maybe I’m just modest.”

“You’re many things. Modest isn’t one of them.”

Before Phainon could retort, someone nearby—a girl in a grey compression suit, sweat already dripping down her forehead—looked over at Mydei and asked, a little too casually:

“Wait. Weren’t you training under Krateros since you were ten?”

Silence fell like a sword.

Phainon stopped mid-step. His brow arched, sharp and slow. He turned toward Mydei with the full weight of someone about to unearth a goldmine.

Mydei turned his head with agonizing calm. Stared at the girl.

She immediately looked away.

Phainon leaned in, voice blank. “Since you were ten?”

“That’s classified.”

Phainon paused just long enough to almost process it, then gave a lopsided grin like it made perfect sense. “Wow. My boyfriend’s a librarian and a Krateros-trained combat prodigy. Dragging me into a civilian program just to let me flex a little. I feel so honored.

“Correct.”

“And you’re still blushing.”

Mydei’s face definitely turned pink.

Phainon laughed, loud and pleased, narrowly dodging Mydei’s retaliatory swipe.

The instructor shot them both a look. Again.

They coughed in unison.

Back to stance.

The break came fast, and the instructors wasted no time splitting everyone up. A few names were called out—some volunteers, some clearly handpicked—and those individuals were directed toward different corners of the facility. A few even got taken aside for what looked like one-on-one assessments, instructors murmuring quietly to them as clipboards came out. It wasn’t subtle.

Phainon lingered near the water station, cup in hand, already plotting his quiet exit from the next half of the session. This was exactly why he’d said no the first time someone brought up this program to him. All it took was showing a little potential, and suddenly you were a “prospect.” Next came the offers—extra sessions, off-the-record evaluations, meaningless government-adjacent missions dressed up like some noble cause. He didn’t need any of that. He already did what needed doing.

He sipped the water like it was wine and kept his eyes away from the crowd.

But then Mydei got picked.

Of course he did—he walked like someone who knew how to handle a blade and stood like someone who hated being watched for it. One of the instructors waved him toward the far side of the room, where the more advanced group was being assembled. Mydei didn’t argue. Just nodded once and started walking.

Phainon, as per plan, stayed planted.

Or he would’ve, if Mydei hadn’t slowed down, turned halfway, and— without ceremony—reached back to grab his hand. Like it was the most natural thing in the world. No look, no words, just a casual come on tug.

And what was Phainon supposed to do? Say no? Yell “Sorry, I can’t, I’m a shadowy antihero who works better alone”?

So he let himself be pulled along. Of course he did.

The second training area was set up deeper in the building, larger and more stripped-down, built less for practice and more for performance. Luckily, they weren’t the only ones shuffled over. A decent-sized group was already filtering in, weapons and training gear issued in orderly stacks, instructors taking positions.

Not too elite, then. Just advanced enough to weed out the ones who couldn’t keep up.

Fine by him. He could pretend.

He was good at pretending.

The third training segment was Simulation Missions.

The next room after was massive—vaulted ceilings, black-tiled walls fitted with emitters that flickered faintly like stars. A series of complex projectors and hard-light generators were suspended from steel beams above, whirring softly. It looked less like a gym and more like someone hijacked a tech lab and gave it more than a few little tweaks.

Once inside, instructors handed out slim wristbands and brief explanations. “These generate your environment,” one of them said, tone bored like this wasn’t the coolest thing Phainon had seen all day. “Your task is simple— rescue and extraction. Keep civilians safe. Contain the threat. Don’t die.”

No pressure.

The “civilians” weren’t basic mannequins either. They were hybrid constructs—part training dummy, part reactive AI, built to simulate panic, injury, and distress. One of them blinked up at Phainon when it activated, mouth opening in a tiny “o” before defaulting to a passive standing position.

“I shall name you… Mydei Junior,” Phainon said solemnly, resting a hand on its shoulder. “You’re braver than your father.”

Mydei, strapping on his own wristband nearby, didn’t even turn around. “I’m not doing this with you.”

“I’m doing this for our child,” Phainon replied, utterly straight-faced.

Then the lights dropped. The simulation began.

Reality dissolved into smoke and static—and rebuilt itself into chaos.

A city street, cracked and flickering with residual energy. The sky above rippled with a diseased, stormy shimmer, and the air vibrated with low distortion, like sound trying to escape a dream. Buildings were warped at odd angles, brick and steel groaning under invisible pressure. The familiar signs of a Black Tide incursion—twisted geometry, air that moved too fast, windows that stared back.

Something screamed in the distance. A corrupted figure burst down the street, limbs writhing in the wrong order. Others followed, glitching in and out, trailing residue like ash and flame.

Phainon drew in a breath. Time to stay perfectly average.

He ducked low, guided Mydei Jr. toward a nearby alley, keeping to the shadows, carefully applying exactly the kind of hesitance one would expect from a civilian-turned-trainee. He didn’t run too fast, didn’t hit too hard. A perfect performance.

Until, of course, the building exploded.

It was a slow, awful thing—walls buckling, the structure groaning like it knew what it was about to do. The Tide twisted its fingers into the foundation, and with a shriek, the floor gave out beneath him. Flames licked the walls. Smoke poured inward. Mydei Jr. let out a piercingly accurate simulation scream and promptly short-circuited in his arms.

“Well, shit,” Phainon muttered, brushing ash off his shoulder. “I’ll get out in a minute.”

Except the exits warped. Doors vanished into the walls. The windows melted like wax.

“I said—” he growled, rolling his neck. The hologram could take a hint.

Then someone kicked the wall in.

Literally kicked it in.

Mydei burst through the smoke like righteous fury wrapped in emergency response protocol. No helmet. No hesitation. Just grabbed Phainon by the collar with one hand and hoisted Mydei Jr. under the other like he did this sort of thing every weekend.

“Dramatic timing,” Phainon coughed as they stumbled outside, still trailing smoke. “I knew you’d come. I believed in you. And in our child.”

Mydei’s breath hitched on a laugh he tried to smother. “You were serious when you named it after me?”

“It screamed like you when it saw a spider.”

“It was a training construct.”

“And yet you’re holding it like you’re about to cradle it to sleep,” Phainon pointed out. “Just saying.”

Mydei didn’t dignify that with a reply. But he was still holding it, still pulling Phainon in a little closer than necessary. His jaw clenched like he had something to say and wasn’t sure how to say it.

Phainon leaned in, singed and smug. “I’d die for you. And our son.”

The simulation signified an end with a sharp bleep. Everything—flames, sky, city—vanished in a wash of static.

They were back in the chamber.

Mydei Jr. lay in Phainon’s arms, slightly melted. Phainon looked down at it fondly.

“He’ll grow up so fast.”

“Phainon,” Mydei said, finally, massaging his temple.

“Don’t thank me,” Phainon murmured. “Being a father is the real mission.”

The simulation fully disappeared with slow fade to white. Holograms dissipated, environments crumbled into digital ash, and the training room’s sterile light returned with a vengeance. Instructors clapped once—just once —as if that was enough to signal both “well done” and “don’t get cocky.”

People started filtering out of their pods or standing from their training zones, some flushed with adrenaline, others looking like they’d just survived actual urban warfare.

Phainon, ash-covered and triumphant, strolled to the evaluation station with Mydei Jr. half-cradled under one arm like a charred baby koala.

A clipboard-bearing official waved him over, barely looking up. “Name?”

“Phainon.”

They tapped the screen. “You were assigned a mid-tier threat level scenario. Scored high on agility, responsiveness, and teamwork. Low marks on regulation protocol.”

“That’s my entire personality,” he said brightly.

The official gave him a slow blink, then turned to Mydei. “You—excellent recovery time. Precision response. Strong marks on environmental adaptability and leadership tracking.”

Mydei nodded like it was a grocery list and not a glowing report.

Phainon held Mydei Jr. closer. “So… can I keep him?”

Both evaluators looked up—finally—and opened their mouths, clearly ready to hit him with a firm no, probably followed by a speech about proprietary government tech.

Then their eyes slid to Mydei. And paused.

Mydei stared back with that same mild, unreadable expression that somehow implied ten layers of both irritation and diplomatic influence. It wasn’t quite a threat. It wasn’t quite anything.

“…I guess,” the official mumbled reluctantly. “Just… don’t get it wet.”

Phainon beamed. “You hear that, Mydei Jr.? You’re free now. You’ll grow up strong and dramatic, just like your other dad.”

He made it five glorious seconds.

Someone behind them—tired, sweaty, distracted—uncapped their water bottle too fast and fumbled the grip. A sudden splash, a sputter of fizz, and then—

SPARK

Mydei Jr. twitched violently in Phainon’s arms. A soft, warbling noise escaped the construct’s speaker like a death rattle in binary. Its eyes

flickered once. Then went dark.

Phainon stood frozen, mouth slightly open. His arms cradled the now-limp husk of what was once his pride and joy. Water pooled around their feet.

The room went dead silent.

Even the person who spilled the water had backed away like they’d just assassinated a diplomat.

Mydei shifted awkwardly beside him. “I—um.” He cleared his throat. “There’s… only one or two more scenarios left today.”

Phainon didn’t move.

Mydei tried again. “We could… name the next one Junior Junior?”

Still nothing.

“…I’ll take that as a maybe.”

Phainon didn’t even blink. He just slowly turned, gaze vacant, Mydei Jr.’s damp frame still in his arms like a fallen soldier.

A single tear might’ve fallen. Or maybe it was condensation.

Either way, the loss was real.

Phainon didn’t speak.

He hadn’t spoken since the tragic, watery demise of Mydei Junior. The synthetic citizen unit lay in his arms, lifeless and short-circuited, its once-vibrant simulation eyes now replaced with a blinking red X and a vaguely mocking shutdown chime. Some off-duty participant had muttered an apology and fled the scene, but the damage was irreversible. Phainon had not moved since.

Mydei lingered near the him awkwardly hovering in solidarity. His hands twitched every few seconds—hovering close to Phainon’s shoulder like he might pat it. Every time, he stopped himself short and pulled away, as if afraid physical contact might make the grief worse.

“Phainon. We’re…Almost done.” Mydei offered quietly, his voice too unsure to count as real comfort.

Phainon’s reply was the softest, most pitiful: “He was barely a day old.”

They were summoned before Mydei could figure out what to say to that.

The next training scenario loaded while the previous team cleared the simulation space. A wide, steel-walled chamber slowly shifted around them, projectors flickering to life as the lights dimmed. The environment shimmered into shape—another fractured city square surrounded by half-demolished buildings, cracked pavement, and emergency tents.

Somewhere, faintly, a simulated siren looped.

The instructor’s voice cut through the illusion: “Crisis Convergence.”

Digital walls rippled with projected smoke once again and distant shouting. The space had expanded to nearly stadium-sized, the air cool from environmental controls. Portable crates appeared with coded markers, supplies highlighted by faint glows in their corner of the staging area.

“Civilians are stranded in a compromised zone. There are structural risks. Some may be infected. You will need to provide first-response aid, screen evacuees for contamination, and ration limited resources.”

Three crates. One labeled medical. One rations. One equipment.

Also present: twelve “citizens.” Semi-sentient constructs—not quite synthetic people, but not inanimate either. Their faces rendered with uncanny humanity, pre-programmed with a dozen personalities, needs, and conflicts. Phainon didn’t name any of them this time.

Probably for the best.

“Teams will split responsibilities. Rescue. Supply. Screening. Choose wisely. Some evacuees may lie.”

That last line was delivered with far too much amusement.

Mydei turned to him slowly. “Which do you want to take?”

Phainon, still mourning, gestured vaguely. “Whichever job lets me avoid emotionally connecting with another fake child.”

Mydei paused. “…Screening?”

“Perfect.”

And with that, they stepped into chaos.

A few hours into the scenario, the fake sunlight hadn’t dimmed once. The simulation’s clock ran off something uncanny, bright and sterile as all things were here and humming faintly over their heads. Most participants had shed their jackets or tied their sleeves back, soaked in the sweat of virtual stress and civilian panic.

Phainon leaned against the edge of the folding table they’d been assigned, hissing under his breath as he clutched his arm. “That woman bit me.”

Mydei didn’t look up from his tablet. “You denied her clearance.”

“She growled at me.” Phainon peeled back the sleeve. The bite wasn’t deep, just impressively toothy. “What was I supposed to do, hand her a juice box and let her in with a souvenir infection?”

“You also called her a walking test tube.”

“It was meant to be educational.”

Across from them, a few other trainees were watching with thinly veiled interest. Phainon straightened his posture slightly, masked the wince as he

flexed the arm, and then leaned on the opposite side like that had been his plan the whole time.

Mydei stepped closer—not to check the injury, but to skim through the flagged profiles in their queue. He’d somehow been handed senior access, no explanation, no complaints. If Phainon had to guess, the system just recognized competence by scent.

Or maybe leadership had just seen the look in Mydei’s eyes earlier—quiet and cunning. He’d slid into the coordinator role with minimal fuss, redirecting confused participants, approving calls without waiting on instructor feedback.

Phainon could respect that. He just wished it didn’t make him want to show off.

A new civilian model was escorted in—disheveled, twitchy, fake bruises stamped onto their cheek. They slumped into the screening chair.

Phainon watched them, carefully this time. Mydei watched him. Neither said anything.

When Phainon finally moved to retrieve the scanner, he made sure not to favor his bitten arm.

“Totally normal simulation,” he muttered under his breath. “No emotional baggage. No crisis of conscience. Just got attacked by a discount grandma with dentures.”

Mydei didn’t laugh. But he did nudge the bandage roll toward him in silent offering.

Phainon took it, wrapping it on himself. The bite still throbbed, but it looked cool from a distance. Probably.

He was halfway through bandaging his bite with one hand, still mumbling something bitter about “carnivorous civilians,” when the lights dimmed

slightly. Not enough for alarm—maybe the simulation’s way of saying the sun was setting.

Then came the announcement: “Warning: Potential hostile presence detected in the perimeter. Please proceed with standard civilian containment protocol.”

Phainon blinked, pausing mid-wrap. “…Containment?” He looked over at Mydei, who had already turned toward the sound, brows furrowed, but otherwise calm.

“Don’t worry,” Mydei murmured. “It’s likely just an escalation test. They’re probably going to introduce some corrupted figures or simulated panic to test our judgment.”

“Cool, cool,” Phainon said, nodding. “That definitely sounds like something they told us about. At registration. In the… documents I totally read.”

“…You didn’t read anything, though.”

“I liked the font.”

Then the music—a faint, generic hum in the background—cut out. Not slowly. Like someone yanked the aux cord out of the simulation.

Phainon blinked and looked down.

There, directly below the table, was a grown man folded the wrong way. Limbs contorted, neck at a ninety-degree angle, face twisted into a grin that didn’t match his eyes. Just staring up at him.

Phainon froze. So did the man.

For about four solid seconds, they simply… stared at each other.

Like a polite but deeply cursed tea party.

Then the man skittered.

Phainon jolted back a step—too late. A clammy hand grabbed his ankle with shocking force, and he yelped, scrambling for grip as he was dragged under the table like it was a horror movie and this thing had been waiting to audition.

“MYDEI I’M TOO YOUNG FOR THIS,” Phainon yelled as he slammed elbows into the floor, flailing wildly while being hauled backward. “TELL MY FANS I WENT OUT BRAVE.”

“You don’t have fans,” came Mydei’s very unhelpful reply from somewhere far, far too calm.

“YOU’RE MY NUMBER ONE FAN—DON’T LET THEM TAKE ME—”

Whatever the thing was, it didn’t talk. It hissed. It clicked. It smelled weirdly like pennies.

And just as Phainon felt his brain hit that calm oh my god I’m gonna die in a fake environment phase, something cold settled over him. His mind stilled.

Oh right. I kill people.

He twisted his hand, something sharp igniting under his palm—not a real dagger, but the shape of it—and just as he prepared to send this simulation freak back to the corrupted code he crawled out of—

“Simulation failed. Trainee extracted.”

His body fizzled out in segments, light blue lining cutting across his limbs like an upload glitch.

And then he was outside.

Sitting on a chair. Alone.

“…Huh.”

The screens displayed the rest of the scenario as it continued, the dome shimmering slightly with projected movement. Mydei was still in. Of course he was. Probably looking heroic. Probably winning. Probably not getting dragged by Uncle Error from under a table.

Phainon leaned back, staring at the ceiling for a moment. “This is not what I signed up for.”

Technically, he reminded himself, I didn’t sign anything. I just scrawled something vaguely resembling a signature on a clipboard and hoped for the best.

He huffed out a slow breath, resigned. Might as well wait. He’d check his evaluation after Mydei was done. Maybe see if the simulation offered snacks. Or therapy.

The floor was cold, the lights dimmed. Somewhere in the background, a voice droned out instructions, then crackled into silence. Phainon had somehow slouched all the way down on the waiting bench, legs half-draped over one side, arms crossed loosely, one foot twitching now and then. His head tilted back, breathing soft and slow.

He hadn’t meant to fall asleep. He just… closed his eyes a little too long.

Then came the sharp buzz of the simulation ending. Lights flicked to normal.

A soft ding signaled the end of the final scenario.

Phainon’s head snapped up like a cat hearing food hit the bowl. “Mm— what’d I miss?” He blinked, squinting as the door slid open—then brightened instantly. “Oh hey, look who survived!”

Mydei walked in, brows furrowed, expression unreadable—except for the faint, traitorous twitch at the corner of his eye. He zeroed in on Phainon’s sprawled figure, taking in the sleepy smirk, the bedhead, the way his boyfriend looked like he’d taken a nap in the middle of an apocalypse.

“You’re impossible.”

“I try.”

They joined the small cluster of other trainees shuffling over toward the evaluation stations. Digital displays flickered to life as files queued up— individual rankings, performance assessments, behavioral markers.

Mydei tapped through his results efficiently, like he already expected the outcome. And of course he did—his screen was glowing with full marks. Leadership score, reaction time, coordination, even tactical execution under pressure. Flawless.

Phainon peeked over and gave a low whistle. “Someone’s going to be recruited into herohood at this rate.”

“I’m not joining the Heirs,” Mydei muttered, but didn’t elaborate.

“Aw, and here I was picturing us in color-coordinated armors again.”

Mydei shot him a look.

Then Phainon’s screen blinked to life.

For a moment, he looked almost smug. Then he read it.

…Then he scrolled.

Then his expression soured.

“‘Reasonable engagement. Subpar hazard judgment. Failed to follow Black Tide infection protocol. Treated contaminated wound with unapproved civilian bandages.’—That was a premium wrap,” he said defensively.

“You were going to use a floral-patterned scarf you pulled out of your own pocket until I gave you the bandages. Don’t even deny it.”

“It was absorbent!”

Mydei pinched the bridge of his nose.

“It also says,” Phainon went on, eyes narrowing at the screen, “‘Subject displayed emotionally unstable behavior upon contact with corrupted figures. Requires reevaluation of panic response.’ I was not panicking. That was strategic screaming.”

“You yelled ‘save me, you’re my number one fan.’”

“And look! You didn’t!”

Mydei exhaled through his nose, looking away, but not before Phainon caught the very faintest quirk tugging at his lips.

“Still,” Phainon said, stretching a little and swiping the report off the screen like it personally offended him, “not the worst score. Could’ve been worse. Could’ve died.”

“It was a simulation.”

“A simulation with very real teeth, thank you. That grandma bit me.” He held up his bandaged arm like proof. “And not a gentle nibble either.”

Mydei stared at him, then rubbed his face. “There is only one scenario left.”

“One chance to redeem myself,” Phainon said brightly. “Or crash and burn with style.”

Mydei sighed. Hard. But he didn’t correct him.

An overseer finally stepped forward a while later, clipboard in hand, their presence marked by the mechanical hiss of the doors sealing behind them. The room quieted with the kind of anticipation only mild dread could conjure. Phainon leaned sideways, eyes half-lidded, already bracing himself for whatever weird test came next.

“This final simulation is a little… experimental,” the overseer began, with the exact tone of someone who legally had to say that. “One of you has been duplicated by our AI system to simulate an impersonation threat. Your

task is to identify and isolate the impostor before they compromise the scenario. The duplicate will behave as close to the original as possible.”

Phainon blinked, then squinted. “Didn’t some guy try to clone his ex last year? This city’s weird.”

Still, no one questioned it when sleek, practice-weighted blades were distributed to each of them—light enough for civilians, dull enough to not kill anyone, but just sharp enough to get the point across. Phainon turned his over in his hand and muttered, “Neat,” even as his eyes narrowed.

He was pretty sure the officials had long since stopped expecting anything from him. Now they were just running these for entertainment. Honestly? Fair.

The setting for the final scenario was deceptively quaint—suspiciously so, if you asked Phainon.

Instead of a high-tech facility or eerie simulation chamber, the group was led into what looked like a perfectly normal neighborhood house. Cozy, suburban, obnoxiously average. The kind of place with throw pillows that matched the curtains, wood floors that creaked politely underfoot, and the faint smell of chamomile that definitely didn’t come from tea.

Phainon stepped in, eyebrows raised. “Either this is a training scenario or we just broke into someone’s grandmother’s house.”

No one answered, probably because they were too busy gawking at how aggressively normal the place looked. There was a living room with a modest TV setup, a round kitchen table with mismatched chairs, even family photos on the walls—though if you looked too long, the faces blurred just enough to remind you this was still government-issue uncanny valley material.

Participants spread out, situating themselves on couches, leaning against doorframes, milling into the kitchen where a fake fruit bowl sat on the counter. People started chatting, some relaxed, others keeping a wary eye

on the others like they were already trying to figure out who among them wasn’t real.

Phainon plopped down on an armchair with a quiet oof, flipping his practice blade in his hand once before laying it across his lap. “So. Casual small talk or casual suspicion?”

Mydei sat beside him on the armrest, arms folded, gaze scanning the room like he’d been given a script but wanted to burn it. “They said someone’s pretending to be someone else.”

“Mhm.” Phainon slouched deeper into the chair. “And all we have to do is point fingers and hope we don’t stab the wrong guy.”

Mydei didn’t reply, though Phainon could feel the tension already knotting into his shoulders.

Yeah. Homey or not, this place was about to get real uncomfortable.

It had been hours.

Tension simmered beneath the surface like an unattended kettle— occasional side-eyes, whispered check-ins that weren’t really check-ins, someone suspiciously polishing their practice blade in the corner like they were prepping for a murder mystery dinner party. The chatting had long since died out, replaced by a strained silence and the quiet hum of everyone pretending to relax.

And then it happened.

A scream rang out from the hallway.

Someone yelled about a body (a body? Really? Cliche.). Another about a broken lamp. The sounds of footsteps thundered down the fake wood floors, chairs scraped, people tripped over the aggressively normal living room rug. The air snapped from boredom to full-blown chaos like a rubber band.

“There’s two of him!”

And just like that, the accusations began.

Finger-pointing, shouting, wild theories spun like bad soap opera plots.

“I saw him twice, I swear!”

“He was in the kitchen, and then—in the kitchen again.”

“That guy? With the white hair? I knew he looked too smug.”

Phainon blinked. “Me?”

“Yes, you!”

He stood, hands raised halfway like he was being arrested for tax fraud. “Okay, first of all—how dare you. Second of all, if I were a clone, would I know that Mydei’s favorite tea blend is cherry plum hibiscus with a dash of cinnamon? Which, might I add, he pretends not to like but always drinks when he’s tired?”

Everyone paused.

Mydei looked like he was about to be forcibly removed from his own soul. “That’s not—”

Phainon turned toward him, full showman mode. “Would a clone know how your eye twitches exactly 0.3 seconds after someone leaves a mug on the table without a coaster? Would a clone recognize your ‘I didn’t make breakfast for you’ neck tilt when you absolutely made breakfast for me this morning?”

He spread his arms to the group like this was closing night at the theater. “Would a clone look at him the way I do?”

Mydei looked ready to dissolve into smoke. Or commit a minor felony.

Then the front door slammed open.

And there he was.

Clone-Phainon. Identical. Perfect. Too perfect. Like someone asked AI to generate Phainon based on his student records and filtered selfies.

Same hair, same face, same lazy stance—but wrong. Like someone bought his personality off the discount rack.

Phainon stared, horrified. “That is not how I walk.”

The room erupted. People dove behind furniture, blades came out, a few people screamed. Someone tried to grab the fake fruit for defense.

And in the middle of the chaos, Phainon could still be heard protesting over the noise, “Look at him! He’s walking like he makes spreadsheets for fun. I have personality!”

Eventually, the room settled. Not because anyone trusted each other, but because there was no energy left to keep throwing accusations.

Two Phainons sat side-by-side in the middle of the room like some twisted art exhibit. Both of them wore the same half-sleepy smirk, both leaned with that exact same infuriating slouch like they weren’t in the middle of a social breakdown. Someone had moved a lamp closer just to make sure they weren’t seeing double. They weren’t.

“So,” someone finally said. “We just… ask them stuff?”

“Until one cracks,” someone else offered.

“We’re gonna be here all night,” muttered another.

Still, the questions began.

“What’s your date of birth?”

“Name every Heir in the Chrysos system, backwards.”

“What did you have for breakfast?”

“Toast,” said the one on the left.

“Technically, leftover pie,” said the one on the right. “And a cold egg tart. You stole half of it, Mydei.”

Mydei, seated a few feet off with his arms crossed, didn’t even blink. “You offered.”

“After you gave me that look.”

“Which look?”

Phainon-Right mimicked it. Raised eyebrow, small squint, the faintest downward curl of the lip. A perfect imitation.

Phainon-Left’s eye twitched.

More questions. Dumb ones. Serious ones. Questions neither should’ve known but somehow both answered anyway. The room kept circling, restless, getting nowhere.

And then, as the tension simmered in its own confusion, Clone-Phainon— Phainon-Right—shifted.

“Alright,” he said lightly, “then let me prove it this way.”

He turned a little, directing his words more toward Mydei than the crowd. “Your coffee was too bitter this morning.”

Mydei didn’t look at him.

“You said it wasn’t,” Clone-Phainon added, quieter now. “But you kept stirring it like you were hoping it’d change.”

He didn’t say it like a gotcha. He said it like an observation.

The room started to quiet.

“You always stir things when you’re thinking too hard,” he added. “Tea. Soup. Paint. You get this furrow between your brows that you probably don’t even know you make.”

Mydei’s fingers twitched against his arm.

“And the last time someone asked how you were doing,” the clone went on, “you said fine, but scratched your wrist with your thumb.” He lifted his hand, mimicking the exact movement. “You always do that when you’re lying.”

A small sound escaped someone in the back. The room was entirely motionless.

Mydei didn’t look away, but his expression was hard to read. Just too still. A faint flush crept to his ears.

Across from him, Phainon sat too still.

Not stiff, not obviously tense—just thoughtful. His arms remained folded lazily over his chest, his legs crossed. His expression didn’t change. But his tongue swept once across his teeth, slow, thoughtful.

He was listening. That much was clear. Watching, too.

He didn’t bother pretending not to.

The clone kept speaking, voice low and familiar, threading memories into something intimate. Making it look easy. Making it look real.

Phainon didn’t interrupt. Didn’t even blink for a while.

Just sat there.

Watching this cheap replica play house with moments that weren’t his.

And it wasn’t the accuracy that bothered him—he could live with that. What got under his skin, what itched behind his ribs like an old bruise being pressed too hard, was the fact that the bastard didn’t even hesitate. Like he

thought he belonged here. Like knowing a few tells was enough to make him the one who mattered.

Phainon’s jaw flexed once.

He tilted his head slightly to the side, eyes narrowing—not in disbelief, but in the way someone might look at a stain that wouldn’t come out of a shirt they actually liked.

Annoying.

He shifted his weight just a little, a move so small it almost didn’t register —but it bled purpose.

Just a quiet signal: you’ve overstayed.

The clone kept talking, unaware—or maybe pretending to be unaware.

Phainon’s gaze flicked toward Mydei then. Not for confirmation or reassurance. Just to watch. To see how much of it Mydei was letting slide. And to remember it.

Then he turned his eyes back to the other version of himself.

Cool. Unimpressed.

And very much done with this game.

The temperature in the room hadn’t changed, but something about it still felt colder.

Phainon leaned back slightly, letting the edge of the chair bite into his spine. The room had quieted into a tense kind of fatigue—civilians slouched in their seats, murmuring theories under their breath, others still too wired to sit, pacing near the walls as though they’d find the truth in the paint.

Across from him, the clone hadn’t moved much. Still mimicking his posture. Still looking just close enough to make people squint. But it was

too polished now. Like a version of him rendered in clean lines and angles, missing the uneven rhythm of a real person.

More questions were being thrown at them—harmless enough, but useless.

Phainon crossed one leg over the other, resting his arm along the back of the chair.

He could feel Mydei watching.

That flicker of focus, sharp and measured, cutting between him and the other version. Trying to see something invisible. Something only Mydei would notice.

Eventually, Phainon straightened and spoke—carefully. Flatly.

“Alright. Let’s just end it here.”

A few heads turned. Even the clone blinked.

“I’m the fake. He’s the real one. Job done, right?”

There was a beat of stunned silence. Then someone scoffed, “Seriously?”

Phainon offered a half-shrug, expression unreadable. “Why not? If I were the real one, I’d have walked out twenty minutes ago.”

It was meant to be dismissive. To mislead.

But the clone twitched.

Not physically—at first. Something flickered behind its eyes, like a light dimming behind faulty glass. Its smile faltered, then reassembled, piece by piece. Too slow.

Phainon sat still, eyes narrowed.

The clone’s gaze swept the room—too fast, too focused—and then locked onto one of the civilians standing near the edge of the group. A teenage girl,

maybe seventeen, had been nervously watching the whole thing from a corner.

And then it stepped toward her.

Not with aggression. Not at first. Just calmly. Quietly.

Like it had made a decision no one else was aware of.

Phainon stood up, already tense. “Hey—”

The girl took a step back, but the clone reached for her anyway, hand outstretched in a mechanical approximation of reassurance.

“I wouldn’t,” Phainon warned, low.

But the clone didn’t stop. It moved faster now, grip shifting from open to forceful in a blink. Fingers curled around her arm—not hard enough to break it, but tight enough to hold. Tight enough to make her flinch.

Then came the sound—an ugly, grinding static—like something internal had misfired.

And in the next moment, the clone jerked, too suddenly, movements disjointed. Its head tilted slightly off-axis, and its voice—when it tried to speak again—came out warped, distorted with feedback.

“…confirming…target behavior…reset—reset…”

The girl cried out.

Now people were moving. Chairs scraped, feet stumbled, someone shouted for an instructor, but no one stepped forward. No one expected the simulation to break like this.

Phainon’s hand was already halfway to his weapon—training blade or not —but before he could close the distance—

Mydei moved first.

One step. Two.

Then his fist connected with the side of the clone’s face in a clean, brutal arc. The impact sent the figure crashing to the floor. Sparks cracked along its jaw as it twisted unnaturally, back arching in a seizure of code. Limbs locked. Skin shimmered—and then collapsed into a facsimile of composite plating, tech and frame now visible where skin used to be.

Silence.

The girl scrambled away. People stared. One man near the back sat down slowly, stunned into immobility.

The dummy fizzled, glitching softly against the floor, its systems fried beyond repair.

Phainon stared at it, then turned to Mydei—who stood, hand still partially raised, breathing calm and steady, but eyes sharper than they’d been all day.

There was a beat. Then Phainon snorted, shaking his head once. “So… you knew.”

Mydei didn’t answer at first. His expression didn’t shift, but the silence was enough.

“You hit him faster than I’ve seen you blink,” Phainon muttered, mouth quirking up at the corner. “Violent, decisive, deeply romantic. But if there’s a next time—I’m begging you. No more clones. No more robots. No more existential crises in moderately furnished living rooms.”

The official debrief came two hours later.

And it was exactly as satisfying as getting stabbed with a retractable training blade.

Most participants were crammed into a too-bright multipurpose room where someone from the administrative board—flanked by a Chrysos Heir liaison

and an official from the Civic Engagement Division—stood at the front and tried very hard not to look like this had been a total disaster.

They failed.

“…a systems miscalibration,” the woman was saying, tone overly rehearsed, “that bypassed intended safety thresholds. While the impersonation module was cleared for advanced defense programming, it was not meant to be deployed in a public civilian setting—”

Phainon stopped listening halfway through.

His arm still ached faintly from the earlier bite. His nerves were twitching from residual adrenaline. And across the room, someone was crying while eating a granola bar, which felt like a perfect summary of the day.

It wasn’t supposed to happen. Everyone kept saying that.

Which was reassuring, in the same way someone telling you “this plane shouldn’t crash” mid-flight is reassuring.

A collaboration between the Chrysos Heirs and the Government—years in the making, funded, tested, backed by oversight committees—and yet a full malfunctioning impersonation unit somehow slipped past every checkpoint and nearly dislocated a seventeen-year-old’s shoulder.

The trainers assured them this had never happened before.

The looks on their faces said it better not happen again.

Half the room filtered out as soon as they were told they could go. Some stayed behind to file informal reports. Others mumbled about lawsuits. And somewhere amidst it all, Phainon sat in a chair against the wall, filling out a feedback form he didn’t remember picking up.

“Overall satisfaction with today’s session?” it asked.

He drew a box between Neutral and Dismal and checked that instead.

Mydei appeared beside him a few seconds later, holding both their bags and what looked suspiciously like an unopened ice pack.

“You done?” Mydei asked.

“I regret to every deity I’ve ever learned about that I signed all those waivers without reading them.”

Mydei didn’t smile, but the look in his eye was half an apology, half an I told you so.

They left quietly. No dramatic exit. Just a few nods to the coordinators and a shared, tired glance between them as they stepped out into the cool evening air.

It was quiet outside.

Too quiet for the day they’d had.

“…So,” Phainon said after a beat, “how long do you think until I start dreaming about punching my own face?”

Mydei adjusted the bag over his shoulder and exhaled slowly. “Depends. Was it satisfying when I did it?”

Phainon gave him a look. “A little too much, honestly.”

They kept walking.

The streets were mostly empty by then, save for a few lights still glowing behind café windows and the soft hum of a distant train crawling across the horizon. Mydei walked a little ahead, quiet in that observant way of his, and Phainon trailed beside him, hands tucked into his coat pockets, shoulders slack with exhaustion.

A few paces passed in silence.

Then, casually—maybe too casually—Phainon tilted his head. “So… hypothetical.”

Mydei didn’t glance over. “Hm?”

“What would you do if I had been replaced?” Phainon asked. “Like— actually swapped out. Not a test, not a simulation. Just one day, new me. Would you know?”

It was said with a light lilt, like a joke. But it hung there, just a second too long.

Mydei finally turned, his expression unreadable.

Phainon met his gaze, still walking, still looking faintly amused, but his eyes were quiet. Thoughtful. There was a pause where it was clear he wanted to follow up with something else—another line, another joke, another way to pretend it didn’t matter.

But he didn’t.

He just waited.

Mydei stopped walking.

And that was enough to make Phainon do the same.

For a moment, Mydei just studied him—really studied him—the small shift of his weight, the tired draw at the corners of his mouth, the way he kept his chin lifted like he was daring someone to challenge him, even now.

“You’re asking,” Mydei said, voice low, “if I’d notice if something happened to you.”

Phainon’s smile flickered. “I mean. You did hesitate earlier.”

“Because I thought the test was going somewhere worse.”

“Oh.”

Another beat of silence. Then—“Would you have known if it was me?”

Mydei’s answer came without hesitation. “Yes.”

Phainon blinked.

Mydei didn’t elaborate. He didn’t list the reasons, though he could’ve.

He didn’t say how Phainon had a habit of fiddling with loose threads on his sleeves when he was thinking too hard—never pulling them, just turning them over between his fingers like he was grounding himself in something small. Or how he always tapped his heel twice before taking a step toward anything dangerous, as if giving himself a beat to change his mind—though he never did. Or how, when he was about to say something self-deprecating, he always glanced up first, almost like checking to see if Mydei was still looking at him.

He didn’t say how all of that, stitched together, made a person no clone could copy.

And more than that—how no clone would ever stop in the middle of an empty street, under flickering streetlights, just to ask a question like that. One that was half-joke, half-promise, and all Phainon.

So Mydei didn’t say any of it.

But the answer still sat plainly between them.

Phainon looked down, a little overwhelmed, a little thrown.

“…Okay,” he said quietly. “That’s a good answer.”

Mydei gave the barest huff of a laugh. “It’s the only one.”

They kept walking again. The city moved around them, slow and distant.

And somewhere in that stretch of silence, Phainon let out a long breath he didn’t realize he’d been holding.

Phainon bumped his shoulder into Mydei’s, light enough to pass for a joke, steady enough to say I’m still here.

“You’re lucky I’m so damn charming,” he said, a grin tugging at the corner of his mouth. “Otherwise that clone might’ve actually had a chance.”

Mydei huffed a laugh, soft but real. He didn’t move away.

Instead, he let the quiet settle for a moment, long enough that Phainon thought it might’ve ended there—until Mydei spoke again.

“Thank you. For coming with me.”

Phainon blinked. His grin faltered—not gone, just… gentler now.

The warmth of Mydei’s words crawled beneath his ribs, unexpected and earnest. He looked away, then back, because it mattered. Because it was Mydei.

He said, voice low but sure, “I’d go anywhere if it meant walking beside you.”

And for once, Mydei didn’t correct him. Didn’t scoff or roll his eyes.

He just stood there, shoulder still brushing Phainon’s, as the last rays of sun dipped behind the city’s spires—quiet and full of things unspoken, but understood all the same.

Chapter End Notes

Next chapter is probably gonna be delayed a bit since I’m working on sm else, and I’m thinking of a way to combine two ideas I had for the next chapter to make it sm enjoyable AND drop some Phainon lore if I can so uhh, sorry💔

Anyway, you guys are always welcome to criticize or add new ideas for this fic since it’s pretty open-ended and anything can work really (Worst things worst if the criticism goes too hard I’ll develop a degradation kink or sm idk) so yeah😚

PS: just wanna add sm irrelevant and probably forgotten but stuck in my head. Abt the whole Mydei screaming abt the spider, Mydei screamed not at the spider, but because he’d nearly blurted out something hero-related—mid-kiss (Their first kiss probably), dizzy, bleeding just a little from getting his head smacked in by some guy an hour ago, and absolutely not thinking straight—and panicked to cover it. The spider just happened to be there, so he pointed and screamed like it was the problem💕

chapters.title: Boyfriend’s Childhood Friend
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei just wanted a quiet day in the library. Instead, a mysterious vigilante dropped by with ghost problems, emotional trauma manifested in horrifyingly personal ways, and a battle that nearly got him shredded. On the bright side, he survived, helped neutralize a major threat, and hey—now he gets to surprise his boyfriend with a reunion years in the making. What could possibly go wrong?

Chapter Notes

Stuck making a delinquent x nerd au from Mydei or Phainon’s POV. Decisions decisions…Also not sure if I should make Mydei the nerd or delinquent, I was originally gonna go with the second option but idk now😩

For once, the library was quiet in the right way.

Not the kind of quiet that came after someone triggered a defense glyph (Don’t ask why he had that here) or spilled coffee on a restricted section. The peaceful kind—no alarms, no echoing footsteps, no undergrad sobbing into their third energy drink. Just the hum of the overhead lights, the gentle rustle of a turning page, and the soft clink of a teaspoon tapping porcelain.

Mydei sipped his tea, cross-legged behind the front desk with a stack of unsorted horror novels at his elbow. Some were barely holding together with cracked spines and yellowing pages, others shiny and obnoxious with dust jackets that claimed to “redefine fear.” He’d believed that once. At sixteen. Now he just wanted to figure out if The Third Mouth belonged under psychological thrillers or allegorical body horror. Alphabetizing was

easy. Themes were harder, and themes that lied about what kind of book they were were the bane of his afternoon.

Still, he wasn’t in a bad mood. Caelus had actually returned his books without needing to be hunted down this time—which was nothing short of miraculous. Even better, it was during a term break, so there’d been no throngs of panic-induced crammers. Mydei hadn’t even bothered to make a joke (Not really) about charging late fees. Not out of mercy. He just didn’t feel like it.

Which was, for him, a sign of rare and possibly worrying contentment.

He glanced at the digital planner floating off to the side of his desk, the pale blue light casting soft reflections over the surface of his tea. The reminder was still pinned at the top: Meeting scheduled: Garden Hall @ 18:00. Guest: Cyrene.

That was the other thing.

He leaned back in his chair, arms folded loosely across his chest, and allowed himself a small, private sense of satisfaction. Cyrene had reached out a week ago—soft-spoken, hesitant, asking if she could surprise Phainon. “Just to talk,” she’d said. “He probably doesn’t even remember me well, but I thought maybe… it might be good for him.”

Mydei had said yes without thinking. And then he’d spent the next four hours reserving the space, coordinating schedules, and checking for surveillance nodes. Twice. No one was ruining this. Especially not him.

It was a dumb thing to be proud of, maybe. Setting up a simple meeting. But it was more than that. Phainon didn’t know yet, but he’d be happy— probably talk too much, or forget to eat, or smile in that weird way where his nose scrunched up a little. Mydei already liked the idea of seeing it.

He wasn’t the sentimental type. But every once in a while, when he wasn’t being stalked by cursed abominations or dragged into vigilante nonsense, he could be a decent partner. He’d scheduled a surprise. Coordinated it down

to the minute. Hell, he even made sure the lighting in the garden would hit Phainon’s good side.

The day had started well.

Which, of course, meant it was about to be completely ruined.

He was halfway through labeling a misfiled edition of The Weeping Engine when the front doors opened.

He didn’t look up at first. People came in sometimes—students looking for a quiet place, researchers who still thought everything could be solved by finding the right obscure reference. He was ready to nod politely, maybe even offer directions if they looked sufficiently lost.

Then he heard heels. And humming.

He looked up.

Cipher.

In civilian disguise, technically. Which in her case meant a loose hoodie, reflective sunglasses despite being indoors, and an oversized messenger bag probably full of stolen access cards and questionable gum. She sauntered in like she’d personally paid for the floor tiles, waved cheerfully in his direction, and immediately veered past the reading area into the staff-only section with the sort of aimless confidence that only a true menace could radiate.

Mydei stared. Blinked once. Set his pen down very carefully.

There were signs. So many signs. “Authorized Personnel Only.” “Surveillance in Use.” One with a cartoon cat holding a ‘NO ENTRY’ placard. He’d added that one specifically to see if she’d take it seriously.

She had not.

“Out,” he said flatly.

Cipher glanced over her shoulder, eyebrows up, as if she was the one being inconvenienced. “Why? I’m not doing anything yet.”

“I can change that.”

She grinned. “Aw, come on, don’t be like that. I’m just here for a book.”

“You’re banned.”

“That was weeks ago.”

“For life.”

She wandered over to a shelf anyway, flipping through a random volume like she hadn’t heard him. “Ooh, this one’s got diagrams. Creepy little— wait, is that blood or ink?”

He reached under the desk.

Cipher’s head snapped up. “You wouldn’t.”

“Try me.”

There was a brief, tense silence—her eyes locked on the drawer handle, his hand hovering just above it.

“You bring that cucumber spray out and I swear I’ll scream,” she said.

“You’re not supposed to be here.”

“It’s a ridiculous weapon. Who carries weaponized vegetables? And why cucumbers? They’re smug.”

“You said they were ‘visually aggressive’ last time.”

“I stand by that.”

Mydei didn’t move. Neither did she. Eventually, Cipher sighed, dropped the act, and let her shoulders fall into something closer to serious.

“Okay, look. I didn’t come here to steal anything. Or break anything. Or touch the ancient cursed binder you keep pretending isn’t cursed.”

He raised one eyebrow.

“I need your help,” she said.

The tone shift was subtle, but unmistakable. Her voice didn’t pitch upward at the end of the sentence like it was a punchline. It was just honest for once.

Mydei frowned. “With what.”

“Something’s wrong,” Cipher said. “Weird-wrong. And it’s not the fun kind this time.”

Mydei didn’t bother answering her directly. He just sighed—long and tired, like her presence had physically aged him—and gestured for her to follow. As he turned, he made a point of slipping the cucumber spray into his pocket slowly, eyes never leaving hers.

Cipher huffed. “You’re dramatic.”

“You’re a thief.”

“Not today.”

He didn’t respond.

She trailed after him, hands visible and well away from anything valuable. It wasn’t fear—Cipher wasn’t the type—but she did know better than to provoke him in his own domain. The library echoed faintly under their footsteps. His office door was at the back, past the main stacks and locked behind three separate mechanisms: one electronic, one physical, one biometric.

She whistled under her breath. “Still overcompensating, I see.”

“It’s not paranoia if people like you exist.”

Inside, the office was… warm. Somehow. Wood shelves lined with annotated folders and battered paperbacks, a reading lamp that threw a golden pool of light over the desk, a second mug that might’ve been used by someone else recently—or maybe just wishful thinking. Cipher flopped into one of the guest chairs, slouching with the practiced ease of someone who didn’t respect furniture. Mydei remained standing.

“You said something’s wrong,” he said.

Cipher didn’t answer right away. She reached into her bag—not quickly, but Mydei still tensed—and pulled out a cracked datapad. She set it down between them and pushed it forward.

“People are seeing the dead,” she started with abruptly, tone shifting. No foreplay, it seems.

Mydei didn’t flinch. “Go on.”

“Loved ones. Friends. Someone they haven’t spoken to in years. Sometimes just in a crowd, sometimes directly in their homes. Always personal. Always intimate.”

Mydei didn’t sit. He skimmed the logs, eyes narrowing.

“It’s not hallucinations,” Cipher added. “Not some localized psychic echo, not emotional bleed. The encounters follow the same pattern. First sighting. Then conversation. Then blackout.”

Mydei frowned. “You mean they faint.”

“No.” Cipher leaned forward now, more serious than he’d seen her in… maybe ever. “They shut down. Coma-level. Neural responses drop off the chart. You get people lying there like they’re dreaming, but you run scans and the brain’s just… off.  I’m not sure how to describe it.”

He processed that. Quietly. Cipher watched him do it.

“How many cases?”

“Not enough for public panic. Yet.” Her voice dropped slightly. “But enough for a pattern.”

“Why not alert the others?” he asked. “The Heirs. Or the agency.”

Cipher hesitated. Just for a second. “Because the more people you involve, the more chances this thing has to spread. Every encounter leaves a trace. Every retelling does too. It adapts, learns. Once you’re in its sight, it won’t let you go. That’s why I didn’t call Castorice until I had to. She picked up something in Sector 5—might be a linked anomaly. She’s tracking it now.”

“And what? You decided I was safe?”

“You’re immortal.”

“That’s not immunity.”

“It’s better odds than anyone else I know.” Her voice wasn’t flippant this time. “And frankly, you’re harder to replace.”

Mydei didn’t bother responding to that. His eyes stayed fixed on the logs, parsing every detail.

“They’re not just illusions,” he murmured. “They’re entities. Artificial. Possibly sentient. Definitely invasive.”

Cipher nodded. “I think someone—or something—is replicating them. Mimics. Not projections. They’re built. From data. Memories, emotions, patterns. Everything personal, down to the tone of voice and favorite arguments.”

He closed the pad. “How?”

“That’s what I need your help figuring out. But I’ve been digging, and I’ve found traces of something deeper.” She paused. The next words came slower. “There are anchor nodes. Places that stabilize whatever this is. I’ve found two for sure. The third is still buried—maybe even mobile.”

“Hive system,” he muttered.

She nodded. “Yeah. Everything branches back to the center. But if we can pull out two legs of the tripod…”

“The third collapses. Or at least stumbles.”

“Exactly.”

Mydei finally sank into his chair, fingertips pressed together.

“This is a lot of effort for someone who thinks cases are boring,” he said.

Another pause.

“…Yeah.”

Just that.

Mydei looked at her for a long moment. Cipher—who once rerouted an entire museum’s security grid just to leave a glitter trail in the shape of a middle finger. Who broke into a tech lab for a snack. Who said laws were more like “polite suggestions, if you’re into that.”

She was scared.

Not panicking or anything. But scared. It showed in the way she tapped her foot—small, unconscious. In the way her eyes didn’t linger on the datapad too long, like the logs might bite. In the way she said “yet” like she was already counting down to when she’d be next.

“I wouldn’t have come here if it wasn’t serious,” she said, voice quiet.

“I know,” he said.

Mydei sighed. For the second time that hour. And with markedly less resistance than the first.

“I’ll help,” he said, like it was a resignation. As if she was gravity and he was tired of fighting physics.

Across from him, Cipher immediately perked up. “Knew you’d come around,” she said, cheery again with all the grace of a car crash. “You’ve got that face. The ‘dammit, fine, give me the demon files’ face.”

“I have never made that face.”

“You’re making it right now.”

“I will throw you out a window.”

She grinned, pushing to her feet. “Cool, great, perfect. Gear up. We’re hitting the Archive first.”

Mydei arched a brow. “You’re assuming I’ve agreed to be seen with you in public.”

“Oh, please. Like they won’t all be too distracted wondering how no one’s figured out you were Godslayer.” She tossed that out casually, like a pebble into a pond. “I mean, come on, you didn’t even change your walk.”

Mydei’s hand drifted up, thumb and forefinger pinching the bridge of his nose with a kind of quiet grace, as if physically holding back the sheer wave of secondhand stupidity radiating off her.

“I operate under layered dissonance algorithms, reinforced by a reactive cloaking system calibrated to my voiceprint, gait, and signature field,” he said calmly. “People see what they expect. They hear what they want. And no one ever suspects the cranky librarian.”

Cipher blinked. “Wow. That almost sounded cool.”

Mydei turned toward the door.

“Except,” Cipher added, cheerfully malicious, “I did figure it out. So clearly your little disguise system doesn’t account for me being smarter than your average idiot.”

He stopped.

“My voice was run through a triple-phase modulator and my physical presence was blanketed by quantum masking, dumbass.”

The word snapped out harder than intended.

Cipher grinned like she’d just won a game she’d invented mid-conversation. “There he is.”

“Get out.”

“What?”

“Go, Cipher. Prep your plan, plot your route, pack your weird little grenades—whatever it is you do. I’ll be ready in twenty.”

“Wow. Rude.”

He was already opening the office door.

Cipher gave him an exaggerated bow on the way out. “You know, for someone who keeps a literal library of cursed books, you’re shockingly bad at dramatic exits.”

“And you’re still banned from the special collections.”

“I put that book back! Mostly.”

The door shut behind her with a decisive click.

Mydei stood in silence for a moment, letting the absurdity of his life soak in like the world’s worst tea. Then he moved toward his hidden gear cache and started suiting up. After all, it wasn’t every day someone asked you to go hunt memory-eating death mimics.

Getting inside wasn’t difficult. Not with Cipher.

She didn’t exactly pick the locks. She bypassed them entirely—moving through the lower access tunnels with the kind of precision that made it

hard to tell whether she was fast or just chronically disrespectful of the laws of physics. Either way, the surveillance was useless. The biometric scanner didn’t so much glitch as… give up.

The deeper they descended, the quieter it got.

The freight elevator they took shuddered like it hadn’t moved in a decade. Past a certain floor, the lights above stopped responding. Emergency strips lined the walls instead—pale, battery-fed, and dying slow. Each step echoed too long against concrete and metal, and the air started to feel compressed. Not stale exactly—just still. Like nothing had breathed here in a long time.

Cable conduits ran along the ceiling, many snapped open or ripped clean through. Old security plating had been scorched and rewelded. And here and there, splashes of abandoned signage peeled from the walls, warning about radiation or protocol tiers that no longer mattered.

A set of autonomous doors finally slid open ahead of them with a delayed whir. Cipher had to slap the side panel twice, then give it a swift kick before the biometric lag caught up.

“Very advanced,” she muttered. “Love what they’ve done with the place. Real minimalist apocalypse.”

“Keep your voice down,” Mydei said.

She did.

They spoke in clipped bursts, low voices.

“Tell me you have a map,” Mydei said, eyes scanning the long, sterile hallway ahead.

Cipher waved a small holotab over her shoulder without looking back. “I memorized it. You really think I’d break into a ex-government-esque death maze without doing my homework?”

“Last time you navigated with intuition, we ended up in a collapsing maglev tunnel.”
