“That tunnel was mostly intact.”

They passed a rusting security checkpoint. A flicker of motion down the hall turned out to be a wire swaying from a cracked ceiling tile.

They were still cautious. Banter didn’t mean blind.

They reached the vault.

A broad circular chamber opened before them—once sealed by layers of reinforced steel, now cracked just wide enough for someone to squeeze through. Inside, everything was too quiet. Consoles sat dormant around a central core, though faint glows still pulsed under the surface—like a sleeping heartbeat.

Mydei frowned. “This is it?”

Cipher’s usual smirk faded as she took a step forward, scanning the tall server racks along the walls. “Not what I expected.”

“Neither did I,” he said, stepping in after her. “This was built.”

Then he saw the center column.

A tall, humming core encased in crystalline housing, flickering with pulses of light—and beneath the crystal: neural threads. Rows upon rows of memory fibers. Each labeled with Chrysos codenames. Some still active.

Mydei froze.

Cipher didn’t speak.

He approached slowly, eyes narrowing as he spotted a familiar strand, labeled with a numerical code that shouldn’t have existed outside classified Chrysos archives. One he knew was tied to him.

“This is a Chrysos archive,” he said, voice lower now, more deliberate. “Not just general data. These are personal logs. Mission footage. Thought patterns.”

Cipher looked genuinely disturbed. “No one outside the Heirs should have this.”

“They don’t even share it internally,” Mydei muttered. “Not unless you’re cleared. Even then, only in fragments. How the hell—”

“Someone stole the archive,” Cipher said, voice flat. “And fed it to a quantum server.”

They exchanged a look.

Neither of them said it, but the implication hung heavy between them.

Whoever built this node didn’t just want to replicate memories.

They wanted to understand them.

To crawl inside.

And build something out of what they found.

Cipher after a moment, peeled off to the far end of the vault, slipping behind stacks of corroded processors and tangled cords with a practiced lightness. Mydei stayed near the central servers, watching the sluggish blink of interface lights across the old paneling. The air carried the sterile sharpness of disuse, like ozone and forgotten code.

He tugged on a pair of gloves, knelt by the mainframe, and began to trace the input feeds. “Interface activity’s still semi-live,” he muttered, half to himself. “Residual power. This wasn’t mothballed right.”

“Because it wasn’t supposed to be found,” Cipher replied from somewhere behind the server stacks. “This place wasn’t on any of the listings.”

“Of course it wasn’t.” He pressed his hand to the biometric override, waited for the low chirp of denial, and reached for his Chrysos ID instead. “I’m bypassing the failsafe. Keep an eye out for redundancy triggers.”

“Duh,” Cipher said, but the usual edge in her voice was dulled. “You think it’ll scream?”

“Something worse.” The panel clicked open, revealing a narrow feed of code windows—sluggish, fractured, but still learning.

They should have stopped there. Should’ve taken the coordinates, corrupted the chain, and left it to rot. But curiosity had never been kind to the Chrysos Heirs. Especially not the immortal ones.

Mydei linked in.

The interface recognized them instantly.

The lights overhead flickered—sharp, sudden—and the silence of the vault thickened.

Then the system started to speak.

Not in code.

Not in language.

But in voice.

Not just any voice.

“Mydei.”

His spine straightened. Just slightly. A pause in the breath, a stiffness behind the eyes. Nothing more, but Cipher, looping back around, caught it anyway.

She slowed to a stop beside him. “Who was that?”

He didn’t answer.

The voice came again. Warmer this time, a little playful. “Don’t pretend you didn’t hear me. You always try to look so serious when you’re

concentrating.”

And then the figure stepped through the far wall of servers—no warning, just a shift in the lighting, a tilt in perspective—and Gorgo was there.

Or something wearing her.

Cipher’s hand went to her belt immediately. Mydei didn’t move.

The projection wasn’t faded or holographic. It wasn’t a rough approximation built from low-res memory scans. This was sharp. Every detail was in place, down to the silver burn mark on the edge of her left gauntlet, the uneven twist in her braid.

And the look in her eyes. Proud. Tired. Softened by something that felt like recognition.

“You never came back to the house.”

Mydei stopped.

“You left everything as it was. Even the tea tins.”

It blinked slowly. Too human. Not human enough.

“The one on the shelf… You kept that sealed. Thought I wouldn’t notice?” A slight tilt of the head. “You were always good at pretending you’d moved on. You never were.”

“How is it doing this?” Cipher asked under her breath, unreadable now.

“Pulled from logs. Audio files. Mission reports, memories.” Mydei replied quietly, eyes still locked on the projection. “Chrysos archives don’t just track kills. They record everything. Even when they’re not supposed to.” That included your head apparently.

“And someone dumped that here?”

“No. Someone stole it.”

The figure tilted its head. “Still talking over me. You used to mumble back then, remember?”

Its smile was wrong. Perfect on the surface, but too smooth—like wax warmed just enough to warp.

Mydei stayed quiet.

He could feel the tension in his shoulders, but it wasn’t fear. Not exactly. Just a cold stillness. One he hadn’t touched in years.

The last time he’d heard her voice, it hadn’t sounded like this. It had been sharp. Annoyed. “Duck faster,” she’d snapped—right before it happened. Not some grand sacrifice, not a teary farewell. Just pissed she had to die doing something stupid because her son was too slow that day.

He’d replayed it more times than he’d admit.

And yet here this thing was, speaking like she’d never left. Telling him how proud she was. How well he’d turned out. As if it had a right.

As if it knew.

His hands twitched.

“Don’t,” Cipher said softly. “It’s baiting you.”

He didn’t respond.

The projection stepped forward. “I’m proud of you, Mydeimos. I always have been.”

Its face flickered.

For a fraction of a second, the skin smoothed over where her scar should have been. The pupils rotated wrong. Then the glitch passed, like it had never happened.

Mydei’s jaw clenched.

It wasn’t her. He knew that. But the voice… it sounded like her. And part of him—stupid, aching, traitorous—wanted to listen anyway.

“I miss you,” it said.

Then again.

“I miss you.”

It started to loop.

“I miss you.”

“I miss you.”

“I miss you—”

The voice stuttered mid-sentence, volume peaking just enough to spike the speaker output.

Then: a crackle. A sharp whine of overclocked circuits frying as Cipher jammed a spike charge directly into the access port beside them.

The illusion shattered with no fanfare. Just a blink—and gone.

The room fell quiet again, save for the hum of cooling processors.

The charge burned through the remaining memory strings, glitching the server until even the automated voice couldn’t rebuild itself. Static hissed for a few seconds. Then silence.

Mydei stood still. For a long time.

Cipher didn’t speak.

She just shifted a little to the side—just enough to stand in the line of sight between him and where the projection had been.

When he finally moved, it was to turn off the feed. A flick of the switch.

She still didn’t ask.

And he didn’t explain.

Cipher crouched by the still-flickering remains of the access port, visor flicking through data overlays as she scanned what was left of the corrupted server. Static danced along the edges of the projection glass—brief ghost-frames flashing, then dissolving.

“Someone hardwired this thing to pull from blacklisted archives,” she muttered. “Not just scraps. Direct uplink. Memory logs, audio stamps… someone’s been siphoning for a while.”

Mydei didn’t respond. He leaned against the wall with a hand braced near the switchboard, face unreadable.

Cipher’s tone shifted, quieter. “This shouldn’t even be possible. Chrysos archives are supposed to be locked behind three identity firewalls and a temporal checksum. You don’t just… find this kind of thing.”

She stood. Gaze lingering on the ruined projection panel.

“Someone wanted this to feel personal. That would’ve made it harder to shut down.”

He finally looked up at that. “They almost got their wish.”

Cipher nodded once, grim. Then kicked the access unit hard enough to spark a trail of dying blue light across the floor.

“One down,” she said, turning away. “Two more to go.”

Mydei followed, slower this time. The vault hissed shut behind them, and the silence that followed felt heavier than when they’d arrived.

The tunnels beneath the metro grid stank of ozone and old power. Low, thudding hums echoed off the walls, mechanical heartbeats pulsing somewhere deep ahead. Mydei barely said a word the entire descent—just

watched their surroundings, the way the lights shifted, the way Cipher walked without her usual dramatic flair.

That, more than anything, put him on edge.

“Is there a reason we’re walking directly into a place that gives off obvious mind-control energy,” he asked, dry, “or do you just enjoy ignoring basic survival instinct?”

Cipher glanced back with a smile that didn’t quite reach her eyes. “Didn’t peg you for claustrophobic, Book King.”

“I’m not. I just like knowing if I’m walking into a place designed to peel my brain open like fruit leather.”

“Ugh, gross.”

She turned a corner, crouched, and scanned the wall for a biometric seam. When her glove lit green, the panel slid open, revealing an old stairwell reinforced with psych-steel plates. Reinforced from inside.

Mydei stared at the layers of shielding. “This place was meant to keep something in.”

“Technically? Minds. Lots of them.” Cipher didn’t look back. “It’s called the Mirror Room.”

“And how, exactly, did you find it?”

“Luck. Gut instinct. A vaguely threatening dream about elevators.” She shrugged. “You ever follow a feeling so weird it had to be something?”

“I avoid feelings as a general rule.”

She grinned.

They descended. The door sealed behind them.

The room opened slowly—more facility than chamber. White, pristine, but wrong. Mirrors lined the walls in seamless rows, reflecting too much light. There were no frames, no angles, just endless glass. One flickered faintly, and Cipher immediately covered her eyes.

“Don’t look directly into them until we break the primary feed,” she warned. “This place reads your emotional map and tailors stimuli to it. That means—”

“I’m aware what emotional feedback loops are,” Mydei muttered.

“Okay, nerd.”

A monitor blinked to life above them, a silent stream of data pulsing across the screen. There were tags. Names. Brief flashes of faces, expressions mid-panic or reverie. Cipher paused beneath it, reading.

“This whole node was a psychological experiment,” she said after a moment, voice tight. “Run by something codenamed Voxcore. They tagged people—implants, minor enough to pass as headaches. Then ran simulations. Trauma exposure. Cycles. Like AI-driven therapy, except not.”

“Except weaponized.”

Cipher nodded. “It’s using this data to pacify or destabilize. Depending on who walks in. Guess what that means for us.”

“I’m going to see something I’d rather not. Again.”

“Yep. And I’ll probably see something that makes me want to punch a wall. Again.”

They exchanged a glance.

Then Cipher cracked her knuckles. “Alright. You hit the core; I’ll handle the reroute from the server spine. We move quick. Mirrors aren’t mirrors. They’re interface panels. Don’t let them catch your reflection for too long.”

Mydei didn’t reply. Just set his jaw, adjusted the strap of the reinforced glove on his left hand, and walked in.

They split the moment the floor panels lit up.

Cipher bolted left, slipping between panels with inhuman grace, each step timed between sensor flickers. Mydei moved with practiced, deliberate force, weaving past the mirrors with just enough peripheral awareness to map the room without catching his reflection.

Data arced above them—lines of code bleeding into the air like spectral veins. Somewhere deeper in, something pulsed once, faint and rhythmic, as if the entire facility had a heartbeat.

Mydei reached the core housing first. The vault was sealed behind reinforced plating, rigged with logic puzzles and outdated encryption cycles. Child’s play. His fingers flew over the interface, bypassing most of the system’s interactive layers and slipping beneath, directly into the skeleton of the feed.

“Spinal reroute in place,” Cipher’s voice crackled through the comms. “About to overload the primary channels.”

“Wait for the loop to hit forty-two percent,” Mydei replied, still focused. “Any earlier and it’ll just reroute to the mirrors again.”

“I know how to fry a loop, Mydei.”

“Then don’t talk while doing it.”

“Rude.”

He heard her laugh, faint and sharp through the earpiece—but it cut off too soon. Static crackled.

Then nothing.

“Cipher?” he asked. No response.

Mydei straightened from the console. “Cipher, report.”

No answer.

He moved.

The halls here weren’t uniform—stretched too long, corners angled just slightly off-center like someone had built this place in a dream. The air grew colder the deeper he went. Not temperature. Not really. Just… quiet. Like something had pressed a hand over the world.

He found her two junctions over, standing frozen in the middle of a mirrored corridor. One foot lifted, mid-step. Her arm was still halfway up, like she’d meant to wave something away. But she wasn’t moving.

Her eyes were locked ahead.

Mydei followed her gaze—and stopped.

Standing directly in Cipher’s path was… Cipher. Younger. Blood on her cheek. Hair tangled. Eyes wide and tearful.

“Don’t go in,” the younger version whispered. “Please. Don’t go in. It’s a trap. You’ll die. I—”

She stepped back, hands trembling. “I shouldn’t have come. I shouldn’t’ve done it. I told you. You never listen—”

Mydei took one step forward, reaching to grab Cipher’s shoulder.

She flinched like she hadn’t even realized he was there.

The projection glitched—once. A flicker, like static under skin. Then the young Cipher vanished.

Just gone.

Cipher exhaled sharply. Her hand clenched and unclenched at her side.

“She wasn’t part of the data feed,” she muttered. “I scanned the whole thing. There was nothing from that year. No mirror should’ve pulled that.”

Mydei said nothing. He just waited.

Cipher didn’t look at him. “I’m fine,” she said. Then louder, with more bite: “I said I’m fine.”

He nodded once.

And they kept moving.

Mydei didn’t comment on what had just happened.

He saw nothing in the corridor ahead—no flickers—but that meant very little in a place like this. Silence could be a lull or a lie. Cipher had gone quiet, and he respected it, shifting his attention instead to the path ahead, mapping the remaining grid lines and redirecting power flow.

Behind him, he heard the faint hitch of breath as she collected herself. No careful tone. He’d never insult her with that.

Instead, he asked, “You scanned the archives before we came. No entries from that year?”

Cipher exhaled hard through her nose. “I triple-checked. That memory shouldn’t be here. Not even close. My tagging was wiped by the time I joined Aglaea. I made sure of it.”

“Then the system’s pulling data it shouldn’t have access to. Unindexed memories. Possibly pre-verbal imprints.”

Cipher snorted. “You say that like it’s a comforting theory.”

“It’s not.”

They reached the anchor point three minutes later. Deep in the heart of the loop chamber, tucked behind a half-glitched array of emotion-mapping

relays, stood the core: a tangle of optic threads and mirrored neuromesh, glowing faintly blue beneath a stretched surface like skin over circuitry.

This wasn’t just a storage vault. It was active processing. Multiple minds, thousands of signatures, all crammed and indexed by trauma severity.

Cipher rubbed her temples. “Why do I feel like this room is screaming at me without making a sound.”

“Because it probably is.”

Mydei stepped closer, careful not to catch his reflection in the walls. The pulse from the anchor was stronger here, vibrating through his shoes into bone. It wasn’t a conscious force—but it wasn’t unconscious either. It was built to watch, built to feel. And now that it had been disturbed, it was lashing back with the only weapons it had: memories and mimicry.

Cipher moved around the other side, flipped open her modified Chrysos terminal—sleek, almost skeletal, with glowing threads crawling across its frame like tattoos. Her own design, of course. “Alright, we’ll hit it from both sides. Mydei, prep for sync. I’ll spike the top layer.”

He nodded once, linking his interface through hers. There was a flick of static, then—

Pain. Like memory itself had turned to shards and decided to burrow straight through their skulls.

He gritted his teeth as Cipher hissed, staggering back a step.

“This isn’t a normal node,” she bit out. “It’s a convergence point. All the tagged signatures? They’re not just stored—they’re looped. It’s running them. Endlessly. Like a fucking simulation engine.”

Mydei’s eyes narrowed at the code bloom unfolding on the shared display.

It was mutating.

He watched the lines writhe—once-sharp logic pathways now folding into themselves, data loops splitting and forking into tangents. Each cycle made it more complex. More cohesive. Not random.

“Adaptation,” he muttered. “It’s learning from every emotional imprint. Reconstructing its interfaces with borrowed behavior.”

Cipher was pale now. “You mean the mimics.”

“They’re not just images. They’re evolving constructs. The longer they’re active, the more information they pull from the surrounding network. Eventually…”

“They won’t need the anchors,” she finished, voice tight. “They’ll be real enough to stand on their own.”

They both went still.

That had been the plan—hit two of the three, destabilize the system, and let the third unravel on its own. But now…

“This place wasn’t a foundation,” Mydei said slowly. “It was a womb.”

Cipher gave him a sharp look. “So what—you’re saying we’ve just been playing midwife to a parasitic dream machine?”

“Something like that.”

There wasn’t a dramatic countdown after that. Just a shared glance, a flick of synchronization between their terminals, and a discharge so sharp and bright it fried the neuromesh like a snapped nerve.

The core screamed—not audibly, but in sensation. The room convulsed. And then it died.

They stood in the sudden dark, both of them breathing harder than they realized. Something behind Cipher sparked once, then stilled.

“…Two down,” she said, pressing a hand to her temple. “One left.”

Mydei’s voice was low. “And if the third’s already stable…”

“Then it’s not a node anymore,” Cipher said grimly. “It’s a nest.”

They hadn’t slept. Not once. Cipher looked like hell, and Mydei hadn’t said a word about it—because she, miraculously, had refrained from commenting on the bags under his eyes.

Wind skated across the rooftop, tugging at Cipher’s hood as she leaned against the rusted railing. Mydei stood a few paces back, arms crossed, eyes fixed on a flickering billboard across the city. Neither of them had spoken in a while. There wasn’t much to say that hadn’t already been said in fragments over the last ten hours.

The second anchor was gone. Destroyed. And yet—

“It’s slowing,” Cipher said, finally stopping her pacing. “You were right. The first two anchors hit it hard. Spread’s down. Mimic activity’s staggered. But—”

“But it’s not regressing,” Mydei finished, not looking up. “It’s consolidating.”

“Like it’s bracing itself.”

“Or hiding,” he muttered.

She pulled out another protein bar, stared at it, then pocketed it again. “You know what pisses me off? We actually did everything right. Blew the anchors. Tracked the feeds. Burned the backups. And it’s still slithering around like it’s waiting for an upgrade.”

They went quiet again. A loose pipe rattled in the wind. Sirens murmured faintly in the distance.

Then, quietly, Cipher said, “I can’t trace it.”

He looked over.

“My network,” she clarified, jaw clenched. “Even the back channels. It’s not on the grid anymore. If it ever was.”

Cipher sighed. “If the third anchor exists, it’s wearing a mask. And wearing it well. No energy signature. No signal bleed. It’s either mobile, cloaked, or —”

“Disguised as a person.”

Silence again.

Cipher leaned back, arms folded. “If it’s wearing a human face, we’ve already lost.”

“We haven’t lost,” Mydei said sharply—more to himself than to her. “But we’re running out of time.”

The third node wasn’t just another link in the chain. If the first was storage, and the second was evolution, the third was the heart. The control center. The stabilizer that allowed the mimics to function independently. Once it reached maturity, destroying it might not matter. The system would be too far along—capable of surviving without support.

After a long silence, Cipher pulled out a comm device and scrolled through a list. Mydei caught a glimpse—she hovered over Aglaea’s ID for a second, then switched tabs. Not a friend. A protocol line.

She clicked it.

“Cipher, transmitting incident code Black Echo Three. Requesting joint investigation support from the Chrysos-Gov oversight unit. Immediate response window. Full access permissions.”

The reply came fast.

“Received.”

Just one word. But even Mydei felt the weight behind it.

Cipher locked the device and shoved it back into her jacket. “Well,” she said. “Guess it’s officially a party now.”

Mydei didn’t respond. Just stared out at the city.

The third anchor was still out there.

And it was learning how to be real.

The debrief took less time than it should have.

Cipher and Mydei were brought in fast—no waiting lines, just silent nods and biometric scans as the guards ushered them through steel doors and sealed checkpoints. They didn’t even get questioned until after someone shoved them both into a heated bench seat and handed over standard-issue emergency blankets. Cipher had laughed dryly at that, but didn’t complain. Mydei just wrapped his around his shoulders and leaned back, grateful not to be standing anymore.

They explained everything. The anchors. The projections. The mimic of Gorgo. The memory absorption pattern and the evolution protocols. By the time they reached the part about the third node, even the high-ranking agents had stopped asking clarifying questions. Aglaea herself stepped in soon after—listened to their rundown, brows knit, arms folded. When they were done, she gave a tight nod and walked off without a word.

Cipher whistled low. “She’s either really impressed or really about to gut someone.”

Mydei didn’t answer. He was half-asleep under his blanket, chin resting on one hand.

Cipher shifted, nudged his leg lightly with her boot. “So that’s it. We’re done, right?”

He opened one eye. “Yeah. Our part’s over.”

Cipher sat back, expression unreadable. “Weird, isn’t it? We tear through all that, almost get mimicked to hell, and barely a few hours later they already have a lead on the third node.”

“That fast?” Mydei sat up.

She nodded. “Didn’t tell me much—shockers. But they’ve got someone sniffing it out already. Chrysos-Gov are freakishly efficient when they want to be.”

He rubbed his temples. “I’d rather be moving.”

Cipher raised an eyebrow.

“I mean it.” Mydei stood, blanket still around his shoulders like a makeshift cloak. “I’m not useful sitting around here. I’ll cover ground, even if it’s nothing. Keeps me sane.”

Cipher didn’t argue. She leaned forward, elbows on her knees. “I figured you’d bounce. Honestly, I’m thinking I’ll stick around here a bit longer. Maybe poke at some of their auxiliary feeds, see if anything slips through. If that third anchor’s got a face, it’s only a matter of time before it blinks wrong somewhere.”

He nodded. “Keep me posted.”

She reached out, patted his shoulder with a tired smirk. “Will do. I’ll update you once Princess Homebody decides to grace us with her divine return.”

Mydei chuckled under his breath. “Castorice always has timing.”

“Too good,” Cipher muttered. “Girl’s a damn oracle.”

He moved toward the exit, blanket still trailing behind him like some reluctant cape. “Good luck.”

Cipher saluted lazily with two fingers. “You too, Godslayer.”

He didn’t turn back. Just lifted a hand in farewell and disappeared down the corridor.

The city hadn’t quieted. Not really. But it moved differently now.

Mydei walked with his hands in his pockets, blanket finally ditched back at the agency drop-off. The streets still buzzed faintly, transit lines rumbling underfoot, light pollution dusting the sky in faint orange. But there was a lull in the air.

He wasn’t just walking. Every few blocks, his eyes swept the rooftops, tracked faint movement across crosswalks, watched for glints of unnatural light or static skipping across the edges of glass. If there were residual signals, if anything lingered from the anchors… he wanted to see it first. Just to know.

But that was only part of it.

The other reason—well. That one made his pace pick up a little when the old garden district finally came into view.

The park wasn’t large. Most of the trees were grafted biogenics, and the grass had a telltale grid pattern from whatever underground wiring powered the garden’s humidity systems. Still, it was green. It was quiet. It was enough.

He turned a corner.

And there he was.

Phainon sat on one of the swings, bundled in a too-big hoodie, kicking the toes of his shoes against the dirt path. Head tilted up, watching the way the artificial leaves rustled in the night breeze. The kind of calm that looked effortless, but Mydei knew better—Phainon wasn’t fidgeting, which meant he’d been waiting.

Mydei didn’t say anything. Just walked over, settled into the swing next to him, and let the chains creak a little under his weight.

Phainon didn’t look surprised. Just glanced over, smile tugging at his mouth, soft and warm.

“You’re late,” he said.

Mydei tilted his head back, feigning thought. “Am I?”

“Not by much,” Phainon admitted. “I gave you a fifteen-minute grace window because I figured you’d get distracted saving someone’s cat.”

“Bold of you to assume I didn’t.”

That earned a small laugh. “Okay, now I’m picturing you in a tree trying to talk a cat down.”

“I wouldn’t talk it down. I’d negotiate.”

“Bet you’d lose.”

They sat like that for a moment—just the soft sway of the swings and the hush of the wind skimming over steel and synth-leaf. The streetlights flickered lazily, casting long shadows across the worn rubber beneath their feet.

Phainon bumped his swing into Mydei’s, just barely. “You look like you haven’t slept in two days.”

Mydei glanced over. “You’re not wrong.”

“And yet,” Phainon said, voice light, “you still showed up. Swing and all.”

“I’d rather die than miss this.”

“Dramatic.”

“Accurate.”

Phainon smiled again. Not the usual crooked smirk or the half-laugh kind of grin he wore when teasing—but something more sincere. Seems like he wasn’t the only one who had a bad day. He looked down at his hands, then back at Mydei.

“I’m glad you’re here.”

Mydei didn’t answer right away.

The swings creaked again, and the city moved on around them. For now, there weren’t any sirens. No flickers of corrupted light. No weight dragging down Mydei’s shoulders except the usual kind—the kind that felt a little lighter when Phainon was close by.

And tomorrow could wait.

Mydei stood first. He glanced once down the path, then said, “We’re going on a walk.”

Phainon leaned back slightly on the swing, sneakers scraping the dirt beneath him. “That’s ominous,” he said, not moving. “Is this a trick? Are you leading me into some obscure alley to yell at me about misusing the stovetop again?”

“It was on fire, Phainon.”

“Briefly.”

“You ignited a sound sculpture in the shape of a plate rack.”

“I was exploring the intersection of form and vibration! …Also I thought the metal would vibrate less if I microwaved it first.”

Mydei turned his head just enough to give him a slow, unimpressed look.

Phainon stood with a sigh, brushing nonexistent dust from his sleeves. “Fine. Lead the way.”

They fell into step together easily. The streets ahead curled through the edge of the residential sector, which had mostly quieted for the night. Buildings softened from sleek mirrored glass into older stonework, accented with green tiles and scattered signs of aging infrastructure. Phainon kept talking the whole way, hands stuffed in his hoodie pockets, hopping from one thought to the next without much coherence.

He went on about some bizarre theory he read involving vibrational memory patterns—how certain materials might absorb and re-emit emotional frequencies—and how he’d been testing it by yelling compliments at spoons. “You laugh,” he said seriously, “but the one I praised all week stirred my tea smoother than the others. The other ones were…judgy.”

“You’re scaring me.”

“You don’t understand the emotional range of flatware.”

Mydei didn’t say much. He just let Phainon ramble, which was both strategic and affectionate. He was listening. He always did, even when the logic spiraled off into the abstract.

They turned another corner and the noise of the city dropped off almost instantly.

Ahead of them, tucked between the shadows of a cluster of highrises, a narrow walkway opened into something more carefully designed. Mydei had chosen it precisely for that contrast—a quiet, enclosed courtyard nestled between a gallery and a government archive, overgrown with flowering vines and soft gold lighting that spilled down from the glass canopy above.

It wasn’t a flashy place, but it was serene, with tall stone arches bordering a reflecting pool and hanging plants swaying faintly in the controlled breeze.

Phainon slowed as they approached, his footsteps naturally easing back from their earlier rhythm.

“You do know how to set a scene,” he said, half-impressed, half-suspicious. “Is this the part where you propose? Because I will faint.”

Mydei didn’t reply.

His gaze had already shifted toward the far end of the garden.

Beneath one of the arches, standing in a soft spill of overhead light, was someone waiting.

She wore a long, pale jacket. Her posture was calm.

Her hair—long, pink, unmistakable—caught the light in a way that made it almost shimmer.

Phainon followed Mydei’s line of sight.

He stopped mid-sentence.

The silence between them didn’t feel immediate. It was more like the world itself quieted by degrees, one layer at a time—first the rustle of leaves, then the distant drone of a tram, then the hum of lights overhead.

Phainon didn’t say anything.

Mydei started to step back, already easing himself a little out of the way, giving space the way someone would before a private reunion. What a good boyfriend I am, he thought, not without a touch of smugness.

Then Phainon turned and reached for him.

Not a gentle reach. His hand closed around Mydei’s wrist, firm and fast.

Mydei blinked, caught off guard. “Phainon?”

But Phainon didn’t answer. His grip tightened, and he pulled.

It wasn’t a sprint exactly. Just a quick, focused departure, like they were late for something.

“Hey,” Mydei said again, confused now, glancing back over his shoulder. “Phainon, what—?”

“We need to go,” Phainon muttered, curt but clear.

They were already halfway back through the arch when Mydei slowed his steps, resisting slightly. “That’s her. You knew she—”

“No,” Phainon cut in, his voice sharp now. “We’re not doing this.”

He wasn’t looking at Mydei anymore. His gaze was fixed straight ahead, and there was something in his jaw—something too tight.

“She’s waiting,” Mydei said carefully, testing.

Phainon’s grip only locked harder. “I know. That’s why we need to leave.”

The last words fell into the space behind them like stones.

And though Mydei didn’t say anything else, he couldn’t help but glance back one more time.

Cyrene was still standing there, exactly where she had been. Her head slightly tilted. Not waving. Not calling out.

Just watching.

They didn’t run far, but the turn they made was sharp, instinctive—guided more by Phainon’s grip than any actual destination. Mydei’s boots scuffed tile, and before he could voice the hundred questions crowding his throat, Phainon yanked open a rusted utility door nearly hidden by the garden’s layered vines and dragged them both through.

It was a service alcove. Small. Barely enough room to turn around without brushing metal pipes or the uneven concrete walls. The door clicked shut behind them, leaving only the distant hum of automated fans somewhere deep in the ventilation above.

Then Phainon slammed his palm into the wall beside Mydei’s head—his other arm still pressing him back, pinning him.

“Okay,” Mydei started, breath catching from the momentum, “what the hell is—”

He stopped.

Phainon wasn’t looking at him. His head was bowed slightly, breath short, uneven. Mydei’s voice faltered as he registered the slight tremble running through Phainon’s shoulders. The shallow, almost panicked rhythm of it.

The last time he’d seen Phainon look remotely close to this had been years ago—and even then, it hadn’t looked like this.

The silence folded in tight.

Phainon’s voice, when it came, was quiet. Raw. “That’s not her.”

Mydei didn’t move. He felt the tension in Phainon’s arm still caging him in, the way his hand clenched and flexed as if unsure whether to hold on or run.

“I didn’t think,” Phainon said again, barely audible now, “I thought I’d imagined it the first time. That it was just someone who looked like her. But I saw her again. Three nights ago. Not there, not… not like that, but on the train. Same jacket. Same way of tilting her head. Same voice when she turned to a stranger and said ‘excuse me.’ Exactly the same.”

His fingers curled tighter against the wall.

“I told myself I was wrong. That she couldn’t look that young anymore, that she wouldn’t wear her hair that way. But tonight—” He finally looked at Mydei, face pale in the low light. “She looked just like she did when we were fifteen. And she smiled.”

The silence that followed wasn’t awkward. It was final. Like a door slamming shut inside him.

“She’s dead, Mydei.”

Mydei felt the weight of the words settle into the room like dust. Heavy. Undeniable. And for the first time since stepping into this entire garden, he understood the look in Phainon’s eyes when they’d seen her.

It hadn’t been shock, it had been recognition.

Not of a person though, but of a ghost that shouldn’t exist.

Mydei reached for him—not to stop him, not even to pull him back, just to make contact—but Phainon wasn’t really present anymore. He stood with both hands braced against the wall like he needed the pressure to keep from unraveling. His breathing had steadied, but it didn’t sound right. Like he was focusing on getting through it, not coming down from anything.

Mydei opened his mouth. “I didn’t know.”

“I know.”

There wasn’t room in his voice for anything beyond that. Not blame. Not comfort.

Then Phainon straightened and turned toward him, not completely relaxed, but no longer visibly shaking either. His expression had gone still, not blank —measured. He didn’t ask permission or explain when he leaned forward and pressed his lips briefly to Mydei’s forehead. It wasn’t affectionate in the usual way. More like giving someone—himself—a reminder of who he had with him to keep safe.

“If you’ve ever trusted anything I’ve said,” he murmured, “I need you to go when I tell you. I’ll pull it away from here.”

“Phainon—”

“I’m not asking.”

He took a step back toward the entrance, adjusting his footing, but didn’t move further. His body was still half-blocking Mydei from the gap in the

wall when the sound hit.

A long scrape echoed across the surface behind them—metal bending slightly under pressure, the edge of something hard dragging across it, like someone was testing for weak points. Mydei’s breath caught. He turned to the source, but there was no shadow passing under the door. No shuffle of movement. No sound of breathing.

Phainon’s arm came up to hold him in place, not roughly, but without hesitation.

It hadn’t spoken once. It hadn’t called out or glitched or tried to trick them. It didn’t need to.

Mydei stood still, his thoughts running too fast now to sort through. The way it moved. The timing. The silence. It had followed them without alerting a single sensor, tracked them through an unlisted garden path, and arrived here already knowing who it needed to reach.

That wasn’t mimic behavior. It wasn’t projecting from stored footage. This thing was learning. Every twitch of Phainon’s hand, every breath out of place—it had been watching and refining itself in real time.

It didn’t need to pretend to be Cyrene. It had found something more efficient than memory.

It had learned Phainon.

And that meant this wasn’t just another echo.

This was the third node. The core. Alive and adapting.

Phainon started toward the exit, already crouched, ready to move.

Mydei’s hand shot out and grabbed his wrist, tight.

Phainon halted instantly, but the way he turned back wasn’t gentle. His face was tense, expression tight like he was counting to ten in his head.

“Mydei,” he said, not harsh, but unmistakably serious.

And that tone—that flat, quiet insistence—set something off in Mydei that had nothing to do with fear. He stared at him, disbelieving, heart still pounding from the sound outside.

“You’re seriously going to pull that stunt?” he said, low. “You think you’re doing me a favor by throwing yourself at it?”

Phainon’s eyes narrowed, his whole stance wound up tighter. “If we both stay, we die.”

“And you don’t?”

“I’m faster than you.”

“Bull—”

The wall groaned.

They both stopped.

It didn’t creak or splinter—it groaned, like something was prying against the frame from above. A beat later, metal screamed overhead as the roof was torn away in a single, effortless wrench. Wind slammed down into the space like a wave. Debris scattered. Dust and glass rained down. Neither of them moved.

They turned around at the same time.

She was standing on what used to be the ceiling, limbs too long, joints bending just enough in the wrong directions to make it impossible to ignore. Her face still looked like Cyrene’s. But the smile that spread across it wasn’t human.

There was no twitch. Nothing indicating something robotic or glitching. Just a widening grin that opened further than it should have, inky black sliding into the corners of her eyes.

Neither of them spoke.

They just ran.

Phainon shoved the loose door off its hinges and pulled Mydei through it. Mydei didn’t let go of his wrist. They moved fast, cutting across the overgrown garden paths, weaving between hedges and statues and rusted benches half-swallowed by moss. The thing didn’t crash after them. It didn’t roar or shriek.

But they knew it was coming.

And for the first time, Mydei didn’t care how much noise they made. There was no point in hiding anymore.

They didn’t look back.

Phainon was fast, but Mydei was faster. No hesitation, no wasted movement —he tore across the broken paths, weaving between hedges and shattered glass domes, dodging collapsed trellises and blown-out fountains like he’d trained for this exact garden layout. Phainon kept pace behind him, close, but Mydei could hear the ragged edge in his breathing and didn’t waste time pretending otherwise.

“She’s gaining,” Phainon muttered, breathless.

Mydei didn’t answer. He already knew.

They cleared a stone railing and dropped into a lower courtyard, feet hitting the ground hard enough to rattle bone. Mydei didn’t slow—he grabbed Phainon’s wrist and pulled, dragging them toward the service tunnels. It wasn’t perfect, but it was enclosed, and the exit looped back toward the edge of the district. Isolated enough to cut through without risking civilians.

A sound slammed down behind them—dirt and stone crunching in rapid succession.

“She’s not running,” Phainon managed between breaths. “She’s skipping.”

Mydei didn’t ask what that meant. He could feel it. The way the mimic closed distance was wrong. No footsteps. No rhythm. One moment far, the next nearly brushing their backs.

He kept his grip locked, hauling Phainon behind him through the shattered archway. Branches caught on their clothes, shattered glass bit through fabric, but they didn’t stop.

He finally spoke, short and direct. “Service corridor. North vent shaft. If we can reach it—”

“It’s sealed.”

“Only from the outside.”

He turned a corner, yanked open the grate hidden behind an overgrown statue, and shoved Phainon through first. The mimic didn’t scream or claw at them—nothing so dramatic. But Mydei felt it the second he climbed in after him. It was right behind them. Too close.

He slammed the grate shut. Metal warped in his hands.

And still—no sound.

Mydei pulled himself up beside Phainon in the dark, both of them breathless, scraped, bleeding in places they hadn’t noticed yet. The vent was tight, barely enough room to crawl, but for now it was cover.

Phainon leaned his head back against the wall, eyes shut.

“Still think you’re faster than me?” Mydei muttered.

Phainon didn’t smile.

“We’re not done yet.”

The vent was silent for a few minutes. Just the sound of their breathing as it evened out, slower now but still heavy. The worst part was that Mydei couldn’t hear her anymore. Not even scraping.

Phainon shifted beside him. His knuckles were still pale from how hard he’d gripped the vent walls earlier.

“So,” he said, voice steadier than it had any right to be. “What’s the plan?”

Mydei hesitated, only briefly. “There’s a maintenance hatch a few meters ahead. If we time it right, I can hotwire the exterior latch before it resets. That should get us out into the train depot. From there, we cut across to the west block. That side’s been cleared since the gas line breach. She won’t follow where there’s no one to watch.”

Phainon didn’t argue. Not with that. But then he turned, eyes sharp, his tone more clipped now.

“If something goes wrong,” he repeated, “you run.”

Mydei exhaled through his nose, already shaking his head.

“I’m serious,” Phainon went on. “She’s after me. I don’t know how, but she is. And if you try to get in between that, it’s going to end badly.”

Mydei bit down on the reply, the first one that came to him. Something sarcastic, probably. Something deflective.

Instead, what came out was quieter. “You don’t know that.”

“I do.”

“I’m not leaving you behind.”

“You might have to.”

“I won’t.”

The tension stretched, stubborn and familiar. They stared at each other for a beat too long before Phainon sighed, frustration clear, but not angry.

“You’re not taking this seriously,” he said, voice lowering.

“I’m taking it seriously,” Mydei replied, the edge returning now. “I’m just not planning for you to die.”

Phainon stared for a second longer, then finally looked away, jaw tight. But something cracked between them.

There, in that dim, metal corridor, pressed between steel panels and the distant sound of wind scraping the ruins above, they stopped posturing. Just for a moment.

Phainon ran a hand through his hair, quiet now. “I didn’t mean to drag you into this.”

“You didn’t,” Mydei said. “I walked into it.”

A small pause.

Phainon nodded. “Still…I’m glad you’re here.”

And something about the way he said it—reluctantly honest. It landed heavier than anything else tonight.

They leaned in slightly at the same time, heads resting against the narrow steel wall, foreheads brushing just faintly. It wasn’t a kiss. Just stillness. Breathing the same air again, even if it tasted like dust and iron.

But then—something decided to fuck it up.

A faint change in pressure. A pop in the vent seal behind them.

Mydei tensed instantly. The panel at the rear end of the shaft creaked—no tearing, no booming entrance, just a subtle flex of metal that hadn’t been loose a moment ago.

His eyes widened. “How—”

Then it hit him. Not the mimic. The realization.

The vents. They were insulated, but not completely sealed as he thought. If that thing could trace neurological imprint, if it could adapt based on who it followed—

It didn’t need sound. Or scent. Or light.

It just needed proximity.

The panel behind them caved inward.

Phainon moved first, throwing his arm back to shield Mydei without thinking—but the thing didn’t lunge or strike.

It looked at them.

Still Cyrene. Still pink hair, still soft face. But something in the stance was wrong. She leaned forward on her elbows like someone listening to a lullaby only she could hear. Then she smiled. Slowly. That same smile as before.

And then—

Phainon froze again.

Not flinched or tensed. Froze.

His mouth parted like he meant to say something, but nothing came. His shoulders slumped as his eyes went glassy—not unconscious, but vacant. Like something reached in and turned the volume off.

“Phainon?” Mydei moved toward him instinctively, shaking his shoulder. “Phainon, look at me—hey, what the hell—?”

No response.

He remembered Cipher’s words.

First sighting. Then conversation. Then blackout.

But this wasn’t fainting. Phainon wasn’t drooping, wasn’t swaying. He was sitting upright, breathing steady, eyes open and tracking—but empty.

Like a puppet with no strings left.

Mydei didn’t move. Not yet.

The mimic didn’t either.

For a moment, no one moved. Three bodies, one breathing in a conventional sense.

The mimic stared down at Phainon like it was trying to figure out how to lift him without breaking something. Its fingers hovered above his collarbone, gentle in the way that made Mydei’s stomach twist.

He stepped between them.

It didn’t stop him. Just tilted its head, slow. Studying. Then it moved. Quick —too quick—and drove a hand clean through Mydei’s chest.

Straight through.

There was a beat of silence as it waited.

Mydei didn’t flinch. Didn’t fall.

He looked down at the blackened, clawed arm inside him and then back up. A flat breath pushed out of him—not pain. Closer to annoyance.

The mimic pulled back sharply. Like it had physically been burned.

It stepped away, a few inches first, then more. The lines of its face began to shift. Not morphing exactly, but more so as if it was trying to remember how to be human again and failing. It opened its mouth and no normal words came out—just a sound, somewhere between a hiss and the creak of something too old being forced to move.

Mydei took a step forward, not out of aggression, but curiosity.

It saw him now. Not just as an obstacle. As a problem.

He nearly smiled.

“You thought you were the only freak in the room,” he said, voice quiet, tone dry. “Shame.”

It hissed again, louder this time. The soft face melted back, jaw stretching wider than it should’ve, joints ticking out of place with quiet, wet pops. Its limbs grew longer. Sharper. Wrong.

Perfect.

Mydei’s fingers flexed once. Then, without taking his eyes off it, he shifted slightly and dragged the back of his foot across the floor—catching some debris and tugging it sideways.

The mimic twitched.

There it was.

He’d noticed it a second ago. A repeating detail in its reconstruction. Something off in the way the illusion maintained itself in physical spaces— geometry that didn’t quite update in real time. Almost as if its form couldn’t bend to environmental damage without resetting.

So he made it worse.

He stepped hard on the edge of the bent space and dragged a cracked stone paver back, hard enough that it scraped the mimic’s warped footprint.

It snapped.

The creature let out a jagged, scraping scream, then lunged—but Mydei was already moving, drawing it out with a few fast, brutal steps. Not away from Phainon—around. He was guiding it away, flanking.

It followed him.

Good.

Because now it was mad. Now it wasn’t thinking.

And now, it was his.

The vent shaft opened with a metallic clatter as Mydei kicked through the last grate, dropping hard onto the roof below. His boots hit slick metal, knees bending low to absorb the fall, and then he was already moving— down the slope, across a rusted maintenance ladder, and vaulting the low barrier that marked the edge of the garden’s upper walk.

The mimic was right behind him.

Mydei twisted as he ran, dragging a blade he kept in his jacket and flinging it back. The thing caught it midair like it weighed nothing, fingers curling tight before crushing it to dust.

Alright. No more distractions.

He pivoted hard at the end of the path, using a cracked trellis beam to slingshot himself left. He needed open space. Visibility. Somewhere it could be locked down.

And then—he saw it.

An amphitheater clearing tucked between the artificial riverbanks and ivy-swept stonework. Perfect line of sight, no exits, and most importantly: empty.

Mydei ran faster.

The mimic shrieked behind him—glitched sound torn through corrupted lungs—and the air warped around his shoulders as it closed in. Mydei hit the center of the clearing and turned fast, ready to—

A blur shot past overhead.

Then a sharp sound like laughter and glass.

“Really?” a voice called. “You couldn’t wait twenty more minutes?”

There she was.

Landing in a spin of black-and-purple silk, her boots cracking the tiles with impact, Cipher—no, Kitty Phantom Thief—flashed into view with the theatricality of someone born to make a goddamn entrance.

Her mask caught the light in a gleam of pale violet as she leveled her baton, modified with enough illegal tech to qualify as a war crime, directly at the mimic’s throat.

“Told you I’d bring backup,” she said, voice light.

And backup she brought.

Figures surged in from every side—Heir agents, vigilante allies, a full government tactical unit dressed in containment armor. Spotlights flared from every angle, beams locking onto the mimic as kinetic barriers shimmered to life.

The mimic screamed again. It lashed out, limbs warping in a final attempt to phase out—but the grid was already snapping into place. Traps deployed, energy fields compressed, and Cipher’s baton lit up in her hand with an almost melodic hum before she threw it like a spear.

It hit dead center, and the mimic dropped.

All at once, the air stopped vibrating.

Mydei didn’t even realize how hard he’d been bracing until his knees gave slightly. He sank down on the rough stone, arms resting on them, and finally—finally—let himself breathe.

Cipher padded over, nudging him lightly with the toe of her boot. “Told you we had a lead.”

He looked up, chest still rising fast, and gave her a breathless, half-exhausted glare.

She winked. “Next time, maybe check your texts.”

Behind them, the mimic was already being sealed away—its body flickering, glitching out as containment protocols locked down the last node.

Three anchors. Neutralized.

One goddamn nightmare less.

Mydei’s spine pressed to cool stone, lungs finally working like they were meant to. The chaos was still echoing—shouts from the agents corralling the last of the energy, Cipher rattling off updates to a nearby tech, some poor intern puking behind a planter—but for one small, blessed second, it was over.

He’d survived worse. Fought worse. But this? This had been a slow kind of terror. The kind that followed you around with a fake face and dead eyes.

He exhaled.

And then it hit him.

Phainon.

Still in there. Still unconscious. Alone.

Mydei shot to his feet so fast his knees cracked, chest already tight with panic.

“Shit—”

Cipher turned just as he started to move, hand snapping up to catch his arm. “Relax.”

“I can’t,” he snapped. “He’s still in there, Cipher—he’s still—”

“I know. I know,” she said, gentler this time, gripping his sleeve until he stilled. “Medical already got to him. They’re running checks now.”

He tried to pull away anyway, but she didn’t let go.

“I mean it. The moment that thing dropped, we sent a crew in. And here’s the good news—real news, not the vague ‘we’ll monitor the situation’ bullshit. Now that the anchors are broken, the trances should start to fade. They’ll wake up, eventually.”

He blinked hard, chest still rising too fast, but the pressure eased just slightly.

“And if not,” Cipher added, “we’ve got a few ideas. People smarter than me already running simulations. He’s gonna be okay.”

For the first time all night, the tension in Mydei’s jaw loosened. He didn’t smile. Couldn’t. But he nodded, once, and Cipher let go.

He turned to leave. He’d had enough. He just needed to see Phainon—just lay eyes on him, maybe touch his hand or something equally embarrassing —and then maybe collapse in peace.

But before he got two steps, Cipher called after him.

“Oh, and—Princess Homebody’s back.”

He stopped. “Castorice?”

Cipher grinned, already digging something out of the side pocket of her utility belt. “You know how she is. Went off the grid for a bit, came back with receipts.”

He turned halfway, cautious curiosity winning over exhaustion. “What’d she find?”

Cipher stepped closer. “She found a lead.”

“To what?”

Cipher’s smile was the kind that meant trouble. “Who’s behind all this.”

Mydei stared at her.

She raised an eyebrow, voice calm as a blade. “Tell me, Mydei. You ever heard of the Flame Reaver?”

Chapter End Notes
