Phainon had been awake for a few hours now.

Long enough to memorize the water stains on the ceiling, count the number of soft blinks from the monitor clipped to his finger, and go over—at least six times—what he should have said two days ago.

Also long enough to know that Mydei hadn’t left since he’d come to. The chair by his bed had a permanent crease now, and his posture screamed stubborn concern disguised as casual slouching.

“…I’m fine,” Phainon said, not for the first time.

“You were unconscious for nearly forty-eight hours,” Mydei replied, flat.

“I was resting.”

Mydei didn’t laugh, but the corner of his mouth twitched. “You always pass out after an argument, or was that just for effect?”

Phainon lifted an eyebrow. “You’re the one who decided yelling was more productive than running.”

“You’re the one who looked at me to run like I’m disposable.”

They stared at each other for a long, quiet second.

“…Okay, fair,” Phainon admitted. “That was a bad call.”

“You think?”

“I thought I was protecting you.”

“I thought I was protecting you.”

Another beat passed. Phainon shifted slightly against the pillow and gave a soft sigh. “So what, we’re just gonna take turns playing martyr until one of us flatlines?”

Mydei sat back in the chair, folding his arms loosely. “No. I think we need to actually trust each other. Even when we’re scared.”

Phainon gave him a sideways glance. “Even when you’re being an overbearing, reckless, self-righteous—”

“Yes. Even then.” Mydei smiled slightly, which ruined the attempted sarcasm beautifully. “And even when you’re being a rude, cryptic, self-sacrificing bastard.”

“Oh good. As long as it’s mutual.”

A silence settled again, more comfortable this time. The tension had bled out of the room, replaced by something gentler.

“I’m sorry,” Phainon said. The words felt weird in his mouth but not wrong.

“So am I,” Mydei replied. “You scared me.”

“Yeah,” Phainon murmured. “You too.”

Mydei stood, brushing imaginary dust from his shirt. “I need to go check in on a few things. But I’ll be back tonight.”

“You don’t have to—”

“I want to.”

Phainon blinked at him, unsure how to respond to that level of honesty before caffeine.

Mydei leaned in just enough to cross a line—one he rarely stepped over. He kissed Phainon on the cheek, light and confident, then headed for the door without waiting for a reaction.

“Rest up, professor,” he said casually. “If you flirt with anyone else while I’m gone, I’m breaking your legs. Gently.”

The door shut behind him with a soft click.

Phainon lay there, stunned into silence, one hand still half-raised like he might catch the moment before it faded.

“…Great,” he muttered, “and now I can’t even pretend to brood properly.”

Phainon sighed and let his hand fall to his chest, the corners of his mouth twitching in residual disbelief. He stared at the ceiling like it might offer an escape hatch or maybe just a less complicated form of consciousness.

But then his eyes shifted—slightly, subtly—and the whole mood flipped.

The warmth drained from his expression. That soft, half-lidded haze he’d allowed himself to bask in for the past few hours evaporated, replaced by something sharper, more familiar. Like slipping back into armor. His gaze cooled, jaw setting as the weight of reality crept in.

It wasn’t just the hospital room getting to him. Boring as hell, sure, but not unbearable.

No, the problem was the message.

He rolled onto his side with a grunt, reaching for the sleek, nondescript device stashed beneath his pillow. One of Anaxa’s custom rigs—encrypted six ways from hell and ugly as sin. The screen flickered to life with a soft pulse.

The message had come in a few minutes ago, cloaked in a cipher so sloppy it had to be one Anaxa came up with while drunk on expired energy shots and loathing.

rEsuRGENCE:n02//arise//shdwfrm//LOC VAR///BRINGFIRE, dumbass.

He parsed it in seconds, chest tightening.

Translation: “Second Node is reviving. Bring your shit.”

Of course it was.

Phainon flopped onto his back with a groan, dragging a hand down his face. The device sat beside him on the pillow, its faint glow still pulsing like some smug little heartbeat.

Of course it fucking was.

Because nothing in his life could stay quiet for more than five minutes without detonating.

He exhaled slow, eyes fixed on the ceiling—though he wasn’t really seeing it anymore.

This all started three weeks ago.

Standard infiltration op. Basic data siphon job.

He’d gone in as the Flame Reaver, chasing a spike in Council data traffic. Not unusual on its own—the Council was always moving shady shit behind polished, official fronts. On paper, they were the nation’s clean-cut, elite regulatory body. A high-command task force with full government backing, responsible for overseeing vigilante activity, suppressing high-threat crime, and keeping the general population blissfully ignorant of how close to collapse everything really teetered.

Surface role: The good guys.

Reality: A control faction with a vendetta.

Phainon had learned not to buy the bullshit a long time ago.

Sure, they’d slapped on a pro-vigilante mask after the Black Tide fallout, but underneath, they’d always hated them. Especially the powerful ones. The heirs. The off-leash anomalies you couldn’t bribe, leash, or quietly erase. The Council’s real game was slow reclamation: replacing natural vigilante networks with clean, Council-trained agents. Dissecting every last scrap of Chrysos tech under the excuse of “containment” and “public safety.”

Phainon didn’t give a damn about their vendettas. Not usually.

He cared about keeping certain people alive. And, when the opportunity struck, making someone’s life a tactical nightmare.

So when that unusual data spike cropped up in a restricted cluster, flagged under one of the Council’s more obscure black vault tags, he figured it was worth a look.

Expected: A file dump. A corrupt resource ring. Another dirty ledger to pass off to Anaxa for his increasingly unhinged, spite-fueled spreadsheets.

What he found: A mess.

Fragments of documents. Chopped-up sentences. Acronyms stacked on acronyms, tangled with references to nodes, emotional patterning, memory

anchors, and something about cognitive resonance frequencies. Vague as hell—but it made the hair on the back of his neck rise.

He hadn’t thought much of it at first. Government weirdness was basically tradition at this point.

But Anaxa took one look at the pulled data and got that manic gleam in his eye. The one that meant this is your problem now too.

Buried in the jargon was a half-erased set of coordinates.

After a good thirty minutes of arguing—and a healthy, mutually acknowledged we probably shouldn’t, but we’re definitely going to—they decided to check it out. No details. No name on the place. Just a dead location marker deep underground, tucked into a long-forgotten corner of the city’s old sector.

Phainon still remembered the way Anaxa sounded in his ear when they reached it.

“This doesn’t feel like a vault,” Anaxa had muttered, tension crackling sharp through the comm.

“Nope,” Phainon had agreed.

“Feels like a mistake.”

They went in anyway. Because they always did.

They hadn’t known what they were expecting.

But it sure as hell wasn’t that.

The moment they crossed the threshold, both of them picked it up—a weird, low-frequency hum. Not audible, not exactly, but there in the bones. Like the static prickle you felt before a lightning strike. Whatever they thought was hiding down here, it wasn’t just an abandoned vault.

And then Phainon saw the tag.

Not on the walls. Not on the servers. But on the old sublevel’s core housing unit itself—an old, half-scraped-off Chrysos mark.

His blood ran cold.

Even Anaxa went quiet. And that never happened.

It should’ve been impossible. The Council wasn’t supposed to have Chrysos tech. Nobody was. Not outside of heir control, and especially not something like this. Even if you could get your hands on it—which Anaxa, genius that he was, couldn’t—you couldn’t open it. Couldn’t bypass the security layers. There were at least ten, maybe twelve safeguards hardwired into anything Chrysos-borne. Half of them weren’t even mechanical.

The fact that it was here, under a Council site, felt…wrong. In the marrow-deep way only certain things did.

Phainon shoved the shock down fast. Focused on what he could do.

He scoured the terminal banks and found a cluster of heavily encrypted files —data clusters sealed behind some of the ugliest firewalls he’d ever seen. He grabbed what he could, pushed it to an external drive for Anaxa to dissect later. No time for grace.

And even half-corrupted, even through the encryption, it was enough to paint a shape.

The files were fragmented, incomplete. But they spoke in broken lines of a node system, of emotive mapping, of grief and memory as quantifiable metrics. Some half-formed theory about tracing trauma echoes in neural patterns—using residual emotional signatures to flag individuals who’d caused mass suffering.

At first glance, it looked like a forensic tool.

Cruel but justifiable. The kind of thing you could pass off as a moral gray area if you worded it right in a press briefing.

But there was something worse buried in there too. A recurring designation.

A new Council unit he’d never heard of: Containment Integrity Unit. CIU.

Anaxa had immediately zeroed in on that. Deduced that whatever the Council was really doing, this was probably the team pulling the strings behind the node extractions. The CIU wasn’t in any official records they’d seen before—which meant it was either newly formed, or very old and very buried.

Either way, the name fit too cleanly to be coincidence.

That had been the moment Phainon started to get the headache. A sharp, pressure-heavy throb behind his eyes. The deeper into the system they went, the worse it got.

And then everything blurred.

Phainon had pushed through it.

Even with the migraine clawing at the base of his skull, even when every instinct screamed leave it, he’d gritted his teeth and steadied his breathing. The Chrysos Archive sat there—silent, heavy, a relic that shouldn’t exist in Council hands. Locked behind what Anaxa immediately clocked as an Omega Lock encryption.

Which was bad.

Omega Locks weren’t just high-clearance. They were impossible clearance. Built for heir-level command chains and ancient vaults no one had the right to open. You didn’t just crack those. You didn’t even try.

But they did. Because of course they did.

Anaxa guided him through it—or tried to. Voice hushed in his ear, threading out code sequences and workaround theories at breakneck speed. The kind of rapid-fire thinking only possible when you knew you were already too deep to back out now.

For a moment, it almost felt like they had a handle on it.

And then the Archive lashed out.

Not physically.

It hit his mind.

A pressure—wrong and invasive. Like a hand gripping the back of his skull and shoving him forward into something vast and seething. His headache flared white-hot, nausea twisting up his throat. Vertigo hit so fast he staggered, grabbing onto the nearest wall for balance.

He barely heard Anaxa shouting over the comm, voice warping in and out.

Couldn’t breathe. Couldn’t think.

Something had reached back.

He didn’t remember leaving. Just remembered that single survival instinct roaring to the surface—out out out—and then he was on the surface again, drenched in sweat, heart hammering like it wanted out of his chest.

Later, once the worst of it had dulled, Anaxa called it a Neural Burn Protocol. A Chrysos-grade defense mechanism designed to trigger psychological overload in any unauthorized mental signature that tried to tamper with a live Archive. Phainon had bought into it too. Made sense. It was old tech. Dangerous as hell. Half of it probably sentient by now.

At least—that’s what he told himself.

Because it was easier than considering the other option.

That it hadn’t been the Archive alone.

The data Anaxa managed to decrypt after the fact suggested something worse.

The final node system—the third one—was incomplete. It required an anchor. Not just any tether, but an emotional constant. A grief that could stabilize the projection, give the fractured system cohesion.

Anaxa called it the N2 Catalyst. Because of course he did. Couldn’t just say “this is going to get us both killed.”

They’d backed off. Couldn’t afford another incident after the Archive. Not with whatever the hell had happened to Phainon’s head still lingering in the edges of his vision. But even with space and time, it gnawed at him. Anaxa had gone into full obsession mode, chasing threads, linking half-corrupted files, cross-referencing old Council logs. That wasn’t new. What was new was the conclusion they came to.

The system wasn’t for criminals.

It wasn’t a weapon to hunt the monsters outside.

It was meant for the ones inside.

The vigilantes.

Even knowing how bad things were between the Council and the off-leash operatives, they hadn’t expected this. A system built to fracture, map, and possibly erase vigilantes from within their own memories? It sounded like paranoia. It sounded like war.

And then six days later—she appeared.

On the train.

Cyrene.

Pink hair. Small polite smile. The faint skip in her step like she didn’t have a single care in the world.

He’d thought it was a trick of the light. A glitch in a too-long night.

And then the mimic incident happened. Two days vanished from his memory. He woke up here.

The rest…well.

Phainon let out a breath, sinking deeper into the pillow, the recounting hollowing him out more than he expected.

He knew now.

The Neural Burn wasn’t just a failsafe.

It was the trigger.

His memory—of her, of what she’d meant, what she still meant no matter how many times he’d tried to scrape it out of his bones—had been the anchor. The N2 Catalyst wasn’t a random occurrence. His grief gave the system form. His stubborn refusal to forget had been the spark to reanimate a dead project.

He couldn’t undo that. Didn’t even know how.

The room felt too quiet now.

He stared at the ceiling again, but this time the weight of it pressed down like stone.

“So that’s how it is,” he muttered to no one. “My head cracked open a vault and gave it a heartbeat.”

And all she did was smile.

Because that’s what friends do.

Even now, the memory of it—the skip in her step, the too-gentle way she’d held him after everything went to hell, like she was grateful—made his blood run cold.

Because nothing worked around her. Nothing made sense.

And for the first time in a long time, Phainon wasn’t sure if there was a way out of this one.

He dragged in a shuddering breath.

Right. No point lying here waiting for the void to finish gnawing at him.

Time to leave.

The moment he thought it, the crushing weight in his chest loosened just a fraction. Not because it was a good idea—it was a terrible one—but because it was something to do. Something to plan.

And plans meant jokes.

Dark, terrible, aggressively unfunny jokes. His preferred brand of denial.

“Okay,” he muttered, dragging himself upright with a wince. “Time for a good old-fashioned, deeply irresponsible prison break.”

If he played by the rules, Mydei wouldn’t let him so much as walk alone. He’d be handcuffed to this bed, force-fed kale smoothies, and by sunrise he’d be legally married to a heart monitor. And knowing this hospital’s obsession with procedure, probably a third-year med student named Chip.

No. He had to ghost out of here fast, before the staff noticed he wasn’t too concussed to walk.

He grabbed a scrap of paper from the bedside table—probably a patient consent form, but who cared—and scrawled a note in the messiest handwriting he could manage.

Dear students, It’s me or your GPA. Guess who’s more expendable – P

Sincere. Poetic. Half-assed. Perfect.

Phainon rolled off the bed, made a face at the jolt through his side, and limped toward the window. Fire escape. Easy enough. He’d slipped out of tighter lockdowns before.

Of course, those times he wasn’t nursing a migraine the size of a small planet.

The first part was smooth. He slipped through the cracked window, eased onto the fire escape landing, and dropped down two levels without issue.

Then he twisted his ankle on a loose rung.

The sound he made was something between a snarl and a string of profoundly filthy swears in four different languages—one of which might’ve been extinct.

“Fucking chrysanthemum-ass spark plug—you absolute whore of a ladder —”

He gritted his teeth, limped it off, and kept moving.

Because if there was one thing he knew how to do, it was run.

The passage down to Anaxa’s underground bunker felt longer than it had any right to. An old maintenance shaft, crumbling concrete walls bleeding condensation, rust eating through every metal brace. The only light came from the flicker of his own half-dead wrist beacon, and even that was sputtering. His pulse pounded behind his eyes, a steady drumbeat of exhaustion and pain he didn’t have the time to process.

He reached the old service door, punched in the code—a string of numbers Anaxa insisted wasn’t significant but absolutely was—and it hissed open.

The air inside was cold, sharp, too sterile in a way that felt almost alien. Stark white walls, the hum of machines you couldn’t find on any legitimate registry, and lights that never quite seemed to settle on one steady color.

Phainon staggered in, bruised and smelling like hospital antiseptic and asphalt.

Anaxa didn’t even look up from the terminal he was working at.

“Took you long enough,” Anaxa muttered, fingers flying over keys, eyes fixed on cascading streams of incomprehensible data.

Phainon flipped him off without much heat. “Missed you too, asshole.”

That got a faint smirk from Anaxa. Brief, but there.

Phainon dragged himself further in, eyes locking on the containment tank at the room’s center—and the thing inside it. The recovered node fragment floated there, suspended in some viscous, iridescent fluid. It twitched, faintly. Like a heartbeat.

Like breathing.

His stomach lurched.

“That normal?” Phainon rasped, voice frayed.

Anaxa’s smirk flattened. He sighed, finally turning to face him. “Define normal.”

“It’s mimicking an early-stage neural cascade,” Anaxa muttered, eyes flicking back to the readings. “Technically it shouldn’t be possible without a host anchor.”

Phainon limped closer, squinting at the shifting patterns on the screen— some looping, fractal hell of symbols and pulse-lines that meant absolutely nothing to him, except for the parts labeled in angry red. Those probably weren’t good.

Anaxa sighed, like explaining advanced theoretical metaphysics to a half-conscious arsonist was the single greatest burden ever placed upon a man.

“Okay, short version for your concussed ass—the second node wasn’t a projection host like we thought. It was a convergence catalyst. It gathered resonance signatures from active anchors in proximity. Emotional charge, psychic bleed-off, unresolved trauma…you know. Your natural habitat. It creates the perfect storm, generates the conditions necessary for a projection

to evolve, rather than just mimic. An actual sentient construct built off accumulated resonance data.”

Phainon stared at him.

Then, flatly: “So…a womb. Not a mirror.”

Anaxa gave a grudging, almost pleased tilt of his head. “Exactly. And something’s kicking inside.”

He flicked through a series of projections, the screen casting his face in cold, alien light. Code spiked and bled like some malignant pulse across the interface.

“See this?” He pointed to a jagged cluster of readings. “It’s reconstructing a pre-coded entity. Not random. Something embedded from the start. And guess what it’s tethered to.”

Phainon already knew. The weight settled in his gut like stone.

“Your grief gave it teeth,” Anaxa muttered, tone caught between fascination and warning. “It’s synced to you now.”

Phainon’s jaw flexed, the air in the lab feeling heavier.

Anaxa kept going, fingers dancing over keys. “The Council’s not just monitoring anomalies. They’re using anchors—people like you, high-resonance grief cases—to seed sentient constructs. Memory-based projections. Built to destabilize and spy. You can’t fight a ghost that wears the face you miss.”

Silence.

Anaxa’s eyes flicked to another volatile cluster of readings. “And it’s not sustainable. Entropy feedback from anchors like you causes decay loops. Every activation’s another crack in the city’s psychic field. Sooner or later, the whole system caves.”

Phainon stared at the node fragment twitching in its tank.

“Well shit,” he muttered.

Phainon dragged a hand down his face. “So what’s the play here? ‘Cause I’m guessing the Council’s not just gonna politely shut this shit down.”

Anaxa gave a sharp grin. “Actually, this gives us an advantage. Their whole system relies on stable grief anchors. But unstable ones?” He gestured at Phainon. “Volatile. Unpredictable. Dangerous.”

Phainon sighed. “So I blow it up.”

“Not quite. You sync to it directly. Force a resonance spike, overload the cascade. If the node’s built to handle grief anchors, it’s not built to handle one going critical.”

Phainon eyed the flickering node fragment. “What’s the catch?”

Anaxa shrugged, too casual. “Could kill you. Or erase some inconvenient parts of your mind. Minor risks. It’ll especially be rough since the second node already housed thousands of minds for simulated trauma cycles. Which means you’re walking into a hell of leftover resonance patterns.”

Phainon grimaced. “Awesome. Love that for me.”

Anaxa offered a deadpan smile. “Probably fine. Or not. Scientific discovery either way.”

Phainon’s jaw tightened. “We destroy it. Now. Before it stabilizes.”

Anaxa didn’t look away from the terminal. “Wait.”

A pause. The tension in the room crackled like a live wire.

Anaxa finally turned. “Before that, this is our last shot to understand what the Council’s really building. If we torch every anomaly, we stay blind. You want to stop them? We need leverage. Data.”

Phainon’s stare was ice. “If this thing gets out, there won’t be anything left to leverage.”

Neither moved. The node pulsed faintly in its tank—like it was listening.

Anaxa exhaled. “One night.”

Phainon frowned.

“I run a full set of scans, under strict protocol. The second those readings spike—” he jabbed a finger toward the emergency override, “you pull the plug. No hesitation.”

A long beat.

“Fine,” Phainon muttered. “One night.”

They didn’t shake on it. Just turned back to their respective controls—both already regretting it.

As Anaxa adjusted a bank of monitors, he muttered, “You know, maybe if this city’s academic budget wasn’t run by cowards and bureaucrats, we wouldn’t have to jury-rig half this lab.”

Phainon leaned against the console, smirking. “Maybe if you stopped scaring grant committees by citing Lovecraft.”

Anaxa shot him a flat look. “Their fear is validation.”

Phainon snorted.

Anaxa turned back to the controls. “Anyway—if we’re doing this, your Flame Reaver gear’s in the back. Might as well suit up.”

Phainon pushed off the console. “Don’t have to tell me twice.”

The lab was oppressively silent, save for the hum of machines and the soft, rhythmic pulse of the node fragment suspended in its containment tank. Stark white light reflected off its surface—twitching, writhing, the movement almost…breathing.

Phainon stood near the far wall, fully geared now. Black Flame Reaver coat slung over his shoulders, gloves buckled tight. His eyes never left the node.

Anaxa tapped away at a series of terminals, muttering numbers under his breath. Graphs jittered. Resonance signatures fluctuated. The tension in the room thickened like wet cement.

Then came the hum.

Soft, distant—a low, tonal vibration radiating from the containment unit. The pitch climbed, twisted, shaped itself.

A lullaby.

Phainon stiffened. His stomach turned cold.

He knew that melody.

It was a song his mother used to hum when he was little, before everything went to hell. No one else knew it. He hadn’t spoken about it in years.

Anaxa glanced up. “Alright…that’s new.”

Phainon’s voice was a rough scrape. “Can it do that?”

Anaxa was already scanning readings. “Technically? No. It shouldn’t have access to personal memory locks without a direct anchor sync. And I haven’t connected anything to its—” He squinted. “Wait. Resonance bleed… it’s mimicking your neural cascade. That’s why.”

“Translation?”

“It’s copying you, Phainon. Pulling from your unconscious residuals. Early-stage neural echo. It shouldn’t be this fast—we’ve only been running this for twenty minutes.”

Phainon’s fingers twitched near the emergency override. “How bad?”

Anaxa gave a humorless grin. “Depends. If the cascade stabilizes, it’ll build a partial construct. Sentient enough to act autonomously. Drawn entirely from your worst memories, obviously, because gods forbid it be anything else. And if it destabilizes—”

“What?”

“Local entropy spike. Psychic infrastructure fracture radius…probably four blocks. Maybe five.”

Phainon grit his teeth. “And you wanted to study this.”

“I am studying it. You’re welcome.” Anaxa’s tone stayed maddeningly casual, but his hands moved faster, tweaking calibrations. “Good news is— it’s incomplete. See here?” He gestured to the readings. “The resonance harmonics are peaking early. It’s bleeding too much energy to maintain form. This confirms the Council’s prototype isn’t stable yet.”

“Meaning we still have a shot.”

“Meaning if we collapse this now, the feedback might trigger a sympathetic shutdown in any linked nodes citywide. But…”

“But?”

“I need about another hour of data to map the cascade fully. Then we overload it.”

Phainon’s jaw flexed. “You’ve got thirty minutes.”

A grim pause.

Anaxa smirked. “Fifteen.”

Anaxa’s fingers flew over the interface, rerouting feedback loops and adjusting containment field parameters. The node’s glow flickered, shadows crawling along the walls in time with the pulse.

Phainon’s voice cut through the static. “How many more grief anchors do you think there are?”

Anaxa didn’t look up. “Dunno. Could be a dozen. Could be a hundred.”

Phainon scowled. “Comforting.”

“Doesn’t matter.” Anaxa keyed a new sequence. “This one’s the prototype. It’s the convergence point. Without it, they physically can’t finish the chain. No second anchor, no tether stabilization, no third node to start spawning mimics.”

“And the first one?”

“Seized. Chrysos Heir’s people raided the archive days ago—grabbed the core node and half the Council’s indexed resonance logs.” Anaxa’s mouth twisted into something almost resembling a grin. “Wonder how they’re feeling right about now.”

Phainon’s brow furrowed. The glow from the node painted uneasy shadows over his face. “Should we…tip them off? About this?”

The thought made his stomach turn. He didn’t owe the Chrysos Heirs a thing—but neither of them would survive another one of these anomalies blowing a crater in the city’s mindscape.

Anaxa snorted. “They already suspect the Council. You’d have to be a comatose turnip not to, considering where the archive was housed. And whatever they do with that node isn’t our problem.”

“You sure about that?”

“Positive.” Anaxa glanced over his shoulder, eyes glinting sharp in the alien light. “We survive this, we walk. Let them play power games with the Council. I’m not dying for a monarchist middle manager with a personal vendetta.”

Phainon grunted. “Fair.”

Another sharp pulse from the node. The lullaby twisted—faltering, warping into static.

Anaxa’s gaze snapped back to the readings. “Hold onto your teeth, sweetheart. Resonance spike incoming.”

The node’s glow had settled into a steady, sickly pulse—less like a heartbeat, more like something thinking.

Anaxa rattled off data without pause. “Resonance ratio stabilizing at point-four-nine. Lattice integrity’s holding. Neural cascade rate exceeding baseline but—acceptable parameters. If this trend holds, I can isolate the imprint architecture and maybe even—”

Phainon leaned forward against the side of a storage crate, half-listening, the words folding into static in his ears. His eyes stayed locked on the tank. Something about the cadence in the hum…off-key, like a lullaby sung underwater.

And then—

His stomach dropped. Instinct howled.

He moved without thinking.

One arm shot out, grabbing a fistful of Anaxa’s coat, and yanked them bothdown behind a support console just as a shrill, piercing scream tore through the room. The air vibrated like a struck bell, and a surge of unseen force ripped through the lab—tables overturned, glass shattered, stray equipment lifted and flung against walls.

The node’s containment tank bulged inward like it was breathing—and bleeding light.

Phainon blinked. “Uh. I think this’s a real good time to overload the damn thing.”

Anaxa hissed, glaring, half-crushed beneath him. “No! I’m not done yet—”

Another high-frequency shriek cracked the air, followed by a violent crash. A cabinet smashed against the far wall, scattering tools like metal confetti. Phainon didn’t wait—he grabbed Anaxa by the collar again and hauled him bodily into cover behind a toppled table as a sparking coil snapped loose and whipped across the room.

Anaxa coughed, scowling. “…Fine.”

Phainon’s hand lit with heat, ember-crackles flickering between his fingers as he stared toward the node, jaw clenched. “Told you this thing had claws.”

Anaxa wiped blood from his cheek with the back of his hand, voice dry. “In my defense, it was purring ten seconds ago.”

The node screamed again.

“Phainon—!” Anaxa’s voice cut sharp through the chaos as a row of monitors blew out in a shower of sparks. “On your feet, now! I’m rerouting the containment uplink but I need a direct resonance sync to destabilize its lattice.”

Phainon ducked a flying shard of something metallic and charred. “Speak Common, Blasphemer!”

Anaxa’s hands flew over the cracked terminal, lines of code flickering in frantic sequence. “You—touch the tank. Feed it everything. Rage, grief, guilt, all of it. It’s tuned to your resonance signature now, so you’ll override the cascade pattern long enough for me to spike the core. It’ll collapse on itself if we time it right.”

Phainon’s stomach turned. “And if we don’t?”

“Best case—you forget a week. Worst case—Swiss cheese cortex. Stop whining and light up, Reaver.”

The node wailed again, light warping the air like heat off asphalt. Phainon’s hands were already kindling, veins glowing molten beneath his skin as he shoved aside debris and stalked toward the containment tank.

The thing inside looked like a tangle of half-formed faces, blurring between childlike and monstrous, a thousand eyes in no fixed place. And it knew him. He could feel it, latching on, threads hooking into old scars in his head.

He slammed his palm against the glass.

White heat bloomed from his hand, a soundless shockwave buckling the air. The node shrieked in reply, the lullaby-thread in its hum cracking into static.

“Good—good! Hold it there!” Anaxa barked from behind, rerouting energy paths through the node’s stabilizers. “It’s syncing—point-seven-four resonance match. That’s deep tethering, Reaver! I’m initiating the spike charge—when I say now, you pour everything into it. You’ll feel it trying to pull back, override the reflex.”

Phainon gritted his teeth as something cold and wet slithered through his mind, dredging memories unbidden—hands in his hair, blood in snow, that stupid lullaby. His breath hitched, and fire flared along his arm.

“Anaxa—this is bad.”

“I know! Do it, now!”

A red pulse rippled through the node as Anaxa triggered the feedback loop. The tank shuddered violently. Alarms shriek. Phainon suppressed a scream and shoved harder, heat racing up his spine as the room blurred at the edges.

The faces in the node screamed back.

“Now—dump it all! Now, Reaver!”

Phainon let go—a brutal, raw surge of grief, rage, bone-deep fury. The node’s light inverted, a hollow implosion of sound and pressure snapping inward as if the whole world had inhaled at once.

Phainon’s head jerked back—images flickering like burning film—before everything snapped white.

Then silence.

A second later, the tank was empty. Blackened glass. A faint smell of ozone and old blood.

Phainon staggered back, one hand to his temple. His head hurt.

Anaxa limped over, checking the readings. “Collapse confirmed. Containment stable. Neural imprint—” He eyed Phainon. “You still with me?”

Phainon managed a ragged smirk. “Who the hell are you again?”

Anaxa snorted. “That’s the spirit.”

Phainon groaned as his body hit the ground, slumping against a half-melted support beam. The air still stank of ozone and scorched metal, the wreckage flickering with half-dead sparks. His head felt like it’d been cracked open and packed full of burning sand. Every nerve throbbed.

Dragging a hand down his face, he winced. “I’m not even gonna pretend I’m conscious for this,” he muttered, letting his head thunk back against the beam. His eyes fluttered shut, exhaustion settling like a heavy coat.

Across the room, Anaxa limped through the debris of his demolished lab, muttering sharp, ancient curses under his breath. The containment rig was a wrecked husk. Fractured terminals spat out dying lines of code. A notebook lay half-burned in a puddle of something that definitely wasn’t water.

“Two prototype regulators. Gone. Secondary dampeners, slag. That was a one-of-a-kind core stabilizer, you spark-huffing piece of garbage,” Anaxa grumbled at the charred remains, briefly mourning his equipment. He let out a long, ragged sigh. “What’s knowledge without a few sacrifices.”

Grabbing a half-functioning scanner, he waved it over the ruined node with grim focus.

Phainon cracked one eye open, watching from where he lay. “You done giving your lab a eulogy?”

Anaxa didn’t glance up. “You hush. Some of us value progress.”

Silence settled in—only the hiss of a coolant leak and the occasional groan of warped metal breaking the quiet. For a second, it almost felt like the worst was over.

Then a weak, half-melted sensor near the far wall let out a strained, flickering beep…beep…beep…

Phainon didn’t move. “What’s that?”

No answer.

His brow furrowed as he glanced over. Anaxa was frozen, scanner still in hand, staring at the display with a look Phainon didn’t like.

“…Anaxa?”

The man’s voice came low and flat, clipped sharp as a knife.

“They’re here.”

Something cold slid down Phainon’s spine. He didn’t have to ask who they were.

“What do you mean they’re—”

A distant, rising wail of sirens cut him off, growing louder by the second. The steady thup-thup-thup of helicopter rotors followed, making the dust vibrate in the air. A searchlight beam knifed through a crack in the ceiling, casting long, jagged shadows over the wreckage.

Phainon’s stomach dropped.

“Vigilant Integration Bureau,” he muttered, pulse quickening. The Bureau always came smiling—but wherever they showed up, vigilantes weren’t far behind. And neither of them were in shape for round two.

Anaxa snorted, bitter and resigned, shoving what little salvageable gear he could grab into a battered bag. “Guess we made the guest list.”

Phainon exhaled, forcing his aching limbs to move. “Do we run?”

Anaxa shouldered the bag. “You always run.”

Phainon’s pulse hammered as the sirens swelled outside, the faint roar of a helicopter cresting over the gutted lab. He forced himself upright, ignoring the burn in his limbs, and jerked his head toward Anaxa.

“Grab the core remains,” he ordered, voice sharp. “I don’t care if it’s slagged—I don’t want the VIB getting so much as a shard.”

Anaxa hesitated, casting a wary glance toward the ceiling as the searchlight beam knifed past again. His jaw clenched, but he didn’t argue. He snagged the scorched containment housing and what few half-functioning instruments he could carry, stuffing them into the battered bag.

“Don’t die,” Anaxa muttered under his breath, pulling a lever set into the wall. A concealed panel groaned open, revealing a narrow escape hatch lined with corroded rungs. Of course he’d built a secret exit. Of course.

Then he was gone, vanishing into the shadows below.

Phainon exhaled hard, rolling his shoulders. The old, familiar burn settled over his bones—the low, restless heat that came when the mask went on and the world stopped being complicated. He was the only one here geared up, and with Anaxa gone, someone had to hold the line.

He slid the Flame Reaver mask into place, letting the world narrow through the visor’s sharp filters.

Alright…think. The Bureau’s a pain, but manageable. Question is…who’s with them?

His gut twisted.

The Chrysos Heirs didn’t move openly. The actual Heirs even less so. But somehow, it felt like every time shit hit the fan, he ran into one. Or more.

He cycled through the roster in his head.

As long as it’s not Undertaker, I can handle it. Anyone else, fine. Just not—

A sharp whistle of air cut past his ear.

His instincts flared white-hot. He jerked his head aside just in time to feel a burning sting trace his cheek.

The world slowed.

Phainon’s hand rose to his face, fingertips brushing blood.

What the hell—

Then he saw it.

A shimmer. A hairline glint in the low, flickering light. Not one. Dozens. No—hundreds. Thin, gossamer threads crisscrossing the space, stretching from beam to rubble to rig, gleaming faintly gold.

His stomach turned to ice.

No. Not her. Anyone but her.

His throat tightened as the threads caught the flicker of a dying spark—like a spiderweb spun of light, closing in.

Goldweaver.

His heart dropped clean into his gut.

Worse than Undertaker. Worse than anyone.

He pivoted slow, careful not to snag a line. The threads shimmered, so fine they barely seemed real, but he knew better. He’d seen what they could do.

To people. To structures. To everything.

And if she was here…he didn’t have long.

A single string quivered, a predator’s silent herald.

Phainon’s mouth went dry.

“…Fuck.”

Phainon didn’t think.

He moved.

The second his brain registered those threads, those sickly golden strands slicing through the air like a noose closing in, his body was already sprinting. A jolt of primal instinct ripped through him, survival clawing to the surface like an animal.

Get out. Now.

His boots pounded against the scorched floor, vaulting over a half-collapsed support beam. He ducked a low-hanging wire, shoulder-rolled through the smoke curling off a slagged console, his pulse hammering so hard it hurt.

The strings vibrated.

A new glint in his periphery—another thread dropping down like a noose. He twisted mid-sprint, just missing it by a hair’s breadth. His side grazed a jagged steel panel, tearing fabric and skin, but he didn’t stop.

No. No no no—of all people—

His mind reeled as he weaved through the wreckage like a man possessed. He wasn’t just fast—he was trained, refined chaos, moving with predatory precision through a warzone. This wasn’t a fight he could win, and every fiber of him knew it.

Goldweaver.

The goddamn leader of the Chrysos Heirs. The one you didn’t see. The one who didn’t bother with cleanup jobs or chase-downs. If a target warranted her personal involvement, it wasn’t a retrieval mission.

It was an execution.

And if those threads got around him here—in this tight, suffocating labyrinth of debris and half-flooded tunnels—it was over. No fight. No clever trick. No last-second escape. Hell, he wouldn’t even actually be killed.

Just gone.

Why the hell was she here? Why him?

Sure, if they’d figured out this was a node site, it made sense to send an Heir. Undertaker for example, no matter how much he wanted to avoid her. Even Godslayer, maybe.

But Goldweaver?

He’d covered his tracks. Been careful. The serious jobs—the real forbidden ops—were buried. He and Anaxa had burned records, rerouted traces, scrubbed networks.

So why the fuck was she here?

Another thread snapped down. He dove, sliding beneath it, feeling it singe the air inches from his skin. His muscles screamed, lungs burning as he vaulted up a twisted ladder rung, grabbed a ledge, and hurled himself up toward the half-collapsed roof.

The entrance was compromised—front sealed, Bureau forces closing in. Surface extraction was a joke.

Only one way out.

Phainon sprinted along a narrow beam, leaping for a broken ventilation shaft overhead. Caught the edge with one hand, swung up, scraped his

shoulder bloody on the jagged frame—but didn’t slow.

He could feel her now. The threads shivering in the dark. The air itself seemed to hum with pressure.

Every instinct screamed trap.

And still no answer why.

His teeth clenched.

I’m not dying like this.

Another line snapped toward him—he ducked, skidded along the wall, then launched himself through the shaft’s jagged opening, not caring where it led.

Didn’t matter.

Anywhere was better than here.

The crawlspace was a maze of cracked pipes and warped steel, half-collapsed from the earlier blast. His fingers grazed the walls as he moved, leaving smears of ash and blood. Something flickered at the edge of his vision—a shimmer, a brief distortion like the world caught between blinks.

Phainon didn’t hesitate. He grabbed it.

It wasn’t a thing, not exactly. More a ripple in the air, a flicker of broken light where the explosion had warped the structure’s energy lines. His fingers curled around the raw, seething pulse, and with a sharp, instinctive twist—like pulling thread through frayed cloth—he dragged. The shimmer snapped taut, forming a jagged line of fire that lashed out, severing the nearest thread just as it struck.

The air sang with tension. He ducked again, his pulse hammering against his ribs.

The narrow passage spilled him into a lower chamber where the VIB units were sweeping through—black-clad figures with sleek helmets, visor lights cutting through the gloom. No time for stealth. He hit the ground in a roll, grabbed a half-collapsed support strut still radiating heat from the earlier overload, and pulled.

It bent in his hands like softened wax. The metal flickered—its shape warping, splintering into jagged, ember-bright shards.

He flung it forward.

The makeshift projectile split in midair, searing through the first line of agents. It didn’t kill. Just enough to scatter, blind, buy seconds.

Phainon moved like a specter in flame. He didn’t think—every move was raw instinct, chasing the flickers, the warped gaps in reality where energy buckled under stress. Broken data readouts on the walls, still throwing corrupted symbols from the earlier surge—he brushed a hand along them, and the symbols stirred, twisting into unfamiliar, sharp-edged shapes.

A barrier of heatless, smoldering light flared up between him and another wave of agents.

His head throbbed. His vision blurred.

No time.

He forced himself onward, vaulting over debris, one boot kicking a half-slagged rifle away. The exit was ahead—the main lift shaft, scorched, cables swaying loose.

And then his body jolted.

A searing line across his shoulder.

He staggered, blood hitting the floor in a hot spray.

From the far end of the ruined hall — green eyes. Cold. Unblinking. Watching from the wreckage above like a blade waiting to fall.

Phainon’s heart clenched tight.

Not a soldier. Not a Bureau agent. Her.

A figure half-wreathed in shadow, threads of liquid gold curling lazily through the air around her, each one glinting like strands of sunlight on glass. The strings hung suspended, waiting for a single twitch of her fingers to snap them tight.

He bit down a curse. The room was rigged. He could see it now—how the threads anchored to every surface, coiled around debris and bodies alike, tracing a lattice of death. And there she stood, still and patient as a predator, watching him.

Blood dripped from his shoulder, trailing in hot lines down his side. The sting kept him focused.

He forced himself upright, teeth gritted, feigning a stumble. Let her see the wound. Let her think he was faltering. The gaze stayed locked. No command issued. No hand lifted. But he could feel the threads start to shiver.

No way out the front—too many agents, too many threads. And the longer he hesitated, the tighter the noose would draw.

His eyes flicked up.

An exposed conduit, a fractured support beam still slick with coolant mist. A single spot where the threads didn’t quite reach—the burst of the earlier explosion must’ve scorched them there.

It was enough.

He moved.

A sudden burst of speed, raw and reckless. Pain flared bright in his shoulder as he surged forward, ducking low and skimming along the edge of the wreckage. The threads snapped at empty air behind him. A line grazed his arm, hot as wire, but he didn’t slow.

The green eyes narrowed.

Another flick of the strings. They lurched toward him, filling the space he was running for.

Phainon’s hand lashed out, fingers grazing the wall, and something unseen shifted. The air itself seemed to bend, a sharp ripple like heat distortion catching the threads mid-flight. For a fraction of a second, the web faltered.

He dove through it.

Rolled under a collapsing beam, flames licking at his heels. Wrenched a broken length of piping from the floor as he passed—not as a weapon, but a tool. The conduit above was cracked open, exposed.

One breath. One chance.

Phainon swung the pipe, striking a burst junction. A surge of scorched energy burst from the line, sending a wave of volatile heat through the chamber. The threads recoiled. The VIB agents cursed and scattered for cover.

In the chaos, he moved.

Not vanishing—slipping through the seams. Through the space between one moment and the next, trailing flickers of dying flame and bent light. A phantom silhouette, a smear of motion.

By the time the threads lashed out again, the chamber was empty.

And the only thing left of him was blood on the floor and the scent of burned air.

He barely made it three blocks.

Phainon staggered down a side street, half-seeing, half-sensing his way through the maze of alleys. The world pitched sideways around him, a sick blur of neon reflections warping in puddles and grime-slick walls. Every

breath scraped his throat raw. Blood dripped from his nose, hot against his upper lip, and he wiped it away with the back of a trembling hand.

The aftereffects hit harder this time. They always did when he pushed it that far—light distortion bending the corners of his vision, nausea twisting his gut, static crawling under his skin. His blood felt thin, like something vital had burned away with it.

He shouldn’t have done it.

But it was that, or get caught. And he knew what happened to people like him when the Bureau took their time.

The alley dead-ended against a crumbling wall. Phainon let himself drop to his knees there, back to damp brick, pulse hammering behind his eyes.

His hand brushed something cold.

A small vial. Clear glass catching the weak, flickering light. Next to it—a crumpled scrap of encrypted microfilm, flickering faintly as his fingers ghosted over it. Anaxa. Of course.

He unfolded it. Sharp digital text blinked up at him.

Go home. Cameras off for 20 min. Don’t be seen. Use the dose if you’re bleeding out. Get rid of this when you’re done.

Phainon huffed a breath that was halfway to a laugh, though it hurt like hell in his ribs. A smirk ghosted across his bloodied mouth.

“Sentimental bastard.”

He pocketed the vial, thumb hovering over the note’s erase glyph before tapping it. The message dissolved into harmless static, vanishing between blinks.

The worst of it was over. For now.

He dragged himself upright, wiping his face with a sleeve already streaked in red and ash. His stomach lurched. The world spun. But he stayed standing.

Time to go home.

And maybe—just maybe—not die this time.

The window stuck halfway. Typical. Phainon grit his teeth, wedged his shoulder against the frame, and shoved it open enough to squeeze through. Every movement hurt. His ribs screamed. His head spun. But the familiar scent of old wood, incense remnants, and city air slipping through the cracked glass was enough to make his shoulders sag.

Home.

Or what counted for it.

He stepped inside and let the window fall shut behind him. No lights. He didn’t need them. Knew every inch of this cramped apartment in the dark. The loose floorboard near the kitchen. The half-dead plant by the windowsill. The slight dip in the mattress where he always collapsed after nights like this.

No sirens. No strings. No VIB squads.

For the first time in hours, the city’s chaos felt distant. He could almost breathe.

Phainon slowly stripped off his upper body, wincing as the fabric peeled away from dried blood and half-healed burns. Dropped it in a heap on the floor. His fingers fumbled the vial from his pocket, the glass cool and clean against his palm. He stared at it for a moment.

Faint streetlight caught the liquid inside, casting a fractured glimmer on the wall.

Anaxa’s work.

“Son of a bitch,” he muttered under his breath, a weak huff of something close to a laugh pulling at him. Because only Anaxa would leave some prototype concoction in an alley like a care package and expect him to just roll with it.

He uncorked it and downed it in one go. It scorched like liquid fire—acrid, chemical, bitter. His stomach lurched, but almost immediately the worst of the nausea ebbed. The edges of his vision steadied. Pain dulled from white-hot to a persistent throb.

Better.

Not good. But better.

He dropped back onto his bed, the mattress sinking under his weight. For a second, he just lay there. Letting the quiet in. The weight of the night peeling off in layers, leaving nothing but raw exhaustion in its place. He stared at the ceiling, watching faint cracks crawl through the plaster like distant constellations.

He could almost pretend—

Footsteps.

Fast. Unmistakable.

Phainon froze. Every muscle tensed. His hand twitched toward the dagger handle at his belt before he remembered he’d ditched it.

Those steps were inside.

Inside the apartment.

Nobody else had a key. Nobody should be here.

Break-in. Or—

Shit.

He had a heartbeat—less—to move. Rolled sideways, yanking the blanket over himself just as the door to a room slammed open hard enough to make the hinges scream.

The air in the room went razor-thin.

Who the hell—

The room hadn’t even settled from the last slam before the next one hit— the bedroom door bursting open like it owed someone money.

“Mydei—”

“Where the hell were you?!”

The voice could’ve peeled paint. Phainon felt his soul leave his body, circle the ceiling fan once, and snap back in. It was the kind of fury that could shatter a boardroom in thirty seconds flat, vaporize someone’s will to live, and yet here it was—in his crappy apartment.

Under the blanket, Phainon curled tighter, willing his body to stop bleeding, stop looking guilty, stop existing. He coughed quietly into the sheets.

“M’teaching,” he mumbled, muffled by fabric and half a pillow. “Left a note.”

Wrong move.

Wrong move.

The silence was the worst part. Heavy. Nuclear. The quiet before every power station in a ten-mile radius went dark.

The blanket yanked halfway off his head.

“A note?” Mydei’s voice was so sharp it could’ve cut stone. “You left a note. You left the hospital without telling anyone, turned your comm off,

vanished for an entire damn day, and you think a note counts?”

Phainon grabbed the blanket’s edge like it was a lifeline and tried to disappear into the bed.

“I was—uh—grocery shopping.”

“The hospital has a kitchen.”

“Yeah but… uh… no soy sauce.”

Mydei stared. The kind of stare that could split atoms.

Another tug. Phainon dug his fingers in.

“Okay, okay—I was meditating.”

“At an illegal fight club?”

“On the way to the grocery store.”

Another tug. The blanket almost went flying. Phainon clung like a man possessed.

“You have one and a half hours to fix your face.”

Phainon peeked out with one eye, blinking past the pounding in his skull. “Can I get… two?”

“One.”

Door slam.

The walls rattled.

Phainon exhaled, still tangled in the bedding, heart jackhammering.

“…I hate my life.”

He coughed up a little more blood. Wiped it off. Reached for the nearest pillow and screamed into it.

Smooth. Real smooth.

The clock on his wall clicked. A minute lost already.

Phainon cursed and forced himself upright.

The walk to the bathroom was its own personal odyssey. Every step sent a fresh wave of nausea rolling up his throat. His ankle twinged in protest, a dull ache from the earlier sprint over broken metal and debris, and the skin beneath his bandages felt raw, tacky with dried blood. The world tilted unevenly when he passed the mirror, but he didn’t stop to look. Didn’t need to see it to know how bad he looked.

First aid. Right. First aid.

He fumbled under the sink, knocking over a half-used can of something and a cracked mug before finding the battered first aid tin. Opened it. Antiseptic spray, gauze, tape—haphazardly shoved in from the last time.

“This is gonna suck,” he told the empty bathroom.

And it did.

Every sting of alcohol against a split or scrape had him gritting his teeth so hard his jaw ached. He worked fast, patching up the worst of it. Some wounds he left alone. Not enough time. Not enough materials. Not enough everything.

A quick, lukewarm shower came next. The water hit his skin and he bit down a hiss so sharp it made his eyes water. He scrubbed blood from his hands and soot from his hair, careful not to tug the worst spots. Watched rust-red swirl down the drain.

Five minutes. No more.

By the time he dried off, his skin was flushed, raw, and aching, but at least the scent of smoke and adrenaline was gone. He slapped on gauze and tape, a half-assed job at best, but passable.

Clothes. Needed clothes.

He limped back into the bedroom, dropping the damp towel on the floor, and rummaged through the dresser. Most of it was garbage. Ratty shirts, old hoodies, stuff he hadn’t worn in years.

And then his hand brushed something soft.

A worn, faded, ridiculously expensive cotton sweater.

Mydei’s.

Left behind one night, long ago, and never taken back. Phainon kept telling himself he was holding onto it for practical reasons. It was warm. Comfortable. Good for emergencies.

But the truth was it smelled faintly like him for weeks after he left it, and Phainon never quite worked up the nerve to give it back.

He pulled it on now, the fabric heavy and soft against bruised skin, hanging loose on him the way it always had. The sleeves a little too long, the neckline slightly stretched. It shouldn’t have made him feel better, but it did.

Some dumb part of him felt safer in it.

Like he wasn’t entirely alone.

“Stupid,” he muttered to no one, tugging the cuffs down over his hands.

His reflection in the window was a mess—bandaged, limping, sweater-draped, pale as hell—but at least it was presentable. Or close enough.

Forty-two minutes left.

Phainon dragged a hand through his damp hair and squared his shoulders.

Time to act normal.

The apartment was a disaster. Blood smeared the floor near the window, a streak trailing toward the bedroom. Bits of ash clung to the walls, soot-dark fingerprints on the frame. His sheets were beyond saving—torn, scorched at the edges where his suit’s plating had burned too hot. One of the pillows was still stained with a perfect imprint of his face from when he’d screamed into it earlier.

He sighed. Grabbed a rag, soaked it with whatever cleaner was under the sink, and started wiping the floor. The metallic tang of blood clung stubbornly to the air. It didn’t help his stomach any.

He worked in silence. Rinsing, scrubbing, wringing out the rag. Switching it for another when the first one turned dark too fast. It wasn’t the kind of mess that cleaned easy. Dried blood was hell on wood floors. Another thing to deal with later.

The sheets? No chance. He pulled them off the bed, wincing as a muscle in his side protested. Hauled them into a trash bag, tied it shut. That could go out the fire escape later.

Another glance at the clock.

Thirty-four minutes left.

He leaned against the dresser for a second, catching his breath. Then back at it. Wiped a bloodstain off the windowsill. Pushed a cracked picture frame down so it wouldn’t be obvious. Straightened a stack of old sketchbooks.

As he worked, his mind kept circling back to Mydei.

What the hell was he gonna say?

He rehearsed a dozen half-assed excuses.

Traffic. Fell asleep at a friend’s. Got stuck fixing something. Phone died. Didn’t think it was that big a deal.

Each one felt thinner than the last.

“Teaching,” he muttered under his breath, snorting at his own idiocy. “Brilliant, really. Award-winning.”

He grabbed another rag, wiped down the desk. Tossed a busted comm-link into a drawer. Cleaned another streak of red from the doorframe. The minutes bled away while he thought—about what to tell him, how to sell it, how not to look like death warmed over.

Twenty-one minutes left.

The apartment looked less like a crime scene now. Not great. But passable if no one looked too close. Phainon sat on the edge of the bed, elbows on his knees, rubbing a hand down his face.

His head still hurt. The sweater still smelled faintly of old soap and memory. His reflection in the window still looked like shit.

He should’ve eaten. Or slept. Or both.

Ten minutes.

His stomach turned. Not from nausea this time, but from the rising tide of what if.

What if Mydei caught on?

What if he saw too much?

What if this was it—the slip-up that cost him everything?

He hated this part. The waiting. The pretending. The constant rehearsing of a conversation he already knew would go sideways.

Five minutes.

Phainon let out a long, tired breath. Ran both hands through his hair. Prepared to get up.

Time’s up.

Phainon pushed himself upright.

And immediately sat the hell back down with a sharp wince.

“Son of a—” he hissed through his teeth, one hand flying to his ribs.

Alright. Maybe one more minute wouldn’t kill him. Mydei wouldn’t kick the door down again this soon… probably. He could spare sixty seconds. Two, tops.

He let his head tip back against the wall, staring up at the ceiling like it might have answers. His whole body felt like it’d been through a meat grinder set to “extra spiteful.” Every muscle ached. His lungs still burned. The room had that heavy, post-crisis quiet, like the walls themselves were politely pretending not to notice the mess he’d made.

He rubbed his face, groaning quietly into his hands.

But as much as the panic gnawed at him, it came with this weird, warm undertow too. The way Mydei had stormed in earlier—not just furious, but scared. That kind of rage came from somewhere real. From caring.

And if Phainon wasn’t stupid lucky to have somebody like that in his corner. Somebody who cared enough to come find him when he disappeared. Someone who noticed when he wasn’t where he should be. Someone who could level a room with words alone but still left him cryptic little notes and sweaters and safe windows to crawl through.

His lips twitched, soft and stupid, as the thought settled.

“Pathetic,” he muttered to himself. But the ache in his ribs didn’t feel quite as sharp now.

He yawned, long and heavy, his head tipping forward a little.

He really felt like he hadn’t slept in two days. The kind of bone-deep exhaustion that made his skin hum. The room blurred at the edges. His eyelids drooped.

Just a second. Just to stop the spinning.

He let them fall shut. His breathing slowed. The world tilted sideways in a way that felt almost nice.

Surely, closing his eyes for a moment wouldn’t hurt.

The quiet pressed in, thick and heavy, like a blanket all its own.

Phainon’s head lolled to the side as he laid on his bed. His breath came softer now, the ragged scrape of earlier dulled into something slow and steady. The pain faded at the edges, traded for that warm, heavy numbness exhaustion left behind when it finally pinned you down.

He kept meaning to open his eyes.

Any second now.

Any moment.

But the warmth of the room, the faint scent of old detergent and fading cologne clinging to the worn sweater, the way his body stopped protesting now that he wasn’t moving—all of it blurred into a thick, irresistible lull.

His thoughts wavered. Half-finished excuses. Scrambled words. The memory of Mydei’s voice sharp with fury, and the rarer, quieter way it softened when the world wasn’t looking.

The minutes slipped past unnoticed.

And he didn’t hear the door open.

Not until the sigh—sharp, tired, exasperated—cut through the quiet like a thread pulled taut.

Closer.

The covers shifted. Phainon barely stirred, but when fingers brushed his hair back from his face and tugged the blanket over his shoulder, his hand shot out, grabbing a wrist on pure reflex.

“Stay,” he slurred, voice wrecked and drowsy. “Just…tonight. I’ll explain tomorrow. Swear.”

A long pause.

“Oh, you’ll explain, alright,” Mydei said flatly. “In bullet points. With timestamps.”

Phainon let out a lazy, lopsided grin, his thumb absently brushing the wrist he still held. “You love me.”

“Unfortunately,” Mydei muttered under his breath.

And yet—he didn’t pull away.

Instead, he shifted closer, guiding Phainon’s hand to his cheek. The skin was warm. The stubble rough. And for a moment, the world felt a little less like it was trying to cave in on him.

“You look like hell,” Mydei murmured.

“Feel worse,” Phainon managed.

“Good. Serves you right.”

His voice didn’t match the words. It was quieter now, edged with something reluctant and fond. His thumb traced over the back of Phainon’s hand where it rested against his cheek.

“You had me out of my mind, you little bastard.”

Phainon made a weak sound that might’ve been an apology or just the start of a snore. His eyelids drooped again, and his grip slackened a little.

Phainon’s eyes cracked open just enough to meet his. “You’re not really leaving, are you?”

Mydei stared at him. At the mess of damp hair and old sweater and exhaustion written into every line of his face. At the reckless, infuriating, stupidly impossible person he loved in spite of himself.

“No,” Mydei admitted. “Not tonight.”

He leaned down, pressing a kiss to the back of Phainon’s hand. It lingered longer than it should have. Then he stayed right there, crouched by the bed, their hands still tangled together.

“You sleep,” Mydei murmured. “I’ve got…stuff. I’ll be here when you wake up.”

“You always say that,” Phainon mumbled.

“And I always am, aren’t I?”

A faint, crooked smile. “Yeah.”

Silence settled, not awkward, not sharp. Just quiet.

Mydei’s thumb swept once more over Phainon’s knuckles. He let their joined hands rest against his cheek a moment longer, then sighed—not the irritated kind this time.

“Goodnight, idiot.”

“Night, boss,” Phainon slurred, already halfway gone.

And this time, when sleep pulled him under, he didn’t fight it. Mydei stayed right where he was, hand in his, as the room settled into soft, steady quiet.

Mydei didn’t move, and Phainon didn’t let go.

Hyacine pretends she’s not worried. And somewhere in the chaos, a very inconvenient set of dots starts connecting.
