The clock on the wall ticked with the smug, self-satisfied cadence of something that knew it didn’t have to be anywhere else.

Across the room, a vending machine flickered ominously between “Enjoy a NutriBar!” and “Technical Error: Code 731-B.” Someone had scrawled LIAR in Sharpie across the glass. It dispensed nothing.

A holo-poster chirped to life on a glitchy loop, its too-cheerful mascot beaming as it pitched “Join the Aureate Restraint Unit—Because Who Watches the Watchdogs?” The recruit model on-screen hefted what could only be described as an ethically questionable energy cannon with a grin

that implied he had absolutely used it on a co-worker once and would do it again.

Mydei sat in a cracked synthetic-leather chair that felt faintly damp, trying to project the kind of cool, detached professionalism expected of a Chrysos Heir. It wasn’t working. Not when the receptionist—some poor intern whose gold-trim badge was half peeled off—was actively losing a verbal war with a sapient filing cabinet.

“Form 77C, you obsolete slag pile! 77C is for cross-department violent containment! NOT 13-B! 13-B is for hazardous plant-based anomalies! How hard is this?!”

The filing cabinet emitted a mechanical click, popped open a drawer in pure spite, and made a noise that could only be described as a bureaucratic raspberry.

Mydei dragged a hand down his face.

A muffled announcement crackled from the overhead intercom:

“Code Selene in neuroptics. We repeat—Code Selene. Do not engage the levitating patient.”

He let out a long, suffering sigh.

Somewhere behind a glass wall, there was a brief burst of static followed by the unmistakable sound of someone being tased.

A cheery automated voice called out, “Have a nice day, citizen!”

The vending machine flickered again. The clock smugly ticked.

And Mydei, slouched with his elbows on his knees, muttered to no one in particular:

“How did it come to this?”

A groan escaped him, half mortal exhaustion, half spiritual defeat.

And the worst part?

This still wasn’t even the worst waiting room he’d been in this month.

It all started that night.

The night Mydei found himself tearing half the damn city apart looking for him.

Stayed wasn’t even the right word. Hunted down, maybe.

Phainon had left the hospital without a word, vanishing like mist on a bad wind, leaving behind a half-scrawled note that might as well have been ancient cipher code for all the sense it made. Mydei had stared at the jagged handwriting so long it started looking like a Rorschach test. It took five informants, two underground contacts, a heavily bribed kiosk vendor, and nearly twenty-three and a half hours before he found them.

And when he did…

The apartment door hadn’t even been locked.

The room was dark save for the flickering light of a vid-screen on standby, static-blue shadows cutting the edges of the walls. Mydei’s eyes adjusted instantly, trained Chrysos instincts kicking in. He noted the signs the moment he stepped inside—minute things anyone else would miss.

A faint, sour copper tang of blood clung to the air, barely noticeable beneath the chemical clean of a hastily scrubbed floor.

The subtle warp in the fabric of a discarded jacket hung over the back of a chair—stretched at the elbow, suggesting tension in the arm.

A single swollen knuckle on a hand barely peeking from beneath a blanket draped like a defensive barrier on the couch.

Phainon wasn’t asleep so much as crashed, his breathing uneven, shoulders hunched in unconscious guard.

Mydei stood there in the doorway for a long moment, assessing—posture, gait tension, skin pallor, slight bruising at the temple edge where hair didn’t quite fall right.

He didn’t press.

Not this time.

The exhausted set of Phainon’s face made it clear this wasn’t the moment for interrogations.

So, he gave him an hour.

Left, closed the door, came back later, and by then Phainon had managed to pull himself together—washed up, the worst of the evidence gone. A comfortable sweater thrown on, face scrubbed clean, hair damp at the edges. The room smelled aggressively like cheap disinfectant, as if someone had gone ten rounds with a mop in a panic.

But Mydei still noticed the little things.

A faint scrape on the windowsill’s paint. A newly fixed wall panel that didn’t sit quite right. The displaced pattern of dust on a shelf like something heavy had been shoved hastily out of sight.

All of it subtle, smoothed over well enough for most eyes.

But not his eyes.

He clocked it all. Logged it away.

He would’ve stayed longer—wanted to, honestly—but he hadn’t been lying about having business. Vigilante affairs didn’t pause for personal crises, even if they should’ve.

On his way out, he did one last sweep of the apartment. Just habit.

The apartment looked normal, clean even. Too clean.

Mydei frowned.

But he left it.

Let Phainon have this small space of whatever it was.

He didn’t ask, didn’t demand an explanation.

Not then.

And maybe that’s what made everything worse.

It hadn’t even been twenty-four hours before Aglaea called him in.

He was barely out of Phainon’s apartment when the summons hit his comm like a slap. High priority. Encrypted. No details. Just her signature override code and the Chrysos sigil glinting cold on the message.

The Second Node.

He hadn’t wanted to believe it at first—it was supposed to be dead. Cold. Inert. Council records had listed it as fully dismantled, anomalous processes scrubbed, site sterilized and quarantined. A “closed chapter,” they’d said.

But of course, it wasn’t.

Of course.

Aglaea’s office was always curated to perfection. Every paper stack and data slate placed just so. Threads of goldweave diagrams hovering midair above her desk, half-finished constructs left hanging like dissected corpses of thoughts she hadn’t needed yet.

She’d been furious. Not the loud, explosive kind of fury—Aglaea didn’t waste energy on theatrics.

It was in the tightness of her mouth. The way her fingers flexed as if itching to weave some poor bastard into an execution cocoon.

The Node had tried to revive itself.

Not fully—not successfully—but enough to register anomalous activity spikes. Enough to open a broadcast gate. Enough to confirm someone or something had been interfacing with it off-grid for weeks.

It was destroyed now. Beyond salvage.

By, allegedly, Flame Reaver.

And wasn’t that just perfect.

Aglaea hadn’t even tried to hide her disdain. She’d confronted him at the site, left threads woven through his pulse lines to track his movement—but they hadn’t held.

The report described it clinically:

“Subject manifested a recursive, self-consuming sigil during confrontation, unraveling conceptual bindings. Residual frequencies detected in a 2.3- meter radius, anomalous conceptual residue present. Marked reality distortion patterning consistent with digital artifact signatures. Dissolution event followed.”

In plain terms: he’d slipped through her threads like they were smoke. Left behind a glitched, twitching watermark in the air where he vanished, and something about the space felt… wrong after. Stretched thin.

VIB teams reported gaps in their comm logs. Memory blanks. Time discrepancies. Full minute-and-a-half losses where security footage corrupted itself and field agents could recall nothing but static.

The Council’s official explanation?

“Localized chemical weapons leak. Isolated vigilante interference. Unknown suspects.”

Bullshit.

It took them less than an hour to issue the cover story. Less than an hour to scrub civilian witnesses, reroute traffic drones, and seal the sector.

Too fast.

You didn’t pull a narrative that airtight on the fly. Not unless you’d already written it in advance.

And that meant one thing:

The Council knew.

Maybe not everything. Maybe not about him, not yet—but about the Nodes. About what they were trying to build. About the fact that the Second Node should never have been capable of coming back online, and yet it did.

Aglaea had been fuming over it, even if she played her cards close.

And then there was his file.

Flame Reaver.

Flagged Class-Ω.

The highest threat rating the Council issued—reserved for world-altering anomalies, conceptual weapons, and entities classed as “Country-Tier Disruptive.” So in simple terms, not for an allegedly human antihero. And even then, his profile?

Suspiciously vague.

Entire sections were Epsilon-restricted. Not even Aglaea herself had clearance to view it, and if someone like her didn’t, something was broken in the chain. Or rigged.

Which meant whoever was pulling those strings wasn’t just powerful—they were untouchable.

And gods, did Mydei hate him for it.

Hated the way the bastard slipped between gaps in protocol and physics alike. Hated the way agents came back wrong from encounters with him, haunted and unspeaking.

Hated the way his name always showed up at the tail end of when Phainon gets injuried.

He didn’t care how strong Flame Reaver was. Didn’t care what kind of conceptual bending, data-weaving, impossible-logic-born bullshit he commanded.

If, no matter how impossible it was, he was the reason Phainon had ended up bleeding and half-conscious under a blanket, looking like something had crawled out of his chest and gnawed its way back in—then the only question left was how fast Mydei could kill him.

He drew in a slow breath, feeling the memory of blood from the Node site linger at the back of his throat.

Chemical leak, my ass.

The real reason he was here hadn’t started with the Node. Not exactly.

It started when Phainon stopped acting like… Phainon.

Not in a way anyone else would notice.

But in the little things.

The way he used to text Mydei a snide complaint about civilian coffee shop playlists or ugly lobby lighting at exactly the same time every evening— stopped.

The way he’d always pick the left side of the couch and make some smug comment about “prime blanket jurisdiction”—stopped.

The casual little brushes of his hand in passing, the lazy grin that usually curled when he caught Mydei scowling at briefing slides, the obnoxious

tendency to hum old country songs under his breath whilst grading student essays—gone.

Like someone turned the dial down.

It was drigid in a way that left the air weirdly thin between them.

Mydei hadn’t pushed. He told himself it was fine.

People went through shit. Phainon had been through worse. He didn’t want to be that partner—the suffocating one.

So he left it.

Let the distance settle between them like a storm cloud you pretend isn’t there because if you name it, you’ll have to deal with the lightning.

And then came the checkpoint.

It was nothing.

Just a quiet, normal afternoon. Civvie district. They were headed to a street-level market, one of the ones where old-school booksellers and hand-forged jewelry kiosks crammed into narrow alleys because the permits were cheap and no one cared if you loitered.

The kind of place couples went to browse meaningless things and pretend the world outside didn’t exist for an hour.

They were halfway through a conversation about whether or not it was morally acceptable to deep-fry an entire nutrient bar when the Council patrol stopped them.

“Standard bioscan, sir. Routine clearance.”

Mydei barely registered it. Flashing his ID out of habit, expecting them to wave it off.

But the scanner on Phainon pulsed.

And then shrieked.

Not metaphorically.

The thing screamed.

Lit up like someone had just tried to smuggle a micro-fission core through a preschool.

Council officers stiffened.

One of them reached for his comm.

“Detain for secondary—”

No.

No, absolutely fucking not.

Mydei’s second ID was out before his brain caught up, cold authority snapping into place like a blade unsheathed.

Senior Chrysos Heir command override. High-threat incident protocol.

He barely remembered half of what he said. Something about jurisdiction, critical clearance levels, a medical anomaly flagged from residual Node exposure.

Some half-true mix of buzzwords and bureaucratic threats. Enough to make them flinch.

The detail that really set his teeth on edge wasn’t the Council’s presence—it was the VIB team.

They had no reason to be there.

Vigilant Integration Bureau units didn’t run civvie patrols. Their entire purpose, regardless of what they say they are, was to be a last-ditch

authority presence when sanctioned vigilantes got out of line, to cover for Council incompetence and spin favorable outcomes.

They were, by design, reactive. Not proactive.

And yet there they were. Hovering near the checkpoint, like carrion birds waiting for a corpse to finish twitching.

Sketchy didn’t begin to cover it.

Which was how he ended up here.

Dragging Phainon—sullen, silent, and unreadable—to a Chrysos Heir facility under priority override and putting Hyacine personally on the scan.

Because if there was one person in the entire city who knew how to untangle high-anomaly exposure without triggering Council alarms, it was her.

And now…

Now he was sitting in a damp chair, listening to a filing cabinet argue about plant-based hazards, while somewhere behind a reinforced wall his partner was being scanned for gods-knew-what.

A voice crackled through the comm node embedded in the chair’s armrest.

“Designation Mydeimos. Clearance confirmed. Subject’s stabilized for intake—proceed to Bay Two.”

He stood, the motion automatic, ignoring the way his stomach coiled tight like a pulled cable.

Time to see how bad it really was.

The med-bay was all brushed steel and matte glass. Monitors lined the walls, threads of data cascading down like rain, spooling through bio-

readouts and spectral imaging. It smelled like disinfectant and burnt circuitry.

Hyacine stood at the primary console, one hand braced on the glass display, the other flicking through readouts with efficient gestures. Her expression was all business, but the tightness around her eyes told Mydei everything he needed to know. This wasn’t routine.

“Neural burn,” she said finally, voice clipped. “Category IV. Prolonged exposure to high-output Chrysos-thread tech. Restricted class.”

Mydei’s gut gave a sharp, mean twist.

He forced his face neutral, mouth tugging tight at the corners. No. No, that’s not possible. Unless—

“It’s a byproduct,” he said, voice carefully measured, threading plausible deniability into the words before they even left his tongue. “He was linked to the third node when it destabilized. It must’ve mimicked a neural burn signature. Temporary.”

Hyacine didn’t look up. “I ran it twice. Signature spike didn’t appear until two days ago. Well after the incident.”

A silence fell between them, thick and heavy, punctuated only by the faint hum of medical scanners.

Hyacine sighed, adjusting the overlay. “There’s more. I’m seeing disrupted memory sequences. Regression patterns.” She pulled up a visual—a ripple of data fluctuations marked in sickly blue, like bruises on the mind.

“It’s not severe,” she went on. “But it’s enough. Certain memories might be… fragmented. Stuck. Behavioral loops reverting to older personality states.”

Mydei’s throat felt too tight for his liking. He folded his arms to keep his hands from flexing.

“And you’re sure it’s not from the node event?” The words sounded too brittle, like they might snap in half if he wasn’t careful.

“I’m sure,” Hyacine said quietly. “If anything, his baseline physiology’s compensating better than expected.” She gestured to a highlighted section of Phainon’s bio-readout, its metrics stable in ways they shouldn’t be.

“For anyone else, this would’ve killed half their neural lattice. He’s… tolerating it. Better than he should.”

Mydei’s stomach dropped again, this time deeper. He didn’t like mysteries. And he especially didn’t like them tangled up in the one person he couldn’t afford to lose.

He gave a sharp nod, jaw tight. “What’s the prognosis?”

Hyacine shrugged, a bleak little gesture. “Manageable. If the pattern holds. If it escalates—”

“It won’t.” His voice cut sharper than intended, and Hyacine raised an eyebrow but didn’t comment.

She keyed a final command into the system, logging the scan. “You can see him now.”

Mydei didn’t wait for permission.

The door slid open with a quiet hydraulic sigh, but Mydei didn’t bother waiting for it to fully retract before stepping through. His pace was purposeful—not quite a march, but damn close.

The room was dim. Not dark, not bright, just that sterile half-light that Chrysos med-bays defaulted to when they didn’t know what to do with you yet. Monitors lined the far wall, their readouts cycling through neural patterns, vitals, and bio-signature resonance. The steady pulse of data felt louder than it should’ve in the quiet.

And there Phainon sat, propped against the headboard, one hand resting limp on the blanket, eyes unfocused and turned toward the far window like

he could see something on the other side of the reinforced polarized glass. The wash of city lights flickered against his face in cold colors. He didn’t even glance up when Mydei entered.

Which wasn’t like him. Not at all.

Mydei’s throat worked around something dry. He clenched his jaw and forced his focus back where it belonged—on the impossible, spiraling math problem of how any of this made sense.

Neural burn.

Category IV.

From restricted Chrysos tech.

And not from the node incident—after. The rational explanation he’d clung to like a lifeline had dissolved under Hyacine’s readout in a matter of seconds.

But if not that… then what the hell was he touching?

And the injuries. Always the injuries.

Injuries that always, always, lined up with Council disasters. VIB “containment breaches.” Unscheduled blackouts. Emergency lockdowns where security cams glitched just long enough to leave a four-minute gap. Incidents where Flame Reaver was reported active.

His gut coiled tight.

Was he hiding something? Or was Mydei—gods forbid—so blinded by proximity that he never really knew him at all?

He wanted to scoff at the idea. Wanted to dismiss it outright. But the suspicion was there now, gnawing at the edges like a corrosive acid that would keep eating until there was nothing left but truth or ruin.

The data would be flagged. Maybe not immediately—Hyacine was discreet, but Chrysos’ systems ran auto-logs against everyone. It would get picked up. Forwarded. Reviewed.

And if it pointed to something it shouldn’t…

I’ll handle it before they do.

No matter what the hell this was, he wouldn’t let it become a weapon against Phainon.

But gods, his chest ached looking at him like that. Mydei had seen Phainon injuried way too many times this month. How many monitors. How many unspoken near-misses. And somehow, it didn’t get easier.

It got worse.

He cleared his throat, voice cutting through the static hum of machinery. “You planning to acknowledge me at any point, or should I just stand here and admire the wall with you?”

Phainon blinked, like it took him a second to process the words. He turned his head, slow, that familiar sharpness in his gaze dulled but still there, lurking under whatever shell had hollowed him out.

“Mydei,” he said finally, as if remembering he could speak.

And Mydei hated that. Hated how his pulse stuttered at hearing it, hated the worry, hated the suspicion worming its way deeper under his skin.

He kept his face unreadable. “We need to talk.”

Phainon’s gaze lingered on him, sharp now. A flicker of calculation behind those too-dark eyes—not quite the reckless, easygoing sharpness Mydei was used to, but something careful.

And then, softly:

“…Why are we here, Mydei?”

It wasn’t an accusation, not yet—but it edged too close. There was no reason, none Phainon should know of, why a simple civilian with no official clearance would be in a secured Chrysos Heir med facility, let alone walking someone through the front without half a building worth of security detail throwing them both into containment.

And Phainon wasn’t in containment.

He was in an observation suite.

On Mydei’s override clearance.

A cold ripple worked its way up Mydei’s spine. He smoothed his face before the worry could show and forced a wry shrug, looking away like the monitors had just gotten very interesting.

“You gave the Council’s checkpoint scanners a glitch. Some kind of residual neural feedback from that anomaly incident probably. They got twitchy about it.”

He gestured vaguely toward the diagnostic equipment. “I pulled a few favors. Figured it was faster this way than you spending a week in their ‘detention wellness processing.’”

It sounded mostly plausible. Mostly. Enough that it passed on paper— enough that if Phainon wasn’t already suspicious, he might let it slide.

But his expression didn’t ease.

Didn’t crack with one of those crooked grins.

Didn’t soften like it usually did when Mydei bailed him out of something.

It stayed distant.

And it gnawed under Mydei’s ribs in a way he didn’t have a name for.

He sat down in the chair beside the bed, dropping into it with a sigh he hadn’t meant to let slip.

The tension coiled too tight. And like a fool, like an idiot reaching for something familiar, Mydei tried to cut it.

He offered a smile that felt paper-thin even to himself. “Guess you really are defective. Knew there was something off about you.”

It should’ve landed. Should’ve earned an exasperated laugh, maybe a shove. Maybe a muttered, “Only in the ways you like, Mydei.”

Instead, Phainon’s gaze dropped to his hands. He flexed his fingers like he was counting scars no one else could see.

“You’re not wrong,” he murmured.

No edge.

Just a plain, bone-bare statement.

And something in Mydei’s chest stopped.

The breath he took caught jagged in his throat, and he hated how his pulse stumbled. Hated the way those words landed too deep, like an old blade under new skin.

That wasn’t how that was supposed to go.

He swallowed around the guilt, masked it fast. “Hey—” the word came out rough, too rough. He cleared his throat. “I didn’t mean it like—”

Phainon didn’t answer. Didn’t even look up.

And Mydei didn’t know how to fix it.

The quiet stretched long enough to start getting awkward. Mydei, half out of instinct and half to do something with his hands, fished around in his jacket pocket until his fingers closed around a crumpled NutriBar wrapper and the last unopened one he’d grabbed from the waiting room dispenser.

Without ceremony, he tossed it toward the bed.

Phainon caught it one-handed without even looking. Muscle memory. The bar landed with a soft pap against his palm.

“You always bring me these,” Phainon murmured. Voice a little frayed at the edges.

Mydei scoffed, leaning back in his seat. “Yeah, well. Someone’s gotta keep you from passing out every time you forget you’re made of actual flesh and not recycled pipe insulation.”

Phainon didn’t reply, but the bar crinkled softly as he peeled it open.

And for a second, it felt almost normal. Almost.

Mydei grabbed a datapad off the counter beside him—Hyacine’s preliminary scan notes, mostly encrypted, but he could bypass that later— and flicked through it under the glow of the monitors. His brow furrowed as he parsed a particularly dense line of neural conductivity markers.

Without warning, fingers brushed against his temple.

He flinched.

Phainon had leaned forward, still absentminded, and pushed a stray lock of Mydei’s hair out of his face, tucking it behind his ear like it was the most natural thing in the world. His eyes stayed on the datapad, unbothered.

“It was in the way,” he said, like the explanation even mattered.

Mydei stared at him. Words half-forming, a dozen half-baked excuses crashing into one another because that was their thing.

The automatic, familiar touch.

The unthinking gestures neither of them ever talked about.

And his heart did a stupid, traitorous lurch.

He swallowed, made a valiant effort at a scowl. “Next time, ask before you start grooming me like a street cat.”

Phainon’s lips quirked—barely there, but it was there.

Mydei stared at the datapad, absolutely not noticing the way his pulse had picked up or how the air in the room felt the tiniest bit less suffocating.

Mydei set the datapad down with a soft clack, clearing his throat. “Gonna check in with Hyacine,” he muttered, already halfway to the door. “Be right back.”

Phainon didn’t say anything.

But as the door slid shut behind him, Phainon’s gaze stayed fixed on the spot where Mydei had stood—a quiet, unreadable look in his eyes, like he was trying to memorize the shape of his absence.

Well—according to Hyacine, and delivered with the kind of forced professional cheer that meant this was going to suck for both of them— Phainon needed to stay for observation for at least a week. “Neurological stabilization, memory drift mitigation, and protocol-compliant recuperation,” she’d rattled off, sending Mydei a subtle look over the scan logs. Both of them understood without a word: scrub as much of the suspicious data from his file as possible before the Council’s auditors could get their hands on it.

Mydei had agreed. Hell, he even thought it might be good for Phainon. A week. Some rest. Monitored care. Safer here than outside.

Apparently, Phainon didn’t share the sentiment.

Because not even twelve hours into his stay, Mydei caught sight of a familiar mop of messy hair and a very shirtless Phainon trying to shimmy out the window of the med-bay recovery suite like some half-dead delinquent making a break for it after curfew. Bandages loose, a

constellation of bruises blooming on pale skin, one sock on, one sock missing, datapad cables still half-tangled around one ankle.

“Are you serious right now?” Mydei’s voice hit an octave he hadn’t achieved since his teenage years. He stormed over and yanked him bodily back inside.

“Easy,” Phainon muttered, but didn’t fight too hard. “I just needed some fresh air.”

“Fresh air isn’t three stories up through a vent window, you idiot!”

The argument spilled across the room, sharp words and jabs exchanged between someone trying to be responsible and someone whose definition of self-preservation was “die stylishly, probably shirtless.” Mid-sentence, Mydei grabbed Phainon’s wrist to keep him from bolting again.

He never saw it coming.

In one sharp, fluid motion—too fast for someone supposedly disoriented and concussed—Phainon twisted their positions, and the next thing Mydei knew, he was the one pinned to the wall. A forearm pressing lightly against his collarbone, just enough weight to remind him who was more quick-witted, even half-dead.

Phainon leaned in, his breath warm against the curve of Mydei’s ear. Low voice, lazy drawl. “Careful, sweetheart. You’re giving me ideas.”

Mydei’s whole spine locked up. Face flushed. Skin prickling where their bodies brushed, but his glare didn’t waver.

“Try it,” he hissed, “and I’ll break your nose.”

Phainon grinned, all teeth, like it was exactly the answer he wanted.

“Bet you’d like to.”

Same infuriating smirk. Same impossible bastard. Same damn brat. And against every better instinct Mydei had, his pulse didn’t slow in the

slightest.

After physically hauling Phainon back inside—a process that involved entirely too much grappling for someone allegedly in recovery—Mydei barely caught his breath before the man pulled his next move: pure, unfiltered arrogance.

“I’m not staying here,” Phainon snapped, defiance sharp enough to cut. His hair was a disaster, eyes wild, voice frayed at the edges. “Unless you can get me a platinum-suite recovery room with an enviro-control bed, an unrestricted comm feed, synthwave-tinted skylights that actually track the lunar phases, and a minibar stocked with something top-shelf, you can choke on it. I’ll walk.”

He was half-bruised, half-bandaged, still had the audacity to look smug about it.

Mydei just stared at him.

“…That’s it?”

Phainon blinked. “Huh?”

“That’s your price?” Mydei scrolled something casually on his datapad, deadpan as hell. “You’re easier than I thought.”

He tapped the screen once. “Done.”

The silence that followed was immediate. So sharp it was almost comical.

Phainon’s mouth actually dropped open, blinking like his brain had momentarily blue-screened.

“You’re lying.”

“Check for yourself.”

Phainon did. The wall display blinked an alert: Atrium Suite Transfer Confirmed—Patient: Phainon with every absurd request he’d rattled off

listed neatly underneath. Enviro-control bed. Unrestricted comm privileges. Synthwave skylights with real lunar tracking. Minibar. And a note: Authorization: [REDACTED] Clearance, Tier A.

He looked up at Mydei like the man had just punched a hole through the laws of bureaucracy by sheer force of will.

“What the hell—”

Mydei’s expression didn’t shift, but his eyes gave it away—the faintest glimmer of you idiot threaded with the look of a man who’d spent too many nights seeing this idiot in a hospital bed and wasn’t about to add another.

“Welcome to The Atrium Suite, sweetheart,” Mydei said dryly. “Enjoy the synthwave skylights.”

Before Phainon could sputter a comeback, two Chrysos med-techs arrived with reinforced cuffs for “patient stability,” locking him down like a particularly good-looking flight risk. One of them keyed the door to Mydei’s biometrics on the way out.

For once, Phainon had nothing to say.

Mydei let the silence settle, savored it like a rare vintage, before turning to leave—the faint, exasperated fondness lingering in the set of his shoulders.

Might be a brat, he thought. But you’re my problem, you reckless bastard.

The scan suite had glass panels pulsing with quiet light as the bioelectrical lattice array booted up, pale blue schematics hovering midair. Hyacine keyed a sequence into the wall terminal, a lattice diagram of the human nervous system unfurling like a digital spine.

“Alright,” Hyacine chirped. “You’re up, Phainon. Clothes off—I need full contact for the mapping.”

Phainon, already halfway to uncooperative, sighed but tugged his shirt over his head with a lazy roll of muscle, fabric catching for a second before it came loose. He flung it onto the nearby chair and then glanced sideways at Mydei.

“Help me with this, would you?” he asked, casual, fingers absently toying with the waistband of his pants like it was just another Tuesday.

Mydei choked on his own breath. “Do it your damn self.”

Phainon smirked—sharp, predatory, the kind of grin that usually preceded catastrophic decisions. “Didn’t figure you for shy.”

Hyacine, without missing a beat, looked up from her holo-display, smile perfectly neutral. “I can leave if you two need a minute.”

Mydei’s brain short-circuited. “We don’t—He’s—” He gestured wildly at Phainon, who looked entirely too pleased with himself, then at Hyacine. “Just run your scan.”

Hyacine winked. “As you say, boss.”

Phainon tossed a cocky glance Mydei’s way, like he’d won some silent argument, then kicked his shoes off and stepped onto the platform, bare skin catching the soft electric-blue glow of the feedback lattice as the system powered up.

The room dimmed, leaving only the web of bioelectric pathways lighting up along Phainon’s frame—and Mydei, very intentionally, kept his eyes on the holo-monitor and absolutely nowhere else.

Because damn it, this was going to be a long week.

The scan completed with a soft chime, the lattice flickering as lines of bioelectric feedback translated into a three-dimensional nerve map. Hyacine tapped a command, and the rendered silhouette of Phainon’s body rotated lazily in the air—a web of lit nerve clusters and microcurrent readings illuminating in shades of indigo and green.

Mydei wasn’t trying to look.

Really, he wasn’t.

But his gaze snagged on a section of the readout—isolated red markers blinking along old scar tissue buried deep in muscle clusters, fractures in neural pathways rerouted by time and survival instinct. Abnormal stress-response loops. Memory trauma signatures. Combat-related strain patterns no normal civilian—no professor—should’ve racked up.

His gut twisted.

It didn’t add up.

Not with Phainon’s spotless record. Not with the carefully constructed nothingness of his official history. Not with the academic credentials Mydei had only half-cared to check before.

The scan was too clinical to make excuses for. Too damning.

Phainon noticed the silence first. Shirt in hand, half-forgotten, he glanced between the readout and Mydei’s face—something sharp flashing in his expression, instinctive calculation.

“…Something wrong, doc?” Phainon asked, voice light, but his eyes were tracking every muscle in Mydei’s jaw.

Mydei swallowed hard, forcing a smile. “Actually—” he stepped forward, rolling his sleeves up to his forearms, every movement calm, practiced, the kind you used before a bar fight you didn’t wanna start but weren’t gonna lose. “I think I’ll take you up on that offer.”

Phainon’s brow furrowed. “Offer?”

“You know.” Mydei gestured vaguely. “Helping you change.”

A flicker of something like self-preservation sparked in Phainon’s eyes. He grabbed his shirt—caution still intact despite how beat to hell he was—and made a very subtle, very strategic step toward the opposite wall.

“On second thought,” Phainon said, slipping the fabric down over his head, deliberately turning away, “I think I’m good.”

“Oh no,” Mydei drawled, stalking closer, sharp-edged and patient. “Too late for that.”

Phainon bolted for his jacket, trying to slip it on one-armed, one eye on Mydei like he was measuring the odds of a clean getaway versus losing a shoe in the process.

“I swear to every pantheon, Phainon, if you run I’m chaining your ass to that bed again.”

Phainon smirked, but it was thinner now. “Bet you’d like to.”

And then, because neither of them knew how to back down—they both moved at the same time.

Phainon was a miserable, grumpy fixture in the middle of a bed worth more than most officers’ annual hazard pay. The synthwave-tinted skylights above them flickered lazily between lunar phases—precisely as he’d demanded, and now looking more regretful by the second.

Pinned by reinforced restraint bands around his wrists (a precaution, Hyacine had cheerily claimed, since he “kept trying to jailbreak his vitals monitors”), Phainon stubbornly refused to meet Mydei’s gaze. He’d gone full petulant sulk mode.

Mydei leaned against the doorframe, datapad tucked under his arm.

“So,” he asked mildly, tapping a loose knuckle against the wall display, “enjoying your luxury accommodations?”

Phainon’s scowl deepened. If looks could kill, the Atrium Suite would’ve been declared a crime scene.

“It’s been two days,” Phainon snapped. “Two days of cortical sync scans, vasculature density mapping, bioelectrical resonance analysis—and those glorified med-drones trying to barcode my spine while I’m half-asleep.”

“You forgot the cognitive decay latency monitor,” Mydei said helpfully.

Phainon glared, then pointedly turned his face to the side.

Mydei sighed, stepping further into the room and leaning over the end of the bed. “Calm down. We’ve still gotta run you through the neural impulse relay diagnostics and the recursive memory cohesion audit before you’re cleared.”

“No.”

Mydei raised a brow. “No?”

“I’m done,” Phainon said flatly. “That’s it. No more tests, no more lattice mapping, no more whatever-the-hell-you-called-it neural resonance differential sequencing. I’ve had enough. The techs have had enough. You’ve had enough.”

“Actually,” Mydei replied, glancing at his datapad like he hadn’t heard a word, “we haven’t.”

Phainon shot him a dry look. “Name one I haven’t done.”

Mydei opened his mouth, then hesitated.

“…Look—”

“Quantitative microcurrent latency response. Electro-dermal feedback threshold mapping. Deep tissue vibrotactile stim assessment.”

A beat.

Mydei grimaced. “…Okay. That last one’s optional.”

“Bullshit.”

And for a moment it looked like the standoff would reset for round three.

Until Phainon, very quietly, muttered without looking at him,

“I hate hospitals.”

The words hung there, heavier than they should’ve been.

And for all of Mydei’s suspicion, for all the buried doubt he wouldn’t admit out loud, his heart still clenched like a wire pulled too tight. He exhaled through his nose, rubbing a hand down his face.

A beat of quiet.

Then Phainon spoke again, reluctant, jaw tight.

“…Less tests.”

Mydei fought down a smile. “Deal.”

He made a note on his datapad, signaling Hyacine for priority vitals only and essential diagnostics, then glanced down at the scowling man in the bed.

“You’re still wearing those restraints though.”

Phainon deadpanned at him. “You’re a sadist.”

“You say that like it’s new.”

The third morning started with Hyacine frowning at Phainon’s charts, chewing absently on the end of a stylus. She didn’t even bother with preamble anymore.

“Alright, stabilizer flush. He’s spiking too hard. Endocrine’s out of regulation, cortisol’s trying to start a fight with his dopamine, and his circadian markers think it’s 3 a.m. in four different timezones.”

Mydei, already nursing a cup of coffee he didn’t want, leaned against the far wall, arms crossed. “Side effects?”

Hyacine grinned, far too cheerful for someone about to chemically scramble another person’s brain for therapeutic reasons. “Nothing lasting. Maybe a little disorientation, mild inhibition drop. He’ll be fine.”

Which, in retrospect, should’ve been a warning.

By the time the stabilizer drip hit Phainon’s system, the effects were embarrassingly immediate. His head tipped lazily against the med-bed’s headrest, lids fluttering half-mast as his pupils dilated, the tension bleeding from his frame like someone had cut his strings.

He slurred out a soft, “Mm’ feel weird.”

Mydei tried not to react. “It’s the stabilizer. You’ll be fine.”

Phainon turned his head, hazy gaze locking on Mydei like he’d just now noticed him standing there. A slow, crooked grin crept across his face, something looser and too genuine.

“Mydei…” he drawled, voice warm and wrecked-soft in a way that was absolutely going to kill him later. “Y’know you’re… gorgeous, right?”

Hyacine snorted so hard she had to turn away, pretending to check a monitor.

Mydei, face instantly heating, scowled. “Shut up. You’re delirious.”

“Mmhmm,” Phainon hummed, reaching out like he might actually try to grab him. His fingers grazed Mydei’s sleeve, and it was nothing, stupidly light contact, but Mydei’s pulse stuttered all the same.

“Could kiss you right now,” Phainon murmured, eyes slipping closed, lashes casting faint shadows over flushed skin. “Bet you taste good.”

“Stars, you’re worse than a blackout rat on stim fumes,” Mydei growled, roughly batting his hand away, but it wasn’t sharp. Not really. And his ears

were red enough to fry with no.

Hyacine coughed into her hand, grinning as she scrawled a note on the datapad. “Vitals stabilizing. Endocrine’s leveling. Might wanna bottle this mood for later.”

“I will set your lab on fire,” Mydei deadpanned, glaring at her.

Phainon slumped back down, a lazy, contented sigh escaping him. “So bossy,” he mumbled, barely audible now, head lolling toward the side. “Lucky you’re cute.”

And then—mercifully—sleep claimed him, stabilizer knocking him out cold. The medbay monitor let out a steady, even pulse. Hyacine shot Mydei a look, one brow raised in smug amusement.

“He won’t remember a thing.”

Mydei stared at the unconscious idiot on the bed, heat still stubbornly clinging to his face. “…Good.”

But he didn’t leave right away. Just stood there for a long moment, watching Phainon’s breathing settle, the faint crease between his brows smoothing out for the first time in days.

He wouldn’t remember it.

Mydei wouldn’t forget.

The datapad chimed softly in Mydei’s hand. He hadn’t meant to check it again, but old instincts had a way of clawing up at inconvenient hours.

He flicked through the logs—standard vital checks, stabilizer balances, sensory recalibration files. Then he saw it.

Adrenal Response Curve: Flagged.

A spike right where there shouldn’t be one. Not under sedatives, not at rest.

He swiped again.

Situational Awareness Index: 92.7%

Mydei’s tensed. That wasn’t just above average—that was combat active. Field-ready. Numbers like that didn’t come from a civilian with neural scarring. Not even one with irregular anchor residue like Phainon’s.

Gods above…

Another soft ping. Reflex Latency Test Results.

He opened the file.

Visual latency: 0.142 seconds. Auditory response: 0.219 seconds. Neuromuscular coordination: 0.105 seconds.

He stared at those numbers. Chrysos-vetted enforcers barely clocked those in controlled simulations.

Phainon had blown through them like it was nothing.

Hyacine’s note at the bottom:

“Not standard civilian baselines. Re-test pending.”

Mydei didn’t breathe for a full second.

Across the room, Phainon was reclining in his ridiculous luxe enviro-bed, one hand lazily tossing a nutrition bar into the air and catching it again like some overgrown street rat who’d lucked his way into a royal suite. Smug, cocky—entirely unaware of the storm curling tighter around him.

“0.105,” Mydei muttered under his breath.

Phainon glanced over. “Talking about how impressive I am again?” he smirked.

Mydei gave him a thin, humorless smile. “Something like that.”

He scrolled further, cross-referencing the flagged readings against old mission logs, against old Flame Reaver field reports he wasn’t technically supposed to have archived. Situational awareness spikes in high-conflict nodes. Adrenal overclocks during flare riots. Reflex scores that only two known agents had ever clocked higher than.

And one of them was dead.

His stomach turned.

He didn’t say a word, though. Not yet. Just closed the datapad with a sharp flick of his thumb and forced his expression back to neutral.

Could be a neural burn side effect.

Could be trauma pattern crossovers.

Or it could be something worse.

He wasn’t sure what terrified him more.

The soft click of a releasing restraint band met Mydei the second he stepped through the door.

He looked up from his datapad, raising a brow.

Phainon was seated on the edge of his enviro-bed, one wrist free, a stripped stim patch casing pinched expertly between two fingers like a lockpick. The restraint band lay slack against the mattress, seconds from falling away entirely.

They made eye contact.

A beat passed.

“They slipped,” Phainon said.

Mydei stared at him. “Uh-huh.”

Another beat.

Mydei crossed the room, plucked the stim patch casing from his fingers, and re-secured the restraint—a little tighter this time.

Phainon gave a token tug. Scowled. “Abuse of power.”

“You’d know,” Mydei muttered.

Just then, Hyacine popped in, chipper as always, holding a tray with a nutrient paste blend that looked like it’d been extracted from a sewer runoff and smelled worse.

“Neural repair blend,” she announced brightly, setting it down with a flourish. “Formulated to regulate endocrine spikes and stabilize post-burn neurotransmitter crossfire. Tastes like shit.”

Phainon eyed the cup warily. “I’m not eating that.”

“Not optional,” Hyacine sing-songed.

“I’ll starve.”

“Can’t. Monitored intake protocols,” she said, then winked at Mydei. “You’ve got this.” and ducked out before the explosion.

Mydei sighed, grabbed the spoon. “Open your mouth.”

“You wouldn’t dare.”

He dipped the spoon into the sludge. Held it out.

Phainon glared. “I swear to God, Mydei—”

“Say ‘ah.’”

“You say ‘ah.’”

Mydei lunged.

They wrestled.

Ridiculous, undignified, elbows and half-choked insults. Phainon had one hand still cuffed but still managed to disarm Mydei, sending the spoon arcing in a graceful, traitorous arc across the room.

It hit the wall with a wet splat.

Silence.

Phainon grinned, breathless and smug. “Told you.”

Hyacine, from the hallway, let out an audible snort and vanished before either could retaliate.

Mydei let his head drop back with a groan. “You’re an absolute menace.”

“And yet you keep showing up,” Phainon shot back, and for a split second, there was a flicker of something softer under the banter.

Mydei caught it. Didn’t comment.

Just sighed, grabbed a fresh spoon, and muttered, “We’re not done.”

Mydei strode in, datapad tucked under one arm and a cheap ration chocolate bar in hand like it was some rare, coveted artifact. He flicked it onto Phainon’s chest with a practiced, unimpressed motion.

“Congrats,” Mydei announced flatly. “You survived Day Four. Here’s your prize.”

Phainon, lounging against the luxe enviro-bed like he owned the place, didn’t even bother to look. One hand absently palmed the ration bar, thumb running over the wrapper, eyes half-lidded and faintly amused.

“If this isn’t a striptease, I’m not interested.”

Mydei’s brow twitched. He sucked in a sharp breath, exasperated, and rolled up his sleeves with slow, deliberate intent—knuckles cracking for dramatic emphasis.

“Keep talking.”

There was the faintest smirk at the corner of Phainon’s mouth. That infuriating, self-assured curve that meant nothing good for anyone within a ten-foot radius.

Before Mydei could commit to murder, Hyacine poked her head in, datapad in hand and a too-innocent grin on her face.

“Hey. Neural sync leads need a manual recalibration. System flagged a misalignment in the upper conduits.”

She didn’t even wait for a reply, already tossing Mydei a portable relay patch and gesturing at the overhead node ports. “You’re closest.”

Mydei shot her a glare. “You’re joking.”

“Nope.” She winked and was gone, door sliding shut behind her.

Phainon arched a brow, finally turning his head to glance at Mydei. “Looks like you’re on top of me again, sweetheart.”

“Gods, you’re exhausting.”

Muttering curses under his breath, Mydei climbed up onto the edge of the bed, one knee digging into the mattress near Phainon’s hip, the other braced for balance as he stretched for the overhead interface. The position was a mess of awkward angles and far too much proximity, especially with Phainon’s wrist restraints still locked down.

And of course, because the bastard couldn’t leave well enough alone—

“If you wanted me tied down and begging, you could’ve just asked.”

The words were dangerously close to his ear. Velvet-smooth and unapologetic, like it wasn’t the first time he’d thought about it.

Mydei’s whole body tensed. A spark of heat shot up his spine before he crushed it, jaw tight, pulse in his throat.

“Say one more word,” Mydei warned, voice soft and lethal.

Phainon’s grin widened, sharp and satisfied, gaze heavy-lidded and too fucking pleased with himself. The air between them went thick enough to cut. For a beat, neither of them moved.

Somewhere in the background, a monitor beeped. The datapad in Mydei’s hand trembled slightly from the tension in his grip.

It took every scrap of discipline not to look down, not to acknowledge the proximity of their bodies or the heat radiating off Phainon’s skin, or the fact that Mydei’s thigh was pressed tight against his side.

But gods, it was a near thing.

And just like that, it was the fifth day.

Phainon, against all odds, was actually doing better. The color had come back to his face, his vitals were stabilizing, and most importantly—the bastard was getting cocky again. Old self inching its way to the surface with every smug remark and unrepentant grin.

Mydei figured it was safe enough to step out for a bit. Cipher was in the city —rare, considering she ghosted in and out of networked grids like mist, and when she showed herself it usually meant valuable intel wasn’t far behind.

And Mydei had been meaning to confirm a little suspicion of his own. It seemed their elusive antihero might’ve picked up a partner. Someone else running the streets, someone good—good enough to stay off the Council’s scanners and Hyacine’s encrypted tracers. The kind of dangerous, alluring problem Mydei could sink his teeth into.

He left with barely a glance back, Hyacine cheerfully waving him off and Phainon looking entirely too pleased to be unsupervised.

Of course, it would be the one time something went wrong.

Chrysos Heir medical centers didn’t fail. Not on mission, not off. It happened maybe once a decade—and apparently, this was their lucky day.

Hyacine had been running a neural integration stabilization procedure. Standard. Smart, even. The goal was to reinforce neural pathways destabilized by trauma-adjacent memory displacement, smoothing over erratic resonance spikes, clearing junk data.

It should’ve helped. It was helping. Right up until it didn’t.

Residual trauma triggers.

The system flagged a priority amber spike halfway through the recalibration phase—a surge of hyperactive node feedback. Which, in clean tech terms, meant Phainon’s brain decided to play back some very bad things at full volume.

And the worst part?

It happened when Mydei wasn’t there.

It went from bad to worse sometime around the fourteenth hour.

The logs Hyacine sent later painted a brutal picture. During the Neural Stabilization Recalibration, a residual trauma spike hit—higher than anything they’d seen. Feedback flooded the synapse lines, and Phainon panicked.

Bolted.

The Aureate Restraint Unit was deployed, fast and professional. Or at least they were supposed to be.

By the time they got him down, two had cracked ribs, one a dislocated shoulder, another a fractured ulna. Neural tech ruptured, monitors shorted out in a ten-meter radius, half the floor’s lighting grid glitched so bad it left everything flickering like a failing pulse.

They called it a systems anomaly. Hardware degradation. Power loop cross-interference.

Nobody said the obvious. That it happened centered on him.

Now, hours later, Phainon was locked in the room. Not caged—they weren’t animals here. It was still his room, with its ridiculous huge bed and adjustable enviro-temps and far too many pillows for one man. But the entrance authorization grid was restricted, sedatives loaded into the wall injectors if needed.

For his safety. And everyone else’s.

Hyacine waited for Mydei by the observation pane. She looked tired for once—tired and small in a way she never did, leaning against the wall in loose scrubs, datapad clutched to her chest.

“I don’t recommend going in,” she said softly. “Not yet. He’s… not himself.”

Mydei’s gaze flicked toward the sealed door. No flicker of concern in his face, just that unreadable composure he wore like armor. He exhaled through his nose, slow and unhurried.

“I’m not here to fight him,” he started with carefully. “And he wouldn’t lay a hand on me. Couldn’t, even if he tried.”

Hyacine opened her mouth, then thought better of it. She stepped aside without another word, letting him pass.

Mydei keyed the lock, stepped through without hesitation, the door sealing behind him in a hush of pressurized air.

He didn’t puff his chest or make a show of readiness.

He just walked in, and if Phainon came at him, he wouldn’t strike, wouldn’t flinch—would catch him, hold him down if it came to it, and let him calm because that’s what you did when someone needed help.

But they both knew it wouldn’t come to that.

It never would.

Phainon looked like hell.

Sweat-dark hair clung to his forehead, the sharp line of his jaw shadowed with stubble. Bruises mottled his collarbone, ugly and blooming against pale skin. The restraint bands at his wrists had been resecured, red marks ghosting along the skin beneath them. He didn’t spare Mydei a glance.

Mydei crossed the room without a word.

The half-spilled water pitcher sat abandoned on the side table, condensation beading down the glass. He righted it, poured a clean glass, set it within reach. Still nothing from Phainon.

Not until Mydei leaned back against the wall, arms loose at his sides, voice soft.

“You hurt?”

A beat.

Then, dry as scorched earth, Phainon muttered, “You offering to kiss it better?”

The air pulled tight between them, a breath before a storm. Tension like a drawn string, neither of them willing to ease the hold.

Mydei didn’t smile. Just arched a brow, gaze steady and unreadable.

Then—the lights overhead stuttered.

A monitor on the far wall glitched, its feed warping for a heartbeat, data bleeding into static. A near-imperceptible distortion in the pulse of the room.

Mydei clocked it instantly. No comment, but his eyes narrowed, a flicker of calculation sparking in that sharp gaze.

Across from him, Phainon’s jaw clenched. Not at the water. Not at the restraints. At that.

He’d felt it too.

And neither of them said a word.

Mydei exhaled, the sound soft, weary, like some heavy weight settled deeper into his chest. He pushed off the wall, closing the distance between them, his movements unhurried, almost careful.

Phainon tensed the moment he stepped close.

Mydei crouched slightly, one hand ghosting near Phainon’s shoulder—not touching, just there. “What did you see?”

For a second, nothing. Just the uneven cadence of Phainon’s breath, the twitch in his jaw.

Then—a sharp flinch, like instinct snapping through brittle nerves. He recoiled, not much, but enough. Shoulders tight, throat working like swallowing glass. His voice came hoarse, cracked.

“You said they’d do less tests.”

The words landed harder than they should’ve. Like a blade between ribs. Mydei felt it—the way those words lodged under his skin, brittle and aching. His tongue pressed to the roof of his mouth, trying to shape something, anything in defense.

But no words came.

Phainon’s hands flexed in his restraints, colorless knuckles shaking with effort. And after a moment, quieter, eyes fixed somewhere past Mydei’s shoulder:

“…You weren’t there. It doesn’t matter what I saw.”

The room felt too still after that.

The comm crackled softly at Mydei’s hip. Hyacine’s voice came through, subdued, careful.

“Vitals are stabilizing, but the restraints… it might be doing more harm than good now. If he’s lucid—you can ease them. I’ll approve it.”

Mydei didn’t hesitate. He reached down, unfastening the restraint bands with efficient movements. The final one slipped free. Phainon didn’t react beyond a sharp flicker of his gaze, a look that landed somewhere just shy of resentment and exhaustion. He turned his head away, jaw tight. Conversation, clearly, over.

Mydei exhaled slowly.

He should’ve left. Every instinct said to.

Instead, he lowered himself to Phainon’s level, crouching again—not crowding him, just there, weight braced on one knee. Close enough to be felt but not pressed.

His voice was quiet. Steady.

“It matters to me.”

That earned a flicker of motion—a glance, wary and tired.

“You’re safe here,” Mydei added, words simple, heavy with the kind of certainty that didn’t beg for belief. “It’ll be alright soon.”

He rose, about to turn, knowing better than to linger. The quiet pressed in, thick as fog. The faint hum of the overhead monitors, the steady pulse of

the vitals feed—it all felt louder in absence of conversation.

Mydei’s hand brushed the door control, the cool touch of the panel grounding. He should’ve left it at that.

But something made him glance back.

Phainon hadn’t moved. His gaze fixed somewhere past the far wall, lashes low, jaw tight enough to crack. Beneath the bruises and the exhaustion, there was something fraying—an old fracture threatening to split open.

Mydei didn’t speak. He just waited.

The seconds stretched, brittle.

Then—like something forced loose —

“…Back then,” Phainon started, the words rough as gravel, “the only thing you could hear at night was the screaming.”

A pause. A breath, sharp through his teeth.

“And the sound it made when it touched them.”

His voice thinned at the edges, breaking down to something raw.

“You don’t forget a sound like that.”

The room held its breath.

And Mydei, for all the things he could’ve said—didn’t.

He let the quiet settle around them like a shield. Then moved for the door, tension low in his frame, leaving space where no words would fit.

He knew when someone wanted to be alone. And sometimes mercy wasn’t words—it was the space you left behind.

The door slid shut in his wake.

Mydei lingered there a moment, the faint sound of the lock cycling into place unusually loud in the stillness. He let his hand drop from the panel, flexed his fingers once, and drew a slow breath.

The hallway beyond was dim, quiet in that late-hour way only medical wings ever were. Hyacine was waiting a few paces down, leaning against the wall with her datapad half-forgotten in one hand. She straightened at the sight of him, scanning his face for something she didn’t bother to ask aloud.

“How is he?” she murmured.

“Alive.” Mydei’s voice was rougher than he meant it to be. “Lucid enough to be pissed off. That’s something.”

Hyacine’s lips tugged in a tired, fleeting half-smile. “Vitals stabilized while you were in there. If it holds through tonight, I can start the recalibrations early. Two days ahead of schedule, if we’re lucky.”

He grunted softly, the edge of a smirk flickering at his mouth. “Spoil him too much, he’ll start expecting special treatment.”

“I think he’s earned it,” she said, quiet.

They let the moment settle there, the hum of nearby equipment filling the space between them. It was a fragile kind of peace — the kind built on mutual exhaustion and too many unspoken things.

Then Mydei spoke again, too casually.

“When was the last time Flame Reaver sightings and power grid malfunctions happened in the same district?”

The words hung there. Heavy. Unwelcome.

Hyacine’s expression froze, the datapad screen flickering faintly in her grasp. A second passed. Then another.

When she spoke, her voice was careful, laced with something wary. “Are you implying—”

“No.” The denial came fast, harder than he meant it to, but he didn’t soften it.

His gaze stayed fixed on her, unreadable in the dim light. Not an accusation. Just a dark, restless thing twisting behind his ribs.

“Goldweaver’s got a lead now, doesn’t she?” Mydei said, quieter this time. “It won’t be long.”

He pushed away from the wall, steps measured, the weight of the night heavy on his shoulders.

Hyacine didn’t stop him. Didn’t speak.

The hallway stretched on ahead, empty but for the low flicker of the overhead lights — one of them stuttering faintly, unnoticed.

And Mydei didn’t look back.

Not because he didn’t want to.

Because some part of him already knew.

Chapter End Notes
