Chapter Summary

Phainon accidentally glitches half the campus while having a breakdown, bleeds everywhere, ends up in his boyfriend’s library (again), gets caught (again), and proceeds to emotionally unravel in Mydei’s lap while aggressively cuddling him. Threats are made against innocent shelving units. Affection is weaponized. Somewhere in the distance, Anaxa’s migraine worsens

Chapter Notes

Oof this one was a doozy, y’all think I can finish this before 3.4? I’m gonna try to get to chapter 12-13 before version 3.3, wish me luck😍

Phainon was ninety percent sure his nutrient paste was plotting his murder.

It stared up at him with the consistency and flavor profile of wet cardboard abandoned in a server room. He jabbed at it with a spork—because in this wretched, chronically underfunded hellscape of an academic institution, forks had been declared “a hazard to metaphysical integrity” after last semester’s Incident. Capital I.

Next to him, Dan Heng existed in his usual state of unbothered neutrality, methodically eating cubes of something that might’ve once been chicken while reading an ancient-looking book titled Entropy and the Artificial Soul: A Treatise. In Latin.

Dan Heng wasn’t even enrolled in his department. Or his lectures. Or his building. Phainon was a debates professor; Dan Heng was a literature and cybersecurity dual-major with the social presence of a very well-read cloud of passive-aggressive fog. And yet, without fail, every time Phainon’s life

derailed, this man materialized within a five-foot radius like a cursed NPC bound by invisible proximity triggers.

Phainon sighed, resting his face in one palm.

Rock bottom, he thought grimly, is trauma-dumping to a guy only here for the vending machine.

“Did you know,” Phainon began, poking his nutrient paste hard enough to make it shudder, “that these nutrient cubes are technically made of repurposed protein strings salvaged from terminated simulation loops?”

Dan Heng didn’t look up. “Makes sense. Entropy recycles.”

“Right?!” Phainon gestured emphatically with his spork, like this was a TED Talk attended exclusively by himself and one very tired-looking student. “Which means technically we’re all just repurposed glitches pretending to be real.”

Dan Heng turned a page. “You sound unwell.”

“Thanks, man. That means a lot.”

Phainon listlessly resumed stirring his paste. It made a wet, squelching noise like someone rebooting a corpse.

He sniffled.

And with a quiet, muted pop—the spork in his hand abruptly rethreaded itself into a perfect, polished metal pretzel.

Phainon blinked at it.

The universe, apparently, was doing bits now.

Carefully, without moving his head, he shifted his eyes to Dan Heng.

Nothing. The man didn’t so much as twitch.

Phainon cleared his throat. “Just uh… metaphysical turbulence. Happens to the best of us.”

Dan Heng, still reading, deadpanned, “You should see an educated professional about that.”

“I am an educated professional.”

A long, contemplative beat.

“Well. Get a second opinion.”

Phainon dropped the pretzel-spork back into the nutrient paste with a resigned splorch.

This was his life now.

It had been, what… a week? Two? Time blurred when you were neck-deep in metaphysical crises and minor war crimes. Since detainment, since that place, since he’d woken up in a hospital bed with his powers twitchy and his mind full of holes, staring at Mydei’s stupid, annoyingly flawless face.

He still didn’t know how Mydei pulled it off. Getting him out of the Council’s clutch should’ve been impossible—even for a Librarian. Especially for a Librarian.

Unless it wasn’t just him.

He didn’t like thinking about it. Which was why he hadn’t made eye contact with Mydei in nearly nine days, three hours, and twenty-six minutes. Not that he was counting.

Because if he did—if he so much as held that gaze a second too long— Phainon was ninety percent certain he’d spontaneously confess to treason, accessory to digital sedition, several counts of high metaphysical misconduct, and at least one incident involving the unauthorized reconfiguration of Council property into a giant flaming middle finger.

And the worst part was, somewhere under the jokes and deadpan banter, the dread sat.

Heavy.

Because he remembered what he said in that room. What he gave away.

And if anyone else did too—if it was on record, if it slipped through—he was already dead.

“Entropy recycles,” Dan Heng murmured again, turning another page like he hadn’t just dropped an accidental prophecy.

Phainon glanced over.

“Seriously, man,” he said, voice a little too loud, a little too sharp. “Stop saying shi—ahem, stuff like that.”

Dan Heng raised a brow, unbothered. “You started it.”

Fair.

Phainon grinned at the room like a man standing on a ledge and daring gravity to try him.

“Alright, moral degenerates,” he announced, dropping his datapad onto the desk with a dramatic clack. “Today’s debate prompt: If given access to an infallible predictive algorithm, should governments be allowed to preemptively detain citizens based on potential future crimes? Discuss.”

A beat.

The class stared at him.

Caelus, bless his eternally half-awake soul, raised a tentative hand. “Uh… isn’t that basically that one old dystopia sim?”

“Which one?” Phainon snapped, spinning to face the board like he was about to write down the secret to immortality. “We’ve had like fifty. Name your totalitarian flavor.”

“The one with the psychic cops.”

“Oh. Preemptive Judgment Eight-Three-Seven. Good reference. Two points for Caelus.”

He scrawled a giant, barely legible “+2” on the board like it meant something. It didn’t.

Stelle side-eyed him. “Professor, are you good? You’re kinda—” she made a vague spiraling motion with her finger “—today.”

Phainon grinned wider. “Define good, Stelle. Define today.”

The students exchanged looks. None of them moved to leave. They knew better by now.

“Debates,” Phainon declared, pacing like a caged apex predator. “A battle of wills, wits, and the occasional legally inadmissible threat. Real life application: how to talk your way out of government custody without crying.”

A long, slightly deranged beat.

“Hypothetically.”

Another beat.

He clapped his hands. The lights flickered. Nobody even flinched.

Somewhere in the back, one of the power conduits made a sad little bzzt.

Phainon’s smile faltered for half a second before snapping back into place like elastic.

He was fine.

He was great.

He was totally not spiraling into metaphysical paranoia because his morally dubious hopefully and lovingly still boyfriend hadn’t looked him in the eye for over a week and might be plotting either a date or a public execution.

“Anyway,” he said brightly, gesturing to the class. “Split into pairs. Someone defend the algorithm. Someone oppose it. Winner gets… I dunno, one of my backup access codes.”

“Is that legal?” Caelus asked.

“Debatable,” Phainon chirped.

And just like that, the students moved into groups, like this was perfectly normal.

Because for them, it was.

Phainon grabbed an eraser off the desk, mind still halfway in his own impending existential collapse, and absentmindedly squeezed it as he paced.

It burst into flame.

A small, miserable aetheric fire, flickering a sickly blue at the edges.

No one even turned their heads.

Not a single student flinched. No one asked if it was part of the lesson. Caelus didn’t even blink.

Stelle sighed, reaching into her bag like a veteran of too many low-grade supernatural crises, and pulled out a standard-issue fire suppressant stick. She pointed it at the burning eraser, pressed the button, and a puff of white foam snuffed out the flame with a pathetic fzzzt.

“Three this week,” she muttered, checking something off on her phone.

Phainon didn’t even stop pacing.

Because again, this was his life now.

While the students bickered over some ethics-of-televised-trials debate topic he absolutely didn’t remember assigning, Phainon slumped down onto the edge of his desk like a man freshly mauled by a metaphorical bear. The wood groaned beneath him in solidarity.

God, he was tired.

Not in the I stayed up too late doomscrolling Council leaks again way. No —this was marrow-deep, head-splitting, can’t tell if I’m hallucinating or astral-projecting but either way I’m gonna throw up tired.

He rubbed at his temple, and felt the faintest trickle of blood from one nostril. Cute.

The thing was—and this was a thing—at some point over the past week or two (post-detainment, post-interrogation, post-fucking-nightmare), his internal scaffolding had cracked.

He didn’t have a better word for it. Anaxa called them his “ideal form templates.” Little mental blueprints he kept in the back of his brain— structures for how reality should behave when he reached out and twisted it. They made things neat. Predictable. Safe.

Without them?

Well.

Now his power ran off subconscious, half-feral dream-logic. Instinctual belief systems forged in grief, caffeine, and denial. Every emotional spike a potential catastrophic misfire. Every burst of frustration or god forbid, fond thought a chance for the nearest pen to combust, reality seams to knot themselves wrong, or that one time yesterday when his comm decided it was a moth and tried to fly out the window.

It wasn’t even that he used his power that much. Not unless he had to. But now the barrier was hair-trigger thin. It bled through in the margins, in

headaches that felt like his brain was trying to fold itself inside out, in flashes of static in the corners of his vision. In little things.

Like setting an eraser on fire.

Phainon sighed, leaning his head back against the wall.

As Anaxa liked to call it—Conceptual Creation. Reality-bending, if you wanted to sound pretentious. Which he often did.

But it wasn’t creation in the true sense. No summoning something from nothing unfortunately. It was structure. Imposing pattern on chaos. Reconfiguring broken threads of reality and code, reworking corrupted aether, glitching systems, raw energy fields. If a place was stable, if everything was ordered and proper? He was powerless.

If it cracked? If it buckled, if entropy bled through, if the code frayed at the edges or the aether warped under pressure—then he could slip a needle in. Then he could stitch.

Weapons, sigils, doorways, conceptual barriers. Made not of matter, but of bent logic and realigned cause-and-effect. A flame-shaped dagger formed because he believed a dagger could hold the shape of flame if you threaded a reality seam just so.

Dream-logic engineering.

The more complicated the weave, the worse the backlash. Which was fine, back when his templates kept things tethered. Back when every creation came with clean edges and a neat little cost.

Now, without those, it was chaos. Every jagged spike of grief or anger or— god help him—affection could trigger a misfire.

It was partially another reason why he’d been dodging him.

Phainon made a noise, covering his face with one hand.

God, he missed his boyfriend.

There it was. The absolute state of him.

He didn’t even have it in him to self-censor anymore.

From across the room, a half-hearted argument about legal personhood rights for rogue AI floated over.

He groaned louder.

Phainon dragged both hands down his face now, took a deep, ragged breath through his nose—and immediately regretted it because blood.

He forced his head sideways, ignoring the sharp throb in his temple, and squinted blearily at the clock mounted above the classroom’s front console.

Two minutes.

Two goddamn minutes.

The only thing standing between him and blissful, dead-eyed solitude.

For a moment, he debated just growling “Get the fuck out,” and calling it pedagogical tough love. But some dim, flickering remnant of professional shame made him hold his tongue. He didn’t have the energy for the complaints form that would generate. Again.

Instead, he sat up abruptly—a little too fast, the room tilting nauseatingly— and slapped both hands onto the desk with a wide, unhinged grin.

“WELL,” Phainon declared, loud enough to make at least three students jump. “Fantastic discourse today! Excellent ethical chaos. Remember, kids: when in doubt, argue in bad faith and see what happens.”

A student gave him a look.

The rest of the class stared in wary, collective silence—not the is this part of the lesson? silence of week one, but the if we stay very still, maybe he won’t snap the laws of physics again silence of seasoned survivors.

Phainon clapped once, the sound sharp and a little too enthusiastic.

“Class dismissed!” he chirped.

Chairs scraped. Bags rustled. No one spoke. They shuffled out like cautious evacuees from a structurally unsound building, giving his desk a respectful five-foot radius.

Even Stelle didn’t bother putting the fire suppressant back in its case. She just left it on the front row seat like a grim little offering.

Phainon slumped back against the desk, exhaling through his teeth.

Merciful silence.

He stayed exactly where he was for a long, dragging second.

Eyes half-lidded. Breathing shallow. Head pounding like some ancient god was using his skull for percussion practice. He waited for the worst of the ache to pass—the sharp, searing bolt behind his eyes fading into a dull, electric throb.

When he could move without retching, Phainon sluggishly reached into his coat pocket, fumbling for the slim, battered comm tab.

Thumbed it open.

No sarcastic voice message this time. Just a quick, quiet ping sent straight to Anaxa’s secure line:

[ hurry the fuck up. ]

A beat.

[ u said a few days at most. i am rapidly approaching ‘most.’ ]

He closed his eyes and let the device rest on his knee, waiting for the inevitable snarky reply. He didn’t care what it said. As long as it came. As long as someone out there was fixing this mess.

Fixing him.

Phainon’s break wasn’t so much a “break” as it was him slumped in a corner booth of the empty campus café, staring blankly into a cup of what the vending machine had promised was coffee.

It tasted like rust.

He stirred it anyway, watching the sludge swirl around like the event horizon of some tiny, caffeine-based black hole.

“So this is it,” Phainon muttered to nobody. “Drinking battery acid in the metaphysical equivalent of a war crime, contemplating whether job abandonment constitutes treason if you do it quietly.”

He took a sip. Immediately regretted it.

“God, what is this? Ground-up despair with notes of public transport floor?”

Somewhere behind him, the register made a distressed, warbling beep.

He didn’t look up.

“Kinda wish it killed me,” he told the universe, swirling the cup again.

A figure slid into the booth across from him, casual as you please.

“Careful,” came Anaxa’s voice, dry as ever. “If you die in here, your corpse legally belongs to the Department of Paracausal Waste Management.”

Phainon blinked, dragging his gaze up to meet Anaxa’s. The man looked marginally worse than usual—hair a little messier, eyes a little heavier, like whatever hell Phainon was enduring, Anaxa had met it, shared a drink, and then scammed it for spare parts.

“…Did you just hack the register?” Phainon asked, because one of the wall monitors was flickering GET FUCKED MOTHERFUCTER in corrupted

text strings.

Anaxa, still half-typing on his portable terminal, didn’t even look up. “Wouldn’t pay out my loyalty points.”

Phainon made a sound that was halfway between a laugh and a dying animal.

“God I missed you,” he muttered.

Anaxa snorted. “Yeah, well. Don’t get attached. You’re insufferable when you get clingy.”

“That’s rich, coming from the guy who broke into my server cache to leave me memes.”

“I was being supportive.”

“It was thirty-seven consecutive images of a dog on fire.”

Anaxa finally looked up, the corner of his mouth twitching into something like a smile. “And you’re still alive. See? Support.”

Phainon stared at him for a long, tired beat.

“Anaxa,” he muttered, letting his head thunk against the table, voice muffled against the cold surface. “I’m one minor inconvenience away from setting myself on fire out of spite.”

“Good,” Anaxa replied, going back to his terminal. “I need the energy to finish bypassing government firewalls. Stay mad, princess.”

Phainon sighd. The absolute worst part?

That was supportive, in Anaxa-speak.

“Nancy’s doing the waltz in Sector Seven.”

Anaxa said it like it was the most normal thing to utter in the middle of a half-condemned university café.

Phainon blinked. “…The hell does that mean?”

Anaxa didn’t answer right away—just stared at him, the subtle kind of look that told Phainon to shut up and pay attention. His stomach dropped a millimeter.

“Oh,” Phainon muttered. “It’s one of those.”

“Yeah,” Anaxa said, casually tapping a key sequence. The lights overhead hummed. “One of those.”

They lapsed into a weird, scratchy quiet, the flickering café monitor still scrolling some glitchy nonsense about “SOUL TAX EXCEEDED.” Phainon took another sip of his coffee. It did not improve.

“I swear to god, Anaxa,” Phainon sighed, “if this is another metaphor for you stealing library servers again—”

“It’s not,” Anaxa said, eyes still fixed on the screen. “This time it’s the council’s main grid.”

Phainon almost choked.

“I told you to leave that alone!”

“I did,” Anaxa said mildly. “And then I didn’t.”

A long, jittery beat.

Phainon leaned back, running a hand down his face. “Okay. Talk slow. Explain like I’m concussed. ‘Cause I probably am.”

Anaxa exhaled through his nose, expression flat. “The waltz is their internal sweep protocol. Nancy’s their codename for any asset flagged for high-priority surveillance. Sector Seven’s the upper clearance tier reserved for nation-breakers and abstract anomalies.”

Phainon frowned, brain sluggishly untangling the metaphor web. “Okay… and?”

Anaxa finally looked up, the sharp line of his jaw tensing. “They bumped someone to top-tier clearance officially this morning. Seems like it’s been there for a while before that though. Full immediate termination protocol. No trial. No retrieval. Just wipe.”

Phainon’s pulse hiccupped. A faint, sourceless flicker rippled through the ceiling lights.

“…Who?” he asked, though something in him already knew.

Anaxa held his gaze for a long, stretched moment.

“Flame Reaver.”

The world dropped out for half a breath. The café’s old streetlamp buzzed outside, flickering once—in perfect sync with the throb of Phainon’s pulse slamming against his skull.

“That—” Phainon’s voice cracked halfway. He cleared it. “That doesn’t make sense. We’ve been careful with the important things. We’ve been ghosts. Even if they suspected, top-tier’s for things that can glass continents or...”

Anaxa’s face was stone, fingers twitching at his terminal. “Yeah. That’s why I hacked the grid.”

Phainon sat back hard, head pounding in a way that wasn’t entirely metaphor.

“God,” he muttered. “What did I miss.”

Anaxa didn’t answer. The absence of explanation was a bullet in its own right.

They sat there for a while, the brittle quiet only broken by the distant hum of server fans and the dull pulse of his own panic. Then Anaxa stood,

shouldering his bag.

“Anyway,” he said, his voice the same easy, wry thing it always was. “If you see Nancy…”

Phainon looked up, throat tight.

“Tell her the waltz is over.”

And then he was gone.

Leaving Phainon alone with his coffee sludge, a throbbing headache, and the creeping, awful knowledge that something had gone terribly, impossibly wrong.

The day, against all odds, got worse.

Phainon forced himself into everything’s fine mode with the sheer, unhinged commitment of a man on the edge of his third consecutive breakdown. He graded finals in his office like an actual educator, as though the entire infrastructure of his life wasn’t actively collapsing beneath him.

“Let’s see here…” he muttered, flipping a paper over. “‘Debate Question 3: In a closed system of moral decay, who holds authority over the unverifiable self?’” He squinted. “Okay, not bad, a little pretentious—”

The text shimmered.

His brow furrowed.

It flickered again, letters warping into something sharp and jagged before settling into neat, eldritch cursive:

”I saw the god beneath the latticework of stars and fed it my name.”

Phainon blinked. “…Okay, so, uh… bonus points for thematic commitment?”

He grabbed a red pen, circled it, and wrote ‘citation needed’. Moved on.

Across his desk, the paperweight shivered.

A tiny, anguished chirp rose from it.

Phainon glanced up just in time to watch the glossy metal orb sprout brittle, beady eyes and a rapidly flapping set of wings. It screamed. A shrill, existential wail of tiny avian horror.

Without missing a beat, he grabbed a coffee mug and slammed it over the thing. The shriek muffled instantly. He slid a sticky note onto the cup that read “DO NOT OPEN—metaphysical hazard”.

“Anyway,” he sighed, reaching for the next exam.

The lights in the office flickered.

A knock came at the door—which then politely opened itself before he touched it.

He didn’t even flinch.

A student poked their head in. “Um, Professor Phainon? You’re, uh… bleeding again.”

Phainon dabbed under his nose. Came away with a smear of dark red.

“Yeah,” he said tiredly, “I do that sometimes.”

The student lingered a second too long, then quietly closed the door.

He sighed. The shadows under his desk stretched, curling like ink dropped in water. The reflection in his monitor blinked out of sync with his own.

“Normal,” Phainon muttered. “Perfectly normal. This is fine.”

The debate final in front of him rewritten itself again.

“The lattice will break. The tide is coming. Only the hollow king endures.”

“Okay,” Phainon muttered, capping his pen. “Pass.”

Phainon shoved the debate finals into a folder that didn’t actually exist. One second it was a folder, the next it flickered out of phase, and honestly? Same. He rubbed at the smear of blood beneath his nose with the heel of his hand and rose to his feet, ignoring the way the text on the last paper twisted into confessions of forbidden rites performed beneath the twin moons. That was probably fine. He gave it a B+ for creativity.

He slipped out of his office, shoulders stiff. A couple of students passed him, one of them snorting out a laugh over some brain-dead meme about a sentient machine uprising in Wing C. Their chatter blurred, words stretching and thinning like sound passed through static.

A decorative plant by the wall bent away from him as he passed, leaves shriveling at the edges. He ignored it.

Phainon ducked into the nearest supply closet with all the grace of a man fleeing tax evasion charges. Pulled the door shut behind him and slumped against the wall, cold metal biting through his shirt. Dust motes spun lazy constellations in the single beam of flickering light from the ceiling.

His head felt like a radio tuned to the wrong frequency. Thoughts overlapping thoughts. Memory bleed. The leftover static of a thousand thoughts trying to scrape meaning out of him. The soft, ever-present buzz of reality straining under his skin.

A laugh scraped out of his throat. Bitter.

“Damn,” he muttered to himself, “I am two bad hours and a government-sanctioned blackout away from buying a one-way ticket to the void.”

The supply room smelled like old printer toner and something vaguely lemon-scented. He tilted his head back against the wall, letting his eyes

half-lid, just for a second, until the afterimage of strange symbols he hadn’t meant to see scorched his eyelids.

Somewhere behind the stacked boxes of requisition forms and abstract-approved markers, a faint tapping started. He didn’t check.

His gaze snagged on the glass pane of a cabinet across the room. His reflection stared back—but the edges of his face rippled, blurring and warping like heat haze. Eyes too cold. A unreadable frown where his mouth hadn’t moved.

He looked away.

The tapping stopped.

“Not now,” Phainon told the room, voice brittle. “I’m booked ‘til Thursday.”

He shoved the door open and stepped back into the hallway like nothing happened.

Phainon barely made it three steps down the hall before March appeared, materializing out of nowhere like some aggressively optimistic poltergeist.

“Professor Phainon!” she beamed, practically bouncing in place. “Hey, are you—um, are you okay? You look kinda…” She made a vague gesture around her own face, a circle of concern. “Like, headache?”

He managed a crooked grin. “March, if I were any more okay, I’d be dead.”

She blinked. “That’s… not comforting.”

And before he could slap together another quip, his abilities surged.

The lights overhead flickered, stretching into long, twitching streaks of color. Time hitched, the sound of March’s voice warping like a tape spool unraveling. The walls breathed.

Phainon felt the pulse of it—like something inside his skull tuning every radio in a five-mile radius to the wrong channel.

He cleared his throat. “Office hours are over.”

And without waiting for a response, he spun on his heel and power-walked away at a speed just shy of undignified.

March stood there, watching him go, baffled. The lights settled. The air stopped crackling.

“…Kay, see you next week!”

A metallic tang hit the back of Phainon’s throat a second before the umpteenth nosebleed did—a single, sharp drop onto the floor, flickering faintly like old TV static before settling into ordinary crimson.

He dabbed it with the cuff of his sleeve, sighing. On brand.

The hallway ahead was empty, save for the soft buzz of ceiling lights and the scuff of his boots against tile. Except… then it wasn’t.

A low hum bled through the walls. Not music surprisingly. His own voice.

Layered, warped, fragments peeling off one another in messy overlaps.

“I don’t know what you want from me—” “They’re not supposed to—” “I’m fine, Anaxa. It’s fine. I’m fine.” ”I’ll tell you whatever you want, just don’t—”

It bled out of the walls like radio static, old grief folded over itself. Faint, at first. Then louder. The closer he moved toward the door at the end of the hall, the more it closed in. The floor felt thinner. The air warped.

Phainon slowed.

Stopped.

The sound cut like a switch flipped.

A long, hollow silence.

He stared at the door a beat longer than he should’ve.

“…Nope.”

Pivoted clean on his heel and took the long way around.

Phainon stood in the elevator, shoulders hunched, back to the mirrored wall, clutching his phone like it was the only thing tethering him to the waking world. His thumb tapped anxiously against the case.

The hum of the fluorescent lights above gnawed at his ears. Too loud. He forced a breath in through his nose, out through his teeth.

Grounding exercises.

Anaxa’s rules. Count. Focus. Stay inside your skull, don’t let the seams unravel.

Phainon lifted his gaze to the ancient floor panel display above the doors. The numbers flicked by—3… 4… B7… 44… ∞… 03:AM… ERROR.

His eye twitched.

“Nope. Totally fine,” he muttered, voice a frayed thread of mock reassurance. “Normal elevator things. Definitely real numbers. Couldn’t be more regulated.”

He counted the pixels in the faulty display. Forty-nine. Forty-eight, no— forty-nine again. They pulsed, jittering in and out of alignment like reality buffering on a bad connection.

The mirrored wall behind him caught his reflection a beat too late, movements half a second off. His reflection blinked when he didn’t.

Phainon’s fingers twitched. A stray, silver-blue spark crackled at his knuckles. The fluorescent lights above stuttered, throwing the cramped metal box into a half-second strobe. He shoved his hands into his coat pockets, jaw tight, forcing his breath steady.

Name objects. Count anchors. Hold it together, Phainon.

“Ceiling light,” he rasped to himself. “Floor panel. My phone. My… dignity. Somewhere.”

The elevator lurched, brakes catching, the hum of the world snapping clean. The display, mercifully, settled on 2. No ERROR, no infinity, no 03:AM.

The doors slid open.

A student waited outside, earbuds in, backpack slung low, nodding along to some track Phainon couldn’t hear. The kid’s face went still the moment their eyes met. Something primal, subconscious, like a deer realizing the trees aren’t trees at all.

The kid flinched.

Phainon, exhausted, managed a tight, weak smile.

“Not a good day for elevators, kid. Take the stairs.”

He didn’t wait for a response. Just stepped out, brushed past, the hum of the elevator closing behind him.

His pulse thrummed sharp in his ears. He didn’t unclench his fists until he turned the next corner.

His next location was the courtyard behind the lecture hall. A cracked, overgrown stone path, rusted-out benches swallowed by ivy, the occasional stray energy lamp flickering overhead. Perfect spot for anxious breakdowns, illicit deals, or pretending you didn’t exist.

Phainon cut through it on autopilot, boots scuffing over loose gravel, the pounding in his head getting louder by the second.

He rubbed a hand over his face. His skin felt too thin, stretched too tight over the bone. The aether currents in the air were wrong. Off-key. Subtle pressure drops in his peripheral vision. Everything about this day had been wrong.

“You’re fine,” he muttered under his breath. “Totally fine. Doing excellent, ten outta ten mental health. It’s not like you’re about two decibels away from turning a student into a conceptual cipher. Definitely not.”

A leaf blew past. It spun in the air in a way leaves shouldn’t spin.

He picked up his pace.

Started counting steps. Listing colors. Running through grounding exercises Anaxa drilled into him back when his head was clearer.

One, two, three—

“Professer?”

His name, called soft behind him.

It hit like a bullet. His entire body jolted, muscles seizing. The world tilted.

Not metaphorically.

Literally.

The ground under his feet warped, a fracture line splitting across matter. It was subtle at first—a shimmer in the air, like heat rising off asphalt. Then sharper. The sky twisted at the edges of his vision. The courtyard stones spiderwebbed beneath him, cracks forming not on the surface, but behind it, like a pane of glass held up against the world was shattering.

A static hum bled through the air.

He turned, pulse slamming so hard it echoed in his ears.

Dan Heng was there, a book in one hand, brows drawn in quiet concern, oblivious to the teeth of dimensional fracture snapping open a breath behind him.

A rift. Silver-blue, jagged like the world had been peeled back.

For half a second, Phainon didn’t move.

He felt it rise inside him—the place bucking loose, unspooling, licking at the seams of reality, eager to make something worse.

Stop. Stop. Lock it down—

His hands shook.

He slammed the brakes, locking every frayed thought into place by sheer instinct. His head screamed, pressure building like his brain was going to split at the seams. Blood broke from his nose again, thick and hot, crackling with static like old TV snow for a heartbeat before settling into normal crimson.

Dan Heng’s eyes flicked to it. Not to the rift. Not to the warping air. Just the blood.

“You’re bleeding again,” he said, voice cautious but steady as ever.

Phainon swallowed back bile, his grin sharp and splintered.

“If I tell you to leave right now for your own safety, you’ll do it, yeah?”

Dan Heng hesitated. Not long. He knew Phainon’s serious tone when he heard it.

“…Yeah.”

He backed away, slipping out the way he came, quick, efficient.

The moment he was out of range, the rift hissed closed with a wet, too-real sound. The world flexed. Reality rethreaded itself with a whisper, the

courtyard settling like a body exhaling after a held breath.

Phainon just stood there.

The taste of copper in his mouth. The burn in his sinuses. Blood on his hands, drying sticky against his skin.

If that’d slipped just a second faster—

No.

He didn’t finish it.

Couldn’t.

Instead, he wiped his face on his sleeve, let out a sharp breath, and laughed —brittle, humorless.

“Yeah. Okay. Normal fuckin’ Tuesday.”

And kept moving.

Phainon left the courtyard behind like he always did—fast, head down, pretending it didn’t happen. It was a one-off. Glitch in the system. He’d had worse. Statistically speaking.

He cut through one of the older back wings of campus, the one no one bothered to renovating. The overhead lights flickered with the kind of lazy indifference only decades of bad wiring could produce.

But it was quiet.

And quiet was good.

His boots clacked against the floor in steady rhythm. One, two, three, four. A pattern. He focused on the sound, the weight of each step. It helped. Until it didn’t.

Because about halfway down the corridor—another set of footsteps joined in.

Soft. Half a beat behind his own.

Phainon slowed. The second set didn’t.

Okay.

He glanced over his shoulder. Empty hall. Nothing but dim overheads, a warped window pane, a crooked bench against the wall. He waited. Silence.

He sighed. “Alright.”

Kept walking.

But the sound came too. Always a little off, just slightly behind, like something almost learning the rhythm of his steps but not quite getting it right.

He passed a wall scuff—a jagged little scrape shaped like a lopsided crescent moon.

Then passed it again.

And again.

The third time, his gut went cold.

A door on his left, one he could’ve sworn was supposed to be boarded over, hung slightly ajar. Beyond it: nothing but dark. Something moved inside. A sound like paper dragging against stone.

Phainon didn’t stop. Didn’t look in.

The floor underfoot sloped. Barely. But enough.

The overhead lights began to hum. Not a normal electric buzz—a frequency he wasn’t supposed to hear. It rattled in his teeth, made his molars ache. The

air thinned out. His skin prickled.

In the glass of a long-forgotten trophy case, his reflection flickered—a second behind, lagging like a bad video feed.

His throat tightened. “Totally fine,” he muttered, pulling his coat tighter around him. “Normal hallway things. Definitely real numbers on these doors. Very cool.”

A twitch in his vision. A ripple at the edges of his sight like heat off asphalt.

He swallowed. Willed it down.

The fountain in the courtyard outside the window froze mid-flow, water jittering in place, flickering between solid, liquid, something else. A dead branch curled inward, folding into itself like an origami figure handled too roughly.

Don’t look. Just walk.

The posters on the wall shifted every time he passed them—Debate Club Meet Tonight, then a Memorial Vigil for a name he didn’t recognize, then a stark, blood-smudged warning: DO NOT FOLLOW IT HOME.

His stomach flipped.

Still—sarcasm.

“You know, would love if literally anyone else was seeing this. Just for fun.”

His own voice sounded wrong. Thin, high in his ears.

He picked up the pace.

The hallway stretched, elongated just a little more with every step. Doors on the left now on the right. Windows vanishing when not looked at directly. The sound of footsteps behind him doubled. A half-beat behind. Close now.

He forced a bitter laugh, speaking louder.

“Hate it here. Hate it more now. Not a huge fan of whatever fresh Blair Witch found footage glitchcore bullshit this is.”

It was a joke.

It felt like the last one he had left.

Then—a window ahead.

His reflection stared at him. Lagged half a second behind. And smiled.

He stopped cold.

The air thickened. The sound of his own pulse slammed in his ears.

No footsteps now. None needed.

The walls on either side of him breathed—expanding on the inhale, contracting on the exhale. The posters on the wall all showed his own face now. Not quite right. The eyes empty, a little too wide.

His sarcasm evaporated.

His feet moved on their own—from a quick stride to a sharp jog. A desperate, brittle half-run.

The corridor blurred around him. Doors stretched impossibly tall. Light fixtures flickered, one sparking blue-white. Tables and chairs jittered in and out of place like buffering video frames. The hallway turned—and deposited him right back at the same corner, same scuffed wall, same open door bleeding darkness.

And still, something behind him.

He could feel it in his teeth. In the static charge on his skin.

Blood slicked warm from his nose again, down his upper lip.

He wiped it away with a trembling hand.

Didn’t dare look back.

The floor beneath him shivered. The walls twitched like muscle. The posters blinked with static.

His jog turned to a run.

Didn’t care if it looked insane. Didn’t care if someone saw.

Because something was behind him.

And if he looked—he knew it would have his face.

He didn’t remember when the run became a full on sprint.

Didn’t remember deciding to move faster—his body just did. His boots hammered against the floor, each step landing a fraction out of sync with the world around him. The corridor twisted as he moved, angles bending wrong, windows tilting down at him like watching eyes.

Every door he passed shuddered open an inch without him touching them.

A cold wind followed. From nowhere. Carrying the dry scent of old dust.

The lights snapped and buzzed overhead—one flaring too bright, then dead black. The hum set his teeth on edge. His ears ached with it. The walls seemed closer than before. Or maybe he was getting bigger. Or maybe the hallway was folding in on itself like an origami pattern made of brick and plaster and glass.

His breath scraped ragged in his throat.

He reached for a wall, meaning to steady himself, and the brick there pulsed under his palm—like flesh. Warm.

He yanked his hand back like it burned.

“Nope. Nope nope nope nope—”

The posters around him blurred. His own face. Names he almost remembered. Warnings meant for no one. He couldn’t focus on them now. Couldn’t focus on anything. It was like the air itself had weight, pressing down on him, crushing through his skull.

The floors shuddered.

A light fixture popped overhead, a single, sharp burst of blue-white that made the shadows stretch thin like oil across water. His own shadow dragged a half-second behind him, limbs too long, head tilted the wrong way.

Phainon stumbled. Didn’t stop.

A fountain he passed in a side alcove was glitching in and out of frame, water rising, freezing, then snapping into reverse. The plants in a corner planter recoiled from him, leaves curling, vines twitching like disturbed snakes like before but worse.

Just get outside.

The thought barely made it through the noise in his head. Every nerve sang with wrongness, his abilities clawing at the edges of things, warping everything he brushed against.

Windows blinked out. Door handles melted into the wall as he passed them. Every corner turned only led to another hallway that looked the same—but slightly off. Too long. Too narrow. Ceiling too low. Another half-step toward impossible geometry.

His vision blurred. The floor tilted.

Blood slicked his upper lip again, thick and hot.

He wasn’t even looking where he was going anymore, his focus shattered, steps uneven, limbs too heavy and too light at once. His heartbeat an arrhythmic pounding he could feel in his gums. Everything he touched

sparked—doors creaked open, shadows jittered, lights flickered like a warning.

“Get outside. Just—get—outside—”

He slammed through a final door without even registering what it was. The hinges screamed. Cold air hit him like a shock, sharp and biting, dragging a gasp from his lungs.

Grass underfoot. Distant floodlights bleeding into fog. The smell of damp earth and air.

It didn’t register.

Phainon kept running, not seeing the figures of other students scattered across the campus lawn, not hearing the muffled beats of someone’s portable speaker, not noticing the wary glances thrown his way.

The world felt thin. Loose at the seams. Like one bad thought might unravel it completely.

He finally saw an opening—a dark, narrow doorway set in a stretch of old stone wall. Half-open, light bleeding faintly from the other side like a slit in the night.

It could’ve been a sanctuary or a death sentence. Didn’t matter which. He didn’t think about it.

Phainon sprinted for it, boots skidding over damp ground, breath ragged. His hand slammed against the heavy wood, forcing it open. The hinges wailed like something dying, but he didn’t slow.

He staggered inside.

The moment he crossed the threshold, the air changed—cooler, dry, and dense in a way the outside hadn’t been. The world flexed around him, another pulse of invisible pressure like something uncoiling, then pulling tight.

He spun without thinking, grabbed the edge of the door, and slammed it shut behind him.

The heavy latch caught with a metallic clack. The echo of it shuddered through the space around him, too loud, too final.

For a moment, there was nothing but his own breathing, harsh and broken, blood running hot down his upper lip, his pulse roaring in his ears.

He leaned back against the thick wood, one arm braced against it as he fought to slow down, fought to pull the static back from the edges of his vision.

Didn’t register the warmth of polished stone under his feet.

Didn’t register the faint scent of paper in the air.

Didn’t notice how the world felt contained here.

Didn’t see the rows of tall, dark shapes in the gloom beyond him, shelves stretching high and far, lit by a few scattered lamps that hummed soft and steady.

Didn’t care.

His knees gave, and he sank down against the door, legs sprawled gracelessly, head tipping back to rest against the wood.

Blood slicked his palms, his ears, probably his throat now too.

Didn’t matter.

Didn’t open his eyes.

Didn’t want to.

“Alright,” he muttered to nobody, voice thin and cracked and almost a laugh. “Big fan of this. Ten out of ten. Just gonna sit here. Real normal choices happening tonight.”

And he did.

Too far gone to notice where he was.

Too far gone to realize it wasn’t over.

He let his head tip back, eyes half-lidded, staring up at nothing.

Delusions.

The thought came unbidden, lazy and offhanded, like an old friend dropping by to whisper in his ear.

They’d been worse lately. Shit like this—warped reflections, wrong doors, sounds with no source. Flickering walls, bleeding sky. The hum of his own voice in the static.

Some of it was real.

Some of it wasn’t.

And he was losing track of which was which.

Phainon let out a long, shaky breath, closing his eyes, pressing the heel of his blood-slick palm against one temple. His head throbbed like a muscle too long under strain, like a thousand tiny teeth gnawing at the edge of his brain.

It’s fine, he told himself.

Anaxa will fix this. He said a few days.

He exhaled again, tension bleeding off in a long, tired line.

It wasn’t fine. But he’d pretend a little longer.

The quiet around him felt too thick, the kind of silence that clings.

And then—as if the universe finally realized it owed him one good gut punch for the evening—a sharp, shrill voice cut through it like a siren.

“Oh, oh dear! Are you alright, son?”

Phainon’s eyes snapped open. He squinted up.

An elderly woman, tiny, white-haired, one of those perfectly assembled types you knew had once run entire neighborhoods by sheer force of will alone, peered down at him over a pair of delicate glasses. Her expression hovered between concern and polite alarm.

For a moment, it didn’t connect.

The space around him came into focus in pieces—the tall shelves, rows upon rows of old, meticulously arranged books, the heavy, steady tick of a clock somewhere nearby, the faint scent of paper and aged wood.

A…library.

Wait.

A very specific library.

Shit.

This was Mydei’s library.

It hit him like a lead pipe.

He practically shot upright, too fast, blood rushing to his head in a dizzy lurch. He pasted on the most brittle, too-wide smile known to man.

“Oh, no worries at all, ma’am! Totally fine, you know, just taking a breather —love a good breather, me.”

As if half his face wasn’t smeared with drying blood.

He quickly stepped aside, opening the heavy door for her with a little flourish like a perfectly sane, perfectly unhorrifying individual. She offered him one last wary glance, clutching her book bag, and shuffled out.

The second the door shut behind her, Phainon’s pulse spiked.

I gotta go. I gotta move. Now.

He turned on his heel, intent on making a break for it before anyone—

“Who the fuck—” a sharp voice started from somewhere between the shelves, edged with irritation and sharp timing, a stack of books cradled under one arm.

It softened at the end, the syllables folding into something wary. Familiar.

“…Phainon?”

He stopped cold.

Every muscle in his body locked up.

He knew that voice.

Knew it like a pressure point. Like gravity.

And it was, without question, the absolute last person he wanted seeing him like this.

He didn’t even turn around. Just internally drafted his will and considered reincarnation.

Of course. Of course it’s you.

Phainon sighed, and turned, half a grin already crooked at his mouth. “Heeeyyy.”

Mydei didn’t react at first. Just a glance up from the books in his hands, a flicker of surprise. The usual.

And then his gaze landed, locking onto Phainon’s face.

The blood. The pallor. The too-bright sheen to his eyes. A streak of dried red across his neck like a collar.

The books slipped from his grip, hitting the floor with a flat, dull sound.

Phainon winced. “Okay, not my most photogenic moment.”

Mydei didn’t laugh. He crossed the room in three strides, snatched a clean cloth from a counter like it was routine—because it was, wasn’t it? How many times had this happened now?

“Sit down,” he muttered, already locking the front door with a sharp flick of his wrist. The lights dimmed a little. The shopfront stilled.

Phainon hesitated, then dropped into the nearest armchair, hands loose on his knees, watching the way Mydei moved. Sharp, efficient, annoyed on the surface.

Except—

There. The smallest hitch.

A tremor in his hand as he rung out the cloth. Gone a second later, but Phainon caught it. And he didn’t know why, but it sat wrong. Lodged like a splinter under his skin.

The cloth was cold against his face, dragging away blood in clean strokes. Neither of them spoke for a long stretch. The only sounds were the faint tick of the clock overhead and the quiet rasp of cloth against skin.

“…Are you alright?”

Phainon opened his mouth, words already lining up.

Just peachy.

But then—again—that hand. Quick, steady. But a twitch, a tremor on the downswing. Not enough to notice unless you knew what Mydei’s hands usually looked like. And Phainon did.

And something in him gave.

Not a dramatic collapse. Not some grand epiphany. Just a slow, creeping press of weight in his chest.

When had it gotten this easy to lie to him?

Phainon’s throat worked. He tried the grin again. Couldn’t quite find it.

“…No,” he said quietly, voice scraping out of him like a bad wire. “It’s not alright.”

The cloth stilled.

Mydei didn’t press. Just made a low sound in his throat—a frustrated, exhausted little huff—and kept cleaning the blood away like it was any other day.

And suddenly, he hated it. Hated knowing exactly how this would go. Hated that it wasn’t even the worst scrape Mydei had cleaned up for him this month.

And before he could stop himself, he reached out, grabbed a fistful of Mydei’s shirt, and tugged him down. Not hard. Just enough.

“What the—”

Phainon hauled him down until Mydei half-fell against him, braced awkwardly against the arm of the chair. Phainon tucked his face into the crook of Mydei’s neck, the scent of old paper, ink, and sharp clean skin grounding him.

“It’s really not,” he mumbled, words feathering against skin.

Mydei let out a sigh. Not annoyed. Just tired. One hand came up, settling on the back of Phainon’s head, fingers threading through tangled hair.

“Yeah,” Mydei muttered. “I figured.”

Neither of them moved for a long time.

At some point, Mydei must’ve fully slumped into his lap.

Phainon wasn’t sure when. The world had softened at the edges, blurred into the steady warmth of another person against him, a grounding weight that made it a little easier to keep breathing.

His fingers moved absently, tracing nonsense patterns against Mydei’s side through his shirt. Spirals. Loops. A jagged line.

Mydei shifted slightly, one arm draped lazily around Phainon’s back, the other smoothing a stray bit of hair from his temple.

“Do you wanna talk about it?” Mydei asked. No gentle act—just there. Like the weight of his hand. Steady.

Phainon gave a dry little huff against his throat. “Not really.”

“That’s fine,” Mydei murmured, the corner of his mouth twitching into something too tired to be a grin. “I can make fun of your haircut instead. That’s still on the table.”

Phainon snorted, the sound too close to a laugh for how hollow he felt. “Bold of you to insult a man literally bleeding on you.”

“Occupational hazard,” Mydei deadpanned.

The quiet stretched again. Phainon let it. His thumb catching along a seam in Mydei’s shirt, grounding himself in the small, tangible things. The warmth beneath it. The steady, living thing that wasn’t glitching apart.

He hadn’t meant to say anything. He really hadn’t.

But the words edged out like splinters from a wound that wouldn’t close.

“…What if I’m not who you think I am.”

It was soft. A fact he was unintentionally testing the weight of, seeing if Mydei has a reaction to it.

Mydei tensed—not much, but enough for Phainon to catch it. His hand stilled against the back of Phainon’s neck.

“Okay,” Mydei said after a beat, voice cautious. “You gonna elaborate, or should I guess wildly?”

Phainon smirked. It didn’t touch his eyes. “Could be fun. ‘Turns out I’m a cryptid’ was always my leading theory.”

“Phainon.”

His name hit harder than it should’ve.

Phainon sighed, forehead pressing tighter to Mydei’s shoulder. “I just… I don’t know. Some days it feels like I’m faking it. Like none of this—me, here, with you, teaching, existing—was ever supposed to stick.”

The air between them hung heavy. Phainon braced for it—the sarcastic jab, the harsh retort. A wall he could lean against.

But Mydei’s hand moved again, carding slowly through his hair. Not what Phainon expected. No lecture. No storm.

“You’re a fucking idiot,” Mydei muttered. But it was almost gentle. “A bleeding, sleep-deprived, emotionally constipated idiot. But you’re mine.”

And something sharp cracked in Phainon’s chest, quiet but clean.

“Yeah,” he rasped, eyes shutting. “Yours.”

And for right now—for this small, warped piece of quiet—it was enough.

The quiet settled again, less suffocating this time. Phainon’s fingers slowed, tracing the faint line of a seam beneath his hand—then paused.

His brow furrowed.

“Wait,” he murmured, squinting in the low light. “Is that a new scar?”

Mydei stiffened just a little, a muscle in his jaw ticking. “…No?”

Phainon leaned back, just enough to catch the curve of it along Mydei’s side beneath the hem of his shirt. His gaze sharpened in that way Mydei had learned to be immediately wary of.

“I swear to every god left in this rotted plane,” Phainon growled, voice dropping, “who the hell touched you?”

Mydei blinked. “First off, what the fuck—how did you even notice that?”

“I memorized your body since, like, week two.” Phainon said it too casually, like it was a normal, healthy, non-unhinged boyfriend thing to confess. “I know every inch of you.”

Mydei stared at him, deadpan. “…You are not well.”

“Not the point. Who did it?”

“For the love of—” Mydei tried to shift, but Phainon’s grip tightened around his waist like a steel trap. “It was a shelf box. A sharp one.”

“I’ll kill it.”

“It’s a box.”

“I’ll burn it and salt the ashes,” Phainon said, entirely serious, though his lips twitched with a grin as Mydei squirmed against him.

“Okay, psycho, let go.”

“Nope.” Phainon buried his face against Mydei’s neck, tightening his grip further. “You’re injured. You require immediate, life-saving affection.”

Mydei made a sound halfway between a scoff and a laugh, though he was visibly fighting the upward pull of a smile. “You’re disgusting.”

“Correct.” Phainon pressed a quick, obnoxious kiss to his jaw. “But I’m your problem now.”

“Unfortunately,” Mydei muttered, but it was softer than before.

Phainon grinned against his skin, then peppered a line of quick, teasing kisses along Mydei’s cheek and temple, the kind of half-annoying affection he knew would drive him up the wall but also melt him down.

Mydei flinched like a startled cat, making a half-hearted attempt to escape, but his grin finally cracked through.

“Let go, you damn leech.”

“Nuh uh,” Phainon laughed, arms tightening possessively as Mydei groaned in theatrical suffering.

And for the first time in hours, the static in Phainon’s head eased.

Phainon kept his grip firm, lips brushing the corner of Mydei’s jaw, his temple, anywhere he could reach without getting headbutted. Mydei grumbled through it, too lazy—or maybe too content—to fight it properly now, one hand still tangled in the back of Phainon’s shirt like it was second nature.

The world didn’t flicker anymore.

No warping walls. No glitching reflections. No gnawing static in the corners of his vision.

Just warmth. Steady breathing. The scent of old paper clinging to Mydei’s clothes.

Huh.

Phainon’s fingers curled a little tighter at Mydei’s waist, brushing the edge of that damn shelf-box scar, committing its feel to memory like everything else. And maybe it was stupid, maybe it was reckless, but he let himself sink into the feeling of Mydei’s weight against him. The way his heartbeat steadied against Phainon’s ribs. How the world had gone utterly, improbably still.

He missed this. Missed him. And it struck him then how long it’d been since he let himself feel that without bracing for something to go wrong.

A small, private thought flared in the back of his head—maybe he didn’t break things as badly when Mydei was near.

But he didn’t want to test the theory. Not now.

Not when the risk was Mydei.

And then—the sharp buzz of his phone against his hip.

Phainon groaned, dragging a hand from Mydei’s back to fish it out while keeping the other locked securely around his boyfriend’s waist. “If this is one of your idiot staff asking why the sun’s hot again, I’m throwing your phone into traffic.”

“That was one time,” Mydei grunted.

The screen lit up. Encrypted ping.

From Anaxa.

Phainon’s grin slipped.

The message was short. Just four words.

[ Waltz isn’t over yet. ]

Phainon stared at it, pulse catching—not enough to ruin the moment, not yet, but the edge of unease uncoiled, cold and sharp in his gut.

He thumbed the screen dark.

Arms tightening around Mydei like a shield, he kissed his hair once, just in case.

He wasn’t going to push his luck tonight.

Chapter End Notes

Chapter Summary
