The sun was setting, but the city didn’t care.

Its skyline carved jagged teeth into the bleeding sky, a smear of violet and bruised gold stretching out beyond the balcony rail. Somewhere far below, the endless hum of traffic kept moving—a heartbeat Mydei had long since tuned out.

He sat cross-legged on the battered balcony chair, a mug of lukewarm coffee cupped in both hands, staring out like maybe, just maybe, the end of the world might finally put him out of his misery.

From somewhere inside the apartment, Phainon was singing.

Badly.

And loudly.

And off-key.

Mydei closed his eyes and tipped his head back against the chair. “I’m going to kill him.”

It had been like this for a week.

Ever since The Incident. Capital letters. The one where Phainon had kicked down the doors of Mydei’s library, mid-day, red-faced and breathless like a lunatic, before promptly trying to have a full-blown breakdown in Mydei’s arms. No explanation. No warning. Not even a half-assed excuse. And then, just as suddenly, he’d vanished again.

Mydei hadn’t asked.

Partly because he figured if it was something world-ending, he’d hear about it eventually. Mostly because some quiet, anxious part of him didn’t really want to know.

And now this.

A whole week of… whatever this was. The most aggressively clingy, overbearing, borderline manic boyfriend behavior Mydei had ever witnessed. He’d tried, once, to track the logic. See if there was a pattern. But Phainon’s reasoning—if it existed—was a conspiracy board of nonsense.

Quickfire rundown:

One: A dumb horoscope telling him to “cherish his brightest star.”

Phainon had taken it as divine law. Mydei had called him an idiot.

Two: Because Mydei made him coffee that morning.

By “made,” he meant “reheated a cup in the microwave and forgot about it twice.”

Three: Petty revenge for a four-month-old insult about Phainon’s gentle heart.

Which, for the record, hadn’t even been that scathing. Mydei had casually called him “the softest bastard he’d ever known” and apparently it had wounded him on a spiritual level.

Four: A vivid dream where Mydei died heroically stupid.

Details varied by retelling, but the latest involved tripping over a broom and plummeting off a skyscraper while trying to save a cat.

And last but not least: A possible injury Mydei had definitely lied about.

And denied. And expertly covered with a long-sleeve jacket. He was pretty sure Phainon knew, because his gaze kept flicking to the same spot on Mydei’s forearm every time they spoke.

Or, you know.

All of the above.

Who the hell knew anymore.

Mydei took a long sip of his room-temperature coffee and sighed through his nose. Inside, the sound of Phainon’s warbling grew louder, punctuated by the unmistakable shuffle of socked feet on tile.

He was coming closer.

Mydei closed his eyes and quietly wished for death.

And yet.

Somewhere deep down, in a place he refused to acknowledge, the corners of his mouth tugged upward.

The idiot.

The balcony door creaked open.

Phainon appeared, framed by the fading light like some kind of deranged, off-key angel, still howling the same ancient pop remix he’d had on loop for the past hour. The potted plant in his hands wasn’t helping the image.

“Mydeiiiiiii,” Phainon sang—badly, for the record—“you light uuuuup my liiiife.”

Mydei lowered his mug, deadpan. “I will push you off this balcony.”

Phainon only grinned, sauntering over and plopping the plant onto the table like an offering. “Meet Mini-Mydei,” he declared, gesturing grandly at the tiny, mildly wilted thing. “He’s thriving.”

“That plant is dying.”

“We all are,” Phainon said cheerfully.

Mydei huffed out a laugh before he could stop himself. It earned him a smile so bright it should’ve been illegal.

Phainon flopped into the seat across from him, legs sprawled, hair an absolute mess, and launched into yet another verse of his terrible song— loud, unapologetic, and profoundly out of tune.

And, against all odds, Mydei let him.

He leaned his head back against the chair, watching through half-lidded eyes as Phainon butchered the melody and made hand gestures at the bruised sky like he was performing for a sold-out stadium.

It was stupid. It was ridiculous. It was…kind of nice.

His stomach chose that exact moment to betray him, a low, unmistakable growl breaking the quiet.

Phainon froze mid-note. His head whipped around like he’d just heard a proximity alarm, eyes wide and scandalized.

“You’re starving,” he accused, pointing as if it were a crime.

“I’m fine.”

“You’re wasting away.”

“It was one noise.”

“Emergency protocol enacted!” Phainon announced, already leaping to his feet and vanishing inside with the dramatic urgency of someone heading into battle.

Mydei closed his eyes, sighed, and let his head thump back against the chair.

It had been like this all week.

And he didn’t know how much longer he could take it.

At some point—and Mydei wasn’t entirely sure when—Phainon had talked one of his more ethically bankrupt acquaintances (Anaxa? Anaxo? It had an x in it) into rewiring the apartment’s central media hub so it could link to their personal uplinks and blast through the building’s external speakers.

Legal? Not even remotely.

Morally sound? Absolutely not.

Was Mydei about to argue? Like hell he was.

Which was why he was currently sunk into Phainon’s crime-against-interior-design couch, one leg hooked over the back, his boots abandoned somewhere under the coffee table graveyard, cueing up his melancholy, synth-drenched indie-dystopian playlist.

The first notes eased through the speakers, a soft pulse of atmospheric chords and a ghostly vocal line whispering something appropriately tragic.

Mydei let his head fall back against the cushions with a sigh, eyes half-lidded.

And then—

BZZZT.

The connection glitched.

The music cut.

Replaced by what could only be described as aural terrorism—a violently chipper, aggressively saccharine 22nd-century pop remix that sounded like someone had given a hyperactive AI an energy drink and told it to make a love anthem.

Mydei didn’t move. Just stared up at the ceiling like maybe, if he concentrated hard enough, the god of suffering would take him out on the spot.

“No,” he said flatly, to no one.

Reached for the control.

Switched it back.

The synths returned. Beautiful. Wistful. Full of yearning. Just how he liked it.

BZZZT.

The pop remix came back louder.

This time it had clapping.

Mydei sat up, glaring toward the kitchen. “I swear to every last decrepit deity in this system, Phainon—”

From somewhere out of sight: “You’re welcome!”

The sheer smugness in his voice could’ve powered a city block.

Mydei yanked the connection back, swapping to a track that sounded like it’d been composed by a sad android in a graveyard.

Barely two seconds later—

BZZZT.

The same godawful pop remix, now with extra bass.

“I’m going to kill you in your sleep,” Mydei growled.

Footsteps padded closer, then Phainon’s head appeared around the doorway, hair a mess, snack bowl in hand, eyes sparkling like a man who had just chosen violence. “I’d like to see you try, Mydeimos.”

“Stop hijacking my connection.”

“It’s for your own good.” He declared before cranking up the volume.

Mydei groaned, dragging both hands down his face. “This is psychological warfare.”

“This is love,” Phainon chirped, sauntering into the room like a menace made flesh. He dropped onto the couch next to Mydei with a bounce, scattering a few chips.

Mydei didn’t even flinch. Just switched the track again.

This time, a devastatingly bleak ballad about city lights and being left behind by time.

Phainon made a face like he’d just tasted battery acid. “Ugh. You’re so dramatic.”

“It’s called having taste.”

“It’s called needing serotonin.”

“Die.”

“Later,” Phainon said cheerfully, reclaiming the interface. The pop remix was back. Now with a keytar solo.

“I hope you step on a rusted nail.”

“You’re smiling,” Phainon pointed out, elbowing him lightly.

“I’m imagining your funeral.”

“As long as I’m the center of attention,” Phainon grinned, leaning in close, breath warm against Mydei’s cheek. “Love you too.”

Mydei sighed, but the corner of his mouth tugged up, traitorous.

The music war raged on.

No one won.

And both of them knew it wouldn’t be the last round.

Said war had slowed to a truce of mutually assured destruction—Mydei curled into one end of the couch, Phainon sprawled across the other like a cat who owned the place, snack bowl balanced precariously on his stomach.

The unholy pop playlist churned on.

Some chirpy vocalist warbled about dancing through starlight, how love was forever, some line about chasing dawn across forgotten cities—typical overproduced schlock. Mydei was just about to open his mouth and launch another insult when the next lyric cut through, clear and sharp over the saccharine beat:

“I wear ten faces but none are mine.”

The air went still.

Not much.

Barely a hitch.

But it was there—that split-second, brittle silence that hit like the quiet before glass cracked.

Phainon didn’t look at him. Kept his gaze locked on the ceiling, jaw tight, fingers drumming a little too fast against the rim of the snack bowl.

Mydei didn’t look either. Just let out a low, unimpressed scoff and muttered, “Your taste in music is garbage.”

“Yeah, well,” Phainon said, voice light but just a little off-beat, “you’re still listening.”

The next track queued up before either of them could say anything else.

Neither one of them reached for the interface.

The apartment was, in a word, chaos.

Case in point: Phainon was currently stalking Mydei from the safety of the kitchen counter, narrating his every move in a flawless impression of an old-world nature documentary.

“Observe,” Phainon intoned, voice low and reverent, “the elusive Mydeimos in his natural habitat. Note the cautious, deliberate approach to the primitive caffeine dispenser. A creature of instinct, ritual. Noble. Standoffish. Slightly homicidal.”

Mydei, halfway to pouring coffee, didn’t even look up. “I will end you with a dish towel.”

“Fascinating,” Phainon whispered, as if to an invisible camera crew. “Note the immediate defensive display. Classic territorial behavior.”

“You’re about to experience a classic blunt force trauma to the skull.”

Phainon beamed, entirely unrepentant, and continued his documentary voice. “Notice how he bristles. A predator poised to strike. If I move too suddenly, he may—”

A dish towel sailed across the room, smacking Phainon in the face. He cackled like a lunatic.

“Direct hit!” Phainon crowed, peeling the towel off his head. “Aggression confirmed. Highly dangerous. Ten out of ten would provoke again.”

Mydei muttered something dark under his breath and retreated to the couch with his coffee, done with the sheer force of bullshit in his life.

It only got worse.

Because perched proudly on the windowsill was a new potted plant. Small, spiky, ugly in the way only stubborn things survived in this city. A tiny label stuck in the dirt read: Mini-Mydei.

Mydei squinted at it. “When did you get that.”

“Yesterday,” Phainon said, solemnly. “Named it after you. It’s prickly, thrives on neglect, and will absolutely outlive us both out of spite.”

“You’re a menace.”

“I’m your menace,” Phainon shot back, beaming. “Also, check this out—”

He pointed the remote at the system hub. The screen flickered to life and a prompt appeared:

[Commander Click Mydei, authorization required.]

Mydei stared. “You renamed the system remote.”

“Everywhere you exist is mine now,” Phainon declared, entirely too pleased with himself.

“You’re truly deranged.”

“You love it.”

Mydei sighed, took a long sip of coffee, and refused to dignify that with a response.

The plant’s downfall was inevitable.

No one in this apartment had a healthy relationship with gravity or personal space, and Phainon’s long, dramatic gestures while recounting some half-true story about the time he “definitely didn’t almost get arrested for public disturbance” were a recipe for disaster.

It happened in slow motion.

His elbow caught the edge of the windowsill. The tiny pot wobbled. Teetered.

Mydei’s eyes widened. “Wait—Phainon—”

Clink.

Thud.

The plant hit the floor with a sad, brittle crunch, dirt scattering across the tile like tiny, defeated landmines.

The room went still.

Phainon stared down at it. Completely silent. A blank, dead-eyed look settling over his face like the last light had gone out behind his eyes.

“Wait—” Mydei started again, a hand half-raised.

Without a word, Phainon turned and walked out of the room.

Not stormed.

Not stomped.

Just… left. Silent. Stiff-backed. Like a man carrying the weight of too many sins.

“Goddamn it,” Mydei groaned, setting his coffee down with a sharp clink and moving after him. “Phainon, get back here, it’s a plant. You can’t emotionally spiral over a fucking plant named after me.”

Silence.

“Phainon, if you’re planning a funeral for Mini-Me I swear to—”

By the time he got to him, the bathroom was dimly lit, a single candle flickering precariously on the sink’s edge, its light bouncing off the tile in trembling, overdramatic shadows.

Phainon knelt before the sink as if preparing to summon ancient spirits. His hair was a mess, one sock halfway off, and his face bore the kind of dead-eyed solemnity normally reserved for memorials and corporate performance reviews.

Mydei leaned in the doorway, arms crossed, expression caught somewhere between exhausted fondness and what the actual fuck am I witnessing.

“I,” Phainon began, voice grave, “gather us here, in this most hallowed of resting places, to honor the life, the legacy, of our fallen comrade—Mini-Mydei. A brave sprout. A steadfast soul.”

“It was a succulent,” Mydei deadpanned.

Phainon shot him a glare over his shoulder. “A warrior,” he corrected. “Struck down in the prime of life by senseless gravity.”

“You knocked it over while trying to moonwalk to a remix of Neon Love Crisis, Phainon.”

“That remix slaps, and your blasphemy has been noted.”

Mydei sighed, dragging a hand down his face as Phainon turned back to the candle.

“May his leaves photosynthesize in the eternal light,” Phainon murmured. “May his roots find fertile soil in the afterlife. May his tiny, judgmental soul finally know peace.”

“You’re so weird,” Mydei muttered, though he suppressed an exasperated chuckle.

“Shhh.” Phainon made a solemn, ‘moment of silence’ gesture. The candle flickered. Somewhere in the apartment, the sound of a neighbor’s holo-TV blared out a 21st-century sitcom laugh track.

Without warning, Phainon stood, face deadly serious. “I’ll grow a new one,” he declared. “A worthier heir. Stronger. Smarter. Braver.”

“Oh gods, here we go.”

“I shall name him… Mydei the Second. No. Mydei II: Leafborn Betrayal.”

“That’s the dumbest thing you’ve ever said and you once declared war on a vending machine.”

“That thing ate my credits.”

“You punched it so hard the security drone tried to tase you.”

“I dodged it.”

“You tripped over your own foot and face-planted into a recycling bin.”

“A tactical feint.”

Mydei made a strangled sound and stormed over, grabbing the fallen plant carcass from the counter. He scooped the limp dirt back into the pot with his bare hands, jammed the two least-dead leaves upright, and stabbed a bent fork into the soil like a flag in enemy territory.

“There,” he said, tone flat as dead space. “Resurrection complete. Your grief period’s over. Get a grip.”

Phainon stared at it like it was the most beautiful thing he’d ever seen. A single, melodramatic practically glimmered in his eye.

“You… you saved him.”

“I hate you.”

“I’m naming it Mydei Eternal.”

“I will drown you in this sink.”

Phainon grinned, unrepentant, and wrapped his arms around Mydei’s waist from behind, pressing his face against his shoulder.

“Everywhere you exist is mine now, you know.”

“Shut up, you leech.”

He did not shut up. In fact, he started humming Neon Love Crisis again.

And against all odds, Mydei once again, let him.

The city at night was a different kind of beast.

Mydei leaned his head against the window of Phainon’s beat-up cruiser, watching the world smear past in streaks of half-dead neon and hazy puddle light. The streets were slick from a late rain, still steaming faintly against the glow of signs advertising everything from noodle carts to questionably legal tech repair.

The seat creaked when he shifted. An abandoned cup of iced coffee sweated into the cupholder beside a crumpled receipt for six different pastries and what appeared to be a novelty keychain shaped like a knife.

Typical.

Phainon hadn’t said much since he picked him up. Just leaned across the seat, popped the passenger door, and grunted what might’ve been a

greeting, or possibly a threat. Hard to tell with him. And now he was driving like a man with something to prove—jaw set, eyes fixed ahead, one hand drumming out some twitchy, offbeat rhythm against the wheel.

“…Alright,” Mydei said finally, squinting at him. “What’s eating you?”

“Nothing,” Phainon answered, a little too quick.

“Convincing.”

Silence.

Phainon took a turn slightly sharper than necessary, and Mydei grabbed the door handle on reflex.

“You’re driving like you’ve got a body in the trunk,” he pointed out.

“No body,” Phainon replied without missing a beat. “We’re going somewhere important.”

Which was categorically the worst thing to hear from someone acting mildly sketchy in the middle of the night. Mydei gave him a look.

“Important like… ‘illegal back-alley cyber deal’ important, or ‘found a haunted relic on the university black market’ important?”

“You ask a lot of questions for a guy whose taste in tea is objectively criminal.”

“I swear, if you bring up that hibiscus blend one more time—”

“It was pink, Mydei.”

“It’s a floral infusion, you uncultured gremlin.”

Phainon’s lips twitched. “Still looks like cough syrup.”

“Says the man who drank half a can of ‘Riot Venom: Extreme Combustion’ before noon.”

“It was on sale.”

“Yeah, because it’s banned in three states.”

Another beat passed. The radio hummed on, some upbeat remix of an old-world track with aggressively auto-tuned vocals about burning daylights.

Mydei let his head fall back against the seat with a sigh. “Work was a nightmare.”

That earned him a glance. “Yeah?”

“One attempted theft of The Black Archive Codex by a kid who panicked so hard he dropped it on his own foot.”

“Solid.”

“Security had to carry him out. He was crying.”

“Outstanding.”

“And then,” Mydei continued, “some poor bastard tried flirting by asking where the ‘spicy medieval murder texts’ were.”

Phainon blinked. “The what now?”

“Exactly.”

A beat.

“You smite him on sight, or…?”

“Tempting. But no. I sent him to Agricultural Histories.”

A grin cracked across Phainon’s face, sharp and delighted. “You beautiful, petty bastard.”

Mydei smirked. “Figured he could get lost in the thrilling accounts of 14th-century barley disputes.”

“You’re my favorite person alive.”

“That’s sad for you.”

The banter settled into a comfortable lull. The car rolled past shuttered shops, the scent of rain and street food thick in the air. Somewhere in the distance, an inflatable tube men flayed helplessly.

Phainon’s fingers tightened subtly on the wheel.

“We’re almost there,” he said, voice quieter now.

Mydei arched a brow. “Where’s ‘there’? And don’t say ‘somewhere important’ again, I swear—”

“You’ll see.”

“I hate when you say that.”

“I know.”

Mydei shot him a sideways look. “You better not be dragging me to another one of your ‘abandoned but totally safe’ urban exploration spots.”

Phainon smiled, wolfish. “Not this time.”

“Oh good. Last one almost got us chased by an unhinged maintenance drone.”

“That was one time.”

Mydei let out a long, dramatic sigh. “I tolerate you because no one else will.”

“Yeah?” Phainon’s voice softened despite himself. “I cope badly with your face, too.”

“…Was that supposed to be a compliment?”

“I dunno,” Phainon shrugged. “Your face does things to me. Complicates my life. Wrecks my strategic plans. I’m coping.”

“Strong comeback, genius.”

“Shut up and prepare yourself.”

“For what?”

Phainon glanced over, expression unreadable but smug as hell. “Destiny.”

“Oh, gods.”

The car roared on into the night.

Eventually, Phainon pulled the car to a stop without warning.

“We’re here,” he said, too even.

Mydei lifted his head from where it rested against the window, brow creasing. The street outside wasn’t one he recognized—narrow, half-lit, the kind of alley you didn’t find on official maps. Neon signs buzzed in half-dead colors, old paint peeling from the walls. The air tasted like rain on hot metal.

Before he could ask, Phainon was already out of the car, slamming the door and circling around. The passenger side cracked open and a hand appeared, palm up, waiting.

Mydei stared at it.

“What’s this.”

“Chivalry,” Phainon replied, blankly. “Now don’t embarrass me in front of the alley rats.”

A sigh. But Mydei took it. His fingers closed around Phainon’s, the grip warm, steady, and let himself be pulled to his feet.

And then he looked around properly.

It wasn’t the parts of the city he was used to. This was Upper Tier, somewhere in the folds of the city’s cleaner face—but this corner had been left to rot. Faded signage hung overhead, the kind written in languages nobody bothered translating anymore. A soft, irregular drip echoed somewhere out of sight.

No one else was on the street.

Phainon was already walking ahead, one hand tucked in his pocket, like none of it registered.

A cold knot twisted in Mydei’s gut.

Does he know?

It was a stupid thought. An impossible one. But the alley looked too familiar in the worst kind of way. The world felt thinner here, like it did after bad nights. And Phainon—who usually filled the space with words of assurance—was silent now, moving with a certainty that made the hair at the back of Mydei’s neck lift.

“Hey,” Mydei called, voice low. “This one of your backroom deals or are we sightseeing?”

Phainon glanced over, a flicker of affection breaking through. “You ask a lot of questions for a guy who owes me pastries.”

“Could’ve just said no.”

“Where’s the fun in that.”

He reached a battered door at the end of the alley and pushed it open, pausing to look back.

“You coming?”

Mydei hesitated. The door was unmarked. A faint warmth leaked out from the crack, carrying something sweet beneath the damp city air. The kind of scent you didn’t expect here.

His stomach dropped.

He knew this place.

Phainon waited, a question in his eyes but no impatience.

Mydei muttered a curse under his breath and moved.

“Gonna blame you when I get stabbed.”

“Wouldn’t dream of it,” Phainon murmured, holding the door wider.

And with one last glance at the empty street behind him, Mydei stepped through.

The door swung shut behind them with a soft click, sealing out the city.

Inside, it was warmer. The walls were the color of old bone, cluttered with hanging charms, faded paper talismans, and glass jars that caught the weak light and held it hostage. The air smelled like cardamom, baked sugar, and something darker—anise, maybe.

A figure moved behind the counter.

The woman was slight, draped in layered fabrics that didn’t seem to belong to any specific decade, with sharp dark eyes and a gaze that could skin you down to the bone without ever raising her voice. Her hair hung in loose, ink-black waves, and a single silver chain circled her throat.

She zeroed in on Mydei the moment they stepped inside.

Didn’t blink. Didn’t speak. Just stared like she was counting the threads of his soul and finding them… acceptable.

Mydei stiffened. He knew those eyes. Not because he remembered her name—if he’d ever known it—but because he’d seen that look on long nights when this was the only place that felt like it existed outside the city’s rotten pulse.

He hadn’t meant to come here with Phainon.

And yet.

“What’ll it be,” she asked at last, her voice a soft, meditative thing.

Phainon, undeterred by the entire funeral rite atmosphere, stepped forward like this was the corner deli. “Got it written down,” he said cheerfully, pulling a slightly crumpled note from his jacket. “Told myself I’d memorize it but, you know. Life.”

He handed it over.

The woman didn’t look at the note. She just held it between two fingers and kept staring at Mydei.

Mydei, for his part, didn’t move. He had the distinct, irrational sense that if he so much as shifted his weight, the walls might fold inward.

Phainon grinned, oblivious to the impending existential reckoning.

“Trust me,” he told her. “It’s the right order.”

A long pause. The shopkeeper’s gaze lingered on Mydei a beat longer, then she gave the smallest, barest nod.

“As it should be,” she murmured.

And then, with a whisper of fabric and a scent of sweet spice trailing in her wake, she vanished into the back.

The moment she was gone, Mydei finally exhaled.

“You are so lucky she didn’t curse you on the spot,” he muttered, rubbing a hand down his face.

Phainon shot him a charming smile, leaning casually against the counter. “What, you mean my impeccable charm didn’t carry us through?”

“I mean you’ve got the self-preservation instincts of a drunk moth.”

“Moths have good instincts.”

“In what ecosystem.”

“This one,” Phainon said, smug. “Now c’mon, you’ll thank me in two minutes.”

Mydei gave him a flat look, but didn’t leave.

Didn’t want to.

He just huffed a breath, watching the bead of spice-sweet condensation on the counter’s edge.

The shop’s seating area was small—more cluttered than cozy, though it tried to pass itself off as both. Mismatched tables, chipped cups, a crooked heater humming in the corner. A radio crackled somewhere behind the counter, low and strange, some old-world string melody curling through the air like fog.

Phainon dropped into a corner booth like he’d claimed the territory by force. Mydei slid in opposite, arms crossed, gaze flicking to the door as it shut behind them.

It wasn’t dangerous.

It just wasn’t a place you brought people to.

“So,” Mydei said, breaking the stretch of silence. “How’d you even find this place?”

Phainon grabbed a sugar packet, flipping it between his fingers. “Hm? Oh. You come back smelling sweet sometimes.”

Mydei blinked. “I—what?”

“Not like your usual paper books smell. It’s this… burnt sugar and spice thing. Cardamom, maybe. Weirdly specific.”

A beat.

“You noticed that?”

Phainon shrugged, like it was nothing. “Coincidentally ran into the scent last week while I was… doing something out here. Recognized it. Thought, huh—Mydei’s sweet cinnamon smell.”

Mydei’s stomach flipped. He looked away, trying and failing not to smile.

“You could’ve just asked, you know.”

“Nah,” Phainon said, almost fond. “You wouldn’t have told me.”

Mydei opened his mouth—and closed it. Because yeah. Fair.

“It’s not like I was hiding it,” he muttered. “It’s just… far. And it’s got that weird occult vibe. Figured you’d think it was stupid.”

Phainon grinned. “Maybe I like weird occult vibes.”

“You don’t.”

“Maybe I do.”

“You don’t.”

Their eyes met. Phainon’s gaze lingered a second too long before it slipped, dropping to the table, fingers stilling.

“What were you even doing over here?” Mydei asked.

That landed.

Phainon’s expression didn’t shift much—just a small, almost imperceptible pull at the corner of his mouth. “Nothing important.”

It wasn’t convincing.

Good enough.

For now.

Phainon was half-distracted, idly sorting the assortment of pastries like it was a battlefield he intended to win.

Mydei’s fingers ghosted over a plain-looking bun, attention caught more by the faint pulse against his inner sleeve.

Or something else entirely.

A presence shifted beside him. Mydei blinked once, letting the thought drift into the mental archive of to be processed later.

A week.

He would take every second.

For now.

That was enough.

The glow of his phone screen cast pale light against the ceiling. Mydei lay sprawled on the couch, scrolling through feeds he wasn’t really reading. The Flame Reaver.

operations they’d overseen for years. And somewhere in that tangle, a new unit had surfaced—unmarked, unlisted, with no formal designation in any of the known branches. Either it was recently built, or worse, it wasn’t new at all. Something old back into play when no one was watching.

He’d have to look into it. Soon.

The water shut off. Footsteps crossed the room, and a moment later Phainon dropped onto the other end of the couch, pulling a blanket over himself tiredly.

Phainon laughed, eyes half-lidded as he tilted his head up into the next pass of the towel, like some smug, sleep-deprived cat.

Mydei sighed again, quieter this time. “You’re exhausting.”

“And yet,” Phainon murmured, voice softer now, “here you are.”

He didn’t have a comeback for that. Just kept toweling, as the bathroom lights hummed overhead and the outside world carried on without them.

Mydei sighed, pressing the towel against Phainon’s head one last time before dropping it in defeat. “Sorry,” he muttered, voice low. “I didn’t mean to—”

There was a beat—something small and sharp tugging at Mydei’s chest he didn’t have a name for.

He squeezed Phainon’s hand back. “Alright. Let’s go.”

[Enjoying your late-night vigil duty, Godslayer? Hope your stray’s behaving.]

Mydei’s grip on Phainon’s hand tightened.

“Mydei?” Phainon’s voice, soft. “You good?”

Mydei’s own.

Tribbie’s breathing hitched on the open comm, shaky and fast.

“Please… what’s wrong…?”

The only sound in return was the crackle of broken systems, the metallic ping of cooling glass fragments, and the steady drip of blood.

The Archive howled.

A synthetic shriek that didn’t stop, grinding up and down in pitch like some ancient predator’s dying scream fed through a thousand layered speakers. Warning glyphs strobed to life across every surface, crimson and jagged, data streams spasming into corrupted static.

[RESONANCE BREACH DETECTED.] [CONTAINMENT FAILURE.] [DEPLOYMENT TEAMS EN ROUTE.]

Lights stuttered, the chamber locking itself down by reflex. Shutters hammered shut on peripheral exits. The reinforced vault trembled as defensive lattices activated with the sound of a thousand knives scraping over glass.

And Mydei… didn’t move.

He stood at the shattered terminal, hand slick with blood, glass lodged deep in the meat of his palm. The Archive’s panicked security grid spat out error after error as it struggled to reassert control. Sirens stabbed through the vault like needles, lights flickering hard enough to leave afterimages behind his eyes.

A crackle.

Then:

“Stop it, you’re scaring us!”

Tribbie’s voice—sharp, small, ragged. Not through the comms anymore. In the room.

He didn’t turn.

Didn’t blink.

Didn’t hear her.

The alarms blurred into a single unending wail, one endless red chord of warning, and still, his mind registered only a single, savage truth.

It was him.

The words struck like a nail through bone.

Clean. Absolute.

Everything before it—denials, careful logic, the hundred rationalizations crafted in brittle moments of calm—collapsed like paper before a flame.

Another blaring announcement crashed overhead.

[CONTAINMENT AUREATE RESTRAIN UNIT DISPATCHED.] [RESONANCE VOLATILITY: CRITICAL.]

Doors exploded open behind him, security pouring in. Shouts, boots hammering metal, containment fields snapping to life. Weapons primed, tactical orders shouted over overlapping comm lines. No one knew it was him.

Didn’t matter.

The Archive was hemorrhaging alarms like a wounded animal, environmental lights casting the room in seizure-quick flashes of red and blue. Mydei’s silhouette stood in the eye of it, blood dripping from his fingertips to the floor.

And then his comm vibrated.

A single, clean pulse.

Amid the sirens, blood, glass.

He glanced down.

Phainon☀️:

Hey, you free tomorrow? Thought we could grab coffee <3

The timing was obscene.

A crime against the order of the world.

Tribbie’s voice cracked, panic breaking through training:

“Dei…No—no no no!”

The alarms screamed.

Security barked orders.

And Mydei didn’t look away from the message.

Not once.

Chapter End Notes
