chapters.title: Chapter 14: Mydei’s Big Stupid Feelings Hour
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei wakes up, discovers literally everyone in his life is either lying, dying, or about to be punched. Escapes medical detention with the help of a morally conflicted medic, elbows a guy into next week, and begins his dramatic sprint through a crumbling death facility in search of his maybe-traitorous boyfriend. Alarms blaring, grudges flourishing.

Chapter Notes

Hey everyone! First off, I owe you an apology for how long this update took. I genuinely meant to have it out weeks ago, but then Myphai Week happened, and I got completely caught up in that. On top of that, the original draft I had for this ended up getting sidelined right up until now.

I’m honestly really sorry for the delay, and I appreciate your patience more than I can say. I’ll do my best moving forward to stick to a weekly update schedule for this fic. I really hope you’re all still interested in following along, thank you so much for sticking with me! 🥲

The room was quiet.

Not silent in the pure sense of the word—there was always that low, steady hum of suppression arrays embedded in the walls, a muted resonance you couldn’t quite hear, but felt, like the pressure of a deep current beneath your skin. A soundless thrum that dulled the edges of thought, made you forget how unfiltered air used to feel when you could actually breathe it.

Mydei didn’t know how long he’d been here.

Days. A week. Longer, maybe. Time blurred in places like this. No one kept track, and if they did, they weren’t in the habit of sharing.

His wrists rested loosely against his lap, thin metal bands cinched around them—dull Chrysos alloy, the kind designed to look harmless at a glance. Enough give to move, to eat, to avoid sores at the edges of flesh. But the inhibitors buried inside would surge the moment he even considered pushing past them. Subtle, elegant enforcement.

He sat against the far wall, shoulders sagging. His knuckles were wrapped in sterile strips of med-cloth, flesh beneath still in the process of weaving itself whole, uneven where accelerated healing had botched the symmetry. The Heirs’ med-tech could repair the damage easily. He hadn’t let them finish the job.

This wasn’t a high-containment black site.

He knew what those looked like. The state-run detention cubes for war criminals and rogue operatives. Private facilities built for people whose body counts filled entire reports. The Council’s own disappearing places for dissidents they couldn’t afford to martyr.

And somewhere deeper, beneath the polished veneer of sanctioned justice, the Heirs maintained their own.

This wasn’t one of those.

It was containment, yes—but different in a way you couldn’t name at first glance. There were no kill-switches humming at full charge. No reinforced plates buried behind the walls. No squads stationed outside the door, waiting for a breach order that would never come.

The danger here wasn’t the threat of violence.

It was the absence of it.

A room meant for people they couldn’t leave unchecked, but weren’t willing to treat like outsiders.

For those caught between duty and circumstance—too burdened with dangerous knowledge to be let loose, too familiar to be discarded.

People the Heirs still cared about.

People like him.

He could imagine how many rooms like this might exist across the city. Tucked-away sublevels, repurposed admin suites, forgotten medical wings disguised as emergency shelters. Spaces built for those rare moments when politics and loyalty collided, and the only humane option was to hold someone close while keeping them out of reach.

But this room—this was different.

There were no other cells here. No sounds of restraints locking. No endless surveillance feeds threading through the corners. Only the containment arrays and the faint shimmer of glyph-lines etched along the far wall, gold against cool steel, like the last traces of some half-forgotten script.

Humane, they called it.

The best they could give him, under the circumstances.

Safer than what the Council would’ve demanded. Kinder than what the state would’ve offered.

He understood why they’d done it.

Didn’t mean it was easy to swallow.

Since he’d arrived, no one had spoken his name.

They brought him food, clean bandages, whatever else he needed to keep going, but conversation had thinned to necessities, and even those came sparingly.

He shifted, a slow ache blooming along his shoulders. The wall behind him was cold—a weightless kind of cold that clung to the skin long after you’d

noticed it. Somewhere above, the arrays flickered again, a soft pulse in the stale air.

And for the first time since they’d brought him here—however long ago that was—the thought came, uninvited:

How in the hell did it come to this?

Mydei exhaled slowly, letting his head tip back against the wall. The room’s pale, artificial light hummed faintly above him, a ceaseless glow that stripped the edges from everything it touched. Even memories felt sterile beneath it.

But he remembered.

Too clearly.

It had started in the archives.

He hadn’t known what he was chasing that night. A name, maybe. A trace. Some half-erased report buried beneath layers of the data. Something he could use. He’d expected the search to be quiet, difficult, frustrating.

He hadn’t expected what he found.

And when the alarms screamed—shrill, overlapping, setting every emergency protocol in the room alight—it was already too late to pretend he hadn’t seen it. The containment units powered to full, barrier humming alive, and the restraint teams came in like they had a chance of controlling the situation.

Mydei’s body had kept moving. Muscle memory and instinct, a dull awareness of the room around him, but his mind had already gone elsewhere. Staring down the thing he wasn’t supposed to find.

The commands had come sharp and immediate.

Stand down, Godslayer. Disengage. Step away from the terminal.

The words barely registered.

Not until one of them—a kid, fresh-faced and too green for this kind of job —stepped forward, a hand outstretched like it was possible to reason with a man whose balance had already slipped.

The snap of bone was sharp, sudden, and horrifyingly human.

Reflex before thought.

The scream that followed still hung somewhere in the corners of his memory. A raw, desperate sound, like something primal forced through a throat too young. It clawed at the edges of his recollection.

And that’s when it started to come apart.

Containment fields crackled, slamming into place. More figures flooding in, weapons raised, ciphers burning hot against the air. Orders shouted over each other.

Do not engage. Stand down. Stand down.

His knuckles still ached at the memory of it—metal, bone, maybe both. The archives reduced to molten slag and splintered glass beneath his hands. What had once been history, erased in minutes. The fields had flickered under the strain. Bodies moving too fast. Arrays faltering.

He hadn’t resisted.

Not when the order came to drop him.

Not even when the bindings hit.

And then—the voice.

Small. High. Frayed at the edges.

“Stop! Stop, stop, stop! Leave De alone!”

A child’s voice.

But not a child.

Tribbie.

He hadn’t seen her. Didn’t have to. The sound had cut through everything else like a blade. It made the room pause, breathless. Every weapon lowered a fraction.

The world had gone still in that instant.

He remembered the taste of blood at the back of his throat. Couldn’t say if it was his. Hands raw, the ruined wreckage of the archive at his back, and a line of wide-eyed operatives in front of him.

Then came Aglaea.

He hadn’t expected her.

She didn’t handle breaches herself. Delegated those things, as any of them would’ve. But this wasn’t any breach. And the look she carried wasn’t protocol.

At first, maybe.

The golden threads bonded him tight, coiled like living things. Truth-weaving—the kind that left no room for lies, pulling words from your throat before you even formed them.

He could still feel the faint prickle under his skin.

And she’d asked him one question.

“Who is the Flame Reaver, Mydeimos?”

The name had sat heavy behind his teeth. He could’ve spoken it. Could’ve ended it right there.

But the shape of it wouldn’t leave his throat without breaking something irreversible inside him.

Even dazed, battered, barely standing, he’d seen the flicker in Aglaea’s expression. That moment where detachment cracked, and something quieter —something deeply, horribly human—surfaced. Not for the lost archive.

For him.

Her hand had almost lifted. Hovering just near his face, like she meant to— he didn’t know what. A gesture half-born. A comfort never given. It hadn’t mattered. The intent was enough.

Then the decision came.

No handoff.

They wouldn’t send him to the Ministry’s vaults, or let the state make a martyr of him.

They brought him here.

Not a cell. Not quite.

Isolated.

Safer than the alternatives.

And he understood, truly. He understood all of it. Every reason they gave, every line they couldn’t cross.

Didn’t mean it cut any less.

A long breath rattled from his lungs.

He closed his eyes, tried to slow the riot of thought, but it went where it always did—the one place he’d been avoiding.

Phainon.

The name scraped at the inside of his skull. He didn’t speak it. Couldn’t. His throat worked around it, an ache where the word should’ve gone.

It hadn’t mattered how careful Phainon had been.

The Heirs didn’t have his name, didn’t know his face. But they knew one thing.

He was close to Mydei.

And that was enough.

He could picture it now—patrols thickening around the places he’d been seen, checkpoints blooming like sickness around familiar corners, surveillance fields stretched tight across every space that he’d ever visited.

And the archive…

Maybe that was why his hands had kept moving.

Why he hadn’t stopped until every terminal cracked, every glyph bled out, every file warped beyond recognition.

Subconsciously, even then—protecting him.

Not a calculated erasure.

Just instinct.

A refusal, bone-deep, to leave anything behind that might be used against him.

Against Phainon.

And in those last ragged moments—before the archive was silenced—it hadn’t been the Heirs gnawing at him.

It had been him.

Phainon.

It twisted sharp beneath his ribs.

He should talk about it.

Not to them. Not to anyone here.

But to someone.

Or at least think it through, let it bleed out where it wouldn’t turn rotten in his chest.

The ceiling buzzed on, indifferent.

Somewhere overhead, the hum of the containment systems shifted. A subtle recalibration, a slight drop in the room’s ambient pressure, the faint ripple of field harmonics re-aligning themselves.

Across the far wall, a cluster of proximity beacons flickered to life. Thin lines of interface light traced clean patterns around the door’s frame, dormant blue giving way to soft gold. Lock sequences disengaged in quiet succession—not the jarring stutter of a breach response, but the smooth rhythm of an override someone had the authority to initiate.

He exhaled.

There was no need to guess.

The door slid open with a muted hiss, the pressurized seal breaking cleanly as reinforced alloy panels retracted into the walls. No alarms. No containment squads on standby. No drones crowding the entryway.

Only Aglaea.

She moved like certainty given form—every step unhurried, her presence folding into the sterile hush without disturbing it. No weapons, though the absence meant little; she’d never needed visible threats to command a room.

Her gaze found him where he sat, and for a moment, she simply regarded him.

Then, quietly—a name:

“Mydeimos.”

He didn’t reply. Not immediately.

She spoke again, softer this time.

“May I sit?”

He could feel the ache building behind his temples—a dull pressure at the base of his skull, not from her, but from what conversations like this always asked of him.

“Of course,” he murmured, voice rough from disuse.

Aglaea crossed the room without hesitation and lowered herself onto the floor beside him.

She made no immediate move to speak.

And that, more than anything, told him how serious this was.

Aglaea had always known how to wield silence. Not as absence, but as invitation. A way to let others fill the space, to measure the shape of what they chose to leave unsaid.

And Mydei—despite everything—recognized the mercy in that.

He didn’t need to look to feel her watching him.

She always had.

“What do you need, Aglaea?” He asked.

A soft exhale.

“You already know.”

He allowed himself the faintest tilt of his mouth—not quite a smile, more the suggestion of one. “I’m not giving it up.”

She inclined her head, unsurprised. She’d known before she crossed the threshold, before she’d ordered the locks disengaged. Still, something in her gaze dimmed—not disappointment, merely a quiet acknowledgment.

“I didn’t think you would,” she murmured.

For a moment, nothing else. Then, as if deciding there was little sense in postponing what had to be said, she spoke.

“The Council has formally requested your handover.”

That earned a brow lift from him.

“Of course they have.” His voice was dry, unsurprised. He’d expected as much the moment Aglaea had intervened, claiming jurisdiction before anyone else could. What caught him was how long it had taken for them to escalate.

Aglaea’s gaze never wavered. “It’s been… more persistent than anticipated. Beyond what protocol would require under the circumstances. Repeated demands, direct appeals to the Sovereign Circle. Some not even through sanctioned channels.”

There it was.

He dragged a hand down his face, feeling the faint, residual ache of bruising beneath his palm. “What else.”

She hesitated, though with Aglaea, even hesitation was a deliberate pause rather than uncertainty.

“We’ve increased security sweeps around sectors you’ve frequented. Old safehouses, contact points, workplace.” A glance toward him, slightly apologetic. “But the Council’s mirrored the pattern. Independent

deployments, no formal notice. Civilian grids, former operative corridors, assets long cleared of any actionable threat. They’ve doubled patrol strength, tightened surveillance, deployed active detainment fields in areas you haven’t touched in years.”

A faint line formed between her brows, a sign of thought more than concern.

“On record, it’s nonsensical. The Chrysos Heirs hold purview over this situation. The Council retains no authority here—they answer to separate mandates, govern vigilante designations and rogue oddities, not matters concerning Chrysos operatives.”

Mydei felt his pulse edge higher at that.

“And you’ve confronted them.”

A slight inclination of her head confirmed it.

“We logged the first instance as a miscommunication. The second as unauthorized overreach. By the third, it was clear the pattern wasn’t accidental.”

He frowned at the implications. The Council preferred subterfuge, the sort of veiled manipulations one uncovered only after they’d already served their purpose. Open posturing didn’t suit them.

“There’s more,” she continued.

“They’ve commissioned a new task unit. Code designation: the Cleaners.”

That earned a sharper look from him.

“Never heard the name.”

“Neither had we,” she admitted, a trace of irritation slipping beneath the calm. “Officially, they’re listed as a rapid-response division. Neutralization, asset retrieval, high-risk containment operations. The type of force typically reserved for black-site purges, not citywide civilian grids.”

Task forces didn’t manifest fully operational just like that. Not with this kind of reach.

“How new are they, exactly?”

Aglaea’s expression tightened. “On record, barely a quarter-cycle. In practice… seasoned. Too coordinated for a fresh assembly. I’ve monitored their field patterns, tactical maneuvers, encrypted comm protocols. It’s precise work, Mydei. This is a unit built from experienced hands, repositioned beneath a new title.”

A long breath drew from his lungs.

He didn’t need to ask what came next.

“…They’re after the Flame Reaver as well,” she confessed.

He felt it land in his chest like a weight.

“Why.”

A question for the sake of asking. Neither of them expected an answer.

Aglaea’s jaw flexed, and for the first time since entering, the edges of her composure frayed—not visibly, but in the words that followed.

“I can’t say with certainty. They’ll name their reasons: threat classifications, public security justifications, escalation clauses. But it doesn’t align. Not at this scale.”

She paused, studying him. Weighing the risk of the truth against the futility of withholding it.

“They’ve been watching him for months. Longer than I realized. His operational file’s been elevated beyond reason. Every incident, including the Node collapses, and every sublevel blackout conveniently traced to his shadow, even when evidence pointed elsewhere. The narrative’s been shaped for some time now.”

She let that settle between them.

“I believed it, once,” she admitted.

Mydei closed his eyes.

It struck differently, hearing it spoken aloud, knowing what he knew now.

He’s—

The thought twisted sharp behind his ribs.

Aglaea didn’t press.

“I don’t know what’s true anymore,” she said quietly. “And neither should you.”

He exhaled, a humorless sound. “That lesson came a little late.”

She didn’t refute it.

There was no point.

He angled a glance toward her. “Anything else I should brace for before you tell me whatever the worst part is?”

A faint, weary curve of her mouth.

“You aren’t going to like it.”

He huffed a breath, leaned his head back against the wall. “Didn’t expect to.”

Aglaea didn’t waste time with preambles.

“Someone submitted a private request for you.”

His gaze flicked toward her, brow lifting in quiet inquiry. “Another transfer request?”

“Not to a faction,” she clarified. “To a person.”

That made him still. The slight shift in his posture wasn’t much, but it was enough.

She continued. “It wasn’t processed through formal channels. It came through a flagged echo point—one we abandoned six years ago. Buried deep in an obsolete relay center outside Grid South. Whoever sent it either didn’t know it was still monitored, or didn’t believe anyone would be watching.”

Mydei straightened slightly, a frown cutting through his features. “And you intercepted it.”

“It brushed against an old security protocol I left embedded in the relay’s substructure.” For the first time, a faint edge of displeasure tightened the corners of her mouth. “It was addressed directly. No chain of command, no formal handling. Only your designation, and a set of coordinates.”

His designation.

Godslayer.

A slow breath left him as he weighed his next words. “You know who sent it.”

Aglaea hesitated.

Second time today.

Her expression didn’t shift, but he caught it in the slight furrow of her brow, the subtle tension across her shoulders.

“I have a suspect.”

He didn’t press. He knew she would tell him.

“Caenis.”

The name struck like a stone into still water.

Leader of the Council. The one figure in all their constructed hierarchy who answered to no one.

He didn’t ask whether she was certain. If Aglaea spoke a name without formal proof, it meant her instincts had already outpaced evidence. And her instincts, he’d learned, rarely missed their mark.

“You have proof?” he asked anyway, because some part of him needed to hear it.

“No.” The word came quiet. “Not the kind I could take before a tribunal. The origin code piggybacking the transmission was an obsolete priority designation. Level Grey. Before it was scrubbed, there were three individuals with direct clearance.”

She held his gaze without flinching.

“The other two are dead.”

He let out a quiet curse under his breath and leaned forward, elbows braced against his knees. The pressure in his skull sharpened, a dull ache threatening to bloom into something worse.

“And the request itself?”

“Immediate physical transfer. No review or governmental oversight. Relocation to an off-record holding site. The destination tagged as restricted access, routed through Council internal systems.”

“They want me removed,” he murmured.

“They want you somewhere no one can witness what comes next.”

It wasn’t the same thing.

And it was infinitely worse.

For a long moment, neither of them spoke. The hum of containment fields, the soft shudder of internal conduits recalibrating, filled the room’s quiet.

When Aglaea spoke again, her voice was calm, but softened around the edges in a way few ever heard from her.

“Which is why I need to know what happened in the Archives.”

She didn’t phrase it as a request. Not this time.

Her gaze held his. “What did you see.”

And there was no deflection left to offer her.

He watched her for a long moment, weighing what little he could afford to say against what refusing would cost.

At last, he answered.

“Nothing worth killing over.”

He saw the flicker then—the infinitesimal shift in the line of her jaw, the tightening of her fingers where they rested against her thigh. Anyone else would’ve missed it. But Mydei had known her too long, seen her weather too many impossible hours, not to recognize the fracture when it surfaced.

She was afraid.

Not of him.

For him.

Aglaea drew a breath. She didn’t press further. Not because she didn’t want to, but because she knew him well enough to recognize the futility of it.

“They’ve been watching you longer than you realize,” she said at last. “Since the beginning. After we took you in.”

That one landed.

He didn’t react visibly, but she would have felt the shift in him anyway.

She didn’t remark on it.

“Council assets embedded within external oversight teams. Passive surveillance, mostly. Movement records, incident reports, unofficial logs. No direct interference, at least none I’ve been able to confirm. But the eyes were there, Mydeimos. For years.” A pause. “I only uncovered the extent of it recently.”

He swallowed the sharp taste rising at the back of his throat. He could’ve pretended it surprised him, but there was no point.

It made a terrible kind of sense.

Aglaea didn’t dwell on it.

She glanced toward the sealed door, more a signal than a motion.

“When you decide to stop carrying it alone, you’ll know where to find me.” The words were even, but the steel beneath them remained unmistakable. “We are not handing you over. Not to them. Not to anyone.”

A final look.

And then, as she rose to leave, a last quiet warning.

“You’ll have a visitor soon. Prepare yourself.”

She didn’t wait for his reply.

The door’s locking seals disengaged with a sequence of clean, toneless chimes. She crossed the threshold, and the locks whispered closed behind her.

And then, as so often before, the room was empty.

And he was alone.

He drew a long  breath.

Held it.

And let it out, willing his pulse to steady.

Piece it together.

Slowly.

Cleanly.

Without panic.

His mind, unbidden, drifted to the Archives.

The Heirs’ Archive. The most secure, quarantined data reserve within their entire operational structure. It housed far more than mission logs and threat assessments. Buried within its vaults were personnel dossiers, class-locked biometric records, resonance blueprints, and incursion incident reports no authority outside the Chrysos Heirs had either the legal standing or the extrajurisdictional access to even request—let alone seize.

Its containment protocols were absolute. Unauthorized access didn’t merely trigger a failsafe—it initiated progressive neural degradation, system-induced biofeedback seizures, and, in at least one recorded case, a fatal cascade collapse before the breach could propagate.

It was, in every conceivable sense, untouchable.

And yet—it had moved.

Not a sanctioned system migration. Not a crisis containment measure or routine clearance reallocation.

Moved.

Shifted from its subterranean stronghold beneath Kharon Sector to a Council-designated underground zone.

He’d seen the markers himself. Even through the haze and bloodied fractures of that room, the transfer indicators had burned through the fog of his mind.

The Archive didn’t drift.

It didn’t go missing.

Which left only two possibilities.

Either one of the Heirs had sold them out.

He discarded the thought before it could fully take shape. Not out of sentiment, but because the integrity of their structure had never allowed for such a weakness. If betrayal within the Heirs had been so easily bought, the faction would’ve devoured itself years ago.

Which meant only one other explanation remained.

The Council had orchestrated it.

And by every known protocol, that should have been impossible.

How?

He shut his eyes and ran the permutations.

A forged transfer order?

No. Even under emergency override permissions, Aglaea’s passive trace systems would have flagged synthetic access within minutes. The Heirs’ archives didn’t acknowledge foreign authorization masks. Their isolation protocols were hardwired, immutable.

Repurposed emergency clearances?

Riskier. Technically feasible during a declared crisis, perhaps bypassing surface pings. But even then, multiple biometric confirmations and sequencing protocols existed to prevent precisely this kind of infiltration.

Which left one plausible vector.

An internal Council asset.

Someone with native system clearance. Not a proxy or contract agent—but a legitimate, credentialed figure high enough to move between Council and Heir systems. Someone embedded long enough, positioned precisely enough, to bypass the security lattice entirely, reroute the Archive, and leave no trace until it was already beyond their reach.

And now the pattern could no longer be ignored.

The timing wasn’t coincidence.

The Cleaners.

The sudden scrutiny around his movements.

The Council’s fixation on the Flame Reaver—and, unspoken but undeniable, on him.

It wasn’t paranoia.

It was orchestration.

And the Archive hadn’t been moved for its own sake.

It had been taken.

Why?

His stomach twisted sharply, some instinctive wrongness settling deep behind his ribs, even before the answer emerged.

Because the Archive housed more than operational records.

It contained full profiles. Complete biometric matrices for every active Heir. Command signatures. Enmeshment threads.

And the original function of the Nodes—

His eyes snapped open.

Mimics.

He surged upright, breath catching in his throat.

That was the purpose. The intention. Synthetic resonance constructs— indistinguishable from the original, capable of carrying voice patterns, clearance credentials, even the weaponized abilities of their counterparts.

The Nodes had been designed to weave them.

To replicate authority figures.

To replace them.

And if the Council had gained control of the Archive’s contents—

The mimics wouldn’t be citizens.

They would be them.

Chrysos Heirs.

His pulse thundered against his throat, a cold sweat rising along his back.

The project had been terminated. The Nodes dismantled before replication reached operational scale. But if the data—if the complete resonance matrices and command threads hadn’t been extracted and repurposed—

What had they intended to do if they succeeded?

And worse still—his stomach hollowed—what if those mimics hadn’t been meant for their enemies?

What if they’d been intended for replacement?

One. Two. Ten Heirs at a time.

Removed quietly, without spectacle.

Without witnesses.

Until the originals were gone.

And no one would ever know.

A cold, oppressive weight settled behind his sternum.

He wasn’t sure which prospect was worse—that the Council had attempted such a maneuver, or that they might have already shifted to a newer, more insidious design the moment the first failed.

His hand lifted to his face, pressing against his eyes.

He never thought he’d say it, but with the terrible clarity of what was taking shape, he wished Aglaea hadn’t left.

Then how was the Flame Reaver involved?

He almost groaned.

It always came back to Phainon.

It had to.

For so long, it had been so simple. Easy, even. Blame the Flame Reaver. The faceless insurgent, the ghost woven through half-collapsed sites and destabilized sectors. The dossiers painted him as reckless. A destabilizer. The kind of violent, anarchist thing that didn’t care who burned, so long as the system bled.

And Mydei had believed it.

He clenched his jaw, teeth grinding against the pressure.

But now… now, knowing the face behind the mask, he knew better.

Phainon would never have done it.

Would never have triggered those Nodes with civilians in range.

Wouldn’t have left those children in comas with their grieving parents.

Not unless—

Unless what?

Unless there’d been no choice?

Unless it wasn’t him?

And if it wasn’t Phainon…

Then who?

And worse—why frame it so cleanly? So perfectly? Who benefits from stitching a rebel’s name to a crime like that?

He tried to let it go. Really, he did.

Tried to dig his heels into the facts, to count the patterns, to draw clean lines between logic and grief.

But the fractures were piling too fast.

The oddities stacking one atop the other until the shape of them couldn’t be ignored.

The injuries.

The disappearances he couldn’t explain.

The way Phainon always turned up in the aftermath—bloodied, broken, wearing that same reckless grin like pain was just another language he

spoke fluently.

And the looks. Gods, those looks.

Those sharp, brittle glances when certain Council divisions passed too close. Like old reflexes twitching alive, memories Mydei hadn’t known to name back then.

It all fit too clean now.

Too damn neatly.

He heard Aglaea’s voice in his head, slicing through the noise like a blade:

“They’ve been watching you since the start.”

If they watched him…

They would’ve watched Phainon too.

His heartbeat stuttered.

And then—worse—the thought came.

The one so ugly it felt like something toxic blooming behind his teeth.

What if it was him?

What if Phainon had led them here?

What if every deflection, every ragged smile, every near-miss coincidence wasn’t coincidence at all?

What if he was still an enforcer?

Not against the Council—but for them.

A loyal dog in insurgent’s colors.

A rebellion curated by the very hands it was meant to defy.

His pulse spiked. His hands flexed against the resonance cuffs, jaw tight enough to ache.

No.

No—it was irrational. He knew it was irrational.

But pain didn’t obey logic.

And betrayal didn’t care about probabilities.

Because love blinds.

And for all his sharp-edged pragmatism, for all his clinical detachment, Mydei had believed Phainon’s lies because he’d wanted to.

Because no one else had found him at his lowest and chosen to stay.

Because no one else had seen the thing beneath Godslayer and spoken his name so softly.

Because it was Phainon.

And now—now the storm inside him wouldn’t stop.

Gnawing through memory and speculation, blurring fact and fiction until he didn’t know which would be worse:

That Phainon had betrayed him.

Or that he hadn’t—and Mydei had broken them anyway.

His chest tightened, breath shuddering through his teeth.

His hands wouldn’t stop shaking.

He pulled against the cuffs.

A little at first.

Then harder.

The flare of pain—resonance backlash crawling through marrow like wildfire—punched the air from his lungs. He bit down on his tongue, tasted blood, didn’t care.

Did it again.

And again.

Because pain anchored.

Because it was better than drowning in a mind he couldn’t quiet.

Because if he stayed still too long, he’d start believing the things he was thinking.

And he couldn’t afford that.

He’s not a traitor. He’s not. He’s—mine.

But the ache wouldn’t leave.

He dropped his head to his knees, shoulders trembling, sweat beading at his brow.

Tried to tell himself it didn’t make sense.

Tried to tell himself he would never.

But heartbreak didn’t care about tactical discipline.

He was Godslayer.

He’d kept secrets whole generations of officers didn’t know existed.

Worn a thousand masks, spoken a hundred lies, played ghost in the ruins of dead systems.

It was hypocritical.

But this wasn’t the same.

Because it was Phainon.

And Phainon was—

Was what, Mydei? Yours?

Or was he the knife they turned on you while you weren’t looking?

The ache sharpened.

His hands shook like a fault line before collapse.

The certainty he relied on had abandoned him.

He just hurt.

He pressed his knuckles to his lips.

Closed his eyes.

Hoped, stupidly, for a moment’s peace.

It didn’t come.

And then—beneath the ragged rasp of his own breath—he heard it.

A hum.

Low, syncopated, barely audible. A subtle shift in the containment unit’s resonance lattice.

Someone was here.

A visitor.

His stomach turned. The room seemed to tilt.

He wiped a shaking hand down his face, forced his spine to straighten, ignoring the tremor in his limbs.

Breathe in. Breathe out.

Because no matter what broke inside his chest, no one—no one—got to see him like that.

Not them.

Not yet.

Not until it was over.

And gods help them if it ever was.

The reinforced threshold gave a final, mechanical click.

Mydei tensed.

Some part of him always would.

There was no point pretending otherwise.

And then—through the sterile light and brittle, dead air—Krateros stepped inside.

It struck harder than it should have.

Even through the mire of grief and suspicion, with thoughts unraveling faster than he could catch them, some ancient, bone-deep instinct still knew what to do when that figure entered a room.

Straighten your spine. Center your breath.

Make yourself still.

His age didn’t matter.

Nine. Twenty. Now.

Krateros was Krateros.

And the part of Mydei that had never quite outgrown it obeyed without question.

His fingers stilled against the cuffs. The trembling didn’t vanish, but it pulled deeper, tucked itself into some quiet, hidden place.

The grief stayed. It always did.

But his posture held.

He expected the iron-hard gaze. That careful, assessing stare followed by a precise correction—a reprimand shaped like a lesson.

But it didn’t come.

What met him wasn’t the mentor.

Not the man who’d taught him to wield a blade, to silence fear, to build walls so high nothing could reach him.

This was something smaller.

A man without a mantle.

And without meaning to, Mydei’s shoulders loosened—because some buried part of him recognized, without needing to name it, that Krateros wasn’t here for Godslayer.

He was here for Mydeimos.

“Teacher,” he said.

Krateros inclined his head.

“Mydeimos.”

And then—to his quiet astonishment—Krateros didn’t remain standing.

Didn’t pace like an interrogator.

Didn’t linger at the threshold like a wary emissary deciding how close to risk.

He crossed the room.

Lowered himself to the floor.

And sat.

Cross-legged.

Close.

Deliberately human.

The way he had done when Mydei was small, when nightmares made sleep impossible and the world felt too wide to hold alone.

It was a signal.

Mydei’s throat tightened. The question slipped out before he could measure it, before he could summon the wisdom to leave it unsaid.

“This about them trying to pull something out of me?”

He meant for it to land sharp. Defiant.

It didn’t.

Krateros looked at him—truly looked—with the kind of steady, unimpressed clarity that cut deeper than any reprimand could.

It wasn’t anger.

It was something colder.

A quiet disappointment at the insult to his dignity.

As though the mere suggestion he’d be sent by them should’ve been beneath both of them.

The shame hit sharp and sudden, flushing under his skin before he could stop it.

Of course not.

Krateros wasn’t a man anyone commanded.

Not the Council.

Not the Heirs.

Mydei forced the words out anyway.

“Then why are you here?”

He braced for it—the reprimand, the clipped disappointment he’d always feared more than raised voices. He even shut his eyes for a moment, a pointless instinct, as though not seeing it would spare him the weight.

But the silence that followed wasn’t sharp.

No reprimand.

Only the faint, metallic sound of something moving between calloused fingers.

He opened his eyes.

Krateros sat motionless, save for the object turning slowly in his hand.

A ring.

Plain. Aged by time. Its metal dulled to a soft, worn gray. The crest still legible to anyone who’d ever belonged to them.

It hit like a blow to the ribs.

Krateros’s voice broke the stillness.

“This was your mother’s,” he said, gaze not leaving the ring. “She wouldn’t take it off. Drove your father mad.”

Without ceremony, Krateros set it on the floor between them.

He didn’t offer it.

Didn’t ask him to take it.

Just placed it there.

The dim light caught on its edge.

And in that single, unspoken moment—Mydei understood.

This wasn’t a test.

Wasn’t leverage dressed in familiar skin.

Some debts lived longer than the ones who made them.

And some promises weren’t made to the living.

He exhaled, the breath unsteady.

“So that’s what this is about,” he murmured, not entirely sure whether the words were meant for Krateros, or for himself. “You promised her.”

Krateros didn’t deny it.

The ring stayed where it was.

“I remember the night she came to me,” Krateros murmured, his gaze never leaving the ring. “Stormed into the East Sector, clothes half-fastened in her haste. Blood on her knuckles from a man twice her size who thought to stop her.”

Mydei held his breath without realizing.

“She said she was finished waiting. Finished choking down your father’s lies. She meant to take you that night. Away from him.”

It was a story he’d never been told.

And one he could no longer pretend he hadn’t needed to hear.

“But it didn’t work.” Krateros’s voice lowered. “They’d built contingencies, buried in your blood. Invisible chains wound through your pulse, tied to your proximity. You wouldn’t have made it past the threshold before it unraveled your mind. Or worse.”

Worse.

“She learned too late,” Krateros continued, softer now. “And she made me swear. Swear to you. Not to the Heirs. Not to the Council’s gilded filth. Not to whatever promises that wretched Initiative whispered.”

Krateros’s fingers brushed the edge of the ring, turning it once.

“She said doors were being built,” he murmured. “Doors no one else could see. And if she wasn’t there when they opened, someone had to be.”

Mydei wanted to ask.

To follow the implications down, see where the threads led, no matter how jagged the end.

But not yet. Not like this.

He drew a slow, careful breath, steadying his voice.

“So what’s the point of this?” he asked. “Old history won’t unmake what’s been done.”

Krateros met his gaze—implacable, and sharp as old iron.

“You think this is history?” The words landed like an anvil. “Boy, the ground beneath your feet was laid by that night.”

Mydei scowled, the retort rising, ready to bury this finally. But before the words left his mouth, Krateros’s tone turned, the cold edge of it cutting straight through the air between them.

“And what if I told you the Council was in it from the start?”

The room seemed to contract.

Krateros saw the flicker of awareness—that lethal, subtle shift behind his student’s gaze—and his expression changed.

The fatigue of years gave way to something else—a soldier’s terrible certainty.

Then—without warning—Krateros moved.

In a single, swift motion, he drew a thin, compact blade from beneath his collar. Without waiting he drove it, not into flesh, but straight into the resonance conduit embedded in the cell’s control node near the wall.

The metal struck with a sharp, resonant sound. Sparks burst from the fracture point. A keening whine filled the air as the room’s lattice destabilized.

Alarms exploded to life. A high, shrieking wail. Lights stuttered, then stabilized into a raw, unfiltered pallor. Containment seals slammed down with a brutal, grinding finality.

[WARNING]

The surveillance weave collapsed, flickering out like dying stars.

Containment seals slammed into place with a bone-rattling grind.

The entire cell was cut off.

Panic rippled through the facility’s infrastructure—muted, but unmistakable.

And inside this room, there was only the howl of alarms and the unblinking weight of Krateros’s stare.

He didn’t flinch.

Didn’t so much as shift his shoulders.

When he spoke, his voice was sharp— not raised, not barked, but with a gravity that pressed against the bones of the room itself.

“Listen to me now, boy.”

Mydei’s shocked eyes met Krateros.

“What I tell you doesn’t leave these walls. Because if it does, you’ll be forced to choose which ties you sever—and whether you have the teeth to survive what follows.”

The alarms wailed on. The lights hummed, harsh and pale.

And neither of them moved.

Because in that moment, both of them understood what had just been set in motion.

And the only thing more dangerous than Krateros bearing a secret

was Krateros deciding this was the hour to let it bleed.

The alarms screamed through the sealed room—red light bleeding in jagged streaks along the walls, shadows stuttering with every pulse. Beyond the reinforced doors, shouts rose like a storm surge, the pounding of boots growing louder.

Krateros didn’t hesitate.

“The Council,” he spat, voice raw and vicious, a sound stripped to bone. “They were the spine of Kýklos Thanatou Eikon. The Initiative was never rogue. It was theirs. Eurypon was just a knife they pointed with.”

Mydei’s stomach turned so violently it felt like gravity slipped.

“What—?”

Krateros didn’t let him finish. The words came like a dam burst—not elegant or careful at all.

“They funded it. Ran it. Buried it when the Heirs stormed the site. Erased the names. Burned the files. Lied about rogue cells and broken men. I saw the fucking records. I dug them out with my own hands from the corpse pits they left behind.”

A fist hammered the other side of the door. The reinforced frame buckled. A jagged voice barked for clearance codes.

And then Krateros snapped.

He spun, grabbed Mydei by the collar, his fingers bruising flesh through fabric. His voice cracked wide, a jagged, half-hysterical snarl undercut with the brilliant, precise madness of a man who understood the machinery of power far too well.

“Think, Mydeimos. You were the only one. The only one. Thirty-three corpses in a pit, and you breathing. Why do you think they’ve been circling like carrion since the moment we dragged you out of that hell? Why every

transfer request, every quiet offer, every operation the Council’s shadowed from behind the curtain?”

Mydei’s pulse screamed in his throat. He tried to speak—but his mind was collapsing inward, memories cascading, half-heard conversations, Eurypon’s ragged voice pouring out theories like poison, diagrams he shouldn’t have remembered flashing behind his eyes.

Stabilizer rings. Fail-safe loops. Resonance anchoring protocols.

“They—” he started, breath scraping raw in his chest.

Krateros didn’t give him the chance.

“That bastard,” he spat, refusing even now to speak the man’s name, “started claiming it was about the Tide. Immunity, protection—the usual fucking salvation myth. But it stopped being about humanity the moment he realized he could manufacture immortality.”

The word landed like a hammer to the sternum.

Krateros’s eyes gleamed—not gentle, not sorrowful, but bright and terrible and alive with the kind of knowledge that sickens you just to hold.

“And you, boy—” he rasped. “You’re the one that worked. The one thing death couldn’t hold. A tether they can’t cut, no matter how many times the world falls down around it. Do you understand now?”

It hit.

Not like a revelation, not like clarity.

Like a free fall.

Mydei’s immortality.

Not an accident.

Not a byproduct.

The entire point.

He staggered a half-step back, jaw slack, nausea rising sharp and sour in his throat. The room seemed to lurch sideways. His heart pounded against his ribs like it was trying to claw its way out.

If that’s why they’d been waiting.

If that’s what they meant to claim.

What would they do with it?

Krateros’s hand crushed his shoulder, grounding him through sheer violence.

“I don’t know what purpose those bastards have for it,” Krateros bit out, “but I know men like them don’t leave power lying in the dirt. They’ll harvest you, Mydei. Strip the marrow from your bones. Build new things out of your skin and claim they were born to rule. And I’ll be damned twice over before I watch them do it.”

From outside—a final, gut-wrenching shriek of tearing metal.

Containment seals buckled under a manual resonance breach.

The lattice around the room stuttered, flickered. The doors began to split at the seams.

Krateros leaned in, so close Mydei could see the madness in his eyes, a manic sheen born of terror and rage and a soldier’s bitter love for the last thing in the world he could still protect.

His voice dropped to a feral rasp.

“Listen to me, Mydei. You never go with them. Never take their offer. Never let their words inside your head. They’ll gut you, wear your immortality like a second skin, and bleed others in your name.”

And then—the doors blew inward.

A flood of light. Shouting. Boots. Faces locked in the empty-eyed stare of men given orders they no longer understood.

They seized Krateros. Two guards grabbed his arms, hauling him back. He fought like a cornered animal, a snarl on his lips—not at them, but at Mydei.

His gaze never left him.

And even as they dragged him toward the breach, his voice rose above the chaos:

“Cut your leash, Mydeimos. Cut it before it wraps around your throat. Or you’ll wish you’d died with your mother.”

Then he was gone—swallowed by a wall of armored bodies.

And in the aftermath, in the deafening absence of Krateros’s voice, Mydei stood motionless.

The alarms still howled, but they were distant now, like sounds filtering in from a dead world. The light felt too sharp, every pulse of it like a blade against his skin.

His pulse spiked. His breath quickened—ragged, shallow. A pressure built in his chest, tight, constricting. His hands shook.

A new, deeper terror unfurled in him.

And Mydei, for once in his life, truly felt panic gnaw at the edges of his mind.

He drew in a shuddering breath, tried to steady it—and failed.

His head hurt.

He pressed trembling fingers to his temple, tracing the pulse there—as if anchoring himself to the last, indisputable proof that he was still here.

Think.

Krateros’s voice wouldn’t stop.

Not cleanly. Not as whole words.

Fragments. Shards.

The Council was the spine. They built it. Built you.

And the worst part wasn’t even that.

It was why.

That word.

It hung in his mind like a broken stabilizer coil, sparking and stuttering, threatening collapse.

Why?

If it had only been about him—about the lattice, about Eurypon’s rotten salvation masquerading as science—he could have followed the thread. But it wasn’t. Not just him.

The Flame Reaver.

They’d marked him too.

Why?

What did one have to do with the other? What pattern did two anomalies make when overlapped?

The thought snagged something raw in his memory. A loose edge. Then another. Then another.

And before he could stop it, the betrayal reasserted itself.

Phainon.

The lies. The omissions. The way the man had steered him, always steering, under the illusion of partnership. Every ‘coincidence’ of proximity to power players. Every quiet nudge toward people fated to die. Phainon had likely killed them, one by one, with the same detached precision a surgeon uses to cut away necrotic flesh.

But this wasn’t cleansing.

It was slaughter.

And Mydei tried—tried—to reach for rage, for that cold, beautiful thing Heirs were taught to refine into resolve.

Nothing came.

No fire. No hatred. No righteous vow to burn his name from the earth.

Just a hollow quiet.

And it startled him.

His brow furrowed, lips parting on a breath he couldn’t quite catch.

I should feel something.

He should be furious. Should want to rip the man’s heart out with his bare hands and watch it struggle to keep beating. Should curse his name, spit on the memory of every whispered night, every shoulder-to-shoulder moment pretending to be something like brothers, like comrades.

He should swear vengeance in the name of the people Phainon had dismembered, suffocated, burned alive in locked resonance cages. The girl who’d begged to be shot before the Tide took her. The old operative who’d detonated his own skull node to avoid being devoured inside-out by harmonics. The civilians who never even knew what was being done to them.

Each life another notch in a ledger Phainon never let him see.

But none of it conjured the anger. Not the way it should have. Not the way it needed to.

He didn’t feel hate.

He felt sick.

Not at the blood. Not at the scale of it.

At the lie.

And it was that—that small, bitter truth—that made his jaw clench tight enough to ache.

Because somewhere, somewhere in the marrow of him, Mydei understood the real betrayal wasn’t the atrocities.

It was the silence.

Phainon hadn’t just killed and lied and schemed.

He’d known. And he’d let him wander blind through it all, dangling half-truths like a tether. Had let him believe the world wasn’t quite as monstrous as it was, because somewhere in it, there was one man who wouldn’t lie to him.

And worse—Mydei had let him.

He felt his throat tighten—not grief, not mourning.

A suffocating, gut-deep clarity.

It wasn’t the deaths. It wasn’t even the cause.

It was trust.

The unspoken thing that lived between people when the noise fell away.

And that was the thing Phainon carved up with a scalpel.

He was a hypocrite for mourning it. He knew that. Knew his own hands weren’t clean. Knew he’d buried names they’d never find and faces he’d long stopped remembering. Knew he’d buried the truth of Godslayer under a hundred aliases and quiet, efficient murders.

But none of it was comparable.

Because Mydei’s lies had always been his own cross to bear.

Phainon’s were a leash.

And the fear—the real fear—hadn’t ever been death.

It was losing him.

It had always been him.

And it hit now, fast and sharp, like a spike driven through the ribs.

Mydei swallowed hard, bracing a palm against the cold wall, the room spinning sideways. The realization bled through like a hairline fracture spiderwebbing across glass.

He could survive the Tide.

Survive containment fields. Torture. Calamities.

He could even survive being made a liability in the eyes of the Council.

But the thought of Phainon vanishing—dragged into some Council chamber, into a blacksite vault, into a disintegration pit before he could hear the truth from his mouth, before he could ask him if any of it was real —

That was what made his lungs lock.

That was what left his hands shaking.

And when that settled in.

If they want me…

And they’d marked him too.

It was a tethered operation. A linked outcome. A convergence.

And if Mydei stayed here, pacing this cell without doing anything, the Council would take him first.

And then he’d never know.

Never find out if those nights leaning shoulder to shoulder meant anything. If the warmth in his voice when he said his name was ever real, or just another facade.

He realized, in that moment, that answers meant more to him than justice.

That he would kill to have them.

And maybe worse—he’d forgive to have them too.

Mydei sat motionless, shoulders pressed against cold alloy, the burn of restraint welts stinging at his wrists. For a long time, he let his thoughts slow, disassociate, unspool into something mercifully dull.

It was the footsteps that pulled him back.

Not the nervous, clipped cadence of a rookie. Not the heavy stride of a security enforcer.

Precise.

He didn’t react at first.

Didn’t bother.

In places like this, there were always footsteps.

Only when the door’s lock disengaged with a pneumatic hiss and a sharp, antiseptic scent cut through the stagnant air did he lift his head.

Hyacine.

She entered with the dual presence of a combat medic and a soldier, though he could see the strain ghosting beneath the surface—in the tightness of her jaw, the careful neutrality of her expression.

“Mydei,” she greeted softly, the tone a little too even to be natural. Her gaze swept over him, a calculated assessment. Not just a glance. A full trauma survey.

He knew the steps by rote:

Primary ABC check—airway, breathing, circulation.

Secondary—neurologic status, focal injuries, covert bleed risk.

She knelt beside him, fingers cold through the thin mesh of gloves as they wrapped around his wrist. Two seconds. Three. Pulse irregular but present. A faint tremor under his skin.

“Vitals are marginally stable,” she murmured, more for herself than him. “Neural strain with probable feedback. Suppressants destabilized. Adjusting now.”

He said nothing.

Not even a wince.

Hyacine continued regardless, the steady cadence of her voice a ritual in itself.

“I’m adjusting your neuroinhibitors. You’re experiencing cortical overload symptoms—delirium, disassociation. You shouldn’t even be upright.”

She reached for his ocular line, sweeping the penlight in front of his eyes. Pupillary response was delayed in one, reactive in the other.

His gaze barely tracked her, unfocused, until a sharper flicker of something registered in her expression.

It wasn’t professional.

She hadn’t cleared the room because someone ordered it. Hadn’t risked cross-traffic during an active lockdown for a duty check.

She’d come for him.

And he almost felt sorry for what would come next.

Almost.

Hyacine’s fingers ghosted across the bruised skin near his temple, brushing aside a wayward strand of damp hair.

“Honestly,” she muttered under her breath, an exhale that carried too much weight for casual reprimand, “one of these days, you’re not going to crawl back from these things.”

A long, brittle silence stretched between them.

Then, without lifting his head:

“I need to leave.”

She stilled.

Not enough for the now likely active cams, not enough for a ceiling scope to catch. But to him—it was there. A half-second’s hesitation.

The kind of pause that spoke volumes.

Then she moved again, seamlessly, finishing the adjustment of his suppressants.

“Mydei,” she said, too lightly. Professional. Coaxing. “You’re not cleared to move. Sit tight.”

A flawless deflection.

It would have convinced anyone else.

But it wouldn’t work here.

“I’m serious,” he rasped. “You don’t understand. I have to go. Now.”

Hyacine didn’t answer immediately. She finished checking the raw abrasions along his forearms from where the restraint bands had torn skin, her touch light but unflinching.

He waited for the reprimand, the clinical rebuke.

It didn’t come.

Instead, she murmured, low and neutral, as if discussing an inventory manifest:

“Your gear’s still tagged in C5. Sublevel 2. Same unit they toss your effects every time you decide to dismantle half my medbay.”

His eyes found hers. A flicker of something passed between them.

She didn’t look up.

Her hands moved slower now. Deliberate. And after a moment, he felt the faint, almost imperceptible shift at his wrist—the tactile click of the restraint lock disengaging.

Gone.

Her grip on his forearm tightened, feigning another vitals check, and she leaned in a fraction too close. Not enough to be flagged, but enough for her voice to slip beneath the sensors’ auditory sweep range.

“They’ll sweep this sector in fifteen.”

A breath.

“I won’t condone what you’re about to do. But I won’t watch you get dragged out of here either.”

It caught him off-guard, not the words, but the intent behind them. Hyacine didn’t owe him this. No one did.

And she was giving it anyway.

He looked at her—saw the edges, the strain she didn’t bother to hide anymore. Not weakness. Just a person, still here when she didn’t have to be.

Her lips twitched. The barest ghost of a smile.

“Make it count,” she murmured.

He didn’t hesitate.

Didn’t allow himself the indulgence of guilt or second thought.

In one sharp, precise motion, Mydei surged forward, his hand closing around the collar of her white coat. Hyacine’s eyes widened for a fraction of a second—not with fear, but with understanding.

She didn’t resist.

Didn’t call out.

The strike was clean—calculated for momentary syncope without lasting trauma. Her body sagged against him before he could let her fall, and instinct guided his hands, one cradling the back of her head, lowering her gently to the floor.

She felt smaller in his arms than he remembered.

He eased her down into the shadowed corner of the room, positioning her out of immediate sightlines. Pulled a folded piece of sterile gauze from the nearby kit and slipped it beneath her head to cushion the contact point.

The knot in his chest tightened.

His fingers lingered longer than they should have at her temple.

“Thank you,” he said, the words meant for no one but himself.

And then he stood.

Head pounding. Delirious. Muscles aching from restraint stress and cortical backlash. But steady. The inertia of earlier shattered clean through.

Krateros, damn him, was still raising hell somewhere down the corridor— the muffled echoes of shouting and metallic impacts a distant counterpoint. Most of the security detail would be focused there.

Fifteen minutes.

He wouldn’t waste it.

Not with Phainon still out there.

Not with everything unraveling.

Not anymore.

He closed his eyes.

Drew in a breath, every inhalation scraping like broken glass.

For a moment, everything slowed.

And then something inside him shifted.

A gear locking into place.

The fractured pieces of his mind pulled taut into ruthless, surgical clarity.

He moved.

A sharp, full-body pivot—muscle memory overriding hesitation, the ache in his side vanishing beneath the surge of momentum. His legs carried him

forward in a blistering sprint, the medblock exit already framed in his mind.

The corridors mapped themselves in real time in his eyes, automatic, as if the entire structure existed solely for this purpose.

Medbay A2 connects to Sub-Corridor 7C. Two levels down through maintenance. Storage Sublevel 2. C5 along the northern access bay. Then extraction.

The overhead strips flickered as he tore through the narrow passageways, the cold light warping into smeared streaks in his peripheral vision. Somewhere behind him, alarms would trigger soon—even with Krateros distracting them. Every second counted.

His brain parsed possibilities, firing rapid contingencies as his boots hit alloy.

How to contact him.

A message?

Impossible. The Heirs had his comm grid and phone flagged, every outbound line quarantined, every data thread triangulated within seconds. His signal was radioactive.

Anything traced back would bring a full tactical sweep before Phainon could even read it.

No.

He’d find him the old fashioned way.

Mydei vaulted over a waist-high security barrier, hitting the other side in a low roll before cutting down a side corridor half-lit by emergency reserve strips. A maintenance crawlspace hatch blinked green ahead, status panel on standby.

He didn’t slow.

His palm hit the override, fingers punching the sequence.

Grid pulse, five-second bypass. Manual override. Old Chrysos tech. Fragile sensors. Laughable security.

The hatch hissed open and he dropped into the narrow crawlspace, weaving between cables and old conduit trunks, the scent of machine oil sharp in the recycled air.

The city beyond was too vast to sweep. Phainon wouldn’t be hiding at random. He was smarter than that.

Certain places made sense, if as Flame Reaver.

Places with no active surveillance. No clean data feeds.

The kinds of dead zones both of them had used before.

A flash of movement ahead.

A Chrysos operative—standard tactical rig, pulseblade at his hip. He turned just as Mydei cleared the hatch.

“Hey— wait, aren’t you—”

He didn’t finish.

Two strides, a sharp pivot, elbow driving hard into the agent’s throat, cutting the word off in a strangled gasp. The follow-through was instinct—a clean hook to the jaw, catching him before his body could crumple to the ground.

Efficient.

His pulse barely rose.

Another route.

Ahead, a narrow conduit access—one of the old plasma vent crawlways, long since decommissioned after the last reactor incident. No active scanners, no vid-links.

Forgotten by most.

Perfect.

Mydei ducked inside, the air thick and stale, thick cables coiled like veins along the walls. The passage curved ahead into a deeper sublevel, each step closing the distance between him and what waited at the end of this night.

He could feel it now

His hand clenched at his side.

I’ll find you.

A promise. A threat. A certainty.

And as he picked up speed again, every muscle coiled tight beneath bruised skin, one final thought settled cold and steady behind his eyes.

And gods help you, Phainon—when I do.
