chapters.title: Chapter 15: Anaxa’s Discount Rescue Service
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Phainon goes to a black market info-forum, makes terrible life choices, runs into a rogue Godslayer, accidentally kills him, has an existential breakdown, melts several Council enforcers, gets forcibly sedated by Anaxa (who arrives fashionably late with a gun and zero patience), gets yeeted through unstable space, and wakes up in one of Anaxa’s off-the-books trauma bunkers wondering if he’s lost everything. Again. 10/10 crisis management.

Chapter Notes

Alright, first off, sorry for the delay AGAIN. Technically I could argue I’m only *kinda* late since I still have like 20 minutes before it hits June 10th in my time zone, but let’s be real, by the time I finish editing and posting this, it’ll probably be 12:40 or something. So yeah. Sorryyy.

Anyway, I hope you guys enjoy the chapter! It’s a messy one, but what’s new.

Heads up: guest comments are gonna be temporarily disabled for now because holyyyyy unemployment. Someone apparently had the free time to go through every single chapter and leave some nonsense comments. Honestly idgaf abt them, but I don’t want anyone else scrolling through and getting weirded out or discouraged from reading, SORRYYY😭

The air thrummed.

High above the gutted carcass of the old industrial sector, surveillance drones drifted in lazy, predatory arcs. No flashing lights. You only saw them if you were looking—

and around here, no one with a survival instinct looked up.

The sky sagged low, a smear of sickly cloud dragging pale light across rusting catwalks and half-collapsed heat exchangers. Somewhere in the distance, a patrol crawler let out a mechanical whine, scattering the last of the stragglers like roaches. Officially, the curfew was soft. In practice, it meant the ground belonged to the Council, the air to the Heirs, and every blind corner was a loaded question with a gun for a mouth.

Which was why Phainon stayed off the streets.

He crouched in the shadow of a decommissioned coolant silo, one gloved hand absently rolling a worn coin while the other adjusted the setting on a pulse tool.

A drone shimmered past overhead. Just a faint ripple in the heavy air.

Phainon sighed through his teeth, tapped his comms.

“Nothing says ‘welcome’ like weaponized eyeballs in the sky.”

A click. Then Anaxa’s voice in his ear—clipped, and already several steps ahead.

“Four escape routes mapped. Three scramblers planted. Two fallback points marked. Stay focused.”

Phainon let out a low, slow whistle.

“Somebody’s gunning for a promotion.”

“Shut up and work.”

A grin tugged at his mouth before he could stop it. The place wasn’t kind to humor. If you didn’t bleed out, burn out, or crash out, you cracked. He was batting two for three.

Not that any of this had gone to plan.

The soft lockdown had hardened, thickened into a knot of overlapping patrol corridors and contested surveillance airspace. Council lockdowns were bad. Chrysos Heir counter-nets were worse. Together? A tangled mess of redundant protocols and half-synced tech, creating unstable fields, dead network zones, and interference anomalies where both sides’ systems clashed.

Dangerous.

Which, unfortunately, made them useful.

For the past few hours, Phainon and Anaxa had done the only thing better than surviving: mapping weak points. Plotting where Council and Heir surveillance fields overlapped and failed. Gaps in the signal. Glitches in the feed. Little dead spots you could slip through if you were smart or desperate.

Or both.

Anaxa had whipped up a handful of scramblers on the fly, cobbled together from proximity beacon parts and an honestly alarming number of questionably sourced neuro-sync chips. They mostly worked. The last one had glitched so hard Phainon’s teeth felt like they were vibrating out of his skull.

He eyed the one in his palm now—a fist-sized tangle of emitters and braided filament. Light seeped through the gaps in unsteady pulses, like a heartbeat with a bad rhythm.

Phainon grimaced.

“These things are a disaster waiting to happen.”

Anaxa didn’t miss a beat.

“You fry both our synapses and I’ll bury your corpse with my tax records.”

He snorted, arching a brow at the comm bead.

“Harsh.”

Another sigh. Phainon straightened, pressed a shoulder to the bulkhead, and started moving.

“Yes, your majesty,” he muttered.

The scrambler flickered in his hand. Like it agreed.

He moved without a sound, shoulders brushing peeling metal. He knew this layout. Knew which footfalls wouldn’t echo. Which struts had rotted hollow. The air thickened around him, an oily weight clinging to his skin.

A weak point.

He felt it before he saw it.

The faint warping of space.

A shimmer.

The hazard signage on the far wall rippled, warping in place as his pulse tool gave an irritable buzz.

Phainon’s mouth twitched.

“Well, that’s not ominous.”

He crouched by a tangle of dead junction cables, fished the scrambler from his belt, and thumbed the priming sequence. The sphere gave a flicker, then a sharp pulse. The ripple in the air expanded, jagged and wrong, making the wall stutter between rust-streaked plating and slick, black glass.

“Shit—” Phainon hissed as the thing spasmed in his grip. He slapped a control panel on its side, muttering,

“You couldn’t make this less homicidal?”

Anaxa’s voice crackled in his ear, dry as dust.

“You knew the job was dangerous when you took it.”

Phainon scowled at the scrambler as its glow finally stabilized.

“Next time, I’m wiring the gear. No offense.”

“Noted. Movement west sector,” Anaxa cut in, voice tightening. “Heir patrol rerouting. And there’s chatter about a rogue contact.”

Phainon gave a low whistle, rose, and slipped up one of the support beams with liquid ease. He reached a narrow cross-lattice and hauled himself into the shadowed framework overhead. Muscle memory.

“You wanna elaborate on that, orrr~?” he drawled, hanging from one arm as a patrol’s footsteps rang out below—three figures in matte-black armor, faint glyph sigils shimmering on their shoulders. He watched them pass, close enough to taste the hum of their weapon cores on his teeth.

A beat.

Then Anaxa again.

“Scattered intercepts. One of the Heir’s people went dark. Rumor says they were confined. Rumor also says they got out.”

Phainon’s brow furrowed.

“Seriously? Heirs don’t just lose people.”

“Forget it. Irrelevant. We’ve got real problems.”

The line went still for a half-second. Long enough for Phainon to sense Anaxa wanted to say something else. Instead, what came was a sharp, low whisper:

“You’ve got ninety seconds. My zone’s compromised. Relocating.”

Phainon hissed through his teeth, easing higher into the frame as another drone shimmered past overhead.

“Sure. Meet you at fallback six?”

“Negative. I’ll route you a new path once I’m clear.”

A pause. Then, almost distractedly:

“I picked up something. I’ll tell you when you’re out of this section. You’ll want to hear it.”

“Tease,” Phainon muttered, already moving.

“Anything else I’m clearing out here?”

“Negative. Objectives complete. Recommend access through lower utility grid—service runoff channel. West sewer junction.”

Phainon groaned, tipping his head back against rusted bulkhead.

“You would send me into the sewers.”

“Security’s dense tonight. Patrol vectors are a mess. Took a lot just to get you in there.”

Another pause.

“Your residential echo’s still holding, but it won’t last.”

Phainon smirked faintly.

“Good little trick though, huh?”

Not a clone. Not quite. An echo construct, his own handiwork—projected tight enough to fool proximity scanners and surveillance skimmers. As far as the city grid knew, Phainon was three districts away, passed out in his apartment, sleeping off a hangover.

The fact he wasn’t was the entire problem.

“Yes, yes, bask in your own brilliance later,” Anaxa muttered. “Get moving.”

“On it.”

Phainon scanned for the nearest maintenance hatch. It didn’t take long to find one buried behind a collapsed barrier.

He crouched, hooked his fingers into the grip ring, and hauled it open with a groan of metal. A breath of cold, sour air rolled up from the dark below.

Phainon peered into it, resigned.

“Love this job,” he muttered, and dropped into the dark.

The tunnel stank.

Not just of mold and standing water, but old blood, scorched oil, and something acrid that clung to the throat. Phainon’s boots splashed through shallow runoff as he jogged down the narrow maintenance artery. Overhead, dead fixtures hung like broken teeth, leaving only the faintest glimmers of streetlight filtering through grated slats above.

He ducked beneath a rusted pipe, tapped his comm.

“Hey, Professor,” he panted, voice light despite the gloom. “What were you gonna say, y’know, before everything caught fire again?”

A pause. The faint rasp of Anaxa shifting wherever he was holed up now.

“Keep left at the filtration stack. Drop down the ladder—utility corridor seven.”

Phainon rolled his eyes and veered left, vaulting a cracked barricade.

“You are terrible at meaningful conversation.”

“Occupational hazard,” Anaxa muttered. Then, after a beat, more audible, “Right. Secured you an invitation.”

Phainon nearly missed a step.

“An invitation? What kind of invitation?”

“You’ll like it. Underground forum. Analog only. No links, no grids, no eyes.”

Despite himself, Phainon grinned, weaving past a collapsed support.

“Let me guess—black-tie gala for the paranoid and armed?”

“Closer than you think.”

The line went quiet for a stretch. Only water and Phainon’s breath filled the space as he vaulted a rung ladder, landing on a rust-caked platform with barely a sound.

Then Anaxa’s voice, lower now:

“The reactor complex runs its own dead grid. No connections to the city circuits. I can skim the streets, piggyback unsecured comms, but inside? Only whispers count.”

Phainon hummed under his breath, crossing a brittle catwalk.

“And what’s so important even you can’t dig it out?”

Anaxa’s tone sharpened.

“Council relocation transport. Rumors of a cluster of ‘Bodies.’ Capital B. No manifest yet, but someone’s paying a fortune to find them first.”

Phainon grimaced.

“Yeah, that’s never good.”

“Better we get there first.”

A burst of static cracked over the line as Phainon slid under a low valve assembly.

“And there’s a name circulating,” Anaxa added. “Not confirmed. But it’s… inconvenient.”

“Oh?” Phainon’s brow quirked. “Someone important?”

“Someone problematic. Rumor says she can bypass chrysocite perimeters. Nobody’s sure she exists. But even the rumors are enough to get people killed.”

That got his attention.

He ducked beneath a cluster of warped pipes, lips curling.

“Wait, wait, I know that tone. You know her, don’t you?”

Anaxa didn’t answer.

Phainon pressed it.

“An Heir, wasn’t she? Before she bailed.”

A long pause.

“Leave it,” Anaxa said, curt. “We’re not chasing her. Not tonight.”

Phainon snorted a dry laugh.

“You’ve got more old friends crawling out of the rot than anyone I’ve ever met.”

“Networking is survival.”

Another turn. A narrow crawlspace, black water up to his shins, stinking of rust and worse.

Phainon’s grin faded.

“Alright. When’s this little masked meet-and-greet happening?”

“Tonight.”

He choked.

“Seriously!?”

Static fuzzed. Anaxa, distracted—probably elbow-deep in another bypass— replied absently:

“Also, Council’s starting residential sweeps. Spot checks. Random knock-and-scan.”

“Seriously!?” Phainon groaned, breaking into a faster run.

“How long before someone figures out my charming echo isn’t me?”

“If everything holds?” Anaxa mused. “Twenty minutes.”

“And if it doesn’t?”

“Hope you make it in fifteen. I’ll let you take a five-minute shower if you do.”

Phainon wheezed a breathless laugh.

“Asshole.”

But his pace doubled anyway.

The maintenance crawlspace was narrower than Phainon remembered.

Not that he’d known it long. Discovered it last week, actually—a personal tragedy, considering how many close calls it could’ve saved him from before now.

He twisted sideways, shoulder scraping grime-slick walls, overhead pipes sweating some unidentifiable chemical stink.

“Damn it, Anaxa,” he muttered, wriggling forward. “You and your brilliant shortcuts.”

A low, metallic thud echoed behind him—a bracket, maybe, or something less innocent. Phainon flinched so hard his elbow cracked against a rusted conduit. Biting back a curse, he wriggled faster until the passage opened into a jagged panel of crumbling drywall. He shoved it aside, the brittle surface giving with a muffled crack, and half-spilled into his own closet.

The door rattled in its frame.

Phainon groaned, braced a hand to steady himself, and dispelled the Echo he’d left slumbering in his bed hours ago. A faint shimmer, a soft pop— then gone.

No time to savor it.

Clothes hit the floor as he stripped, sweat-soaked layers peeled off in practiced haste. The comm receiver snagged off his ear, tossed onto a narrow shelf by the door, out of immediate sight.

The shower hissed to life, hot enough to sting. Five minutes to scrub the sewer off his skin. His fingers worked quick through his hair, chasing grit and clinging dust. The steam helped. The pulse in his chest slowed, fractionally.

Maybe he’d made it.

Maybe the sweep teams were sticking to perimeters, tagging clear homes and moving on.

The water cut off with a metallic shriek. Phainon grabbed a towel, wrapped it low around his hips, steam curling off his skin as he padded toward the living room—

A knock.

Sharp. Three precise, unhurried raps.

The sound seemed to reverberate longer than it should’ve.

He clicked his tongue against his teeth.

“Of course,” he sighed.

Another knock. Polite, but firmer.

He cinched the towel tighter, mussed his damp hair with an artful rake of fingers, and pasted on a lazy smile. Then yanked open the door, leaning casually against the frame.

“Evening, officer,” he drawled, eyelids half-lowered. “How’s the sweep?”

The man on the other side wasn’t a rookie.

Mid-thirties, heavyset, close-cropped hair. The matte black of his field uniform caught the low light, datapad flickering in his palm. His gaze swept Phainon’s face, then the apartment behind him.

“Routine check,” the officer said. Clipped. “Mind if I ask where you’ve been tonight, citizen…?”

“Phainon,” he provided smoothly, thumb absently tapping the doorframe. “Been here. Mostly. Sleeping, showering, bit of reading. Quiet night in.”

The officer didn’t smile. His brow eased a fraction, but only barely.

“Alone?”

Phainon’s smile tilted.

“Sadly, yeah. Though if you’re offering—”

“I’m not.”

“A shame.”

The officer made a note on his pad. His gaze flicked up again—across Phainon’s damp hair, collarbones, shoulders—

Then paused.

At the side of his neck.

A thin, fresh scrape. Just under his hairline.

The air changed.

A subtle tightening, a shift in the room’s gravity. The officer straightened, eyes sharpening in a way that made the datapad seem incidental.

“That looks recent,” the officer said evenly. “Care to explain?”

Phainon’s stomach lurched—just for a second. His face didn’t show it. The grin stayed, though it thinned, mouth moving before his brain caught up.

“Oh—that?” He reached up, fingers brushing it with a mock-sheepish chuckle. “Yeah, partner’s been into… y’know. Intense stuff. It’s a thing.”

No flicker of amusement crossed the officer’s face.

“Injury report filed?”

“Mutual fun, officer. No complaints lodged.”

Phainon didn’t blink. Let the smile turn lazy, half-lidded eyes holding steady.

Then—the officer’s posture eased. Not much. A fraction.

“Well.” He tapped the datapad. “Keep it down during curfew hours. We’ve had noise complaints.”

Phainon flashed a razor smile.

“Wouldn’t dream of it.”

The officer gave a curt nod and turned, boots silent as he disappeared down the hall.

The moment the door shut, Phainon let the grin drop. Pressed his back to the door, slid down until he hit the floor, head thunking softly against the wood. His pulse still rattled like it wanted out of his ribs.

The comm crackled on the shelf.

“Your boyfriend, huh?” came Anaxa’s voice.

Phainon sighed.

“Eat shit.”

Anaxa’s voice came through again, quieter this time. Careful in a way Phainon recognized too easily—and hated.

“Speaking of… any contact from him?”

The words hung there.

Phainon didn’t answer.

The smile he’d been wearing slid off his face like a mask cut loose.

The steady hum of the vent fan suddenly was too loud, the distant bark of a stray dog down in the alley sharp and jarring. Lights felt too bright. The air too thick.

He stayed still.

A wire drawn taut.

Anaxa hesitated—Phainon could hear it. The pause before he spoke again.

“I… would’ve expected him to check in by now. I thought maybe—”

“Enough.”

The line went dead silent.

Anaxa didn’t speak again.

Neither did Phainon.

He closed his eyes. Jaw tight, pulse knocking too hard at the inside of his throat. For a moment it felt like his own body might betray him—breath stalling, eyes burning—before he forced it down. Locked it away where it belonged.

When he finally spoke, his voice was wrong.

Too light.

Too sharp at the edges.

“You’re gonna make me cry before my fancy party, Professor.”

Anaxa didn’t laugh.

Neither did Phainon.

The vent fan kept humming.

Phainon exhaled through his nose, the sound rough in the quiet. He rolled onto his side, propping himself up on an elbow, towel hitching low on his hips.

A beat, then—too bright:

“Soooo!” he chirped, a grin pulling at his mouth like it hurt. “Invitation tonight, right? Do I at least get to pick my outfit, or is this one of your formal parameters things again?”

Anaxa didn’t answer right away.

Then, finally—clipped. A little resigned.

“No.”

Phainon let out a long sigh, scrubbing a hand through his still-damp hair as he pushed to his feet.

“Knew it.”

“I had the foresight,” Anaxa added, “to dead-drop a case at your place earlier this evening. Top drawer, left side. It’s marked.”

“Is that so,” Phainon murmured, padding barefoot toward his room, the floor cool against his skin.

He slid the drawer open.

There it was—a slim black case, unmarked save for a pale chalk line at the corner. Classic Anaxa. Always leaving his fingerprints without ever leaving fingerprints.

Phainon flicked the latches and cracked the lid.

Inside: a suit, folded sharp enough to cut. Deep navy so dark it drank the light, shot through with threads of obsidian stitching that caught the faintest gleam. Black gloves, thin and close-fitting. A narrow choker, coiled like a promise of trouble.

And resting atop it all—a half-mask.

Venetian in style, matte black, faint filigree like static caught in glass.

Phainon raised a brow, holding it up between two fingers.

A smile tugged at his mouth, crooked and a little weary.

“Well, well,” he drawled, voice softer this time. “Y’know, if I had my way, I’d be showing up in a Power Ranger suit.”

Anaxa didn’t miss a beat.

“Which is precisely why you’re not choosing.”

That dragged a snort out of him.

He started pulling the suit on piece by piece. It fit like sin, smooth as a secret, the fabric heavy with concealed weavework and tailored to him down to the centimeter. Of course it was. Anaxa didn’t leave things like that to chance.

“Gotta hand it to you,” Phainon murmured, tugging the gloves snug. “For someone who pretends to have no sense of style, you’re disturbingly good at dressing me up.”

“Because one of us has to be.”

Phainon smirked, the gesture small and sharp as he set the mask aside for now. His fingers brushed the choker, tracing the clasp.

He rested an elbow against the shelf’s edge.

“Okay,” Phainon said. “Explain this place to me again. Masked info rave for revolutionary blackmailers, yeah? Got a proper name, or are we just calling it ‘the spooky reactor basement’?”

A pause on the other end. Faint background noise—a click, the shift of a tool or a keystroke.

Then:

“It’s called the Epitaph Court,” Anaxa replied at last. “Used to be a place for quiet negotiations between government defectors and rogue mercenaries. Now it’s a ghost market for anyone with dirt to trade and a death wish.”

Phainon gave a low whistle.

“And here I thought my social life was bleak.”

He picked up the mask, tilting it in the light, watching the way the dark filigree caught it like frozen lightning.

“Alright, boss,” he murmured.

“Showtime.”

Phainon’s fingers found the seam in the wall panel again.  A flick of his wrist, a grunt, and the thing came loose with a soft metallic groan. It clattered to the floor, sending up a breath of stale air thick with dust, brittle wiring insulation, and the oil-slick tang of long-decayed lubricant.

He wrinkled his nose.

“Still can’t believe I didn’t notice this for months,” he muttered, ducking his head as he slipped into the crawlspace beyond.

He worked his way down the narrow shaft, grime smearing his gloves, until the crawlspace spat him out at a rust-caked access grate. The thing hung half-off its hinges, damp with condensation. Phainon gave it a sharp kick and dropped through.

His boots hit metal platform with a hollow clang, the impact rattling the framework and sending a lazy sheet of dust billowing. The sublevel stretched out before him in the dim glow of failing emergency lamps. Crimson pulses blinked at uneven intervals, painting the space in alternating bands of light and shadow.

Phainon stretched his arms overhead in a long, theatrical sigh.

“Home sweet home.”

His voice fell flat in the cavernous hush.

He made his way along the walkway, the rusted grating echoing under his boots. Another maintenance door yielded under his shoulder with a groan, and the corridor beyond opened into a narrow alley—a scar between two industrial service blocks.

Phainon rolled his neck, a sharp crack breaking the stillness.

Anaxa’s voice came through.

“You have fifteen minutes. Recommend making that ten.”

Phainon huffed a breath, one corner of his mouth quirking.

“Loud and clear.”

And with that, he moved.

He slipped through blind spots he knew by heart. Down a forgotten service lot, into a stairwell barely wide enough for one person at a time. The deeper he went, the colder the air became, the walls sweating rust and condensation. Graffiti layered the walls in old spray paint, slogans bleeding through in palimpsest:

DON’T TRUST THEM THE TIDE COMES FOR US ALL

Most of it half-erased by now. The only ones left intact felt deliberate.

The stairwell finally coughed him out onto a long-dead subtram platform. Steel rails lay rusted and broken, choked in rubble and water stains. Faded directional signs still clung stubbornly to the walls in blocky, corroded text:

REACTOR ACCESS—RESTRICTED PERSONNEL ONLY

Phainon grinned, dropping down onto the old tracks with a soft grunt.

“Never gets old.”

A narrow corridor opened ahead—the walls curved and close. No emergency lights here.

He reached for his pocket.

Didn’t find what he was looking for.

Frowned. Checked the other.

Nothing.

A tightness gathered at the base of his throat.

“…Shit.”

He even spared a quick glance back toward the tunnel mouth, as if some miraculous twist of narrative would have left the access card lying right there, next to the towel he’d left behind like some rogue laundry deity had intervened.

“Anaxa?” he hissed under his breath.

A dry crackle of static in his ear, then Anaxa’s voice, too amused for the situation.

“Left side. Inner pocket.”

Phainon froze. Slid his hand along the inside lining of his jacket. Cold plastic met his fingers.

He sighed. Long. Put-upon.

“…You’re lucky you’re pretty.”

A beat.

“I know.”

The dry fondness there was almost worse.

Anaxa’s voice shifted back to pragmatic.

“Surveillance’s near-zero down here. Proximity sensors still trip if you’re careless. It’s another dead zone—good for a meet like this, claustrophobic for the rest of us.”

“Charming,” Phainon muttered, pulling the card free and adjusting the mask where it hung around his neck. He scanned the dim corridor ahead, feeling the hair at the back of his neck itch.

“Alright, so where’s my hatch?”

“Rusted bulkhead, left side,” came Anaxa’s reply. “Hidden behind a loose panel. Two meters ahead.”

Phainon sighed, cracking his knuckles as he moved forward.

“Knew you were gonna say that.”

The darkness pressed in around him as he searched.

It didn’t take long before his fingers brushed cold, corroded metal beneath a film of grime. A pressure hatch, half-swallowed by debris and broken conduit piping. The faded outline of a hazard placard clung stubbornly to the bulkhead, its warning symbols still visible through layers of rust.

Beneath it, a narrow keycard slot blinked a sullen red.

Phainon exhaled through his nose. He fished the card from his inner pocket, rolling it between his fingers for a moment.

“Once you’re inside the conduit—keep left. Ignore the first two ladder shafts. The third one leads to the substructure threshold. And whatever you do… don’t linger at the door.”

Phainon scoffed.

“Stars above, Anaxa, it’s a club, not a death cult.”

No reply.

He slid the keycard through the reader.

A muted beep. The hatch shuddered against its own age, locking mechanisms grinding before the seam split open with a sluggish hiss.

The passage beyond made him grimace.

Half-collapsed walls slouched inward, streaked with water stains and old mineral blooms. Pipes overhead ran in crooked lines, sagging beneath their own weight.

Phainon gave a resigned grunt.

“On second thought… you might’ve been right.”

And stepped inside.

Twice he passed ladder shafts, their iron rungs slick with condensation, vanishing into darkness above and below. He didn’t look. Didn’t slow.

The third waited where Anaxa had promised—dented, the paint long peeled away. Rust—or blood—flaked along the edges. He didn’t stop to check.

The path twisted once more before dead-ending.

Or it would have, to anyone else.

A slab of matte-finished metal stood embedded in the wall. Seamless. No handle, no terminal. Only a shallow indentation set beneath a blinking red light—and a figure waiting beside it.

Cloaked. Masked.

A pallid curve of ceramic, cracked with age, obscured the face beneath. Hollow eye slits stared through him. The figure didn’t speak.

Phainon slowed.

Anaxa’s voice returned, softer than before—a thread of a whisper:

“Do not look at the guard too long. Do not speak unless addressed.”

His jaw clenched. But he obeyed.

Eyes down.

No words.

He stepped forward, slotting the card into the reader.

A polite chime.

The metal slab split down the center, parting just wide enough for a rush of warm, close air to spill out. From somewhere beyond, music bled through —analog strings tuned to a minor key, the sound of a half-forgotten orchestra playing for a room no one had left in years.

Without waiting, Phainon stepped inside.

The door sealed behind him with a soundless hush.

And the air changed.

Warm, oil-sweet and thick with wax smoke and something medicinal. It clung to his throat, settled in his lungs.

Faded murals bled down the reactor walls, ghostly shapes half-lost to corrosion and time.

Somewhere ahead, a string quartet played. Not a recording—live. A quartet partially veiled behind drooping curtains, dressed in tattered formal wear. One of them dragged a viola bow across the strings, pulling long, dissonant notes that crawled along his spine.

Figures moved through the chamber, no two masks alike—some baroque, others grotesque. All designed to obscure. Eyes flickered through narrow slits, catching the light, marking his arrival.

Phainon rolled his shoulders loose, letting his pulse settle.

“Stay at the edges. Listen first. No trades until you know who’s here.”

He gave a shallow nod,

“Copy.”

The entry vestibule gave way to the main hall—a low, wide chamber held together by old reactor pillars. Thick curtains divided the space into makeshift alcoves and private enclaves where sharp whispers were traded.

Across the room, a trio he recognized from Anaxa’s dossiers—the Augurs’ Circle. Ink sigils marked their hands as they murmured over a glitching projection of black harmonics. Phainon didn’t slow.

The string music caught on a sour note.

“Seven faces not on the last manifest. Three Circle. One Vault broker I don’t trust. That’s Hyracian’s fixer by the east curtain. No deals till you clock him.”

Phainon’s lips barely moved.

“Copy. Taking a lap.”

He let himself drift. A peripheral presence, neither lurking nor conspicuous.

Near the south curtain, the Traders’ Cluster had gathered, their enclave loosely ringed around a scattering of brittle printouts and analog schematics.

Phainon angled himself beside a rusted support strut, posture casual. Close enough to catch voices. Far enough to remain forgettable.

“…clearing the manifest ahead of schedule.”

A gravel-voiced trader spoke, his mask cobbled from an old control panel casing, grime streaking the metal.

Another gave a derisive snort. “Cleanup protocol?”

“Would be, if there was a registry.” A third voice this time—younger. “No locational tag, no terminal codes logged. The entire manifest’s floating dark.”

That drew a pause.

“Another breach containment op?” someone ventured.

The gravel-voiced trader gave a humorless grunt. “Or a harvest pull.”

A fourth leaned in. Thin, breathy, words carrying just far enough:

“Synthetic-binding requisitions went out last cycle. High volume. But no accompanying retrieval logs. Not yet.”

That one landed.

Phainon felt a knot tighten at the base of his throat. So Anaxa wasn’t wrong — not exactly. The body transports weren’t a fabrication… but neither had they happened. The manifests were real, the prep work in motion. They just didn’t have the bodies yet.

Which meant the Council wasn’t covering up an event.

They were anticipating one.

Or worse, orchestrating it.

Anaxa’s voice came like a thread through the haze.

“Move along, lingering isn’t gonna help.”

Phainon exhaled through his teeth and peeled away, folding himself back into the wandering tide of masked shapes.

Near the east alcove, the Augurs’ Circle huddled around a magnetic map display. Its surface flickered with unsteady light. Ghostly flares bloomed across its surface, tracing the Black Tide’s latest spread along the outer parts.

Phainon adjusted his pace, letting their conversation bleed into the space between movements.

“…pattern shifts over the last cycle aren’t natural,” one old voice rasped, thick with an accent he didn’t recognize.

A half-mask in tarnished bronze turned toward a leaner figure swathed in Council-issue cloth—though the insignia had been scorched away.

“It’s moving like it’s being drawn,” the dissident murmured. “Tether points shifting without correlation. There’s no logic anymore.”

Phainon’s brow tightened, reading the tension in their postures more than their words.

Then one of them spoke, too soft.

“I saw her.”

The entire circle tensed.

A dry voice followed, laced with dread.

“By the breach perimeter. A woman. Dark hair. Violin in hand. Played like she wasn’t fully there—torso transparent like water.”

A ripple of sharp, quiet curses circled the group. Someone made a warding gesture with inked fingers.

Phainon’s pulse skipped, stomach giving a cold twist.

There was only one person that could be.

And only one rule Anaxa had ever delivered with absolute finality.

He couldn’t stop himself.

“‘We’re not chasing her. Not tonight,’” he muttered, just loud enough for Anaxa to hear, mimicking his words from before.

Anaxa’s response came as a low growl in his ear.

“If you get yourself pulled down by that specter, I’ll come find whatever’s left and finish the job myself.”

A smile tugged at the corner of Phainon’s mouth as he moved on.

Near the far end of the hall, the Vault guards stood. Two of them. Mirrored half-masks, cut from the same black glass, faces reflecting the restless light. No insignia, but their posture told the story.

They clocked him instantly.

One extended a gloved hand toward an embedded wall reader, silent.

Phainon retrieved his keycard. Ran it through.

A soft chime.

A nod from the left-hand guard. The curtain beyond parted just enough to admit him.

Anaxa’s voice returned, tension coiled around it.”

“This is primary circle territory. Confirm the broker’s presence before you so much as breathe about a trade. No assumptions. Half the Vault’s Council-aligned tonight, and you won’t know who’s who until it’s already too late.”

Phainon stepped through, the heavy curtain closing behind him.

Phainon moved with practiced ease.

He let his gaze drift, noting the faces—or masks.

A lean figure with a hex-glass visor that caught the light like a fault line.

Twin women in mirrored porcelain masks, their expressions unreadable, seated so still it unsettled.

And then—her.

Seated alone at a tarnished brass table near the east wall, half-veiled behind swaying chains sat the one known here as Ferris. Not her true name, but her reputation traveled well—a broker of classified manifests, embargo intercepts, and the sort of information that could make corpses long before morning.

Her mask was simple. A lacquered woodplate cut in the style of a mourning veil, the lower half of her face left bare: thin mouth, a sharp chin, and a pale scar that split the corner of her lip.

Anaxa had named that as the tell.

Phainon let his stride slow as he passed a nearby table, where two men bent over a map. His eyes caught on the empty chair across from her, then moved on—just long enough. He turned, stepped in, placed a single token chip on the table’s worn surface, and spoke the code phrase Anaxa had sent him minutes prior.

“A fine evening for ghosts.”

Ferris didn’t look up.

Her hand moved instead, fingers tracing the rim of a glass.

“The dead travel quickest when the lights go dark,” she replied idly.

Acknowledgment passed between them.

Without invitation, Phainon claimed the seat across from her.

A beat stretched.

“You’re late,” Ferris murmured, eyes flickering up, the scar at her lip tugging faintly.

“Unavoidable,” he returned. “Freight lines were a mess.”

The edge of a smirk ghosted over her mouth.

“Always are.”

The niceties spent, she leaned in—not by much, just enough for the words to slip beneath the vault’s thick hush.

“So. What’s your ask, traveler?”

Phainon tapped a knuckle once against the table’s edge, considering.

“Class-F transports. Manifests. Traffic patterns.”

That stilled her.

Just a slight pause, head tilting faintly, as if recalibrating the stakes.

After a moment, she reached beneath the table and drew out a narrow notepad—old paper, the edges browned—and flipped it open with a thumb.

“Those are sealed movements,” she said.

Phainon’s shoulders lifted in a loose shrug.

“Didn’t ask for the minutes. Just curious what’s shifting beyond the glow of polite company.”

A long, thoughtful silence.

Then, finally:

“Manifest code T-FLUX PRIMA.”

She tapped the page once, then angled it toward him, her fingers never leaving the edge.

“Council requisition. Two containment units. No contents listed.”

Phainon’s brow furrowed, an artful mimic of detached interest.

“Stasis caskets?” he asked.

“Empty ones. For now.”

Something in his gut twisted.

It wasn’t the confirmation—it was the implication.

Ferris let the words settle before continuing.

“The intended cargo’s marked viable carriers. Acquisition status: pending. No registry logs. Destination terminal’s blackout-tier. No comm traces, no preclearance pings. Too clean.”

Phainon exhaled softly through his teeth, murmuring without much inflection,

“Sounds like someone’s clearing a path for a bloodbath.”

A flicker of something—distaste, maybe, or grim familiarity—passed over Ferris’s face.

“Two options,” she said. “Either they’re prepping to sanitize a site no one wants traced. Or…”

She let the word trail, studying him.

He let a brow rise. “Or?”

“A projected incident,” Ferris murmured, eyes narrowing. “Casualties. Enough to merit containment units. If the Council’s clearing lanes this early, the bodies aren’t on the floor yet. But they will be.”

Phainon let the manifest code imprint itself in memory. T-FLUX PRIMA.

“An internal purge?” he asked, letting the note of naïve curiosity feather his tone.

Ferris gave a wry, humorless half-smile.

“Everyone here wagers on the things we’re paid to forget, traveler.”

She was closing the notepad when her hand stilled, fingers splaying briefly against the cover.

“Wait.”

Phainon tensed, a flicker of caution rising.

“The timing,” she murmured. “It’s too fast. Faster than Council procedure should allow. It isn’t some long-game purge. This feels like someone’s aligning stars. Tonight, maybe tomorrow. Before word spreads.”

A long breath.

“If you’ve any sense, you’ll be nowhere near it.”

She rose without another word, chain strands parting as she vanished into the veil of haze and oil-smoke.

Phainon remained seated.

Then, in one smooth motion, he rose, flicked the spent token chip toward the pool of candle wax at the table’s edge, and made for the exit.

He thumbed the comm bead by his jaw.

“You hear that?”

A beat.

“…Yeah. I heard it.”

Phainon ducked beneath a low sconce, sidestepping a pair of masked traders swapping chip vials.

“So,” he muttered, “I’m leaving. Obviously.”

A sharp sigh crackled over the line.

“Oh no, you’re not. Do you have any idea how many contacts I burned getting you that invite?”

“And it’s a fantastic party, Professor. Could use an hors d’oeuvre table though.”

“Phainon.”

He winced.

“Look. They’re moving soon, Anaxa. Whatever this cull, purge, sacrificial-theatrics-to-the-stars horseshit is, it’s planned. We hang around too long, we end up on one of those lists.”

Anaxa scoffed, brittle.

“We need eyes on the rest of the Vault. A thread, a route, anything that leads to the target site—”

“And no one here’s going to hand us that. Anyone who knows won’t say it in a place like this.”

Tension coiled tight between them.

“Damn it, Phainon. Don’t run now.”

“Not running. Calculating.”

Anaxa’s reply was poised on the edge of a retort when a sharp chime clipped through the channel—a muffled, distant alert tone on his end.

Phainon sighed.

“I’ll let you take that.”

He kept moving.

You didn’t draft a manifest like that unless you already knew who was going to die.

Forty-eight hours was optimistic. Could be half that. Hell—could be happening right now while he played dress-up in this crypt.

He was nearly to the outer corridor when he brushed a shoulder.

Tall figure.

Didn’t stop. Didn’t turn.

Lion mask.

A flicker of gold in the haze.

Phainon muttered, “Pardon.”

And kept going—but something about it snagged. A fishhook behind the eye.

The frame, the gait, the shape, everything.

Familiar.

He frowned. Have I—?

Gone. Swallowed by another knot of bodies.

“Anaxa,” he murmured, thumb to comm again. “Update?”

Silence.

A flicker of cold static.

A fine sweat prickled between his shoulder blades.

Then Anaxa’s voice came through, with a tightness Phainon had never heard.

“On second thought—get the fuck out. Now.”

It hit like a blow.

Phainon blinked. The sudden shift rattled him more than he’d like to admit.

“Uh, sure. But you wanna explain that dramatic pivot or—”

“Move.”

An order.

His pulse climbed.

“Anaxa. Talk to me.”

A brittle exhale on the line.

“Caught something on a sweep.”

Clinical now, which means he’s totally freaking out.

“Signature pattern. High-tier, masked so heavy I thought it was ambient noise. But it’s fresh. Residual traces riding the internal shielding.”

Phainon’s stomach turned.

“Which means what, exactly—”

“Which means there’s an Heir in proximity.”

His feet stopped moving.

He forced his voice steady.

“Who?”

A pause.

One beat too long.

Then:

“Godslayer.”

Silence.

A sharp, acid weight settled behind his ribs.

He swallowed.

“Anaxa,” he whispered, already moving again. “I need a path out.”

Phainon’s gaze flicked toward the last place he’d seen the lion mask.

His skin crawled.

The deeper he went, the more the station seemed to forget itself. Old service alcoves sealed by corroded gates, abandoned maintenance bays drowned in layers of dust thick as felt. The walls wept condensation, and half-dead cabling twitched in the gloom like nerves beneath scarred flesh.

“Anaxa,” he muttered, ducking behind a loose ventilation panel as a pair of traders passed. “This path is shit.”

“You’ll live,” came the reply, but there was an edge to it. “Front’s compromised. Too many unknowns shifting lanes. Take service passage Gamma-Seven-Five—tagging it now.”

A marker blinked in his retinal overlay, a faint ochre pulse bleeding through the haze ahead. It led toward a side corridor sagging under collapsed bulkheads and the ruin of flickering hazard signs.

He brushed his fingertips against the pitted wall as he moved, warping the thin skein of reality along the edges—slipping fractures into seams, fraying borders, turning angles just enough to be overlooked.

The din of the Merchant Vault faded behind him to cracked durasteel walls slick with reactor sweat.

He found the service passage.

A battered grate hung askew, one hinge rusted through. He slipped inside, boots hitting the greasy floor in absolute silence. The corridor narrowed to a maintenance tunnel barely wide enough for two men shoulder to shoulder, overhead bulbs guttering between dull amber and dead black.

“Alright,” he murmured, breath misting in the cold. “In. Alive.”

“Good. Stay sharp.”

The tunnel forked ahead. He veered toward the narrower passage instinctively, crowded with discarded vent covers, old stasis clamps, coiled transfer cables knotted like dead serpents. Perfect.
