“Get through it, princess. You can invoice me later.”

He ducked inside, pulling the warped panel closed behind him.  He moved on hands and knees, the air dense enough to taste, every sound amplified.

And then—footsteps.

Not rushed. Not hesitant. A steady, deliberate tread, pacing the corridor just beyond the vent wall.

Phainon froze.

His breath shallow, heartbeat ticking up not in panic, but in cold, efficient thought. Probably a scavenger. A stray trader. Nothing. He waited, spine pressed to the freezing metal, gaze fixed ahead.

“False alarm,” he murmured into the comm. “Someone passing through. No big—”

The footsteps slowed.

Drew parallel to the vent.

Stopped.

Phainon’s brow furrowed. The hairs at the nape of his neck lifted. It was the silence that did it. Not the pause itself—but the sense of it.

The tread moved on.

He exhaled slowly, tension bleeding out. A faint smile tugged at his mouth.

“See? Nothing. You get paranoid at your ag—”

A gauntleted fist punched clean through the vent wall beside him.

The shriek of tearing metal was a jagged, living thing in the dark. Before Phainon could even curse, a hand clamped around his ankle with unerring precision—inhumanly strong, cold fingers crushing down to bone.

“What the fu—”

It yanked.

Metal ripped like old cloth. He was dragged bodily from the crawlspace, his back slamming into the corridor’s grating hard enough to knock the wind from his lungs.

Instinct took over.

His hand snapped out, seizing a warped conduit. A pulse of resonance twisted it into a jagged spike and he drove it up toward his attacker’s throat.

The figure came through the torn vent in a single, terrible motion.

Godslayer.

Tall, built like a monument meant for executions. The lion mask from before—cracked now, its left side splintered like fractured bone. His presence hit like a shifting pressure, the air itself turning thick, resisting breath.

Phainon struck.

The jagged spike snapped forward, only to be caught mid-motion. Fingers closed around the weapon and crushed it to shrapnel.

“Shit—”

Phainon rolled, pulling the gravity around them into a warping lurch. Debris ripped free, conduits burst in showers of sparks, quick-flare snares detonating in his wake.

The Heir advanced through it as though moving through smoke.

“Stop,” the man’s voice said cautiously. “We can talk.”

“Not interested.” Phainon spat the words, twisting raw geometry into a barrage of shrapnel spikes. They drove at the Godslayer’s chest. It barely slowed him.

“Dearest Blasphemer,” Phainon snapped into the comm. “Plan B. Now.”

“Run.”

Phainon spun, slamming resonance threads into the floor to launch himself forward. Debris screamed behind him, the corridor buckling under the strain.

He ran.

Behind him, the Godslayer didn’t give immediate chase. But his voice followed, cutting through the din like a knife through cloth.

“You don’t know who you’re running from.”

Overhead conduits split apart, showering sparks. Lights burst in rapid succession, plunging whole sections of the corridor into stuttering half-dark. Pipes twisted inward, the walls warping themselves into crude, makeshift barricades behind him—not enough to stop what was coming, but maybe enough to delay it by a few precious seconds.

The footsteps didn’t falter.

“He’s still coming,” Phainon snapped, his voice brittle, breath ragged from the sprint.

“No shit. Listen to me—you’re close. Two levels down there’s a reactor sub-chamber. Cut through there. South wall’s got a service exit. That’ll drop you into an exhaust conduit I can patch into. Keep moving!”

Anaxa’s voice wasn’t steady either. There was a rawness to it, something uncharacteristically frayed. Not anger.

Fear.

The air ahead shimmered, a rupture yawning open along the tunnel wall—a narrow tear in the weave of space, unstable and half-born, edges flickering like heat haze caught inside fractured glass.

Phainon didn’t hesitate. He dove for it shoulder-first, the distortion pulling at his skin like wet static. Reality bent, folded, snapped, and he tumbled through, hitting cold durasteel on the other side hard enough to jar his teeth.

The sub-chamber stretched out around him—vast and hollow, the dead heart of a long-abandoned system. Reactor conduits rose like fossilized bones, crusted with corrosion, vanishing into the blackness overhead.

“I’m in,” he panted.

“Good—good. South wall, you’ll see a ladder, right side. It’ll—”

A burst of static swallowed Anaxa’s voice. When it returned, it cracked with urgency.

“Wait—wait, fuck. He’s rerouting. Phainon, don’t stop. Don’t stop moving.”

Phainon moved along the chamber’s edge, weaving between corroded supports and half-collapsed conduit runs. His eyes tracked the catwalks above, searching for any movement. Nothing.

His pulse slowed, just for a moment. A cold sheen of sweat traced the side of his face.

“Anaxa… how the hell did he—”

A flicker.

It wasn’t movement. It was something else—a wrongness in the air, a presence his instincts registered before his mind could name it.

He turned.

Too slow.

A hand clamped around his wrist, fingers encasing bone and tendon like iron bands. The cold shock of contact drove his heart up into his throat.

He hadn’t heard a thing.

No rush of breath. No ripple in the air. One heartbeat there was nothing, and the next—Godslayer.

“Stop,” the voice practically hissed. “I don’t want to hurt you. Just listen to me for one second.”

Every nerve in Phainon’s body screamed at once.

Go. Now.

“Go fuck yourself.”

He wrenched free, lashing out with a pulse of raw distortion from his palm. The space between them shattered like brittle glass, jagged lines cracking outward. The Heir raised his gauntleted hand, and the energy dispersed against it, harmless as mist breaking against stone.

Phainon’s other hand snapped up. Threads of force tangled in the air, coalescing into a flickering shield of warped space. He drove it forward like a battering ram. It struck with a sound like a freight train collision—the shield spiderwebbed, buckled, and burst.

Pain rattled his arm down to the shoulder.

He didn’t stop.

A conduit coil snapped loose with a flick of his wrist, reshaping mid-air into a jagged spear. He thrust it forward. Godslayer parried with an almost contemptuous motion, metal on metal.

Another pulse of force rolled between them, space distorting violently under Phainon’s feet. He hurled himself back, calling every last fraying thread of resonance to him. Hovering lengths of conduit and sheared metal shivered and lifted, spinning around him in a ragged halo.

But his grip on them was tenuous. The fatigue was setting in. His threads faltered, the makeshift weapons flickering unsteadily, shapes warping under his own failing control.

“Damn it,” Phainon hissed. “Route me an exit. Now.”

“I’m trying! Just buy me thirty seconds. That’s all I need!”

Godslayer advanced through the debris, moving like a shadow behind firelight, sidestepping the burst of collapsing gravity and the shrieking

distortions of his thrown spikes. Three launched. One shattered. Another spun wide as warped air knocked it off course. The last came apart mid-flight, dissolving into useless fragments.

Phainon’s heart thundered.

Fissures splitting the floor, spatial tears forming like wounds in the air, the strain of his overtaxed abilities turning reality brittle.

The Heir came on, unhurried.

“I’m not your enemy,” the masked voice said cautiously.

Phainon’s fist connected with the mask in a wild, furious swing. A sharp jolt of pain ran up his wrist as bone struck hardened composite. Godslayer didn’t so much as reel. The mask turned, fractionally, a slow pivot as though assessing.

“You don’t have to do this.”

“Then stop chasing me!” Phainon snarled, teeth bared, sweat burning his eyes.

Anaxa’s voice cut in, sharp and breathless. “Exit’s open! North vent— behind that coolant manifold—move, now!”

He sent a final destabilizing pulse behind him, the floor cracking as gravity inverted for an instant. Debris shot upward in a lethal scatter.

It wasn’t enough.

He ran, every muscle screamed, nerves lit to fire, the edges of his vision tunneling. Warped space trailed behind him in flickering arcs as he sprinted for the coolant manifold.

He didn’t look back.

The pressure of that presence lingered at his heels.

And it was gaining.

The tears he forced open were collapsing faster than he could hold them. His grip on his abilities was slipping, and fast.

“Anaxa,” Phainon hissed into his comm, voice fraying. “I need a path—”

Only static answered him. The comm cracked, hissed, then fell silent under the crush of interference. The line was dead.

He was alone.

A weight struck his side with brutal force. Phainon’s world spun, the breath punched from his lungs as his ribs collided hard against the frozen curve of a coolant pipe. The shock of impact jolted through his spine, a strangled sound catching in his throat.

The blow wasn’t clean. It hadn’t meant to be. There was restraint buried somewhere in it, like whoever hit him had pulled back at the last second— enough to stop him without breaking anything.

Before he could recover, a hand closed over his shoulder, another around his wrist, pinning him against the ice-flecked metal.

The lion-faced mask hovered only a breath away.

“Phainon.”

The name hit like a hammer, a shattering crack through the fog in his head.

His chest seized.

No one should know his name.

Not here. Not now.

Panic surged, rising so fast it blurred his vision, making his skin prickle cold. He twisted violently, straining against the grip, abilities lashing out in wild, jagged arcs around him.

“Let me go,” Phainon rasped, the edge of raw panic threading his voice in a way he didn’t have time to hide.

The hands didn’t tighten, didn’t strike back—they just held firm.

“Phainon.” The voice again, lower this time, softened beneath the distortion field of the mask. There was something beneath the artificial grit, a cadence that should not have belonged here in a place like this. “It’s alright. Breathe.”

His vision shimmered, tunnelled at the edges. His heart hammered so hard it felt like his ribcage would splinter beneath it. He kept fighting—instinct and terror demanded it—though some part of him registered that the hold wasn’t cruel. It anchored, rather than crushed.

“Listen to me,” the figure said quietly. “You don’t have to keep running. You’re safe, right here.”

Safe.

The word barely meant anything anymore. It ricocheted uselessly against the inside of his skull, swallowed by adrenaline.

Phainon bared his teeth. “I don’t know who the fuck you think—”

“It’s me.”

A murmur. Barely more than breath, softened in a way that made no sense. It slipped between the cracks in his panic, threading through the din of his pulse in a way nothing else could’ve managed.

His hands shifted, loosening by the smallest margin. Not enough to let him bolt—but enough to ease the strain. A hand like that didn’t hesitate without reason.

Something about it made him falter.

He could have torn a metaphysical gate wide and fled, could’ve shattered the air itself and vanished into whatever frayed geometry this place had left.

But instead…

“I’m not here to hurt you,” the masked figure said again. “I swear it, Phainon. You’re alright. I’ve got you.”

It shouldn’t have worked.

But somehow, it did.

The violent pounding of his heart didn’t stop, but it staggered. His muscles trembled beneath his skin, on the cusp of fight or flight, but something about that tone—the weight behind those words—slowed the inevitable. The way it was spoken, not desperate, not cruel, but steady, almost gentle.

It was disarming in a way Phainon didn’t have the language for.

The gauntlet shifted again. This time, two fingers brushed against his pulse point at his throat.

“You feel that?” the voice asked. “You’re here. Stay with me.”

His throat bobbed in a swallow he didn’t remember choosing.

He should’ve fought. Should’ve ripped reality open and left this place bleeding behind him. But still, he didn’t move.

It made no sense. Nothing about this did.

“It doesn’t have to be like this,” Godslayer said softly. “You’ll be fine.”

A ridiculous promise in a place like this. And yet…

something inside Phainon unspooled, just a fraction.

For the briefest instant, it felt like the air around them thinned. As though a different version of this moment tried to force itself through.

Phainon’s voice cracked when it finally came. “What… what do you want from me?”

Godslayer leaned a fraction closer, vapor curling between them.

“To talk to you.”

And then—

The air split with the sharp, rising howl of an alarm. A blaring, violent wail that knifed through the chamber, fracturing the fragile quiet between them.

Both men stiffened.

Voices cut down from the catwalk above, distorted through amplifiers, sharp and cold.

“By authority of the Council—designation Flame Reaver, you are hereby claimed into custody for high resonance destabilization, unauthorized breach of containment, and reckless destabilization of restricted sectors. Stand down immediately and prepare for retrieval.”

Phainon’s stomach lurched, blood turning to ice.

He jerked against the grip instinctively. “What the fuck—”

The sound hit like a hammer to the skull, reverberating through bone, every syllable a dull, concussive pulse inside his head. His heartbeat surged, a nauseating heat flooding his limbs, his chest straining against itself.

The grip on his shoulder tightened. He felt the gauntlet flex against bone and muscle, tension bleeding through the metal.

“Wait—Phainon—I didn’t—” The voice cracked, something desperate threading beneath the sound.

But none of it mattered.

The catwalk blurred, figures smearing into shadowed shapes. Every bootfall, every word, every echo slammed into him like shockwaves.

His chest seized.

Of course. Of course.

This had been it. The setup. Draw him out. Pretend to ease him down. Get him to lower his guard. And then deliver him straight into the Council’s hands.

A trap.

The coolant mist thickened around him. Pressure pressed against his temples. His stomach turned. The sound of his own breath came in sharp, ragged gasps he couldn’t control.

“No—you planned this,” Phainon spat.

He shoved violently against the grip. Pain lanced down his arm as his shoulder jarred. He didn’t care. Couldn’t care. Instinct hijacked thought. His elbow struck him with a dull crack. Resonance bled out from him in uncontrolled slashes, sharp arcs of volatile light breaking against the gloom.

“Don’t—don’t touch me, get the fuck off—let me go—I’m not—I won’t—”

His voice broke.

Then the comm roared to life in his ear, a burst of static that spiked through his skull like a blade. Anaxa’s voice beneath it, jagged and desperate.

“PHAINON MOVE—GET OUT—MOVE MOVE MOVE—”

Too loud.

Too much.

His breath hitched in sharp, shallow pulls. Couldn’t fill his lungs. Couldn’t think. The coolant vapor crawled against his skin. The walls warped. Every edge buckled. The sound of boots on the catwalk above blended into a single relentless drumbeat behind his ribs.

I’m trapped. They’re gonna take me. Strap me down. Cut me

Rip through my head. Dig through my bones. I’ll never come back. I won’t—I can’t—

He could see it.

The restraint rigs. The cold straps across his arms. The sharp press of metal against his throat. Needles in his spine. White light over his face. The sound of his own scream, distant and thin, a thing disconnected from the body it came from.

Godslayer’s voice tried to cut through, ragged and frayed.

“I didn’t call them—I swear it—”

It barely registered. Muffled, drowned out, like shouting underwater. Phainon clamped his hands over his ears, thin crackling tendrils flickering uncontrolled. The coolant mist twisted, shapes moving where nothing should’ve been.

Anaxa’s voice merged with Godslayer’s with the pounding boots and the scream of the alarm—no separation anymore, just noise, one suffocating, deafening crush that filled every corner of him.

I’mgonnadieI’mgonnadieI’mgonnadieI’mgonnadieI’mgonnadie—

His knees buckled.

A choking, high sound escaped his throat. His vision blurred at the edges. The room spun, walls folding in. Every thought, every instinct spiraled.

They’re gonna cut me open. They’re gonna open my head. Dig through me. Pull the pieces out. I won’t come back this time. I can’t—I can’t—

And then —

silence.

Not real, but enough.

A flicker.

A single memory cleaving through the suffocating dark.

“Thoracic. Upper mid-spine. Somewhere between T7 and T11.”

A pinpoint.

A single, impossible anchor in the flood.

His fingers twitched.

One small, unsteady movement.

His breath stuttered, catching on the ragged edge of a sob he never fully made.

His other hand fumbled, scraping numbly against the cold coolant pipe at his side. He didn’t even know he was moving, his body following instinct.

The world narrowed to a single, flickering point between T7 and T11.

Everything else—the voices, the pounding footsteps, the alarms, the crushing walls—fell away.

Just a target.

Just one desperate, dying chance.

His knees hit the grated floor with a sharp clang. Arms scrabbled weakly against Godslayer’s frame. The hold around his shoulders instinctively loosened. A hand clamped at his ribs, steadying him.

“Hey—” The voice cracked, a frayed edge of concern bleeding into it. Too close to something Phainon knew but couldn’t name. It slipped under his skin like a needle.

And that was the opening.

His fingers twitched.

A fractured pulse of energy gathered in his palm—not a clean resonance spike, no neat construct, but a jagged, unstable splinter of ambient charge scavenged from the chaos around them: bent conduits, collapsed magnetic seals, the room’s gravity fields knotting and flexing like a storm surge.

It burned in his palm. The skin split, thin strands of flickering white-gold light bleeding through his fingertips. Blood mixed with it. His nose leaked crimson.

Good.

It was real enough.

In the heartbeat of feigned collapse—as Godslayer’s grip shifted, one hand moving to brace him—Phainon surged what was left of his strength into that single, desperate strike.

And drove the crude spike upward.

Straight into the narrow, lethal gap between thoracic plates.

T7 to T11.

Exactly where Anaxa had said.

The effect was immediate—a sickening, resonant crack as the spike punched through pulse fields and nerve bundles. The charge lashed out, sending a jolt through the other man’s frame. Godslayer’s body recoiled. A strangled, guttural sound burst—halfway between a grunt and a choked curse. His hold spasmed, locking for a half second… then gave.

His knees buckled.

Phainon shoved himself free, stumbling back, his whole body screaming in protest. Vision blurred, chest heaving in sharp, thin pulls. Every nerve lit with raw, static agony.

But he was up.

Alive.

And then it happened—a sound he hadn’t expected.

Godslayer staggered against a coolant pipe, one hand pressed hard against his side. Blood welled between his fingers, staining the gauntlet, thick and dark.

And in a raw, guttural rasp, so low it barely registered over the alarms—

“…How?”

A word ripped from somewhere primal. Not a curse. Not an accusation.

A question.

One no one should ever need to ask.

Phainon froze. Just for a breath. Just long enough to feel it—the weight of what he’d done hanging between them like a loaded charge.

Godslayer’s gaze—dark through the cracked visor—locked on him. Wide. Disbelieving. There was no vengeance in it. No anger.

Only that stunned, uncomprehending horror of a man who thought he was unkillable realizing, for the first time, that he wasn’t.

Phainon’s pulse hammered in his ears. The spike dissolved in his hand, motes of unstable light unraveling into nothing. His skin stung where the energy had burned him.

He turned—because he had to—scanning for a way out. Every step felt unsteady, like moving through water, his legs uncertain beneath him.

Behind him, something small struck the floor.

A metallic clink.

A soft, steady roll.

A ring.

Simple. Plain. A worn signet catching the coolant haze as it spun, tracing a lazy arc across the grated floor.

It came to rest against the side of his boot.

Phainon’s foot twitched.

He stared.

Not at the bloodied man crumpled against the pipe.

Not at the Heirs above, shouting, closing in.

At the ring.

At the insignia carved into its face.

And for one single, stuttering heartbeat—the whole world stopped.

The noise, the alarms, the pressure—all of it fell away.

Nothing but the ring.

And the terrible, impossible recognition curling in his stomach like a blade.

The world spun, and somewhere in the background, Godslayer’s ragged, fading breath choked out again —

“How…?”

Phainon didn’t move.

Couldn’t.

And then the moment shattered.

He crouched, his knees creaking against the grated floor. His hand didn’t feel like his own. It trembled as his fingers closed around the ring, the small, unassuming weight of it somehow heavier than the weapon he’d just forged.

The metal was cold.

It bit into his palm.

A smear of blood clung to the underside, drying in a thin line.

For a moment, nothing else existed.

No alarms.

No closing boots.

No screaming comms.

Only that object—the ring, the impossible familiarity of it, and the quiet rasp of his own breathing stuttering against the back of his throat.

Anaxa’s voice snapped.

“Phainon.”

Another burst of static, rough, ragged, his voice frayed in the way it only got when something was already too far gone.

“What the fuck are you doing—”

He didn’t answer.

Couldn’t.

His gaze stayed locked on the ring, the insignia etched into its surface, the way light caught against a faint, uneven mark near its edge. His pulse thudded in his ears, drowning the rest of the world to a dim, distant hum.

His throat worked. A breath caught.

Then words came, breaking apart in his mouth before they fully formed.

“Rings are common,” he murmured.

The sound of his own voice startled him. It didn’t sound like something he’d said. It was thin, loose, disjointed, as though spoken by a stranger standing just to his left.

“People have them.” Another breath. “It’s not… it doesn’t mean anything. It’s just a ring.”

A beat of silence on the comm.

Then Anaxa again, stumbling.

“What—?”

“It’s normal.” His words sharpened, an edge creeping in unbidden. “Anyone could have one. People wear them. It’s just a thing. Just a piece of fucking metal.”

A breath huffed out, something too harsh to be called a laugh.

“It’s a coincidence.”

A sound behind him.

Not a curse, not a snarl—something softer, cracked and hoarse, a threadbare remnant of a voice dragging his name like it hurt to speak.

“Phainon…”

The word crumbled in the air.

It hit him harder than the alarms ever could.

His spine stiffened.

A cold, animal terror settled in his stomach—not the sharp, bright kind that came with battle, but something heavier. The dread that crept in when your mind recognized what your heart hadn’t yet, when you knew something was wrong in the way gravity sometimes felt heavier just before a fall.

His fingers turned the ring in his palm.

And there it was.

The scratch.

A thin, diagonal gouge along the outer curve of the insignia. Stupid, meaningless damage. A mark from a half-forgotten night in a back alley years ago, a piece of fencing, a fight Phainon had mocked him for afterward, grinning through split lips while warning him to stop getting involved in things that didn’t matter.

That scratch shouldn’t be here.

Couldn’t be here.

Not on a Heir-issued ring.

Not on a dead man’s hand.

His pulse surged.

The comm kept crackling—Anaxa’s voice rising now, strained, desperate, but it might as well have been radio static.

None of it mattered.

The only sound was the rasp of a shallow breath behind him.

And his own heartbeat, loud and relentless in his ears.

Phainon stood.

His legs didn’t want to. It took effort. The ring bit deeper into his palm, the edges sharp against his skin.

He crossed the floor.

Each step felt longer than the last.

Metal groaned above.

The cooling systems hissed and stuttered.

The storm of movement on the catwalk blurred to a distant, inconsequential clatter.

His hand reached out.

Fingers found the fractured edge of the lion mask—cracks radiating from the place his strike had landed. His grip closed over it, the modulator sparking against his palm in protest.

And then he pulled.

A single, steady motion.

The mask came away.

Blonde hair, matted with blood and coolant vapor.

A face beneath it, pale and battered, lips parted on a shallow, ragged breath.

Phainon stared.

Every detail landed like a blow—not a sudden impact, but a slow, crushing weight.

The curve of the jaw.

The line of the brow.

Every impossible detail.

The ring slipped from his fingers. It hit the floor with a dull clink and rolled lazily to a stop.

His knees gave out.

He dropped, not with violence, but like a man whose strings had been cut. A sharp, broken sound clawed from his throat—somewhere between a gasp and a sob, though his eyes stayed dry.

He didn’t speak.

Couldn’t.

Could only kneel there, frozen, the breath torn from his lungs as the impossible face of Mydei bled quietly in front of him.

Phainon’s hand trembled as it brushed the side of the bloodied face, fingertips ghosting over skin gone clammy with coolant mist and blood. Too cold. Too still.

“Mydei…”

The word broke in his throat, thin and brittle.

He eased him down, cradling Mydei’s head against his chest. The floor dropped away. The walls seemed to breathe, the air gone thin and sharp as glass. He could barely feel the weight in his arms. Everything felt stretched, too far.

“You’re fine,” Phainon murmured, voice catching. “You’re okay. It’s—it’s nothing.”

It wasn’t a lie.

It was a prayer.

His voice came out high and breathless, a raw insistence, like if he could just string the words together fast enough, reality would remember its shape and obey.

“Hey. C’mon. Look at me. You always—”

A laugh snagged in his throat, brittle as cracked glass. It came out wrong. Too bright. Too sharp.

A faint sound from the figure in his arms—a broken breath that might have been a word.

“…m’sorry.”

Phainon froze.

The world tipped, something cold sinking teeth into his stomach.

“No,” he whispered, breath hitching. His grip tightened. “No, you don’t— you don’t get to say that. You don’t—fuck—you’re fine. We’ll leave. We’ll —”

The presence behind him arrived like a tide.

Not stealth.

Not subtlety.

The kind of dread you felt in your bones before you even heard them move.

The Council enforcers fanned out across the catwalk and floor, armored boots ringing against metal, the dull thrum of kinetic induction charges humming at his back—weapons primed, safeties off.

One of them spoke.

“Hold position. That’s him. Engage.”

Another breathless half-second.

And Phainon’s mind broke open.

A laugh slipped from him.

Soft at first.

A fractured, unmoored thing.

Then another, louder, bleeding out between his teeth like something sharp.

The sound didn’t belong in the room.

It didn’t belong anywhere.

The enforcers faltered. A ripple of hesitation through them, armor sensors flickering against some invisible pressure spike. Even through visors and synaptic dampeners, something primal in them recoiled.

And then it happened.

Not clean.

Not like an overcharged amplifier popping its buffer.

The air fractured.

Light stuttered.

The walls around him blurred, textures doubling, then peeling apart.

Phainon’s hair kept flickering between white-gold like a glitch, threads of gold spiderwebbing through the veins beneath his skin. His irises caught the failing emergency lights, burning molten amber one heartbeat, normal blue the next.

The pressure in the room surged.

A low, bone-deep hum vibrated through the walls, rattling teeth and glass. You didn’t hear it so much as feel it in the roots of your teeth, in the back of

your skull.

The nearest enforcer staggered, one hand going to his helmet.

“Get out. Disengage—the man is a lunatic!”

Machinery buckled.

A coolant conduit burst overhead, vapor hissing down in thick fog.

Floodlights cracked, the glass breaking in long, languid arcs as though gravity had to be reminded to finish the job.

Phainon didn’t know what he was doing.

Blood slipped from his nose, from his ear, a thin line down his throat.

He didn’t feel it.

The floor beneath his boots warped—not metaphorically. The metal flexed. A concave ripple moved out in a perfect ring from his feet. Golden shards shimmered in the air, fragments of resonance unbound from their logical moorings, hanging like the splinters of a shattered star.

The enforcers backed up.

But too late.

Phainon’s laugh broke again—louder this time, serrated at the edges.

And the collapse came.

His body seized, resonance surging outward in a cascade of concentric waves. Not light. Not heat. The boundaries of space and matter folded like wet paper, walls bending inward, catwalks shuddering, alloy pylons twisting as if they remembered they were never meant to hold this kind of force.

The resonance imploded, then detonated in a pulse so violent the shockwave kicked half the enforcers off their feet.

Sirens blared.

Not the usual incursion protocols.

The system lights shifted from red to a cold, sterile white.

A new warning replaced the alarms.

[CLASS ONE BREACH DETECTED] [BLACK TIDE EVENT PROBABILITY: 72%—EVACUATE IMMEDIATELY]

The walls wept condensation as the temperature dropped.

The floor panels liquefied, then re-solidified.

Somewhere high above, a structural support failed, the screech of metal shearing under strain echoing through the dark.

Phainon barely registered it.

His vision blurred, faces melting to shapes, colors bleeding into one another.

The ring in his fist dug so deep into his palm the skin split, blood mixing with the golden resonance still clawing at the air around him.

He knelt there, one hand still tangled in Mydei’s hair, the other clenched tight, as the world came undone.

And for the first time in years—maybe ever —

He had no control over his abilities.

Phainon’s lips moved soundlessly, cracked, mouthing the same words over and over.

“I’m sorry. I’m sorry. I’m sorry.”

A mantra, a prayer, a death rattle in disguise.

Then—footsteps.

Not one pair.

Many.

From the far corridor, the enforcers poured in, their resonance dampeners slung across their backs, pulse ordnance primed. They moved in formation —rigid, tens.

“Hold formation. Target unstable,” the squad leader barked, visor down. “Deploy containment on my mark—”

He didn’t finish.

The first field flared up—a mesh of light and spatial anchors snapping into place around Phainon.

It buckled in less than a second.

The space around him ate it, the energy net twisting, folding back on itself like a living thing curling from fire. The projection whined, tore apart in a burst of white-gold static, leaving nothing but scorched air in its wake.

“What the fuck is wrong with—”

Another containment net fired. Same result.

A third.

Space itself seemed to ripple with disdain.

Then one of them—desperate or catastrophically foolish—edged closer, trying to flank, hoping for the lucky shot.

The resonance didn’t strike him. It didn’t need to.

A single tendril of that flickering light—thin as a vein, sharp as a filament —brushed the man’s chest.

He locked up mid-step. His scream rose but never left his throat. His veins went dark, then gold, then black, fat strands spiderwebbing under his skin like roots burrowing through rotting wood.

His eyes burst first. Then his skull caved in from the pressure building behind it, helmet splitting like fruit under a press.

Blood. Grey matter. A soft, wet explosion against the wall.

The body dropped, nerves still twitching.

Phainon didn’t react.

Didn’t even blink.

He clutched Mydei tighter, murmuring to no one, words unraveling into cracked, half-formed sounds.

More enforcers hesitated. Some started backing up.

The pressure in the room rose, a deep, concussive weight that pressed into lungs and made breathing a conscious effort.

Sirens shifted again.

[EMERGENCY BREACH IMMINENT—BLACK TIDE ESCALATION PROTOCOL ENGAGED]

System-wide. Not a facility alarm. Not a sector alert.

The whole city.

That was when the dying began in earnest.

One enforcer’s helmet visor spiderwebbed from the inside, the man clawing at his throat as his organs liquefied mid-sentence. His scream turned into a bubbling gurgle as his chest caved in.

Another staggered back, convulsing as blood burst from his ears, his brain tissue boiling inside his skull. He dropped, limbs twitching like severed cords.

The others lost formation.

Someone yelled for retreat.

And it wouldn’t have mattered.

The walls bent inward, catwalks shrieking, steel pylons warping. A coolant line burst, showering the chamber in mist so cold it flash-froze blood mid-air into crystalline droplets.

Phainon’s abilities lashed out without aim or mercy. Tendrils  cracked the floor like glass, split a man’s torso clean through, his upper half peeling away from his waist in a neat, bloodless instant before the spray hit.

It was less a fight and more a massacre.

And then—

A flicker.

Behind the enforcers.

Not a displacement boom.

Just a distortion.

Like heat shimmer on asphalt, the air rippled. A fragmentary, sickening lurch in the space behind the last remaining soldier.

The squad leader spun, trying to catch it.

Too late.

A sharp, brutal crack split the air.

An old, ugly sound.

A bullet through bone.

The leader’s head snapped back, a plume of blood fountaining from the exit wound. He collapsed in a heap.

“Contact, behind—”

Another shot. Skull. Gone.

A third. Through the heart.

A fourth. The base of the spine.

Each shot surgical. Unhurried. Cold.

The enforcers broke, stumbling in blind terror now, some collapsing, others trying to scream commands the air didn’t seem to carry.

Phainon barely noticed.

His breathing rattled in his throat, golden light seeping from his eyes, his nose, from the hairline fractures webbing across his skin. His vision blurred, everything smeared, golden-blue-red.

The air buckled again.

And through it stepped a figure.

The distortion resisted him, the shimmering wall of sickened air reluctant to let him through. The man emerged, smoke still curling off the sleeves of his longcoat, a battered sidearm steady in his grip.

Anaxa.

The prototype phase-slip device flickered at his hip, still smoldering. The kind of tech you don’t use inside a unstable collapse zone unless you’ve given up on coming back whole.

And yet, here he was.

Anaxa sighed.

“Of all the places to spike,” he muttered. “Had to pick the one wired for full-detection response.”

Phainon’s power lashed toward him. Tendrils sharp enough to split steel.

And stopped.

Mid-air.

A shudder.

A flicker.

Like recognition.

Anaxa took another step forward. Then another.

“Easy,” he murmured. His voice wasn’t soothing. It was the kind you used with cornered animals and dying friends. “It’s me.”

Phainon clutched Mydei tighter, shivering, his eyes caught somewhere between hatred and plea.

His voice shredded the air.

“Stay… stay back.”

But Anaxa didn’t stop.

Glass crunched underfoot. Bone. Metal.

The dying field snarled around him, rippling, hissing against his skin, but it didn’t touch him.

He knelt.

One slow, careful motion. Not reaching. Just lowering himself beside Phainon.

He glanced down at the bloodied, ruined thing in Phainon’s arms. The shattered mask. The skin gone pale.

And Anaxa’s jaw clenched.

A breath. A shake of his head, small, broken.

“I’m sorry.”

He moved fast.

Suppressant injector in hand, pressed against Phainon’s throat. A single, brutal push of the plunger.

Phainon spasmed. The light in his eyes flared, cracked, and then —

the world tilted.

Phainon convulsed instantly, a sound torn from his throat so raw it barely resembled a scream—more a ragged, broken noise scraped from the back of his lungs. Pain spiked white-hot from the point of injection, radiating out in jagged, shuddering waves that clawed through his nerves and ignited every frayed thread of his unraveling signature.

His body fought it, violently, lashing cracking out like wild, blood-edged lightning, fracturing the air in sharp, erratic bursts. The room buckled again, tendrils warping into existence and then snapping apart as the suppressant tore through him.

For a sickening second it felt as though his bones would rupture, splitting apart from the inside out, pressure building so fast his vision went blood-

black at the edges. His fingers clenched tighter around Mydei’s limp form as if bracing for the moment his own body gave out.

Anaxa’s hand came down, pinning him by the shoulder.

“Stay down. Let it take.”

Phainon thrashed, muscles seizing in relentless spasms. His vision smeared gold and blue, blood seeping into his eyes. Every breath dragged itself through him like glass, his ribs shuddering with the effort of keeping his heart from tearing itself apart. The suppressant didn’t numb the agony—it gnawed its way deeper, latching onto the last flickers of his spiral and tearing them loose one by one.

The threads stuttered. Broke.

One by one, those razor-edged tendrils dimmed.

The flickering edges of unreality around him began to smooth, the impossible fractures in space retreating like receding tidewater, leaving shattered debris and silence in their wake.

Golden shards of dead light fell from the air, brittle as glass. They struck the floor with a strange, crystalline clatter, like fragments of bone. The oppressive pressure in the room slackened in aching increments, but it never fully left.

And then nothing remained but the hollow rasp of Phainon’s own ragged breathing.

He sagged forward, every part of him shaking, still clutching Mydei’s body as if he could force it back together with sheer will. The blood on his skin glimmered faintly before dulling, tears in his flesh sealing themselves with sluggish, flickering effort. His body tried to recover. It didn’t succeed.

Anaxa moved immediately, catching him before he collapsed completely. He hooked an arm around Phainon’s torso, steadying him.

“You’re alright. I’ve got you.” His voice was stripped bare of softness but still solid. A tether.

Phainon clung to it like a drowning man, fingers fisting into Anaxa’s sleeve, blood-slick and desperate.

Neither of them moved for what felt like an eternity.

Somewhere beyond the breached walls, the wail of sirens began to rise again—a new chorus. Not just the Council’s systems now. Different tones. Higher frequencies. Citywide emergency signatures. Strike-force mobilizations.

They were coming.

Phainon barely noticed at first, too lost in the suffocating weight of his own breathing, the too-sharp ache of his pulse hammering behind his eyes.

Anaxa heard them.

And he snorted, a dry sound.

“I’m shocked the Heirs haven’t landed on your head yet. Guess they’re slipping.”

It should’ve been a joke.

It wasn’t.

Phainon’s stomach twisted, nausea and panic clawing at the base of his throat. The edges of his vision swam. His voice broke, thin and frayed.

“Don’t.”

A whisper, no weight to it.

“Don’t. Don’t do this. Anaxa, don’t—”

Anaxa didn’t respond. His jaw set, something flickering behind his eyes too tired to be anger, too resigned to be grief.

Phainon’s hand shot out, fingers seizing a fistful of his coat, slipping against blood and sweat-slick fabric.

“I can’t—” the words came in a breathless, splintered rush, raw with panic and grief, his throat already wrecked but the words tearing their way free anyway. “I can’t do this without you, don’t leave me here, I’ll fix it, I swear to god I’ll fix it, just—just don’t—”

A sharp shake of the head.

Anaxa’s expression softened in that terrible, exhausted way that felt worse than anger.

“I can’t hold this place, Phainon.”

Quiet. Final.

“You’ve gotta go.”

“No—”

Phainon’s voice broke into something too ugly to be a word.

Anaxa exhaled, a thread of dry, humorless sound, and pulled a battered, half-cracked device from his coat. The last portable foldpoint unit. It shimmered faintly, edges scorched, the casing dented from the jump that brought him here.

“One tether left.” His lips twitched in something almost like a smile. “Didn’t even think. Ran straight in. That’s not me, you know.”

Phainon’s chest caved in around the ache, heart hammering so loud the sirens became little more than distant, meaningless noise.

Anaxa’s grip on the phase tether tightened.

“Find Hysilens when you’re back.”

A beat.

And then, quieter.

“One chance, boy. Take it.”

Phainon barely had time to choke out a sound before Anaxa pressed the foldpoint against his chest, locked eyes with him for one last heartbeat, and slammed the activator home.

The world ruptured around him.

White-hot light. A sickening scream of gravity folding in on itself. The sense of every molecule in his body tearing loose, shredded by unstable space —

and then nothing.

By the time he realized he was still alive, it was because his body struck the floor.

Hard.

The impact sent a fresh wave of pain through his side, sharp enough to catch behind his ribs and stay there, blooming outward in dull, steady pulses. He lay where he landed, half-curled in a patch of his own blood, though the sluggish warmth of it barely registered against skin gone cold.

The suppressant still clung to his nerves like frostbite, numbing him at the edges and leaving only the worst of it—the ache in his chest, the faint tremor in his hands, the hollowed-out space where his resonance used to be. His fingers twitched once, a weak, uncoordinated spasm. No strength behind it.

He couldn’t move.

Couldn’t lift his head.

Could barely manage a shallow breath without everything threatening to seize again.

The world spun slowly overhead, lightstrips smearing into dull streaks against a ceiling he didn’t recognize at first. The air was cold, not sterile, not antiseptic like the Council clinics, but sharp with stabilizers and the faint metallic ozone bite of heavy shielding.

It took him minutes to focus, for the haze to thin enough to piece together where he was.

One of Anaxa’s labs.

Not one of the public ones, or even the deniable safehouses scattered across the city grid. This was deeper than that.

Unlisted. Untraceable. Wiped from every Chrysos archive, Council registry, and surveillance loop alike.

And of course—of course Anaxa had pre-encoded the tether to land him here. It was the kind of contingency he built into everything, always assuming the worst because it usually found them in the end.

Phainon knew the dull gray of the walls, the precise hum of the shielding field overhead. He remembered this place now, though he wished he didn’t.

A faint, rasping breath scraped out of him. It might’ve been a laugh, if there’d been anything left in him to carry it.

But there wasn’t.

He tried to move, and his body revolted. His legs wouldn’t move. His hands wouldn’t tighten. Even the simple act of breathing felt precarious, sharp threads of pain catching with every shallow rise of his chest.

Darkness tugged at the edges of his awareness, a slow, inevitable pull. His vision blurred, the cold creeping deeper, though whether from blood loss,

shock, or suppression, he couldn’t tell anymore.

He wasn’t going to stay conscious much longer.

Still—he tried.

Tried to push up from the floor, to force himself onto his hands, though his arms gave out halfway and left him slumped. His vision swam. The world tilted.

No.

Not yet.

Not—

But the black kept coming, cold and relentless, pulling him under one breath at a time.

And as the dark closed in, smothering the last shreds of strength and clarity, a single thought surfaced, splintered and desperate, a half-formed thing clawing at the inside of his skull.

Did I lose them both?

The words echoed, and then the dark took him.

Chapter End Notes

Alright, I didn’t actually have time to properly beta read this before posting, so if you guys spot any mistakes or weird phrasing, feel free to yell at me nicely. I appreciate the heads up.

Also, I’m gonna take a short break from writing on this fic for a bit. I wanna focus on a couple of my other longfics and a 20k one-shot or two I’ve been meaning to plan out. Hope that’s alright with you guys. It’s not gonna be a month-long vanishing act or anything (hopefully, probably not), but honestly these chapters, ESPECIALLY for this fic since it’s so plot-heavy and sci-fi dense, take a lot of brainpower.

Which is fine! Love the lore. But doing them back to back kind of kills the joy and whimsy after a while. 😭 (For context my goal for 3.4 is to get to 18 chapters and fully finish the thing in one go in 3.5, or earlier actually)

And before I forget, just putting it out there, but yes, that whole Council body transfer thing was actually planned out and for Anaxa and Mydei’s body/for Phainon’s crash out. I realize I probably didn’t imply that nearly well enough in the chapter and I really didn’t wanna delay it any longer for revisions, so… hope at least some of you picked up on it. Sorry if it was vague.

Anyway this was slightly rushed but still, thanks for reading, as always! You guys are the best💕

(Unrelated by anyone wanna try and guess Phainon’s backstory🤨?)

Chapter Summary

Mydei takes a relaxing nap, wakes up inside a memory blender, gets emotionally body-slammed by Caenis, forgets what’s real, remembers too much, almost becomes a USB stick, and then gets forcibly yeeted out of a tank by a feral academic with bad timing and worse aim. Alarms happen. So do feelings. Also, ontology does a thing.

Chapter Notes

I promise next chapter is gonna be less tech/sci-fi heavy, brace with it a bit longer please🥀

The first sensation was warmth—

—but not the kind that consoled. It was dense and unmoving, like the breathless air sealed inside a jar just before the oxygen thins.

He drifted, neither standing nor falling. Suspended in a place without edges. No ceiling, no floor, no orientation—only a vast, humming dark threaded through with veins of silver light, shifting like water disturbed by distant sound.

Mydei floated upright, his spine bowed slightly, arms bent at the elbow as though he had been caught mid-drowning. The pulse of the space moved with a rhythm not his own, pressing in on all sides.

There had been a lab here once.

Or something like one.

Steel consoles hung in the void, disconnected from structure or logic. Tubes drifted like dying tendrils, coiling and uncoiling with no purpose. Everything shimmered faintly, warped and half-dissolved, as if submerged for too long and only now beginning to surface.

Blood had pooled beneath a surgical table—though it didn’t look like blood. It gleamed with a slick, oily sheen, refracting in hues that didn’t belong to this spectrum.

His mother lay motionless on the slab.

Eyes open.

That detail caught. It shouldn’t have.

Her lips moved, slow and deliberate, though no sound emerged—until it did.

𖼆𖼇𖼈𖼄…

Reversed syllables. Her voice played backward, each consonant cracked open and hollowed.

They disappeared down the corridor, alarms shrieking behind them.

On the shattered console, a single readout blinked once—then stabilized.

ONTOLOGY STABILITY: 99% → 100%

chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Phainon, despite actively hemorrhaging, treks into the world’s most unlivable HOA to meet a violin-playing war criminal. Several hallucinations, one childhood trauma loop, and a casual ear bleed later, he leaves with a deal, a headache, and a mermaid (Siren?) business partner. Also, Goldweaver’s invited. Against his will.

Chapter Notes

Gosh, wish me luck in posting chapter 18 before 3.5 drops. On the bright side though, next chapter we’re going back to our roots with comedy (and it’s gonna be the reunion chapter too!!) so be prepared for Mydei, Anaxa, and a special guest’s shenanigans :) (I think it’s pretty obvious who tho😭)

[Zarq Neon District—Repurposed Mechbay M-77]

The coolant leak marked time the way clocks did.

Not loud. Not fast. Just consistent. One drop, then two. A short pause. Then again.

The puddle beneath it had spread wide across the cracked concrete floor, its surface smeared with oil and dull neon. Pink. Blue. Green. Each color bent as it passed through the water, crawling over rusted panels and the bent scaffold bolted to the rear wall.

A man hung from it. Not limp. But close.

His legs buckled slightly at the knees. His breathing rattled through a throat bruised to plum. Steel cord wrapped under both arms, biting deep enough to

leave bone impressions where the skin had worn thin. One hand twitched against the restraints, a reflex that had no fight left in it.

The mechbay still smelled like it’s old original purpose—hydraulics, solvent, scorched wiring—but something else had taken over. Rotted cloth, dried blood, and copper-rich damp.

Phainon didn’t speak right away.

He moved through the flooded garage with steady steps, boots sending faint ripples across the surface. One arm grazed a decommissioned servo claw hanging from the ceiling, its housing peeled open like a cracked rib. The wind outside gave the broken paneling just enough voice to rattle like breath caught in a damaged throat.

Mirel, or maybe Mirin—that had been the name. He couldn’t remember. The man had worked logistics under ECHO/OBELISK, long before they shuttered the Tide program. Not military, but closer than most. One of the ones who’d kept the paperwork moving. Routes. Transit approval. Clearance for deep stabilization zones.

And clearance for her. Hysilens.

A slight sound escaped the man’s mouth. Half cough, half choked laugh.

“She’s gone,” he muttered. “You’re late by a decade.”

He coughed again, deeper this time, and shifted his weight like it might help. His face was swollen on one side, jaw offset. Blood soaked into the collar of his coat and darkened the fabric down the ribs.

“You think she’d leave a trail? She wiped herself off the Earth.”

Phainon crouched beside him, not close enough to speak into his ear, but close enough that the man flinched anyway.

“You don’t need coordinates,” the man said. “You know that already. You’re just hoping something slipped through. A file. A pulse reading. Something.”

The corner of his mouth twitched. “There wasn’t.”

Phainon reached up and turned the man’s head, fingers light but steady, adjusting his gaze until it met his own.

“I don’t care about the files,” he said.

His hand stayed there, thumb under the cheekbone. The man tried to keep his eye steady. For a moment, it worked.

“You think she’d let herself be tracked? Hell, that she wants to be found?” Another bitter laugh. “No one survives that long without going insane. She was already cracking before we sent her in. They wanted to see how far the Tide would take someone. And she showed them.”

A silence passed.

“She flooded the site,” the man said. “Collapsed the entry point and bled the perimeter loop into open recursion. Nothing worked after that. Comms, mapping, scans—dead zones. She turned the whole region into noise.”

His breath hitched again. Slower now. Voice wearing down. “They called it a failure and locked it up. Some coastal subsector. C9. I heard they posted a perimeter, then stopped sending teams. One of the old observatories stayed active—barely. Still caught some residual Tide noise. But no one checked.”

His head fell forward slightly.

“You want a name? Find the archivist who stayed behind. He kept the old logs. Maybe he knows where the drift started.”

He closed his eyes.

Outside, the neon sign buzzed louder. Something in the power grid surged, then dimmed.

Phainon stood.

His coat brushed the scaffold. Water dripped from the hem and vanished into the growing puddle below.

A hand pressed to the side of the man’s head. The other locked under his jaw. Smooth movement, practiced. A short shift in leverage.

The sound came sharp and final.

The man’s body jerked, then stilled. His head lolled at an unnatural angle, eyes glassy and locked upward. His mouth stayed slightly open, lips frozen around the breath that never finished leaving.

Phainon held him there for a moment.

Then he let go and stepped back.

The garage creaked. Wind passed through a cracked overhead vent, carrying the distant sounds of sirens and static. Outside, the “CLOSED” sign flickered, then held steady in red.

The room settled again.

Only the dripping stayed.

The rain didn’t sting at first.

It started like any other—thin sheets slipping down the steel towers, harmless enough. But twenty minutes in, it changed. A faint chemical trace coated the droplets, like aerosolized stabilizer. The burn didn’t cut skin, but it left behind a subtle, plastic itch—like antiseptic that never quite dried.

They called it atmospheric conditioning. A byproduct of the district’s entertainment zoning. Not dangerous, just uncomfortable. Simulated hazard. Keeps the adrenaline high and the cameras running.

Phainon vaulted from a leaning antenna platform to a floodlit rooftop, landing hard with bent knees. The metal underfoot groaned but held. The paneling had been installed as part of a thrill tourism initiative—marketed

as “immersive instability.” Cheap stainless under polymer coating, designed to wobble but never collapse.

Tourists hated it. Residence ignored it. He preferred it that way.

The Verge had been built fast—five years of nonstop vertical development with zoning overrides passed under emergency economic incentives. Towers meant for luxury arcades were repurposed into housing halfway through construction. Security nodes were copy-pasted from older districts without adapting to the new architecture. The result? A sector with layered dead zones and spatial blind spots baked into its foundation.

No one knew where anything actually was, not even the grid. That made it dangerous.

And perfect.

Phainon adjusted his coat and broke into a jog.

He crossed an exposed catwalk with no guardrails, then dropped down into a maintenance alley between two overheating vent columns. Above, a billboard cycled through implant upgrade offers no one could afford—lines of code flickering behind the commercial overlay like it had forgotten which version it was meant to run.

The Verge worked in his favor. Conceptual powers didn’t function cleanly in stable zones; too much internal resistance from infrastructure logic. But here, entropy came built-in. The sector’s metaphysical baseline had degraded to the point where reality warped around its own render errors. No one designed it to fail. It just did.

Every time Phainon used his field—vaulted higher than gravity liked, glitched a camera frame just wide enough to pass unnoticed—it cost him something. Headaches came faster now. Bone-deep strain in his spine. The sense that his body’s inner map didn’t quite match its surface anymore.

Still worth it.

His most effective trick had been diversion. Echoes—Constructs shaped from his profile and seeded across predictable routes. They mimicked thought patterns, energy signatures, movement habits. Not perfect replicas, but enough to convince scanners. He left one behind every few days in former safe zones—just long enough for the Council to triangulate false sightings and the Heirs to send in strike teams.

They’d caught one in Auric Sector last week.

It crumbled under pressure, exactly as designed.

He didn’t expect that tactic to last much longer. Echoes degraded too quickly under observation. The more people watched, the more inconsistencies appeared. And once they realized they weren’t chasing the real thing, they’d come for the quieter zones next.

That’s why he was here now. Not to hide.

To stay ahead of the correction.

Another gap opened ahead—wider this time, between a lightwell and a skybridge. Phainon accelerated and jumped, bending his Conceptual field just enough to tweak the drop. His body shifted mid-air, not lighter, but momentarily less counted by the surrounding logic.

He landed with one hand against a rusted ledge, boots skidding across soaked glass tiles. Stood. Rolled his shoulders until the pop settled the joint.

The rain kept falling, now fizzing slightly against his coat.

He gave himself a moment to breathe.

The city stretched out below. From this height, the Verge looked almost coherent. Blurred neon streaked across rooftops. Drone paths stitched between satellite relays. Steam bloomed upward from broken coolant stacks.

But Phainon didn’t see it like that.

He’d split it into three parts to make

It simpler.

Golden Zones—territory under Chrysos control. Clean. Brutal. Regimented. Biometric gates and perimeter mines. The kind of place where a failed entry scan meant a rail round through the chest.

Glass Curtain—Council domains. Full-spectrum surveillance, sterilized transit hubs, crowds engineered to move in synchronized flow. Every step archived. Every breath tracked.

Deadlight Zones—everything else. Places without upkept records. Sub-levels of half-built towers. Transit lines that didn’t appear on the public map. Slums between testing yards. That’s where he stayed. That’s where the Verge was headed. Maybe not fully collapsed yet—but getting there.

The architecture told the story really.

He walked to the edge of the rooftop and looked toward Sector C9. A broadcast tower blinked at irregular intervals—soft red pulses against the skyline. That was his target. The informant had mentioned something about an “impossible structure.” A phrase thrown around too often when the Tide touched something unfortunately.

He didn’t believe the man completely. But he hadn’t had a better lead in weeks.

Phainon tapped two fingers against his coat pocket. The pills inside shifted slightly—synth-regulators from black market caches. They kept his pulse regular enough to keep moving. Sort of. He hadn’t eaten in four days, appetite hadn’t been an issue. The stomach stopped asking after the third blackout.

He felt the push in his limbs. The familiar pressure under the skin when the field wanted to activate on its own.

Not yet.

There’d be time for that soon enough.

For now, he picked up speed and moved again.

He was almost at the ledge when it happened.

Hands steady. Breath held. Weight angled to the metal. He’d scaled worse in worse condition. But his mind was stretched thin—split between the echo trail he’d left stuttering across three districts and the tideweight headache blooming behind his eyes.

A loose bolt turned underfoot. His boot twisted.

He dropped.

He didn’t even have time to curse. Just enough to brace.

The world snapped sideways—scaffold, wall, steel edge—and then gravity slammed into him like a wall. A bone-rattling thud as concrete met spine. Pain bloomed sharp and immediate through his ribs. The impact knocked the air out of him in a stuttering hiss.

He rolled, arm shaking as he dragged himself up just enough to sit back against the wall. Wet metal pressed cold through his coat.

He groaned. A low, pained sound. Then stayed where he was. Eyes shut. Waiting for his nervous system to sort itself out.

Somewhere deeper in his awareness, one of his decoys glitched and shimmered, sparking against a surveillance line. He let it falter. Not worth the exertion.

He exhaled again. Slower this time.

God. He needed sleep. Real sleep, the kind where his mind wasn’t crosswired to three active zones just to stay ahead of the Cleaners and Heirs.

He let his head tip back against the wall. Concrete kissed the base of his skull.

Five billion dollars for this?

The thought was dry. Bitter. Almost amused. His ribs hurt. His knee was probably bruised to hell. And his shoulder ached from where it’d hit a bracket on the way down.

This sector helped him stay hidden. The energy density here was fractured, slanted, hard to track. His field blended in.

But gods, was it annoying.

The wall opposite had been layered with years of graffiti. Some old, scrubbed halfway off. Others recent, still raw in color. The newest stood out sharp under the glow of a flickering streetlamp. Red paint, half-dried. The year had been crossed off.

“CLASS OF ████—DEAD BEFORE GRADUATION. NO REPAIRS. NO JUSTICE. NO FUTURE.”

He stared at it.

A beat passed. Then he snorted.

“Ain’t that the truth.”

His eyes fell shut. Just a second. Enough to let the nausea ease. Enough to not bite his tongue from the pain.

Clank.

The noise cut through the alley like a blade.

Metal on stone. A spray can hit the ground nearby and rolled.

Phainon’s eyes snapped open.

Three kids stood ten paces away.

Graffiti still wet on the wall behind them. Bandanas. Spray caps. The light from the paint stencils lit their faces just enough to show every inch of frozen horror.

He blinked. Slow.

Right. Kids lived here.

The smallest one whispered, “Dude, did he just fall from—?”

“How the hell is he not dead?”

The girl narrowed her eyes.

“Wait a damn minute. That’s him. That’s the guy. The one with the bounty.”

The silence collapsed.

“Shit.”

They turned and ran.

Phainon’s teeth clenched. He pushed himself up. The pain tore through his leg like glass—his muscles screamed—but he moved. Fast. Fluid. Dangerous.

He hit the pipe with one hand, angled his weight forward. The first step nearly buckled his knee, but he compensated. He used the wall as a brace, kicked off a half-fallen panel for height.

They were fast.

But he was faster.

He caught the first one mid-turn, clotheslining him lightly across the chest and pulling him down.

The second tripped over exposed wiring just as Phainon reached him—he adjusted his angle and delivered a clean elbow to the side of the head, catching the boy’s collar to keep his head from hitting the pavement.

Only the girl was left.

She bolted toward the edge of the alley’s open sector.

He closed the gap fast, even limping.

One long reach caught her by the arm. He pulled her weight around in a circle, eased her to the ground with a twist and a downward sweep. Her body slackened. Unconscious. But breathing.

Phainon stayed crouched beside her for a second.

No injuries, luckily.

Three unconscious teens. A chase. A fall. And still—no one came.

No sirens. No intervention. No guards.

Of course not.

Just three kids tagging protest lines in an acid sector. One misstep from potentially being dead, and no one gave a damn.

His jaw locked. A tight, silent burn coiled under his ribs.

Children lived here. In these ruined spines of metal and half-melted walkways. And somehow, the only stability they had came from risking their lives to scream into paint.

This wasn’t a city. It should be a damn apology. Badly built. Never honored.

Even the Council—twisted, manipulative, rotten—had sent stabilizer drops here when the Verge first started breaking down. Enough to claim credit. Enough to do something. The Chrysos Heirs? They’d ignored this entire

grid. They didn’t come here. Didn’t help. Didn’t care. The government? Even worse.

The construction here was rushed. The terrain never reinforced. Half the underlayers still registered as active sink zones. But the moment complaints surged, the government passed the blame. Let it rot.

Kids still lived here anyway.

He looked back down at them. Quiet. Small. Caught in something they never asked for.

Phainon stood. Limped.

An old canopy jutted out from a sloped corner, its frame bowed but intact. Good enough.

One by one, he dragged the teens there—careful hands steady despite the shaking in his leg. He laid them down under the makeshift cover, shielded from the chemical drizzle falling from above.

When he was sure they were safe, he straightened again. A tremor passed through his thigh. He ground it down.

One of their bags sat open.

He pulled out a simple black face mask. Slipped it on.

His hair was still too pale to hide, but his hood helped. With the coat zipped and his stride steadied, he could pass as anyone. Just another body in the rain.

He didn’t look back.

Didn’t say anything.

He just turned, picked a side route away from the alley, and walked.

No one came to check the noise. No one asked what happened. And above them, the graffiti still bled red down the wall.

The name was almost poetic, if you had the stomach for irony.

Tessera. Tiny shards of colored glass, used to build mosaics—whole images made from ruin.

Locals just called it the Sprawl.

Zone 8A-N, formally. Another vertical coffin welded together during the last Stabilizer Initiative. Urban overflow masked as policy. They’d stacked it high, wired it tight, pumped it full of neuro-ads, then called it progress.

Nobody really used the term anymore.

Phainon moved with purpose—not slow enough to draw attention, not fast enough to trigger suspicion.

The streets were congested with runoff markets and stallfront clinics. Neon signs flickered overhead, half-fused to corrupted code loops—ads for black-market immersion pods, off-brand neural augments, stim-laced protein sticks that boasted military-grade absorption. A vendor barked at a half-sleeping crowd hunched under a tarped awning, waving cyber-cigs and secondhand Tide mods. Someone coughed blood into the curb. The medcart behind him was long dead, its wheels rusted into the pavement.

No one slowed to help. No one had the means.

Phainon didn’t look directly, but he noticed the girl squatting beside the vendor, hands blister-red from heat exposure. Not old enough to be alone. Already had that look.

You had to be careful looking lost in the Sprawl.

A low rattle passed overhead—the hollow buzz of a magline runner, rails groaning beneath its weight. Once meant for district transit. Now it ran on

scavenged pulse and bribes. Three more surveillance halos pinged in his periphery. He shifted his gait just enough to throw off any tracking vector, ducking past a stall flanked by scorched chassis rigs. A woman shouted about “Tide shielding for all zones!” and waved a shattered shoulder plate. The insignia on it had been an VIB unit once.

Someone else would’ve stopped to scavenge. He kept moving.

And then—a flicker.

Upper glass, second tower. Left.

He looked up before he could stop himself.

A public holo-display flared to life across the skyscraper’s side. First came the static. Then the red-letter type, punching through city noise.

❝GODSLAYER DEAD? COUNCIL DENIES ALL.❞

❝HEIR FACTIONS NAME PHANTOM KILLER—VIGILANTE IDENTIFIED❞

He clicked his tongue.

Faster than expected.

Unfortunately it was louder today.

A burst of feed interference made half the plaza speakers whine. The footage stabilized just long enough to cascade into the familiar loop: council-approved anchors in collars, smiling without blinking, their voices flatlined by delay and overcorrection.

The first clips were stills. Damage sites. Melted containment facilities. He knew the images well—they’d been reused since the first leak.

But then the reel snapped sharp.

Grainy. Live-recorded. Stuttering on playback.

His face again.

Pulled from an old university staff registry. Hair short, posture formal. He had a faint smile on his face.

“Have you seen this man?”

The voice didn’t glitch this time. It came crisp and cheery like an automated checkout.

His body didn’t flinch. His mind did.

His hearing fuzzed out—a nice trick he’d learn. Easier to tune out that way.

More screens activated. Different angles. Blurred clips from surveillance cams and helmet feeds. One showed a corridor scorched black at the center —two bodies visible, one kneeling, one collapsed.

He didn’t look.

He caught the flash of movement in a storefront display instead. Another figure had replaced the newscasters.

Goldweaver.

The feed had the Council’s watermark. A sanctioned clip. Which meant it had been cleared before transmission, probably pulled under threat of escalation.

Her face was unreadable. She stared through the lens without blinking, chin slightly tilted as if bored. No backdrop. Just her and the statement:

“We will recover what’s ours.”

That was it.

Just that sentence.

She hadn’t appeared publicly since the body went missing. Not until now.

Phainon exhaled, slow.

Across the city, the broadcast was echoing on loop.

And it wasn’t just her face anymore.

News scrolls updated in real time:

❝GOLDWEAVER TERMINATES ALL COUNCIL OPERATIONS IN JOINT ZONES❞ ❝HEIR UNDERTAKER STRIKES THREE TARGETS IN FIVE DAYS❞ ❝BLACK TIDE CONTAINMENT FAILS—COUNCIL SUPPORT BLOCKED❞

Undertaker had summoned Pollux three times this week alone. The Council called them “thermal malfunctions.” But everyone knew better. Entire teams went dark in zones the Heirs used to co-patrol. Supply convoys, intel drops, even overflow medhalls. Gone.

And the message was always the same.

We asked. You refused. Now we take.

Hyacine had closed her medhalls to all Council ID. No negotiation. She hadn’t spoken to reporters in days following as well.

Goldweaver had shut down all coordination across former collaboration zones. Field teams found across the line were ignored. Not killed. Not rescued.

Just left behind.

Containment teams on Black Tide breaches used to work in tandem. Now? The Heirs held position and watched Council agents die. There’d been a breach two days ago in some sector, and no Heir squad moved to help.

The government’s response was a five-sentence memo about “internal oversight recalibration.”

They hadn’t spoken since.

And in the middle of all of it, they’d given the public something easier to hate.

Him.

Why?

He didn’t deny killing Mydei.

Because he had.

He’d stopped feeling the horror at that sentence a long time ago. Which was, in itself, a deeper horror.

If anything remained—if the Council still had his body, using it, desecrating it—then that needed to burn too.

The footage repeated.

His face. The corridor. A smear of blood and a voice on loop:

[“Have you seen this man?” “Heir forces vow full retribution.” “Council denies all responsibility.”]

He adjusted his coat. Pressed one palm against his side.

He passed beneath a cracked walkway. A teenager crouched near the base column, arms wrapped around a thermal canister, the flicker of a hand-lit match warming their face. A ragged Heir insignia stitched on the coat sleeve. Burned halfway through.

The kid didn’t look up.

Didn’t need to.

Everyone in the Sprawl had learned the same thing:

Don’t look at people. Don’t let them look back.

The Sink didn’t show up on maps anymore.

If you ended up here, it wasn’t by accident.

It had been a maintenance bar once—back when lower sector workers had regular hours and enough credits to drink. Now it sat buried three levels below the Tesserae Sprawl, at the edge of a derailed service tunnel and some forgotten Tide infrastructure. If you knew the code, the entrance unlocked from a rusted keypad on a loading shaft. If you didn’t, you stayed lost.

The Sink didn’t cater to anyone. It tolerated them. The lighting was low enough to misread a face, the booths deep enough to disappear into, and the walls pulsed with slow, rhythmic light from outdated Tide-core wiring— still warm, still alive, but decades behind modern safety protocols.

Most of the regulars were grounders. People who weren’t paid to exist above surface level. Technicians with burnt-out augments. Freelancers who couldn’t afford a second strike. Brokers who used to be higher up, before someone rewrote their chain of access.

The place wasn’t full, but it was never empty. Voices murmured over wet glass. Music came from an analog speaker, soft enough not to interfere with conversation. Someone at the back was patching a neural rig with kitchen tools. A woman at the end of the bar popped open a stim patch with her teeth and muttered something about bad code. Nobody listened. That was the Sink’s only rule:

Don’t be the loudest person in the room.

Phainon walked in with no announcement. Just the hydraulic slide of the door resealing behind him and the faint hiss of pressure equalizing.

The air inside was heavier than outside—metallic, and thick with secondhand chemicals. The light from the Tide-core wiring cast a dull pulse

across the ceiling like a slow heartbeat. Humidity clung to the walls. Condensation fogged parts of the mirror behind the bar. The floor had been swept, but barely.

He stood in the entrance for a moment longer than needed, letting the water run off his coat’s hem. The hood stayed up. His gloves were still damp. A few people noticed him. Not many cared.

At least, not until he pulled the mask off.

It came off with a low snap of seal and magnet. His face, pale under the phosphor glow, wasn’t a surprise anymore. The recognition was quiet.

No shouts. No dropped glasses. Just a slow halt in background movement. The woman with the stim patch blinked, then looked away. The man with the neural rig stood, unplugged, and made for the side door. The couple in the booth didn’t speak as they packed up. Nobody ran. They just left.

It wasn’t panic. It was logistics.

You didn’t stay in a room with a criminal unless you had a reason to.

Within three minutes, the bar was empty. Except for one man.

He sat two stools down, elbows on the bar, swirling the last of a glass with a kind of unbothered grace.

Mid-fifties. Face lined, but not weak. His coat was military-cut but softened with age. An old overlay flickered in his right eye—likely tactical, probably still patched into something passive. He looked up, but didn’t move.

Phainon didn’t speak yet. Just walked forward and sat one seat over, dropping his gloves on the bar with quiet finality.

The man lifted his glass like it was a greeting. “Rough weather.”

Phainon’s voice was steady, tired. “You tell me.”

The man gave a faint smile. “Didn’t think you’d come here yourself.”

“Didn’t think you’d be dumb enough to stay.”

That earned a short laugh. “I get paid to sit. Nobody said anything about running.” He glanced at the bottle beside him. “Drink?”

Phainon didn’t move. “It’s on me. You drink.”

The man nodded once, raised the glass, and tossed it back without ceremony.

For a while, neither of them spoke. The bar ticked with the residual hum of outdated tech, and upstairs, rain continued to find its way through cracked ductwork. Every few seconds, the lights in the wall pulsed, catching faint reflections across metal surfaces.

Then Phainon shifted, speaking flatly.

“I skinned the last person who lied to me.”

There was no pause.

“Didn’t even ask him anything at first. But it took a while. And I can do worse.”

The man met his eyes. Didn’t blink. “So you’re skipping the warm-up?”

“I’m skipping the wrong answer.”

Phainon finally turned his head fully, and this time, his expression made the atmosphere change. Not violent. Not unhinged. Just very, very clear.

“Where is she?”

The man didn’t flinch. Just leaned back slightly, then gave a low whistle.

“You’re gonna have to define she, friend.”

Phainon said nothing.

But he didn’t look away.

He licked his lips once and tapped the empty glass against the bar.

Phainon leaned his elbow on the bar. His posture was relaxed. His voice even more so—measured, polite.

“Apologies. That wasn’t clear. I don’t need what you’ve heard. Just what you believe.”

The archivist hesitated. Tried a smile that didn’t quite reach his eyes. “Look, man, a place like this? You hear a lot. Some useful. Some just noise. Hard to say what’s real half the time.”

Phainon nodded thoughtfully. Then raised two fingers toward the bartender.

“Another round. For my friend here. He’s been helpful.”

The man blinked. “I—thank you?”

“Of course. No pressure.” Phainon didn’t blink. “We’re just talking. You stall, I buy you drinks. You lie, I smile and let you keep going. Then I leave.”

He let that settle.

The archivist glanced down at the glass already in front of him. He didn’t touch it.

“You’re doing fine,” Phainon added. His tone didn’t shift, but it softened slightly. “Better than most. One man yapped for twenty minutes over a location he didn’t even give. Screamed through the sedation. I ended up missing the real detail he tried to say.”

The man swallowed. His jaw tensed.

“You don’t have to—”

“Please,” Phainon interrupted. Still polite. “You don’t need to reassure me. I’m not gifted at this. But people talk. Sooner or later. Something just clicks.”

Silence took its time stretching between them.

The old lighting above their heads buzzed—soft, erratic. A valve clicked somewhere behind the bar. The bartender didn’t move.

The archivist tapped the edge of his glass once with a finger. Then again. Then stopped. He stared ahead like he was reading something only he could see.

And finally, he spoke. Quiet. Tired.

“She vanished. Into a collapsed… spatial sinkhole. It’s not stable. Half-aware, leaking—something. It shouldn’t exist anymore. Should’ve collapsed fully. But it’s still active. Still… pulling.”

Phainon listened. Unblinking.

“She went in,” the man continued. “Walked into it like it was open ground. I don’t know how. It should’ve killed her. But it didn’t.”

Phainon’s head tilted slightly. “Go on.”

“She’s still alive. I’ve seen the spikes—data fragments, metaphasic drift. She’s in there. Not stuck, exactly. Just… inside. And she’s manipulating the Tide like it’s fluid.”

“Where.”

The man reached slowly into his coat. He pulled out a folded square of paper—creased, soft with age—and slid it onto the counter. Then took a pen from his sleeve and scratched something down. Numbers. Slanted writing.

“That’s the closest we’ve tracked it. Not a fixed point. But near enough. It’s not stable. Most people can’t reach it without tearing open a dozen fractures

on the way in. But you?” His eyes flicked toward Phainon. “You might not need the front door.”

Phainon picked up the slip. Gave it one glance. Then folded it cleanly and slid it into the inner pocket of his coat like it was a receipt.

He stood.

“Thank you,” he said, genuinely. It landed without edge.

The man raised a hand—not to stop him, just to get his attention—then pushed the untouched drink across the bar.

“If you really want to thank me,” he said, “you’ll sit and have one.”

Phainon paused. Just a beat.

Then he chuckled.

And sat down.

He didn’t just walk out of the place and vanish. Getting to the edge took time.

A decomissioned service hauler got him most of the way. It still reeked of sun-bleached rubber and mold-slick tide gaskets, but the filters hummed, and the lights worked.
