Cyrene tilts her head at his silence. “Phainon.”

He blinks.

There’s blood on his fingers.

A faint smear. Out of place.

He doesn’t move.

She hops lightly from the fence and walks toward him. Her feet leave no impression in the dirt. The flowers don’t bend as she passes.

She grins up at him, undeterred. “Heeelloo? Did you fall asleep with your eyes open again?”

Still playful. Still a child.

He doesn’t look at her.

“…Oh.”

He stares at the blood. Lifts his eyes to the sky.

“This isn’t real.”

Her smile falters.

“What?”

His voice flattens.

“This already happened.”

Cyrene frowns. She steps closer. “You’re acting weird.”

He finally looks at her—fully this time.

“This already happened.”

The field stills.

Sound falls away.

The birds vanish. The trees lose depth, fading like a stage set pulled too far from the audience. The scent of wheat and wildflowers thins and disappears. Everything begins to lose texture.

Phainon turns in a slow circle. The sun casts no heat. One by one, the fence boards start to vanish.

Cyrene hasn’t changed—not quite. But she doesn’t blink anymore. Her arms hang loosely at her sides. The smile lingers on her face, but it’s become something else—a memory stretched too long in sunlight, faded around the edges.

Phainon steps toward her. He draws a breath, shallow and uneven.

She tilts her head, watching him. Still smiling.

The field begins to fold. Not all at once, not loudly. False panels peeling away. Flat pieces pulled from behind the backdrop.

He stops in front of her.

His fingers twitch.

“…Thank you,” he says quietly.

And then she’s gone.

Not shattered.

Just no longer needed.

He comes back violently.

A sharp inhale tears through his chest—too fast, too wet—as if he’s surfaced from something that wasn’t water. His spine arches with the force of it. His lungs fight to stay filled.

But the room is still.

Dry.

Silent.

The violin has gone quiet.

There’s no field. No warmth. Just the polished stone beneath him this time.

His hand is still raised—halfway to a face that isn’t there. It hovers for a breath, then curls in on itself.

He lowers it.

The hush that follows feels like judgment. The walls give nothing back. There is no sympathy here.

He doesn’t move.

Eventually, he exhales through his nose. Not quite a laugh—more a crack of disbelief.

“That was a low blow,” he mutters. His voice scrapes as it leaves him, roughened by whatever that place pulled from him. “Even for you.”

There’s no answer.

He turns his head, slow. His ears are bleeding. He leaves it alone.

Then he laughs—once.

Short. Bitter. Joyless.

The noise catches at the edges of his breath, jagged and raw.

He wipes the salt from his temple with the back of his wrist.

Lifts his gaze to the ceiling.

“Was that supposed to be hard?”

Silence.

Then, finally, the voice.

Unmistakably clear.

“You pass.”

Phainon’s head tips forward, shoulders rising and falling in uneven pulls.

“…Was that it?”

A beat passes.

“Or is there more?”

Hysilens doesn’t shift. Her posture stays composed, the violin now silent at her side. When she speaks, it’s with the same evenness as before.

“I have one more condition.”

He shuts his eyes for a moment, drawing air in through his nose, letting it out with a thin, humorless breath.

“Of course you do.” His gaze lifts again. “What is it?”

“We’ll need her.”

A faint crease forms between his brows. “…Who?”

“Goldweaver.”

The air in the chamber tightens—sharp and sudden, like stone flexing in frost.

His answer comes without a breath’s delay, iron-edged.

“I’d rather die.”

Hysilens doesn’t blink.

“Then die. But this stopped being about you the moment you stepped in here. She deserves to bury her dead.”

The silence that follows is heavy enough to pull at the walls. Phainon’s jaw works once, the corner of his mouth twitching toward something between a sneer and a grimace.

A long breath leaves him. “…Fine.”

Her eyes narrow.

“You mean that?”

“He died. I didn’t.” His tone is flat. “That’s the only part that matters now.”

Another silence. Not cold this time—simply measured.

“When do we leave?” he asks.

Her gaze tracks over him briefly—the tremor in his breath, the bruising along his shoulders, the faint trickle of dried red at his ears—before meeting his eyes again.

“First,” she says, “we get you into a state where you won’t collapse before the door.”

“And after that?”

The smallest curve tugs at her mouth.

“Why not tonight?”

She extends her arm toward him. An invitation, the kind of gesture that feels rare even to her.

Phainon stares at her hand, then at her. Slowly, his own rises—still heavy, still shaking faintly—and closes over hers.

The cold doesn’t lift from the chamber. But the quiet that follows isn’t the same as before.

Chapter End Notes

Alright, before you get all confused (cause I definitely didn’t explain this well here), here’s the deal on how Phainon’s ass survived and why Cyrene didn’t, and how he ended up with his powers. I was going back through this and earlier chapters and realized I left this way too vague and abstract.

So, like Caenis said last chapter, the “solution” was memory, that applies here too. Long story short: Cyrene was already kinda dying, just like everyone else in the district, but she and Phainon didn’t drop right away because in the final collapsing moment, they both clung to the exact same memory that was in the beginning of the loop where they were talking about Snowy (albeit the scene was slightly different with the blood and setting, though that was because the loop was starting to break)

If you’re sitting there wondering ok so like how the fuck is that relavent, yeah, my bad for not explaining it better, but memories are the bread and butter of surviving the Tide basically in this au.

See, the Black Tide erases meaning by contradiction and entropy, but a perfect, shared memory? That can’t be corrupted. It stalls the Tide right there since, what can it even do? They have a tether that grounds them to the world, which also works as proof of their existence as well (which can’t be erased. The point of this was to connect Eurypon’s theory with this as well so I hope someone caught it💔)

Phainon, barely hanging on, started instinctively bending the breaking space around them to keep that moment intact. Not to escape, but to keep it real, which also meant keeping Cyrene real, since the Tide basically wipes people out on a conceptual level.

Problem is, Cyrene was already dying and couldn’t handle the strain. She started to fall apart, so Phainon, desperate as hell, built the rest of that memory bubble around her corpse. She couldn’t keep the memory going anymore, but yeah, Phainon survived only because they were linked through that memory.

I was gonna explain exactly how he got his powers here too from the incident (Hint: it’s related to how this was quite literally the first EVER breach and sighting of the Tide), but I’ll try to slip it into the story somewhere. If not, I’ll just toss it in the chapter notes later like this.

Anyway, thanks for reading and sticking for this long!!

chapters.title: Chapter 18: Naptime at the Slaughterhouse
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei tries his hand at running away with Anaxa and Cipher while high (read: promptly blacks out), Hysilens plays bodyguard in what may or may not be former… something behavior, and Phainon commits one-handed ultraviolence while simultaneously functioning as the world’s deadliest weighted blanket.

Chapter Notes

Heyy, I only beta-read about 80% of this, so please let me know if I missed anything! Also… I won’t lie, this one was a bit rushed, so if it shows, totally my bad😭.

I also take back what I said about the comedy last chapter, this one’s a bit more lighthearted, but honestly, there weren’t enough funny moments or interactions like I’d originally hoped, so it might come off kinda dry. If I get some free time, I’ll try to fix it, but really sorry if it doesn’t quite hit your expectations. Still, I hope you enjoy it <3

The wind never stopped up here.

It slipped through the jagged wound where the north wall used to be, cold enough to bite. It carried the city’s noise in scraps—sirens, engines, the metallic pulse of some distant club—layered together like static through a blown speaker.

From this height, the skyline looked split in two. The new spires rose in clean chrome and holo-glass, bright enough to cut the eye, while the Old District below crouched in shadow, its skeletal high-rises slick with rain and firelight. Somewhere in that mess of towers and ruin, the Council was still tearing up the city looking for them.

Their hideout had once been a corporate boardroom. Now it looked like a scrapyard someone had decided to stack vertically. Armored shutters leaned at wrong angles. Discarded ad panels had been flipped around, their blank backs hiding the faded grins of spokesmodels who’d probably died before any of them were born. Electrical cables looped across the floor like exposed veins. The stolen generators in the corner rattled and hummed until the whole place seemed to breathe.

Out on the street below, a neon sign tried and failed to complete its loop, blinking eternally between Loa— and S—ing.

Cipher was holding court in a high-backed leather chair she definitely hadn’t paid for, the old company initials still faintly embossed in the headrest. She was halfway through an evidence bag of potato chips, chewing with enough sound that every crunch landed like a gunshot.

On the table beside her, Mydei sat cross-legged, polishing the sidearm he’d liberated from a Council operative twenty minutes ago. He didn’t look up from the task, though the muscle at his jaw twitched every time Cipher bit down.

Across the room, Anaxa was bent over a glowing scanner array, muttering without looking up.

“If one more of you drags dirt into my diagnostic zone, I’m installing a guillotine in the doorway.”

Mydei let the sigh escape before he could stop it.

Now, you’d think he’d be used to situations like this by now.

It’s been… a while since Anaxa had first broken him out of the Council facility, and at that time he’d been convinced they wouldn’t see the light of day again.

Until Cipher.

To this day, he had no idea how Anaxa had gotten hold of her. She had a reputation for being everywhere except the city, yet she’d appeared within the hour, maps spilling out of her bag, rattling off three separate exit routes for a Council building that supposedly had no exits. She’d walked them out like she was returning a library book.

The Council had been in full meltdown since. Losing both Mydei and Anaxa in the same week had been enough to send them into overdrive, locking down half the city in overlapping webs of scanners and drones.

And that—unfortunately—had been Cipher’s topic of choice for the past five minutes.

“But—“

Anaxa cut her off by flicking a feed onto the main screen. The city map lit up in a pulsing red lattice, zone after zone stitched shut.

“You see this? That’s why we don’t step into Heir territory. That is a killbox —one they wrote legal paperwork for.”

Cipher crunched another chip. “We could still—”

“No.”

Mydei tilted his head. “I could—”

“Also no.”

Cipher frowned. “…You didn’t even let me finish.”

“Because your sentence was going to get us killed.”

Mydei set the sidearm down, slowly. “So we’re stuck here. And the Council’s tightening the net.”

“Exactly,” Anaxa said without looking up.

Mydei glanced over at Cipher. “And, correct me if I’m wrong, but you’re officially an actual fugitive now?”

Cipher whistled and found something very interesting on the ceiling.

That answered that. Of all the times for the city to cash in on her laundry list of thefts, it had picked the week she’d been useful.

So here they were—three very wanted people in a tower missing half its walls, staring at a map that promised death in every direction.

And the worst part? This was still the safest place they had.

Cipher broke the silence first.

“So, we’re agreed. The plan is: no plans.”

“That’s not a plan,” Anaxa said without looking up from the scanner array.

“It’s been our only plan for weeks now,” Mydei countered.

Anaxa’s head lifted just enough to aim a flat, unimpressed look across the room. Mydei held his gaze, then let his expression shift into something Anaxa recognized immediately.

Anaxa groaned. “Not this again.”

“Oh, I’m sorry,” Mydei began, voice soft with mock sympathy, “maybe if I’d known my boyfriend was an infamous criminal antihero mastermind— one with a distinguished career in justice-flavored killing sprees—”

Anaxa pinched the bridge of his nose.

“—and that his so-called university professor friend was actually his long-time partner in dismantling institutions for fun—”

“That’s not even—”

“—and that the two of you have been running joint black operations under both the Chrysos Heirs and the Council’s nose for years while I was thinking, ‘Wow, they must’ve met at a lecture on economics,’—”

Anaxa’s jaw worked like he was chewing rocks.

“—then maybe,” Mydei finished, “we wouldn’t be in quite this mess.”

Cipher’s snickered. Anaxa muttered something to the scanner that might have been an insult, might have been a death threat. Mydei gave him a glare so half-hearted it barely counted.

Truth was, they didn’t have a plan because every viable option ended with their corpses in a Council evidence vault. Heir territory was sealed—choked with Council biometric checkpoints and patrol grids tight enough to tag them the second they crossed the line.

And revealing Mydei was alive? Sure, it sounded like the easy win—instant public outrage, Heir leadership shielding him, the Council exposed. Except the Council’s whole strategy hinged on turning the Chrysos Heirs into a political island. The moment Mydei surfaced, they’d make the Heirs a co-defendant in every “terrorist” act the Council had ever manufactured by claiming he’d been working with the Flame Reaver. He’d be trading his skin for theirs.

So they stayed in the shadows. Injured shadows. Mydei was still carrying more internal stitches than blood cells. Cipher had officially made it onto the “do not attempt arrest without air support” list. And Anaxa… Anaxa had been cut off from his playground.

The Council had burned through their own defense budget building a kill switch for him—an active, citywide intrusion scrambler keyed to his digital signature. Anything he touched online spun itself into static before it even reached the servers. That didn’t stop Anaxa though, but even his workarounds had to brute-force their way through it, and the strain was showing.

But if they couldn’t be safe, they could at least make the Council miserable.

The weapons job had been first—an entire convoy redirected to a phantom “Warehouse Zero” that had never existed outside Anaxa’s code. Cipher made sure the crates didn’t sit still long enough to be reclaimed, moving them through a chain of underground cells until they vanished into a dozen different hands. The Council found their guns again only when they were being used on Council patrols.

Then the treasury hack. Anaxa’s mechanical worm (Don’t question it, he doesn’t know either) rewrote the Council’s finance AI’s priorities overnight, redirecting “public security surplus” into binding humanitarian grants for anti-Council relief groups. The money was stuck in escrow contracts designed to auto-trigger penalties if touched—locking procurement lines for weeks and forcing entire divisions to ration.

And the biotech stunt… pure, indulgent malice. Anaxa had swapped vault manifests so precisely that the Council, believing they were receiving high-grade gene sequencers, installed industrial algae bioreactors in sterile labs. The systems self-calibrated. The next morning, the labs were swamped in green foam, and the sequencing teams were wading through ankle-deep slime.

That had been a good week.

Still, every strike they made only tightened the noose. And as Cipher kicked her boots up onto the table, scattering a pile of spent ammo casings, Mydei found himself wondering—not for the first time—how much longer they could keep pushing before the Council finally cornered them.

“Oh, right,” he said. “Remember when I mentioned Caenis planning to use me as a vessel? For—” he made a vague, spiraling gesture “—stealing everyone’s abilities somehow, with Phainon in the mix?”

Of course he’d told them about that the second they got out, he’s not stupid.

Cipher gave a lazy thumbs-up. Anaxa nodded once, distracted by the stream of data finally coming in.

Mydei paused mid-roll, the casing sliding from one knuckle to the next. His brow furrowed. “There was something else, though… I’m not exactly sure what that means in this context. And I think I need your help with it.” He looked at Anaxa. His tone had shifted—less throwaway, more deliberate.

That got Anaxa’s attention. The scanner kept humming, but his hands stilled on the console. “…Go on.”

Cipher gestured vaguely between them. “Cool, so I’m just here then?”

“Pretty much.”

She nodded wisely. “The lion does not concern himself with—”

“Quiet.”

Cipher pouted, but leaned forward in her chair, curious now.

Mydei exhaled. “It might not be relevant. But I’d like some peace of mind. Back in that incubator—” His voice thinned slightly at the word. “—there was a readout I could see from inside. I didn’t understand most of it, but one thing stood out: a reading with an unbalanced pattern. Sometimes spiking up, sometimes dropping—no steady baseline.”

Anaxa tilted his head. “…And? What was this reading exactly?”

“Ontological Stability.”

Cipher blinked. “That’s… a good thing, though? Literally means you existing, right? Like, congrats, you’re real?”

Mydei gave her a look, then glanced at Anaxa. “Tell her.”

Anaxa’s mouth twitched like he might agree with Cipher out of spite, but he didn’t. “She’s not entirely wrong. Ontological stability’s a metric for… continuity. Being anchored. A thing that’s stable in that sense won’t just flicker out of existence if no one’s looking. But—” His eyes narrowed slightly. “—the fluctuations matter.”

Cipher crunched a chip. “Okay, but… why would it fluctuate? Either you’re real or you’re not.”

“That’s the simple version,” Anaxa said. “Reality’s not binary when you start factoring in ontological variables. If the measurement’s moving up and down, it means…” He trailed off, searching for the right phrasing. “…It means something’s interfering with the definition of you. Actively.”

Mydei sat back against the table. “Interfering how?”

“Could be memory edits. Could be causality tampering. Could be someone rewriting your personal continuity in real time.”

Cipher frowned. “That’s—hold on. Wouldn’t you notice if someone was doing that?”

Anaxa glanced at her. “If they’re good, no. By definition, you’d only remember the current version.”

Mydei’s fingers tapped restlessly against the table. “When I was in there, the number didn’t trend up or down. It wavered. Like… they were trying to keep it in a specific range.”

Anaxa’s head tipped, considering. “Holding you below full stability keeps you permeable. Too high immediately and you’re fixed—harder to alter. Too low and you risk collapse. But a controlled middle ground? That’s a staging point. They can shape you from there, slowly increasing.”

Cipher’s brows knit. “Why the hell would anyone want that?”

Anaxa’s gaze slid back to Mydei. “Because it’s easier to graft something onto a self that isn’t fully… settled.”

The words hung there. Mydei didn’t move for a moment. Then he said, almost carefully, “And if Caenis’s endgame was a vessel—”

“They were prepping you,” Anaxa finished.

Cipher let out a low whistle. “Okay. That’s… worse than I thought.”

The three of them sat with it for a moment, the hum of the stolen generator filling the silence.

Mydei’s voice was quieter when he spoke again. “So when we say ‘reality’ here… we’re not just talking about the reality. We’re talking about theirs.”

Anaxa’s expression darkened. “And theirs can overwrite yours.”

The brass casing slipped from Mydei’s hand, rolled across the table, and dropped to the floor with a faint metallic clink.

It sounded loud in the stillness.

“…Shit,” he breathed.

Well, they had a plan now.

At least, on paper, it was a plan.

During the earlier discussion, everyone had been unnervingly calm, there were even moments where it almost felt like they were having a normal conversation.

Now?

It was like watching someone light a match in a room full of leaking gas.

The absence of tech, of any real network access, had finally gotten to Anaxa. He was tearing through the workbench like a man gutting a corpse for salvage—sleeves shoved up, hair sticking out at angles, eyes ringed in sleepless shadows. Dead datapads lay in pieces around him, their guts spilling wire and cracked crystal displays. He didn’t so much work as he attacked each device, muttering a steady stream of half-finished curses, equations, and paranoid observations that tangled together into something just shy of coherent.

Cipher leaned toward Mydei, her voice barely above a whisper.

“…Is he—”

“Look at him,” Mydei murmured back without glancing over. “What do you think?”

As if on cue, Anaxa let out a short, high laugh. Both Cipher and Mydei winced at the sound.

Then Anaxa straightened suddenly, wrench in one hand, the other stabbing the air at Mydei like he was punctuating each syllable with violence.

“Do you get this? It’s not brainwashing. It’s metaphysical eminent domain. They own your plumbing. They own your reflection. Hell—” he leaned forward, teeth bared in something that wasn’t quite a smile “—they own your shadow.”

Cipher couldn’t resist. “At least they didn’t rezone him for condos.”

SLAM. The wrench hit the table so hard that a handful of screws jumped like startled insects.

“…It’s a little funny,” Mydei said after a beat.

Anaxa’s head snapped toward him, glare sharp enough to peel paint. Mydei didn’t blink. He’d found that humor, for him, had become a survival tactic. If you didn’t let the knife scare you, you could turn it into a punchline. If you could keep laughing at the dangerous things, it lost a little of its edge. Or so he kept telling himself.

“It’s horrifying,” Anaxa bit out, “and I’m fixing it.”

Cipher eyed the wreckage on the bench. “…With… broken datapads?”

Anaxa didn’t even acknowledge her, shoving a cracked casing aside to drag a soldering tool into reach.

“You can’t debug ontology,” Mydei said, more out of habit than actual belief.

Anaxa gave a quiet, almost conversational chuckle—and somehow it was worse than the manic one earlier.

“Oh, can’t I?” he murmured, not looking up. “Give me a framework, I’ll rewrite the plumbing. Give me the right lens, I’ll steal back the damn reflection. Then we’ll see who owns whose shadow.”

The generator in the corner let out a faint, uneven whine.

Cipher glanced at Mydei. “You think he’s serious?”

Mydei kept his eyes on Anaxa’s hunched back. “…Yeah. That’s the problem.”

Anaxa hadn’t stopped moving in over an hour.

The workbench wasn’t cluttered anymore—clutter implied intention. This was wreckage.

Cracked datapads lay like dissected animals, their casings gutted, copper veins exposed. Notes—half equations, half jagged diagrams—were scrawled across overlapping sheets, all curling at the edges.

He moved between the mess like a predator in a cage, muttering under his breath:

“…continuity anchors… frame persistence… lattice bleed thresholds…”

Cipher leaned against the far wall, arms crossed. She chewed the inside of her cheek, her eyes tracking him like she was waiting for him to combust.

Mydei just stood there, gaze flicking between them, unreadable as ever.

“You’re just gonna watch him grind himself into paste?” Cipher murmured.

Mydei didn’t look at her. “He’s not grinding out. He’s calibrating.”

“That what you call it?”

“It’s the sound of him convincing himself the problem’s impossible so he can’t be blamed for not solving it.”

Anaxa’s hand twitched, almost sending a tower of stripped boards to the floor.

“It is impossible,” he snapped without turning around, “because it’s built to be. That’s the elegance. That’s the trap.”

Cipher rolled her eyes. “Great. So we’re dead in the water unless someone has the magic phrase to snap you out of your spiral.”

Mydei pushed away from the wall. “Forget snapping him out of it. Standing here feels like watching someone drown from the shore. Anaxa. Talk to me. This ‘frame’—what is it really?”

Anaxa stopped pacing. For a second it looked like he wouldn’t answer, then:

“The quantum-locked identity frame. Imagine a deed. To you. Written into the lattice of your brain at the subatomic level. That’s your continuity anchor. Without it—” He flicked a glance at Mydei. “—you’d vanish. Not die. Erase.”

“So,” Mydei said slowly, “if you take it out, I pop like a soap bubble.”

“Yes. Continuity collapse. Like deleting a file, then setting the drive on fire.”

“…So make a restore point.”

“That’s not how—” Anaxa stopped mid-retort. His pupils narrowed, mind re-routing. “Wait.”

Cipher cut in before the silence could calcify. “Oh, so we just yank the plug, reboot him, and hope the operating system doesn’t blue-screen his soul?”

Anaxa opened his mouth to shut her down—but the smallest hesitation caught in his expression.

She smirked. “Or better—slip him a nice fat virus. Make him so buggy the system can’t even load him.”

It was meant as a joke. Anaxa didn’t laugh.

He went still. Not calm—predatory stillness.

“…Contaminating variable,” he murmured. “Unstable input.”

Now his attention was on the far corner—where a battered console sat under a sprawl of schematics. He was already peeling them back with quick movements, the air around him tightening.

“This isn’t entirely crazy,” Mydei said, stepping closer. “I already mentioned my stability reader wasn’t fixed. Maxing it immediately would’ve—“

Anaxa’s finished for him, repeating what he’d said last time with realization slowly dawning on him. “Too stable and the frame becomes self-defining. They lose the ability to overwrite you. The control depends on keeping you just unstable enough to need their definition.”

Cipher’s eyes lit. “So we shove it the other way. Make it so volatile they can’t hold the definition at all.”

“Yes.” Anaxa’s voice sharpened. “We flood the frame with instability. Force a controlled crash. And in the reboot cycle…” He tapped a schematic—two short, deliberate strikes. “…we seed the identity from your subconscious, not theirs.”

Mydei crossed his arms. “…That’s the ‘rewiring the plumbing’ nonsense you were on about earlier.”

Anaxa finally looked up. His smile was too exact, too dangerous to be reassuring.

“Exactly. And I’m the plumber.”

The Spire Run.

Cipher had said it offhandedly—a placeholder name for the op—but it stuck.

Fitting enough.

Anaxa and Mydei stood in the wind-shadow at the Aeon Spire’s base, necks craned toward a tower so tall its crown dissolved into the sky. The haze swallowed the upper struts entirely. From here, it wasn’t clear if the cloud cover was natural or projected—the Spire generated its own microclimate, after all.

It wasn’t exactly beautiful. More… unsettling. The structure had the anatomy of something that grew instead of being built, a skeletal lattice wrapped in mirrored skin that flexed faintly, as if breathing. When the surface caught the city lights, they slid and warped like reflections in a disturbed pool.

Anaxa’s walkie gave a dry crackle. “Action.”

Across the city, Cipher’s voice came back with a yawn. “Yes, sir.”

Mydei snorted faintly at that and fell into step behind him as Anaxa moved off the edge of the observation platform, under the first support strut’s looming shadow. The air shifted here—unnervingly still, scrubbed of any grit or scent.

“You’re still sure splitting the list was smart?” Mydei’s voice was serious now, all business. “We could’ve run all three targets together, kept mutual cover.”

“Three operators on three objectives is wasted precision,” Anaxa said without looking back. His gaze traced the Spire’s support lattice like he could see the circuitry under the panels. “One ghost for the soft grabs. Two for the hard one. Division of labor.”

The mirrored skin above shimmered. Mydei’s eyes caught on it—the skyline behind them fractured into liquid distortions.

“Metamaterial sheath,” Anaxa murmured, catching where Mydei was looking. “It modulates transparency based on clearance level. At street height, you see a shiny weather tower. Above the third strut, it’s a perfect mirror unless you’re Council-tagged.”

“And we’re not Council-tagged,” Mydei said.

A thin smile. “Not yet.”

The walkie cut in again cheerfully. “For the record, if this goes sideways, I’m selling your faceprint to the blacknet.”

Anaxa thumbed a response without missing a step. “You’d get a fortune. Stay on task.”

Mydei’s glance flicked to the slim device in Anaxa’s coat. “Still not seeing why we start here instead of—”

“Because the Quantum Entropy Generator doesn’t leave the Spire without collapsing into useless slag.” Anaxa’s tone was patient, but edged. “Vault Theta—six sublevels down—is the only place it stays coherent. We get it first by physically tweaking it or the rest doesn’t matter.”

“And it does…?”

“It blinds them,” Anaxa said simply. “Drowns their predictive computation in quantum noise until the surveillance net can’t tell a shadow from a body. It’s like—” he drew a small shape in the air, “—dropping ink into clear water. Every model, every probability map, turns to static. For you…” His eyes met Mydei’s. “…it makes your ontological frame too unstable for them to lock.”

Mydei’s mouth tightened. “So step one in evicting them from my head.”

“Step one,” Anaxa confirmed, “and the hardest to touch without waking every containment protocol they’ve got. Which is why Cipher’s running the

other grabs solo—she’s fast enough to ghost through the sweeps.”

“The other grabs being—?”

“Neural Interface Rig,” Anaxa said, ticking it off like a grocery list. “Direct, unmonitored link between generator and stabilizer. Without it, every transmission screams for attention.”

“And the stabilizer.”

“Biochemical anchor,” Anaxa said. “Locks your metaphysical substrate to your biology during the counter-intrusion. Without it, the ‘de-ownership’ could crack your mind or leave you an empty shell.”

They paused in the lee of an angled girder.

Mydei exhaled slowly. Even talking about these types of components was illegal—the kind of illegal that triggered retroactive sweeps.

The walkie crackled again—Cipher, voice low now. “Rig secured. Stabilizer next.”

Anaxa clicked his tongue in approval, turning to Mydei.

“You ready?”

Mydei’s reply came slowly. “You’re the one with the map. I’m here to make sure you don’t redraw it halfway through.”

Anaxa’s grin was razor-thin. “Redrawing it is the fun part. Move.”

They slipped deeper into the Spire’s understructure, vanishing into the gleam and shadow beneath its mirrored skin—where the city’s reflection bent and broke into ghosts.

Anaxa walked ahead, hands buried in his jacket pockets, eyes skimming the converging cross-corridors as if he were counting them. His pace was easy, but his gaze kept tally—people, cameras, angles where the wall’s light broke into shadows.

“They rotate crews every forty-eight hours,” he said without looking back. “Means Level Seven’s swapping half their techs this morning. And we happen to be two of them.”

Mydei closed the gap between them, voice low. “We happen to be?”

Anaxa’s mouth curved—something between a smirk and a blade being sharpened. “Already in the system. Nexel Safety Compliance, Secondary Division. You’re a maintenance subcontractor. I sign your clearances. Both of us just came off a contract in Sector C.”

“And if someone’s actually from C?”

“They’re not,” Anaxa said, tone flat. “Sector C’s mid-refit. Everyone stuck there is on respirators, babysitting pressure valves, and praying the scrubbers don’t choke. Nobody pulls a double to come here.”

The floor under them shifted from ribbed composite to smoother alloy plating as they followed the corridor’s slow curve. Overhead, a strip of conduit lighting hummed, spilling a tired, bluish glow on the brushed steel walls. The air smelled faintly ionized—circulators nearby.

They reached a junction where the noise thickened: the murmur of voices, the clank of gear against metal, the hiss of a decompression valve somewhere out of sight. The corridor widened into a service concourse—a rectangular space with an equipment rack down one side and a datawall scrolling maintenance alerts in orange text, each tagged with a sector code and urgency rating. Six or seven techs in grey jackets clustered in twos and threes, talking over each other in clipped bursts:

“…intake valves still tripping after the flush…” “…filters running hot again…” “…get the Phase 4 kit loaded before—”

Anaxa slowed just before the threshold, letting a genuine crewman with a heavy tool harness pass them. “Rule one,” he murmured, almost conversational. “Don’t walk in. Walk with.”

He matched his stride to the man’s, letting the crewman’s body language carry him forward into the knot of workers. Mydei fell in half a step behind, close enough that anyone glancing over would assume they’d been part of the same group since the last checkpoint.

A stocky woman with oil smears up both sleeves noticed them first. Her eyes flicked over Mydei’s jacket, then to Anaxa. “New?”

“Transfer from C,” Anaxa said easily. “Safety compliance sweep on your calibration run.”

She groaned in recognition. “Another one? Last week we lost twenty minutes to—”

“Not me,” Anaxa cut in. “If I’m doing it right, you won’t even remember I was here.”

That won a shrug. She turned back to a debate with another tech about whether the new venting firmware was worth the downtime. The noise and motion closed around them, masking their presence better than silence could.

Anaxa brushed Mydei’s sleeve in passing—light enough to be mistaken for nothing.

We’re in.

The knot of workers funneled toward the platform doors, boots scuffing paint that had been worn to bare steel in places. White stenciling on the deck—T-5 → with a stylized chevron—pointed the way to the tram line. Beyond the marking, the platform stretched like a hanging balcony built into the understructure’s ribs, the drop below hidden in shadows.

Overhead, a magline track glinted like a taut black vein, vanishing into a dim vertical throat above.

Somewhere in the queue, a tech in a grease-darkened jacket glanced up from his tablet and grumbled, “Vent B-ninety-four’s still out of alignment.

If I have to hear that seal rattle the whole way up, I’m shoving my head through it.”

Anaxa didn’t miss a step. “He’ll check it,” he said, jerking his chin toward him.

Mydei looked up, slow and flat, but the rest of the crew had already stepped aside to give him space.

“Make it fast,” the tech called over his shoulder, already moving on to a rant about cold drafts in the upper tiers.

Mydei crouched by the wall grille. His fingertips worked the frame like he was checking for warping, but his other hand slipped a coin-sized disc under the lip. Through his glove came a faint vibration—security mesh was old-model, the sensor loops staggered enough to leave neat, predictable blind spots. He traced the gaps with his gaze, fixing them to memory.

Anaxa loitered just beside him. A passing crewman gave him a brief nod, so Anaxa threw him a tired half-smile.

“They ever roll out that intake patch?” he asked, casual. It was quite uncanny seeing Anaxa act like this, Mydei shuddered slightly.

The man barked a short laugh. “Patch? We’re still nursing those vents by hand. Whoever greenlit the last firmware deserves a week in the trash compactor.”

Anaxa sighed. “Save me the trouble and I’ll nominate them myself.”

The man chuckled and moved on, pulled away by someone shouting from farther up the line.

Mydei stood, dusting off his gloves. “Seal’s fine,” he reported, for anyone listening.

“Good enough,” Anaxa said, already steering them toward the boarding queue. “Grab the seven-mil from the bay before we move.” The words were

easy, the tone light—but the subtle angle of his hand pointed Mydei toward a side corridor. On the schematics, that path skirted the service elevator bay.

The tram arrived with a sigh of pistons. It clung to the magline above like a silver fish to a hook, plating scored from years of freight runs. The narrow windows were layered with impact film, more for the crew’s peace of mind than actual safety.

Inside was all brushed metal and industrial efficiency: fold-down perches, standing grips, and wall-mounted consoles lit with dim amber readouts. The air smelled faintly ionized.

The floor gave a muted thud as the clamps took hold, and then the car slid upward. Outside the windows, the view shifted from the platform’s shadow to the cavernous crossbeams above.

The tram shuddered over a junction. Somewhere far below, the echo of dropped metal rang up the shaft, swallowed again by the hum.

Anaxa kept his hands in his pockets, gaze on the window slits, but his focus was on the sound of the crew.

Eventually , the car eased to a halt on a mid-tier platform. Doors hissed open. Most of the crew filed out without slowing, boots clanging on grated decking.

Anaxa didn’t follow right away. He let a few go ahead, then stepped out with Mydei at his shoulder, slowly separating from the group.

The elevator bay was to the left, guarded by a man in a pale vest leaning lazily on a waist-high barrier. To the right, corridors branched into the maintenance maze, each stenciled with sector codes.

Anaxa’s voice was quiet. “Thirty seconds.”

Mydei peeled off, posture still that of someone sent for a tool. His thumb brushed the seam of his jacket, waking the disruptor disc. Two turns later,

he found the dead corridor—dust hanging in its still air—and pressed the disc to a conduit plate.

A soft chirp. A slow red blink on a far sensor.

Back on the platform, the guard’s earpiece crackled. He muttered, pushed off the barrier, and walked off toward the fault, vanishing behind the first corner.

Anaxa’s mouth twitched into the smallest smile. “Bingo.”

Anaxa’s fingers slipped under the coil of black polymer at his belt. The leapfrog card clone sat in his palm, no bigger than a stick of gum, and just as unremarkable—except it was about to impersonate an executive keycard for exactly sixty-three seconds. He pressed it to the reader like he was swatting away a fly. A muted chime, a green diode blink—his timer started ticking down.

63.00.

“Politeness is optional,” he muttered, jerking his chin toward the doors.

Inside, the lift was all cold light and thin metal—less of a passenger space, more of a cargo vein running down into the Spire’s gut. Mydei had one step inside before Anaxa yanked his arm hard enough to make him stumble.

The doors sealed them in. The hum of distant turbines rolled through the walls like a constant, low drumbeat. Mydei’s eyes tracked the sliver of open shaft at the far panel’s edge—a dizzying drop disappearing into strobed shadows.

“Keep staring, and you’ll start imagining what it feels like to fall,” Anaxa said without looking up.

Mydei snorted. “Not planning on finding out.”

Anaxa popped the control panel with a practiced flick, exposing a layered mess of fiber lines and armored circuit boards. From a side pouch, he pulled something that looked halfway between a pocketknife and a detonator.

“This is me,” he said, slotting the device in—a physical key injector, feeding a rapid sequence of authentication spoofs directly into the lift’s onboard system. “You—” He pointed to a panel flush with the wall. “Behind that is a mechanical failover. Pressure sensor in front, rotary lock behind. You let go, the panel slams shut, we start over.”

“Sounds fun,” Mydei said, pressing in until the panel clicked. He found the lock’s ridged edge with his fingertips and began to turn. “So, what’s the plan if sixty-three seconds runs out?”

“Pray,” Anaxa said flatly, eyes on the injector’s scrolling debug feed.

HANDSHAKE // BYPASS LAYER-1 // GOV-LOCK ACCESS AUTHCHAIN: INJECTOR -> LIFT OS -> FAILOVER

The timer hit 12.09.

“Mydei—”

“Yeah, I can feel it tightening,” Mydei said. “You’ve got maybe ten.”

Anaxa’s hand darted to pull a micro-bridge cable from his teeth, clipping it across two live nodes. The lights overhead flickered, the hum deepened. Then—

The floor dropped. Gravity went light, the air rushing past them as the lift tore downward. Mydei bent his knees automatically, back braced to the wall while Anaxa’s grip went white-knuckled on the panel edge.

The freefall ended just as violently. Anaxa’s head almost met the wall; he swore in something guttural and untranslatable.

“This lift’s a disgrace to engineering,” he hissed.

“Yeah, no kidding,” Mydei said, pulling him away as the doors creaked open.

The hallway beyond was sterile, empty—and alive with security. Ceiling-mounted camera domes swept in precise arcs, laser sensors flaring faintly at

knee height. Mydei moved first, dragging Anaxa into the shadows of a wall support.

“Fourteen-second sweeps,” he murmured. “We move on the blind.”

They ghosted through in bursts—five steps, freeze, shift again—keeping to architectural blind spots until they reached an unmarked, reinforced door. Mydei started to pass it until Anaxa’s elbow caught him in the ribs.

“This one.”

They ran.

The impact against the crash bar swung it open into a wall of freezing air. Breath crystallized instantly, the temperature drop sharp enough to sting exposed skin.

“Welcome,” Anaxa said through chattering teeth, “to Vault Theta.”

The chamber beyond spread out like a cathedral to refrigeration—rows of frost-rimmed containment units stretching into the dark, each one humming faintly, each one locked behind its own layer of cold.

Mydei blinked against the glare, scanning the aisles. It was… grand, yes, but not in the way he’d expected. For something meant to house one of the most volatile devices under Council control, there was no ostentatious shielding, no palace-like sanctum. Just industrial frost and steel. Function over theatre.

“…That was easy,” he murmured.

“What?”

“This feels too easy.” His head tilted slightly, as if tuning his ear for alarms or the faint footstep of an approaching guard. Nothing.

Anaxa’s brows drew together, but Mydei was already wandering forward, fingers tracing the cold glass of a containment unit. “Never mind. You know what to do from here?”

There was a pause before Anaxa nodded. “We should be done in less than ten minutes.”

“That fast?” Mydei’s gaze stayed on the frosted etchings of a serial number. “No wonder Phainon could clear so many zones in a night.”

That name lingered in the air like condensation. Anaxa’s steps slowed, voice quieter. “…You’re taking that better than I thought you would.”

Mydei stopped mid-stride. For a moment, his profile was unreadable. Then a small, almost weightless laugh escaped him. “…Trust me. I’m not.” The humor didn’t touch his eyes. He moved on before the words could settle, tone brisk again. “Come on.”

Anaxa said nothing—just followed.

The generator lay at the aisle’s far end, a thing out of place in the utilitarian cold. A dense cylinder, wrapped in layered crystal cores that rotated in slow, hypnotic arcs inside a mag-lev cradle. The light bent faintly around it, its edges refusing to stay fixed.

Anaxa crouched, gloves brushing frost from anchor housings. “Drop it, and we’re dead in three dimensions.”

“Reassuring,” Mydei muttered, kneeling opposite.

The process was surgical. Anaxa clipped copper-gallium clamps to each resonance anchor, their tiny status LEDs pulsing in rhythm with the generator’s hum as they mimicked the frequency signature. The vibration passed faintly through the floor and into Mydei’s knees.

His task was the physical half—unbolting cold-sealed mag-cradle locks, the metal reluctant to turn under the bite of subzero air. Every movement had to be steady; release the pressure too quickly, and the anchor field could snap back with enough force to shear the cylinder in half.

The final lock gave with a brittle crack. Frost hissed into the air as Anaxa’s tools worked seams along the crystalline casing. The shell split open like a

geode, revealing a smaller, denser core no longer than Mydei’s forearm, its surface veined with fine latticework that glowed faintly from within.

“This is it?” Mydei’s breath fogged the space between them.

“This is what matters.” Anaxa slid it into a padded, insulated case, sealing it with a magnetic clasp.

No alarms. No klaxons. Just the hum of refrigeration.

Mydei exhaled, rubbing his hands together for warmth. “I’m assuming we’re not taking the tram back.”

“Originally, yes. But…” Anaxa’s gaze unfocused briefly, running calculations. “…it’s probably compromised.”

“Then try this.” Mydei leaned against the cradle’s frame. “Garbage lift to sublevel waste filtration. Maintenance pod to the neutral-sector hydroplant. Then we cross into the outer sector on foot—there’s an old skywalk. Unlit, but it’s still standing.”

Anaxa blinked at him. For the first time all night, a small, genuine laugh broke from him. “You truly are a delight, Mydeimos. No wonder I never wanted to kill you when you’d visited the university.”

Mydei smirked faintly. “So that’s a yes?”

“Of course.” Anaxa slung the carry-case strap over his shoulder, the generator’s weight settling against his back. “Let’s move.”

By the time they reached the rust-stained safehouse, Mydei’s calves burned from the wind shear across the skywalk and the harness had carved neat grooves into his shoulders. He stretched his arms overhead, rolling the ache from his neck, and glanced at Anaxa, who was busy flexing his hands.

“When do you think Cipher’s gonna—”

“—Now. Glad to hear you missed me.”

The voice came from deeper in the warehouse, loud enough to echo. Cipher stepped into view between two stacked pallets, hair wind-tangled, eyes half-lidded. In one hand, a bag; in the other, an exaggerated yawn.

“Next time,” she said, tossing the bag onto the nearest table with a satisfying thunk, “someone else gets to play fetch.”

The contents clinked together—metal on polymer. Mydei caught a glimpse of the Neural Face Rig’s carbon-fiber jaw frame and the matte-white capsule of the Biochemical Stabilizer as Cipher unzipped the bag and nudged it toward Anaxa.

She tapped the capsule like she was testing if it was ripe. “Can we start?”

Anaxa didn’t answer—already pulling the components toward himself. He hummed low, a tune without melody, hands moving with the precision of someone disarming a bomb. The rig’s microfilament contacts got an inspection under his portable scanner; any speck of debris could scramble skin conduction mapping. He linked the rig’s spinal tether to the stabilizer’s socket, waited for the amber LED blink, then slid a wafer-thin bridge module between them.

“That’s your translator,” he murmured. “Tells your cortex and blood chemistry to shake hands. Without it, you’re signing both death certificates.”

Mydei leaned back in the chair, watching him. “So the fun part’s next.”

Anaxa’s mouth twitched. “Fun’s one word for it.”

He peeled the protective backing from the jaw frame’s contact pads. The adhesive was laced with hair-thin microcapillaries—each ready to draw blood samples the moment the rig came online. He fixed the frame snugly over Mydei’s lower face, pivot arms locking at the temples. Next came the stabilizer: a narrow polymer cuff clasped around Mydei’s wrist, its underside riddled with injectors fine enough to pierce skin without a mark. It looked like an oversized watch until Anaxa slid in the synth-serum

cartridge. The cuff chirped, and green text scrolled: Buffering metabolic interface…

“When this kicks in,” Anaxa said, tightening the last fastener, “you’ll feel heat in your jaw, down your spine, then it’ll build in your skull. Don’t fight it. Eyes open.”

The first wave was almost gentle—warmth blooming under the jaw pads, the way sunlight soaks through a window. Then it spread backward along the skull’s base, trickling into his spine. Mydei kept his breathing steady. He’d done worse. He wasn’t going to flinch.

Anaxa adjusted dials, smooth and unhurried. “Pushing cortical sync rate in half-hertz jumps. Too slow, it drags; too fast, it tears.”

The warmth grew heavy. Pressure gathered in the back of Mydei’s head, patient and immovable. He gripped the ground, knuckles pale, and focused on not letting the muscles in his jaw twitch. Sweat prickled his hairline. The warehouse air felt thinner, like it was being rationed.

Cipher leaned on the table, watching. “He’s turning red.”

“It’s vasodilation,” Anaxa replied. “Stabilizer’s hitting target.”

The pressure edged into ache. Mydei kept his gaze level, refusing to blink more than necessary.

“Ten seconds,” Anaxa said, adjusting a fine-tune slider.

Nine. Eight. The ache thickened, flooding the inside of his skull. Six. Five. His pulse thudded in his ears. Four. The whole room narrowed to heat and noise and the stubborn line of his jaw. Three—

White static ripped across his vision, then cleared so sharply it felt like breathing after being underwater too long. He jerked upright, the tether snapping taut.

Cipher’s hand landed on his shoulder. “Easy, champ.”

He kept his eyes shut, riding the last waves of pain until they dissolved into something feather-light. His shoulders loosened. Breath left him slow.

Then the lightness tilted—slid—into euphoria. His head tipped back, and his lips curved in the faintest smile.

“…Is he dead?” Cipher asked.

“No,” Anaxa said, running a check.

For a beat, Mydei didn’t move. Then after a moment, he sat up with perfect calm. Cipher exhaled. “So it’s all fine now?”

“Yes,” Anaxa said, then hesitated. “…But—”

Cipher gave him a look. “But what—”

Mydei cut in dreamily. “You ever notice if you put your heads together, you’d look like a really judgmental owl? Like… one of those ones that runs a post office.”

Cipher blinked. Once. Twice.

Anaxa, completely straight-faced, nodded. “Yes. I see it.”

Cipher turned on him. “…Is he high?”

“Extremely. Keep him talking.”

Mydei smiled at them both, eyes half-lidded. “You’re all… glowing. Like bread… in a toaster… right before it’s perfect.”

Cipher covered her face with both hands. “We risked our lives so he could become a kitchen appliance critic.”

“Let’s get back on topic.”

Mydei slouched deep into the chair, limbs loose and head tipped back like the ceiling might start telling him secrets. His pupils were blown wide, tracking invisible things in the air.

Cipher leaned on the table beside him, chin in one hand. “Two fingers— how many?”

“Seven,” he answered without hesitation.

Anaxa, crouched behind the rig’s housing, didn’t even glance up from the tangle of cables. “His math’s fine. His vision isn’t.”

Cipher hummed, satisfied. “Figures. Math’s always been crap anyway.”

Mydei’s mouth curved. “I can multiply… sometimes.”

“That,” Anaxa murmured, “isn’t the flex you think it is.” He made a final adjustment, then sat back on his heels. “Here’s the situation—he’ll stabilize in forty-three minutes. For now he’s metabolically hypersensitive. Keep him seated. No bright lights. No sudden movements. Neural mesh is still settling—push too hard and we risk seizures or cognitive skips.”

Cipher straightened a little. “I’m not about to start juggling flares over him.”

“Good,” Anaxa said. “And avoid loud noises. His auditory cortex is spiking —everything will sound amplified.”

Mydei turned his head toward her. “Anyone else hear that humming?”

“That’s your bloodstream,” Anaxa replied without missing a beat.

“Or your brain leaking,” Cipher offered.

He considered that, nodding slowly. “Nice. Feels fizzy.”

Cipher shook her head, chuckling. “You’re a mess.”

“Shiny mess,” Mydei corrected, squinting up at her hair. “Your head’s got twelve little suns… but they’re arguing.”

Anaxa’s eyes narrowed a fraction, but he didn’t look up. “Hypersensitive,” he repeated, like the word itself was a verdict.

They fell into a rhythm—Anaxa explaining, Cipher poking, Mydei wandering off into miniature hallucinations—until a faint thunk in the distance threaded itself into the warehouse’s usual creaks. Neither Anaxa nor Cipher reacted at first.

The second sound—soft metal groan, somewhere high above—made Cipher’s weight shift almost imperceptibly to the balls of her feet. Her gaze flicked past Anaxa’s shoulder, then settled there.

Mydei tilted his head in the same direction. “That’s not my blood, right?”

No answer.

The air seemed thicker now, carrying a low vibration just on the edge of hearing. Anaxa’s hands slowed over the rig controls.

“Probably nothing,” he said, though his tone had lost some of its certainty.

Cipher didn’t move.

Mydei broke the quiet with, “Does anyone smell toast? Like, toast that’s… weird?”

Anaxa started to reply, then caught the fact Cipher still hadn’t looked away from whatever she’d locked onto. Her hand hovered near the knife at her hip.

“Cipher?” he said.

No answer.

He stepped closer, brows drawn, and began to reach for her shoulder—

—she moved in a blur, grabbing his jacket and yanking him hard to her side.

An instant later, an armor-piercing round tore through where his head had been, shredding roof plating before punching into the concrete floor with a brutal, echoing crack. A thin cloud of dust unfurled from the hole, drifting down in slow spirals.

Silence.

Anaxa was frozen mid-breath, eyes fixed on the crater.

The vibration came again, louder this time—low mechanical hum swelling under the faint whine of something airborne.

Cipher’s voice cut through, sharp and cold. “Up. Now.”

Mydei blinked, sluggish but unbothered. “Is this… the part where we get blendered?”

Neither answered.

Outside, the hum split into layers—the rapid pulse of drones riding over the heavier thrum of tiltrotors. The warehouse’s rusted siding trembled faintly in their wash.

Then the loudspeaker crackled to life, voice amplified into a cold, procedural rhythm:

[Attention, occupants of this facility. This is the Council’s Central Intervention Unit. You are surrounded. Lay down all weapons immediately, step into the open with hands visible. Noncompliance will be met with lethal force.]

The words seemed to hang in the air after the speaker clicked off.

“…Fuck,” Anaxa muttered.

Cipher was already moving, sweeping her bag from the table and scanning every angle between them and the exit. She hooked an arm under Mydei’s and pulled him up with practiced efficiency. “Well?” she shot over her shoulder at Anaxa. “You listening?”

He clicked his tongue but fell in behind her, eyes still on the bullet hole.

Mydei stumbled along, mumbling with quiet conviction, “Don’t touch the suns. They bite when they’re scared.”

Five minutes. That’s all Cipher’s trick had bought them.

“No one saw us leave,” she’d said, back in the safehouse. And for those five glorious minutes, reality nodded along. Guards glanced past them. Cameras lost interest. Even the air felt like it had somewhere else to be.

But the lie was fraying now—he could feel it in the way the city’s eyes were back on them.

The first siren confirmed it.

Anaxa took the stairs two at a time, scanning every bend in the railing. “Eyes back on us. Patrol drones, five o’clock.”

Cipher hauled Mydei up the last steps before his boots could eat each other. “Stay vertical.”

Mydei’s brain was drifting somewhere between lucid thought and confetti. Whatever the Council had dosed him with sloshed through his head like bad liquor. “The walls are breathing,” he announced. A beat later: “Anaxa, your hair’s on fire—wait. No, just ugly.”

Anaxa didn’t even look back. He just smacked him in the head on his way past.

They burst through the roof access door into a blade of cold wind. The rooftop stretched uneven and cluttered—vent housings, glass skylights,

antenna arrays buzzing with static. Beyond the ledge, the city’s administrative crown rose in mirrored spires, moonlight glinting off their faces like a warning.

The sky was worse.

Six quad-rotor drones banked toward them from different angles, shock-net launchers twitching in their undercarriages. From far below, shouts rode the wind upward—a vertical echo between the concrete cliffs. Somewhere out there, a Council gunship’s running lights pulsed like a slow heartbeat.

“High ground,” Anaxa said, already moving.

They clambered over a rattling maintenance scaffold, then up a narrow ladder bolted into the wall. Cipher dragged Mydei after her, his boots scraping sparks off the metal. The air up here stank of scorched copper— probably from the east-side Administration vent towers.

A net sang past Anaxa’s shoulder, fizzing as it snagged an antenna.

They kept moving—leaping narrow gaps, ducking under guy wires, skirting skylights that flashed quick glimpses of the world below: rows of identical desks under pale strip-lights, Council clerks hammering keys without ever looking up.

Another siren wailed from somewhere deeper in the district. Mydei, still half gone, lifted a lazy wave at a drone overhead. “No autographs today!”

“Shut up,” Anaxa snapped, eyes locked on the next jump. Rain-slick ledge —half-second slowdown—half a second too long.

A net slammed into the roof in front of Cipher, hissing open like a metal flower. She vaulted it clean, catching Mydei’s sleeve before he could step right into it.

One more jump—then they landed hard on a wide, flat rooftop. Too wide. Too exposed.

“Fuck.”

Drones spread in from one side, their shadows crawling over the tar. From the other, two gunships crept closer, rotor wash peeling grit and paper across the roof.

Cipher scanned the edges: sheer drop. Only one visible exit—a yawning ventilation shaft.

“We could go down,” she offered.

Anaxa didn’t even glance at it. “Not dying in a tin coffin.”

Boots pounded up the roof access, rifles raised. Gunship spotlights cut across the three of them.

Anaxa’s gaze shifted to Mydei. “We jump, or we’re caught.”

Mydei blinked at him, nodding with all the gravity in the world. “Falling’s just flying… if you think about it.”

The wind pulled at their clothes. The sirens blurred into a dull tunnel-hum. For a moment, they just stood there, three silhouettes against the bright steel of the district.

Anaxa’s voice dropped. “We’ll make it.”

A pause.

“I’ll make sure of it.”

Cipher exhaled, patting them both—quick, grounding. “Ready?”

The drones tightened their circle. The gunship’s shadow swallowed the roof.

They leapt.

Mydei went first, laughing, a streak of pale and dark flung into open air. Cipher followed in one arc, boots scraping the ledge before she vanished after him. Anaxa was last, a shadow breaking away from the roofline.

The drop bit at them immediately. Air rushed hard against Mydei’s face, roared past his ears, tore at his clothes until every seam felt loose. The building behind fell away faster than he could think about it. His stomach hung somewhere above.

He didn’t fight it. He let the fall take him, weightless and untethered, a body drawn toward gravity’s quiet certainty.

The skyline tilted back, and then there was nothing but sky.

He tipped his head up. His hand lifted without asking him first, reaching toward the constellations as if they’d drift a little closer if he asked nicely enough. Stars spun slow in the dark, clean and sharp as cut glass—no city haze to dull them. The moon lingered low and round, a pale coin in the dark.

It had been a beautiful night. The kind of night you could get lost staring at without minding if you never found your way back. He let that thought sit, slow and warm in his chest, the air’s bite softening to something almost gentle.

Somewhere in the rush, something else threaded in—faint at first, so soft he thought it was his ears playing tricks on him.

A violin.

One pure note held long enough to tremble, then another. Slow bow strokes, deliberate. Mydei closed his eyes, and the city, the shouts from above, even the fall—all of it slipped back.

The music was patient. Each note stretched so far it felt like it might snap, and when the next came it was like an exhale he didn’t know he’d been waiting for.

He thought of the way the moon seemed to watch the city tonight. Of how the stars looked like they’d been spilled there just for him. Somewhere in that soft haze of sound and air and sky, he realized he missed the sun.

He didn’t mean it as poetry, he meant it plainly.

The violin’s tempo edged forward, heartbeat-quick now. The threads of sound pulled tighter.

And then—everything above them stopped.

The drones froze mid-flight, each one rigid in the air, as if the whole night had been put on pause. Light spilled erratically from their frames, twitching and flaring.

A harsh, metallic scream ripped out from them in unison, stabbing the air with feedback sharp enough to make his teeth ache. Mydei flinched. The drones dropped all at once, heavy metal bodies hitting pavement far below. Floodlights blinked out one by one, leaving the street in cold shadow.

The air felt bigger now. Too big.

Something moved below—fast, thin arcs of light tearing upward from the dark. Gold, but almost alive in the way they curved and twisted.

They reached Cipher first, winding around her torso like ribbons, slowing her descent until she hung suspended, swaying gently. Another coil swept around Anaxa, halting his fall in a more violent, albeit still gentle catch.

Relief loosened Mydei’s shoulders. Good. They’d be fine.

The threads arced toward him next. He shut his eyes again, letting the thought settle in. He could still hear the violin, steady, certain.

The gold touched—

—and convulsed.

The glow shattered into static, flickering between blinding white and nothing at all. In a violent recoil, the threads snapped away from him, retreating back into the dark like something had driven them off.

He barely had time to be confused before the world slammed back into him.

Not gold this time—arms.

A body intercepted his fall from below, the impact a bone-deep jolt. The hold was unyielding, ice-cold through his clothes, crushing in its grip— enough to bruise, enough to hurt.

And yet—he didn’t pull away.

The cold felt like something solid to hold on to. He leaned into it, eyes still closed, breathing slow into the space between them.

When he finally opened his eyes—

The face above him was ghost-pale, eyes wide and empty. And then— something broke.

Shock. Relief so sharp it bordered on madness. Guilt, and the kind of desperate joy that made his breath hitch.

The hand at his back trembled violently. His mouth opened—no words at first, just the sound of breath catching, breaking—and then, hoarse, “… Mydei?”

It sounded like a prayer he hadn’t believed would be answered.

A smile tugged faint at Mydei’s mouth—tired, almost lazy in its quiet acceptance. He shut his eyes again and pressed closer, until there was nothing between them but the cold and the hold and the sound of the other’s heartbeat against his ear.

He had found his sun it seems.

Mydei’s head was still tipped against the shoulder that held him.

The chill seeped through his cheek, but the arms around him were solid in a way that told him they weren’t about to let go. Not even when the impact of their fall had faded.

Breath touched the top of his hair, uneven, ragged in a way that spoke more of disbelief than exertion. Mydei could feel it in the faint tremor under his temple, the way every muscle in that hold seemed caught between crushing and cradling him.

He tilted his chin up. Slowly—like lifting his head through water—his vision sharpened on the face above him.

The eyes were too wide. Fixed on him like he might vanish.

“You look like Phainon,” Mydei murmured. His voice slurred faintly around the edges, his thoughts a little frayed. Then, after a pause long enough to almost forget the first words—soft, almost amused: “Oh. You are Phainon.”

The name hit the air like an explosion in silence.

The grip on him tightened, painfully now, enough to push a faint sound from his throat.

The man’s mouth worked once, twice, as if language had momentarily deserted him.

“Mydeimos—”

It broke halfway out, almost a stutter, but not from hesitation.

He said it again, lower this time, and it scraped raw: “Mydei—”

The name cracked like he’d been holding it in for years.

Glass. That’s what his eyes were made of right now—glassy in a way strangers might take for calculation, but Mydei knew better. Knew he was watching a man actively wrestle tears down with sheer force of will.

Before he could answer, before the half-smile forming on his lips could settle—

A voice cut through the alley, quiet but clear as crystal.

“Did you get him?”

It didn’t belong here, its echo threading through the dead air like it had been waiting for this silence.

“…Hysilens?”

The name slid out before he could catch it. Mydei craned his neck, blinking toward the shadows.

She emerged like she’d been there all along, violin still in hand, bow suspended midair. The pale gleam of the wood caught in the faint light, and her expression barely concealed the way her eyes tracked him first.

Another figure followed.

He already knew who it was before even getting a proper look.

Aglaea.

Her hair caught what little light there was, threads of gold weaving in the dim. The faint shimmer of the threads still faded around her fingers as her gaze swept over him—not fast, not slow. Just precise, cataloguing every detail like she was trying to reconcile it against memory. Her face was the same cool, unshakable calm she’d worn for every Council meeting and negotiation, but there was something taut beneath it. A tension that wasn’t hostility—more like a tether that had been straining too long and had just, without her permission, gone slack.

The violin’s last note faded into the air between them. Hysilens hummed it under her breath, lowering her bow.

“I’ve kept my side of the bargain,” she said, and this time her gaze sharpened on Mydei, the words thinning like glass. “…and more, it seems.” Then, to the man holding him: “He’s yours.”

Phainon laughed once—a short, fractured sound that didn’t know whether it wanted to be a sob or a breath. He pulled Mydei in, so close now the world outside his chest might as well not exist.

Mydei let his head rest fully against him, heavy-lidded, catching the uneven rhythm of his breathing.

From the corner of his vision, movement—Anaxa, standing with an expression that could slice through steel, gaze fixed on Aglaea and then flicking to Hysilens. The air between those two was a drawn wire, humming with tension only they could hear.

“Careful,” Mydei mumbled, wriggling faintly. “You’ll squish me.”

That earned him another sound from Phainon—not quite a laugh, not quite sane—his head bowing over Mydei’s hair, the edges of disbelief fraying into something perilously close to joy.

Cipher, still pale and leaning on Aglaea for support, gave Anaxa a look that plainly said don’t start. He didn’t return it—his focus stayed locked where it had been.

Phainon’s attention shifted toward Aglaea—no, not her. Past her.

“Professor…”

The word barely made it out, cracking halfway.

Anaxa’s expression didn’t shift.

“If you’re about to apologize,” he said evenly, “don’t.”

Silence dropped like another body into the alley.

Then—

A gunshot.

The sound tore through the stillness, loud enough to make Mydei’s mind briefly clear. Nobody moved. Nobody except Aglaea.

She lifted her fingers an inch.

The bullet froze midair as string caught it—spun with a tortured screech of metal—and then hit the ground in a mangled knot.

Hysilens exhaled, bow still in hand. “Pests.”

She adjusted her stance, the bow rising—but then she hesitated. Her gaze flicked to Aglaea.

Mydei had seen Aglaea stop more chaos than this with a single sentence with her presence alone. He expected that here.

Instead:

“No need.”

The words landed heavier than they should have. Even Anaxa’s gaze broke for a fraction of a second.

“I’ve had enough of the Council’s deceit,” Aglaea said. Her tone was eloquent, but under it was an edge like a blade drawn deliberately slow. “And enough of their arrogance. I intend to… correct that personally.”

A pause.

And for the first time, Hysilens smiled. A small, flickering thing—but it sharpened her whole face.

“I thought you’d changed,” she murmured. “Seems you haven’t.”

“…How would you know?” Aglaea’s voice was quiet, but it closed the space between them like a door shutting in someone’s face.

Hysilens didn’t answer after that. After a beat, her expression smoothed again. “Let’s take care of them first.”

Mydei shifted faintly in Phainon’s arms, eyes going a little bright in their haze. “I’ve decided,” he said solemnly, “I’m king now. King of Castrum Kremnos.”

Cipher groaned at the mention of that restaurant. “Oh no.”

“You,” Mydei announced, pointing lazily up at Phainon, “are my shining white knight. Go smite the goons.” He giggled uncharacteristically, entirely pleased with himself.

Cipher stretched, muttering, “I’ll explain later.”

Phainon blinked, like his mind had short-circuited just a little from the whiplash, and then let out a short, breathless chuckle that still had something dangerous and slightly unhinged under it. “…Yeah. Of course. Yeah.”

Farther down the street, a Council enforcer shouted something. The voice broke mid-sentence—glitched into static—then silence.

Hysilens didn’t look up. “Not bad,” she commented, and then the bow came down on strings again, the first slow note blooming into the air.

They didn’t stand a chance in the first place.

He couldn’t say when he lost hold of the moment. Somewhere between the shouts and the crashing floodlights, between the violin’s phantom echo and the plunge of vertigo, his mind blurred into static. When thought returned in fragments, it was only to impressions: Hysilens, sword unsheathed for once, moving with precision as she carved a path toward Aglaea. She gave no sign of urgency—face flat, voice absent—yet her body interposed itself between the blade and Aglaea as though she’d always done so. A sharp kind of tenderness lived in the guard she offered, one Mydei, even half-fading, could almost recognize. Cipher was violence at the edge of vision, every flicker of her knives unspooling another Council life into sparks and ruin.

And Phainon—Phainon was everywhere.

The rooftop had drowned in blood. It blackened the tiles, ran into the seams of shattered stone, matted steel and flesh alike until the floor glistened red.

Phainon walked through it like it belonged to him. One arm crushed Council throats, tore drones apart as though they were made of paper; the other held Mydei close. No blood reached him, no shockwave of violence broke against his body. All the butchery radiated away in arcs of gore, leaving only the steadiness of a heartbeat against which Mydei’s head lolled, dazed.

His weight sagged further, too heavy to hold upright. The world pitched and he felt himself sliding, yet Phainon’s grip was iron, locking him in place while the slaughter went on. His cheek pressed to the man’s chest as his eyelids dragged low. The rooftop shook under the weight of screams and snapping bone, and still he drifted.

He didn’t remember the last bodies falling. Didn’t remember the sound of throats giving way or the sparks of drones cut open.

It might have been minutes. It might have been hours. He stirred only when a rough hand found his cheek, thumb grazing skin with a tenderness so at odds with the battlefield that he thought it hallucination. His eyes cracked open to blurred outlines: pastel face, ragged breath. Then the warmth of a forehead pressed into his hair, voice sinking low enough to be mistaken for dream.

“You can rest now.”

Phainon’s breath stirred him, calm in cadence. Mydei hummed something faint and senseless, words too slurred to hold meaning, then let his eyes fall shut at last. The fight had ended; he no longer had to force himself awake.

So he drifted, sinking deeper into Phainon’s arms, while the rooftop lay heaped with severed limbs and spreading pools of blood. The air stank of iron, bodies stacked like offerings at their feet. Yet even then—

“See you tomorrow, Mydei.”
