chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

The gang argues, panics, trauma-dumps a little, and then somehow manages to cobble together a five-phase plan that sounds just plausible enough to work. Aglaea flexes her “actually I’m in charge” muscles, Hysilens is still chilling with them, and everyone else leaves the meeting looking like they just survived a group project. Meanwhile, Phainon and Mydei quietly reconcile to prove they’re definitely fine now (probably).

Chapter Notes

Oops, did I say 3.5? Totally meant this’ll be finished in 3.6 haha…. (don’t kill me plz I’m sorry🥺)

Money didn’t just move through the city—it engineered it.

It bent streets into grids, sculpted towers out of glass and steel, and redrew skylines with every fluctuation in the market. Down in the financial district, that truth was impossible to ignore. The air itself seemed regulated, filtered until even the smog felt curated, like luxury goods for lungs that could afford it. Buildings shimmered under the weight of commerce, and every reflection in their mirrored surfaces reminded you who really owned the daylight.

And at the center of this engineered order rose the compound.

To anyone untrained, it was another corporate fortress: sleek facades, clean symmetry, logos slapped across the glass to disguise its true nature. But the faint traceries of gold veined through the building betrayed it. At night, they pulsed like capillaries, a steady glow that made the tower feel less like architecture and more like anatomy. A body, a system. And like all systems in this district, its heartbeat was tied directly to the Chrysos Heirs.

The Council would never admit it, but they were tethered to it too. They might sneer at the Heirs in public, call them reckless, dangerous, destabilizing—yet everyone knew half the Council’s budgets depended on the markets that pulsed beneath these streets. A misstep here didn’t just risk bad optics. It risked collapse. To march teams into this block would mean tanking the very foundations that kept their power solvent. In other words: the Heirs had carved out a sovereign state in the one place the Council couldn’t afford to bleed.

Inside, sovereignty revealed itself without apology.

Medical wings gleamed with sterile precision, their walls saturated with the faint hum of resonance machines, tuned to frequencies that never failed, because failure here was unacceptable. Conference halls stretched out in reflective steel and glass, sharp as blades, as if the rooms themselves had been designed to cut down hesitation. Security wasn’t subtle. It didn’t have to be. Men and women in matte uniforms stood like punctuation in the silence, visible reminders that the Heirs didn’t hide their power—they enforced it openly.

It was the safest place he could be.

The safest place they could be.

And still Phainon felt cornered.

He had not left the medical wing in two days. Not properly. Sometimes he drifted as far as the end of the corridor to fill a glass of water. Once, he leaned against the far window, staring at the skyline until the glow of it felt like a weight pressing into his skull. But he always returned to the same chair outside the private suite. Always the same rhythm: sit, wait, tap his fingers against the leather armrest until it felt molded to his shape.

The holo readouts floated in the air like blue ghosts—transparent sheets pulsing with vitals, resonance markers, probability graphs. To anyone else they might have looked like reassurance, proof that the machines were doing their job. To him they were stock tickers before a crash. Each dip

made his teeth grind. Each spike sent a surge of fragile hope ripping through his chest, sharp enough to ache more than despair ever did.

So he gave his hands tasks. Strips of geometry peeled themselves into being, constructs folding out of his palms like blocks extruded from wire. He wove and unwove them, shapes collapsing back into sparks, then reassembling again. He told himself it was practice for his abilities. He knew it was distraction.

Because the thoughts always came, whether his hands were busy or not.

And here, in a fortress that could repel armies, he still felt worried. The Council’s reach pressed against his mind like a shadow stretching from far away. Caenis’s name hung at the edge of every silence. But worst of all were the memories—the ones he couldn’t keep out, the ones no guard could shoot down.

And those, he carried with him into every heartbeat.

Mydei had been under sedation for two days.

The Heirs’ medical team said it was necessary—that his system needed to stabilize, that the backlash had been too severe to risk him waking too soon. They spoke with the calm, clinical precision of people who had seen a hundred emergencies worse than this, but none of it made the hours pass faster.

And as anyone could predict, Phainon hadn’t stepped inside the suite once.

Instead, he stayed in the hallway, locked in his vigil. The holo projections cycled endlessly in the air before him, washed in shades of blue that bled into his vision even after he blinked. Vital signs, resonance maps, brainwave fluctuations—all floating like scripture waiting to be interpreted. He read meaning into every dip and spike, convinced that if he stopped watching, if he gave the data a moment’s freedom, Mydei would slip away again.

Anaxa had told him more than once it wasn’t healthy.

That he was spiraling.

That obsession wouldn’t change the outcome.

Phainon heard him.

He just didn’t care.

The others had busied themselves in their own ways since the escape. The compound’s walls made it easy to mistake silence for safety, but beneath the stillness, tension ran like an undercurrent. They’d basically beaten the Council’s people bloody in the streets, torn through city units, left their pursuit in ruins—and somehow, against probability, every one of them had made it out alive. Anaxa had still been there when the dust settled (he hadn’t prayed in years, but that night he had). Mydei, battered but breathing, had not been ripped out of Phainon’s reach this time. Even Cipher—sharp-tongued, usually so insidious—had guided them through the chaos with the kind of silence only someone experienced could manage.

It should have felt like victory.

But victories didn’t look like this. Victories didn’t leave you pacing a hallway with your throat tight and your stomach hollow, waiting for blue light to tell you if your world still had a pulse.

Chrysos tech was advanced, but it was still working against odds that couldn’t be smoothed over with clean lines and confident assurances.

Still, he watched.

Because logic demanded vigilance. Because reason told him that every system had cracks, and cracks only widened when ignored. He told himself a lot of things. Sometimes things that sounded noble in his head. Sometimes it sounded pathetic. He didn’t know which was closer to the truth.

And underneath all that reason, beneath the data and the graphs and the blue glow soaking into his bones, there was the simpler truth: he was afraid.

Not of the Council, not of Caenis, not even of the next conflict waiting outside these walls. Those were threats he understood, enemies he could deal with.

What terrified him was the quiet—the possibility that when the sedation lifted, when Mydei finally opened his eyes, the fragile thread binding everything together would snap. That after everything, after two days of holding his breath, Mydei would despise him.

So he stayed.

And the hours continued to slip away, one graph at a time.

Phainon sighed.

“I know you’re there, Goldweaver. Don’t bother hiding.”

He didn’t look up right away, just turned his head enough to let her see the exhaustion etched into his face, unapologetic.

“Or should I say—Aglaea?”

Her presence wasn’t a surprise. Of course she’d come. From the moment they’d pulled her into this, it was only a matter of time. The whole ordeal had been a mess barely stitched together—Hysilens stepping in at the last second, keeping Aglaea from cutting him open in the middle of negotiations. He’d measured the risk in that instant with cold clarity. If she struck, he could rebuild. It would have hurt like hell, yes, but survival had never been the problem. What mattered was that they reached an accord. A fragile one, propped up on logic, necessity, and—though she’d never admit it aloud—Mydei.

Since then, they’d called it “bonding.” A polite word for slow dissection. Information traded in careful measures, pieces of themselves offered and withheld. Somewhere in that process, the name beneath the mask slipped free: the Goldweaver was Aglaea, the Heirs’ steady hand. It hardly changed anything—she’d still been here—but knowing was nice.

She stepped into view dressed as if she’d walked out of a council chamber rather than a battlefield: tailored white suit, every seam exact, gold accents pared down to a whisper. She looked untouchable, but the faint shadows under her eyes betrayed the strain. Even Aglaea had limits.

For half a second, instinct moved through him—an urge to steady her, to guide her to the chair and help her down. The thought barely surfaced before he strangled it. Aglaea didn’t need gestures. She didn’t want pity, and he wasn’t about to offer it.

He forced the impulse down where it belonged, iron-bound and buried.

Instead, he inclined his head with politeness.

“Please take a seat, Lady Goldweaver.”

Formality felt safer. He doubted she wanted him to say her name so casually anyway.

But her gaze found him, strong despite the fatigue.

“Aglaea is fine, Phainon.”

The way she said his name lingered, deliberate. If it struck a nerve, he gave no sign. He only waited, still as stone, until she sank into the chair opposite. Then he crossed the space at his own pace, lowering himself into the seat across from her.

Silence stretched. Not empty—measured. A line drawn between them, each waiting for the other to mark the first step. Aglaea’s face smoothed into composure, the kind you only earned after years of swallowing reactions before they surfaced. He could almost respect it.

When she finally spoke, her voice was calm, layered with that cool steadiness that always seemed to hold weight no matter how simple the words.

“Now,” she said, eyes on his. “We have much to discuss.”

Phainon matched her stare. There would be no pleasantries here, at least not tonight.

“Where do you want to start?”

Aglaea didn’t waste time. She leaned forward, arms folded.

“I’m assuming you’ve already pieced together their angle.”

Phainon’s jaw worked, eyes fixed on the wall. “Anaxa confirmed it,” he said flatly. “They want to hollow him out. Mydei’s stabilizer makes him the only viable shell. Immortal. Consistent resonance lattice. And me—” his lip twitched, “—as the key to pull the rest in.”

He didn’t spit the word key, but the contempt behind it poisoned the air.

Aglaea’s gaze flicked to him. “Profiles harvested. Layered into him like executable code. Cifera’s intelligence matched that almost to the letter.”

Phainon’s pulse hammered against his throat. He exhaled slow, forcing the spike down, but it was still there, running hot beneath the words. His hands curled into fists, and he didn’t bother to unclench them.

Aglaea noticed, but didn’t call it out. Instead, she drew in a breath, then released it, softer now. “You understand the reason I told you about that initiative. I wasn’t… volunteering that. You made it clear you wouldn’t let go until you knew.”

“Everyone kept it from me.” His tone wasn’t accusation so much as statement, said bluntly.

“Because it wasn’t their story to tell,” she answered evenly. Then, a beat: “Same as you, Khaslana.”

That landed. Phainon’s silence stretched—not defensive, but conceding. He had pressed her, practically begged her to lay out the Initiative, the stabilizer trials, what Eurypon had done. He’d wanted to tear the curtain back, no matter how it looked on Mydei. And in return, he’d had to put his

own rot on the table: Caenis, the numbered designation, the failed attempts that had left him scarred in ways he couldn’t measure.

Unfortunately, it still wasn’t trust as it was mutual necessity. A ledger scratched open between them.

Aglaea shifted her weight. “The Council never trusted the Heirs. That hasn’t changed. Independence has always been the threat. The Initiative was one blade they forged to cut it down. What happened to Mydei… wasn’t random. It was a prototype in a longer chain.”

Phainon exhaled through his teeth. “I know what prototypes look like. I was one. Caenis had done the same and called it calibrations—breaking us down to raw resonance, testing which lattices held under pressure. When they didn’t, she scrapped them and started over. I wasn’t the only designation, and  I’m assuming it’s the same for Mydei.”

Aglaea hummed in acknowledgement before continuing. “Cifera suspected as much. Taking account this new information, Mydeimos wasn’t chosen later, but earlier. Before Eurypon’s descent to madness, before your breach even went on record. If both your timelines overlap…”

Phainon finally turned his eyes from the monitors, meeting hers. “Then this was laid out years in advance.”

Aglaea inclined her head once. “Exactly.”

The hum of the med-equipment filled the space between them. Neither of them looked away.

Phainon leaned back, eyes narrowing as he tracked the threads in his head. “I always marked the beginning of this while fiacso after Δ7, the project’s name. After the breach. That’s when the Council finally took me seriously in those labs as they realized what I was capable of.” His added thoughtfully. “Weeks after, maybe a month at most. That was my frame.”

Aglaea’s response was immediate. “I’d dated it later. After the first Tide incursion. Public favor swung to the Heirs, and the Council was forced to

shift tactics. Their window to dismantle us closed. From there, the tides changed.”

Her hands rested on the table, fingers still.

Phainon exhaled, exhausted. “So both timelines fail. Which means we’re both wrong.” He tapped the edge of the datapad absently, thought running ahead of his words. “They weren’t reacting to breaches or to us. The Tide was was infrastructure. A resource. Survivors became vital assets to test, refine, and weaponize because of their higher immunity.”

Aglaea tilted her head, processing. “The profiles were stripped down, erased, then folded into new lattices. Different methods between Eurypon and Caenis, but the endpoint aligns.”

Her conclusion slid neatly into his.

“And Mydei,” Phainon said, “was never just anomalous. His tether was the solution they’d been waiting for—stable containment without degradation.”

Aglaea finished his words for him. “Which means his endurance is evidence. Proof their system works outside the lab, and proof they can build on it.”

“Then their oversight was assuming they could isolate every variable.”

Aglaea’s brow lifted a fraction. “You.”

“Me,” Phainon confirmed. “And by extension, him. I don’t intend to let either be used any longer.”

She accepted it as such, giving the smallest nod before leaning forward. “So the adjustment is this: it isn’t a shift in policy but a sustained initiative maturing into application. Decades feeding into this convergence—your functionality, Mydei’s survival. They’ve positioned themselves to believe the framework is complete.”

Phainon’s expression thinned into something like a smile, but there was no humor in it. “Then our work is to strip the board before they can even place

the pieces.”

Aglaea considered, then aligned with him. “Agreed. We’ll map their sequence from the earliest recoverable point. Trials, breaches, cover operations. If they’ve layered this long, they’ve left seams. And seams mean access.”

“Access,” Phainon echoed, leaning forward now too. “And leverage.”

She allowed the faintest curve of acknowledgment at the edge of her mouth. “Then let’s begin. Start with your earliest viable record—we’ll build out the grid, and compare against Heir archives. The overlap will give us their true timeline.”

Phainon’s eyes flickered. “Good. Now we’re talking.”

Brainstorming, huh? Not his usual forte, but he’ll do his best.

“How many survivor accounts did the Heirs catalog after Elysiae?”

Aglaea didn’t glance up. “Fourteen.” A pause. “One held. The rest collapsed.”

Phainon’s mouth twitched as he remarked idly. “Council filed it as one. Guess who.”

Her eyes lifted briefly to him. “Efficient.”

“Convenient,” he corrected. A tap of his stylus set a sharp cadence against the tablet. “Erase the failures, crown the anomaly, and you’ve got a neat origin story. NeiKos496. That’s your Phase Two.”

Aglaea marked a line across her notes. “Which means Phase One is the trail —spending spikes six months before Elysiae. Shell firms, phantom contracts, shadow budgets. They were preparing.”

He gave a low hum, not quite agreement, not quite dissent. “Paranoia before the breach. Opportunism after. They couldn’t have known about the Tide

before, but the warning signs were there. Phase One into Two is seamless.”

Aglaea underlined with a flick. “And Phase Three is Caenis. Calibrations. Prototype work, as they called it. Your testimony matches the ledger surge —‘infrastructure stabilization research.’ Same subsidiaries, but doubled.”

Phainon sighed. “I was the control sample. The first cut.”

Her voice was crisp. “Phase Four belongs to Eurypon.”

A click of his tongue. “Obsession with memory, identity grafts. The Council didn’t just indulge him—they bankrolled him. Ran him in parallel to Caenis.”

“Redundancy,” she said evenly. “Two lines, one project. Fail-safes in human form.”

He leaned back, eyes narrowing at the half-formed sequence glowing before them. “Phase Five, then. Divergence. Caenis yields corpses. Eurypon yields cracks. The Council keeps feeding both, waiting to see which collapses slower.”

“And Phase Six,” Aglaea’s voice lowered, “is the convergence. Mydei.”

For a moment, the room held its silence.

Phainon laid the stylus down, steadier this time. “So. Pre-Breach paranoia. Elysiae’s collapse. Caenis’ calibrations. Eurypon’s obsession. Their divergence. Mydei’s survival. That’s the skeleton.”

Aglaea inclined her head. “And Phase Seven is aftermath. The cover-up. Budgets siphoned into deeper black ledgers. The Initiative scattered, not ended.”

He gave a thin smile. “Which means we drag it back into the light.”

The cursor blinked, patient, expectant. For the first time in hours, their threads aligned, two bodies of notes converging into a structure neither could have carved alone.

Phainon broke the silence, voice low, almost absent. “Do you want to run it through?”

Aglaea blinked once dazed, rare for her, as if surfacing. “Yes. Let’s.”

Turns out when two of the most informed people alive—both on different yet strangely parallel sides of the coin—finally put their notes together, you don’t just get two and two. You get four, then eight, then a whole map forming before either of them can stop it.

She swiped her hand, and the scattered fragments sharpened into a single screen:

⸻

[Joint Draft | Compiled Notes: Goldweaver + Phainon] Working document. Accuracy approximate. Subject to revision.

⸻

╠═══ Phase I: Pre-Breach Foundations ═══╣

(Posture: paranoia → opportunism)

— Council stance prior to the Tide: dismissive. Breaches treated as statistical noise, nothing systemic. Containment funding capped at lowest

tier. — Resource allocation: >70% redirected to Chrysos Heirs contracts

(security, infrastructure). — Council propaganda frames Heirs as unstable radicals, yet underground

credibility of Heirs steadily rising. “Necessary devils.” — Expenditure anomaly flagged: six to twelve months before Aedes Elysiae. Sudden spike in vague budget lines: infrastructure resilience,

anomaly research.

⟶ Goldweaver’s anotation: traced two shell subsidiaries. One posing as maritime infrastructure, one as a charity clinic. Both non-operational fronts. Margin: Already preparing for something. Before the first breach.

Aglaea nodded faintly when he saw his note.

⸻

╠═══ Phase II: First Breach — Aedes Elysiae (Year 0) ═══╣

Designation: The Spark Event

“No can do. I’m thriving. Bonding. Reconciliation arc, you can’t break the trope.”

Mydei pinched the bridge of his nose. “Unbelievable.”

By the time the automatic doors slid open, Phainon had worked himself into full deadweight, forcing Mydei to half-drag him inside.

Three pairs of eyes swiveled toward them.

Aglaea and Hysilens sat in crisp, professional stillness on one side of the briefing table. Opposite them stood Anaxa, arms crossed, mid-glare at Aglaea before turning the full force of it on the late arrivals.

“Well,” Anaxa said, drawl sharp enough to slice, “look who decided to reconcile. Only two hours past our scheduled time. Meanwhile, I’ve been trapped in here with this woman.” His voice dripped venom on the last two words.

Aglaea didn’t so much as blink. “You say that as if my company were punishment. Correct me if I’m wrong, but you initiated the discussion on fringe-colony taxation codes, Anaxa.”

“That wasn’t discussion—that was assassination by boredom.”

“Or perhaps you simply lacked the education to follow.”

Phainon perked up immediately, practically vibrating with glee. “Oh, this is fantastic. You two are like an old married couple who divorced three times and still send each other hate-mail.”

“Phainon,” Mydei muttered, warning heavy in his tone.

“No, no, don’t stop him,” Aglaea said sweetly, still smiling at Anaxa like a portrait in a gallery. “It’s refreshing to see someone else recognize his flair for dramatics.”

“Dramatics?” Anaxa’s composure cracked, eyebrows shooting up. “You staged a thirty-minute lecture on the ‘philosophical ramifications of exile law’ while I asked a simple logistical question about fuel reserves. Fuel reserves, Aglaea. The difference between survival and being stranded, and you gave me a dissertation.”

“It was relevant.”

“It was deranged.”

“It was comprehensive.”

“You’re insufferable.”

“And you’re obtuse.”

“Oh, it’s heating up,” Phainon whispered to Mydei, eyes gleaming. “Bet you ten credits she breaks him first. Look at that smile—she’s ruthless.”

“You’re not betting on this.” Mydei’s tone was iron.

“Fine, but admit it—this is better than daytime theater.”

“Barely,” Mydei said, but he didn’t move to stop it.

Aglaea leaned forward slightly, as if presenting in court. “If you cannot endure basic discourse without whining, perhaps you should reconsider your claim to leadership.”

“Basic discourse?” Anaxa let out a short laugh. “You weaponize vocabulary like it’s a dueling pistol. You don’t converse, Aglaea—you lay ambushes.”

“Perhaps you’re simply too slow to dodge them.”

“Slow? From the woman who takes forty minutes to define the word jurisdiction?”

“It required nuance.”

“You required a muzzle.”

“Oh my god. I’m living for this. They’re gonna start throwing case law at each other like daggers.”

Before Aglaea could retort, a single sound cut through the room.

Hysilens cleared her throat.

Not loud. Not long. But sharp enough to cleave through the tension like a blade.

Instant silence.

Phainon wilted, peeling himself off Mydei with exaggerated reluctance, slouching into the nearest chair. He cleared his throat, far too loudly. “Right. Plans. We need to—uh—come up with one.”

Anaxa seized the pause like it had been his all along. “No need.” He smoothed his sleeve, face snapping back into elegance. “While you two were… indisposed, some of us collaborated with other parties to build a working strategy.”

Phainon whistled low, getting up to all towards him just to drop back into the seat beside him. “God, I missed this. Planning with you—it’s like muscle memory. Everything without you was twice as hard. Three times.”

“Don’t flatter me.”

“Not flattery. Desperation.”

Across the room, Mydei drifted toward Aglaea’s side, only to hesitate when his gaze met Hysilens’. For a beat, the two held still—a flicker of old

history, recognition unspoken. Then both inclined their heads in brief acknowledgment, settling beside each other without a word.

Anaxa rose, Aglaea following smoothly, both straightening into crisp professionalism as if the earlier sparring had never happened.

“Now,” Anaxa said, tone clipped back into precision, “shall we?”

He tapped the console, city-core schematics flickering up in pale light.

“Alright. Phase one: pressure. Aglaea, that’s your wheelhouse. You get the Heirs moving in sync and drag the neutrals into daylight. No more polite nodding from the sidelines—we need them loud, public, staking their reputations. The point isn’t to topple the Council overnight. It’s to make the cracks visible.”

Aglaea tilted her chin, faintly amused. “You make it sound brutish.”

“Good,” Anaxa said smoothly. “Brutish plays. This is theater.”

Phainon, leaning forward now, gave a small nod. “Theatrics work if the optics hold. But if the Heirs overplay it, the Council can spin us as agitators. How are you keeping that leash tight?”

Aglaea’s reply was all teeth. “By picking districts where the Council can’t afford bad press. Let them call us agitators while the cameras roll on grieving families.”

“Fair,” Phainon murmured, sitting back again, calculation flickering in his eyes.

Anaxa flicked the schematic, zooming in.

“Phase two: money. Cipher traces the rot—ledgers, contracts, the payments nobody wants public. If even half of it sticks, Councilors start turning on each other before the week’s out.”

Cipher lounged against the table edge.

Phainon pauses. When did she get there? He swore it was just them—you know what never mind he won’t question it anymore.

“Just remember—people need to believe it. My gift doesn’t run on autopilot.”

“Which is why we back it with evidence,” Anaxa countered. “Documents, testimony, receipts. Dress the lies in truth and they’ll eat it up.”

Cipher smirked. “Propaganda with paperwork. Cute.”

“Phase three,” Anaxa continued, “is disruption. My department. I drip-feed classified directives, enough to inflame outrage without burning our stash. At the same time, I’ll throw false breach signals into the grid—make the Council’s enforcement scatter. They’ll look frantic, guilty, and thin-stretched.”

Phainon gave a quiet huff. “Chaos by bureaucracy. Efficient. Just watch your timing—too many false alarms and they’ll wise up.”

“Noted,” Anaxa said. “Which brings us to phase four.”

The air shifted. Even Phainon straightened a touch.

“Caenis,” Anaxa said simply. His gaze cut to Phainon, then Mydei. “That’s yours. How you handle her—capture, expose, kill—that’s your call. The rest of us clear the stage.”

A silence held. Mydei didn’t blink. Phainon’s expression was carved granite.

“Details?” Phainon asked at last. “Because walking in blind is how people end up dead.”

“You won’t be blind,” Anaxa replied. “Hysilens buys us windows. Cipher floods the cycle with proof so Caenis can’t bury the narrative. The goal is containment and evidence. The moment you two confront her, the rest of us make sure the world is watching.”

Phainon gave the faintest nod, like he’d slot it into a plan already forming in his head.

“Which leads us to surveillance,” Anaxa went on. “The Council sees everything. Hysilens?”

The violinist inclined her head, calm as ever. “I can collapse their nets. Briefly. But you’ll have to be exact.”

“I’ll be exact,” Anaxa promised.

“And if you’re not?” she pressed.

“Then we improvise,” Anaxa said without missing a beat.

Phainon muttered, “Always reassuring.”

Mydei gave him a look. “You’ve survived this long on improvisation.”

He didn’t flinch, only lifted a brow. “Exactly why I don’t recommend it.”

Anaxa cut in, crisp. “The fallout isn’t revolution. The Council survives. But it limps. Plan dismantled. Caenis gone. And the Heirs? No longer pawns— partners.”

Aglaea’s sighed. “Finally, a language I can endorse.”

Anaxa exhaled, almost weary. “Then do me a favor and endorse it punctually.” His eyes cut to Phainon and Mydei.

Phainon lifted his hands in mock surrender. “Don’t know what you’re implying.”

Mydei muttered, “You’re insufferable.”

“Compliment accepted,” Phainon said dryly, but the edge in his eyes hadn’t softened.

Aglaea didn’t say anything at first, letting the quiet stretch after Anaxa’s rundown. Then she leaned in, resting her palms on the console so the light from the schematic washed her sleeves. “Four phases is elegant, but insufficient. We’re not dealing with amateurs. The Council will ride out the storm if we don’t close the cycle. I’m adding a fifth.”

Anaxa arched a brow, faintly skeptical.

“Everything you’ve built covers disruption. Pressure, fracture, exposure, confrontation. That’s strong enough to wound them, yes. But if we leave it there, they recover. They consolidate, rewrite, bury the evidence, and three years from now the Initiative returns with a new face. Phase Five is durability. Long-term locks—oversight structures, redistribution of proof, institutional safeguards that stop them from crawling back into the dark. That part falls to me.”

Her tone left no opening for rebuttal, and for once even Anaxa let the silence pass.

It was Hysilens who broke it. “Then you’ll need cover built in. The Council won’t only fight you in chambers—they’ll bleed you in the margins. Attrition, process, delay. If we mean to keep momentum, I can engineer silence in the right places. Not just blind spots, but gaps in the record— meeting minutes scrubbed, trace-logs lost. When they look back, they won’t be able to prove what they missed. That gives your reforms space to root.”

Aglaea inclined her head. “Exactly. This is a rough framework. I’ll refine the timing, sharpen the distribution, and fold in those contingencies. But tonight we’ve done what we needed: a spine to build around.”

She straightened, gathering her notes in a clean motion that felt very much like dismissal. “That’s enough. We begin preparation tomorrow. Get rest while you can—you’ll miss it soon enough.”

The chairs creaked and slid back, their glow dimming as the projection winked off. Conversation dissolved into low murmurs as they filtered toward the exit.

Phainon fell into step with Mydei, the two of them walking in a silence that didn’t press. He thought nothing of it when Aglaea’s voice carried across the chamber.

“Mydei. Hysilens. Stay a moment.”

Phainon slowed without realizing, glancing over his shoulder. Mydei met his eye briefly, then tipped him the faintest nod. Phainon gave one in return and turned forward again, his stride steady. Maybe it was better this way— let Mydei handle Aglaea without him hovering at his side.

He was nearly at the door when Mydei’s voice followed him.

“Phainon. My room. Later.”

The words caught him mid-step. For a heartbeat, he stilled. Then he dipped his chin once—quick, precise, acknowledgment without theatrics—and kept on.

His face was unreadable as he left the chamber, mask steady as ever. But once the doors slid closed behind him, the weight eased. In the half-lit corridor his steps found a lighter rhythm, and a small, almost reluctant smile pulled at his mouth.

A little spring carried him forward. They were going to be all right.
